Modifier What it does nullable() Allow NULL. Columns are NOT NULL by default. nullable(false) makes it NOT NULL again. defaultTo(value) Set a default value. Strings are escaped, so any text is safe. bool, numbers, null, Map/List (saved as JSON) and DateTime work too. withDefault does the same. defaultRaw('sql') Set the default as raw SQL. It is not escaped. Put expressions in ( ), like defaultRaw('(1 + 1)'), because MySQL and SQLite need it. useCurrent() Default to the current time. The same as defaultRaw('CURRENT_TIMESTAMP'). useCurrentOnUpdate() Set the current time on each update. MySQL only, so on Postgres and SQLite set the time in your code. unique() Add a unique index {table}_{column}_unique. index() Add an index {table}_{column}_index. primary() Make the column the primary key. unsigned() UNSIGNED. MySQL only. comment('text') Add a column comment. Postgres and MySQL only. collation('utf8mb4_bin') Set the column collation, for example so A and a are two keys. MySQL and MariaDB only, and only on text columns. after('column') Put the new column after another one. MySQL only, and only in schema.table. change() Change a column that exists. See Modifying columns.

docs.title: Modifying columns
docs.text:
In schema.table, a column is added by default. To change a column that exists, add .change():

await schema.table('posts', (Table table) {
  table.string('title', 500).nullable().defaultTo('x').change();
});

change() sets the full new column: type, null, default and comment. So give every modifier you want to keep. For example, if the column had a default and you leave out defaultTo, the default is gone.

docs.title: Renaming columns
docs.text:
Use renameColumn to rename a column:

await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.renameColumn('bio', 'about');
});

docs.title: Dropping columns
docs.text:
Use dropColumn to drop one column, or dropColumns to drop many:

await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.dropColumn('age');
  table.dropColumns(<String>['a', 'b']);
});

There are also helpers for the helper columns. dropTimestamps drops created_at and updated_at, and dropSoftDeletes drops deleted_at:

table.dropTimestamps();

table.dropSoftDeletes();

docs.title: Creating indexes
docs.text:
Indexes make lookups fast. You can add one with a modifier on the column:

table.string('slug').unique();

To make an index on more than one column, call the index method on the table. It takes a column name or a list of names:

table.index(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // posts_state_created_at_index
table.unique('slug');                         // posts_slug_unique
table.primary(<String>['post_id', 'tag_id']); // composite primary key

Index names are {table}_{columns}_{index|unique|foreign}. To use your own name, give it as the last argument:

table.unique('slug', 'my_name');

docs.title: Full text indexes
docs.text:
If you want to search text, use fullText. On MySQL it makes a FULLTEXT index. On Postgres it makes a gin index on to_tsvector('english', ...):

table.fullText('body'); // posts_body_fulltext

docs.title: Renaming indexes
docs.text:
Use renameIndex with the old and the new name:

table.renameIndex('posts_slug_unique', 'posts_url_unique');

docs.title: Dropping indexes
docs.text:
dropIndex and dropUnique take the columns or the index name:

table.dropIndex(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns
table.dropUnique('posts_slug_unique');            // or by name

Use dropPrimary to drop the primary key. On Postgres it takes the name, and the default is {table}_pkey. MySQL needs no name:

table.dropPrimary();

docs.title: Checking an index
docs.text:
hasIndex takes an index name, or a list of its columns:

await schema.hasIndex('posts', 'posts_slug_unique');             // by name
await schema.hasIndex('posts', <String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns

The list must have all the columns of the index, in the same order.

docs.title: Foreign keys
docs.text:
A foreign key makes sure a row only points to a parent row that exists. foreignId with constrained is the short way to make one:

table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();

It does the same as this longer form:

table.foreignId('user_id');
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('cascade');

constrained guesses the table from the column name: user_id becomes users, and category_id becomes categories. Dox models use singular table names by default (User is user), so if your table is singular, give the name:

table.foreignId('user_id').constrained('user');

If the column can be NULL, put nullable() before constrained():

table.foreignId('editor_id').nullable().constrained('users');

foreignIdFor makes the foreign key column of a model, like user_id. Then constrained points to the table and primary key of that model. Give a name as the second argument to change the column name:

table.foreignIdFor(User()).constrained().cascadeOnDelete();

foreignIdFor is always a big integer. For a model with a text key, use foreignUuid or foreignUlid.

Same type on both sides

id() and foreignId() are both big integers, so they match. If the parent uses increments() (a normal integer), use unsignedInteger() for the child on MySQL.

docs.title: Foreign key actions
docs.text:
You can say what happens to the child rows when the parent is deleted or updated. Use onDelete and onUpdate with 'cascade', 'set null', 'restrict' or 'no action':

table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('set null');

There are also short methods: cascadeOnDelete(), nullOnDelete(), restrictOnDelete(), cascadeOnUpdate(), nullOnUpdate() and restrictOnUpdate().

docs.title: Dropping foreign keys
docs.text:
dropForeign takes the columns or the key name:

table.dropForeign(<String>['user_id']);

table.dropForeign('posts_user_id_foreign');

dropConstrainedForeignId drops the foreign key and then the column:

table.dropConstrainedForeignId('user_id');

docs.title: Turning foreign key checks off
docs.text:
Sometimes you must write rows before their parent rows, for example when you copy data. Use withoutForeignKeyConstraints for that work. It turns the checks on again after the function, also when it throws:

await schema.withoutForeignKeyConstraints(() async {
  // the post first, its user later
  await QueryBuilder.table('posts').insert(<String, dynamic>{'user_id': 1, 'title': 'Hi'});
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'id': 1, 'name': 'Ann'});
});

On SQLite, run it outside a transaction. Postgres only waits for keys made DEFERRABLE, and Dox keys are not, so on Postgres the keys are still checked. See Foreign key checks per database.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Other column notes
docs.text:
• softDeletesTz is the same as softDeletes, because it is already a time with a zone.
  • With the laravelPostgresTypes flag, a new Postgres table gets TIMESTAMP for timestamps() and softDeletes(), and JSON for json().
  • MySQL only allows a default on TEXT, BLOB and JSON as an expression. The schema builder writes it as DEFAULT ('value') for you.
  • collation on a non-text column throws an ArgumentError. Postgres and SQLite ignore it. Give it again in .change().
  • unsigned, comment, after and useCurrentOnUpdate are ignored on databases that do not support them. after adds the column at the end there.
  • change() with unique() or index() adds the index. It fails when the index already exists.
  • change() runs one ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type on Postgres (with SET/DROP NOT NULL, SET/DROP DEFAULT and the enum CHECK again), MODIFY COLUMN on MySQL, and a table rebuild on SQLite.

docs.title: Index name rules
docs.text:
• The primary key is named primary on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. On Postgres it has its real name, like posts_pkey.
  • hasIndex compares names like the database does. MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite ignore the case. Postgres needs the exact case.
  • The longest index name is 63 characters on Postgres and 64 on MySQL. SQLite has no limit.

docs.title: Foreign key checks per database
docs.text:
disableForeignKeyConstraints() and enableForeignKeyConstraints() do the same as withoutForeignKeyConstraints, in two steps:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await schema.disableForeignKeyConstraints();
  // ...
  await schema.enableForeignKeyConstraints();
});
Database SQL Limits SQLite PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF It is for the one connection of the isolate, so other code of that isolate is not checked either while it is off. Inside a transaction it does nothing. MySQL, MariaDB SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0 It is a setting of one pool connection, so disable and enable must run inside a transaction, else they throw a StateError. Turn the checks on again before the transaction ends. Postgres SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED Only keys made DEFERRABLE wait, and only until the checks are on again. It must run inside a transaction too.
  • On MySQL, MariaDB and Postgres, withoutForeignKeyConstraints runs in a transaction, so all its queries use the same connection. Inside another transaction it uses a savepoint.
  • A migration runs in a transaction, so disable and enable work there on every database. On SQLite, a migration already runs with the checks off.

docs.title: SQLite notes
docs.text:
SQLite ALTER TABLE can only add, rename and drop columns. So for change(), for foreign(...) on an existing table and for dropForeign(...), Dox makes the table again. It makes a new table with the change, copies the rows, drops the old table and renames the new one, all in one transaction. It keeps the columns, primary key, AUTOINCREMENT, foreign keys, indexes and enum checks. It fails on tables with other CHECK constraints or with generated columns.

Other SQLite limits:

  • primary(...) on an existing table is not supported.
  • fullText and dropPrimary throw an UnsupportedError.
  • renameIndex drops the index and makes it again with the new name.
  • A new NOT NULL column needs a default. A new column can not default to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
  • dropColumn fails when the column is in an index or a foreign key. Drop those first.
  • On MySQL and MariaDB, schema changes save right away and are not part of a transaction. On Postgres and SQLite they are.

docs.title: See the SQL
docs.text:
Every change is a Table blueprint. A grammar turns it into SQL without a database. The grammars are PostgresGrammar, MysqlGrammar and SqliteGrammar:

Table table = Table('users', creating: true)
  ..id()
  ..string('email').unique();
print(table.toSql(PostgresGrammar()));
// [CREATE TABLE "users" ("id" BIGSERIAL NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, "email" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL),
//  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "users_email_unique" ON "users" ("email")]

On SQLite, the changes that need a table rebuild (and renameIndex) only run on a database.

docs.title: Seeders
docs.text: A seeder puts data in your database, like sample data for development or a list of countries your app needs.

docs.title: Writing seeders
docs.text:
Use the make:seeder command to make a seeder:

dox make:seeder UserSeeder

This makes db/seeders/user.seeder.dart. It also writes db/seeders/seeders.dart, the list of all seeders, and bin/seed.dart, the script that runs them. Do not edit the list, because Dox writes it again on each make:seeder and db:seed.

A seeder has one method, run. Put your code there. You can use factories, models or the query builder:

db/seeders/user.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../factories/user.factory.dart';

class UserSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await UserFactory().count(10).create();
  }
}

docs.title: Calling other seeders
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs DatabaseSeeder by default. So you use DatabaseSeeder to call your other seeders, with the call method:

dox make:seeder DatabaseSeeder
db/seeders/database.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import 'post.seeder.dart';
import 'user.seeder.dart';

class DatabaseSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await call(<Seeder>[UserSeeder(), PostSeeder()]);
  }
}

call runs the seeders one after another, in the list order.

docs.title: Running seeders
docs.text:
Use the db:seed command to run DatabaseSeeder:

dox db:seed

If you want to run only one seeder, use --class:

dox db:seed --class=UserSeeder

You can also seed right after the migrations. Add --seed to migration:run, migration:refresh or migration:fresh:

dox migration:fresh --seed

migration:fresh drops every table of the database, also tables that no migration made. So do not run it on a production database.

The seeders use the same database as the migrations. See Database settings.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A seed runs in one transaction. If a seeder throws an error, nothing is saved, and the command exits with code 1.

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE save right away, and a rollback can not undo them. So keep schema changes in migrations.

A very large seed can turn the transaction off with withinTransaction. Only the seeder you run decides this. For dox db:seed it is DatabaseSeeder:

class BigSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    // ...
  }
}

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A seeder is a normal class. In a test, call run after you set up the ORM:

await DatabaseSeeder().run();

docs.title: bin/seed.dart
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs dart run bin/seed.dart. You can run it yourself too, for example in a deploy script:

dart run bin/seed.dart
dart run bin/seed.dart --class=UserSeeder

bin/seed.dart is made only when it is missing. SeederRunner sets up the ORM, runs the seeder and closes the ORM:

bin/seed.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/seeders/seeders.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(seeders: seeders).run(args);
}

By default it reads the database from .env. Pass config: to use your app's database config instead:

import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(
    seeders: seeders,
    config: databaseConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• migrate:fresh and migrate:refresh are short names, so dox migrate:fresh --seed works too.
  • migration:refresh --seed undoes all migrations, runs them again, then runs DatabaseSeeder. migration:run --seed runs the new migrations, then DatabaseSeeder.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction runs many queries as one unit, so either all of them are saved or none of them.

You need a transaction when some changes only make sense together. For example, you create an order and take the items out of stock. If one step fails, you do not want the other one saved.

docs.title: Running a transaction
docs.text:
Pass a function to QueryBuilder.transaction(). When the function ends, the transaction commits. When the function throws, the transaction rolls back, and the error is thrown again:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  await QueryBuilder.table('actor_info').insert(<String, dynamic>{
    'actor_id': actor.id,
  });
});

All queries and models inside the function use the transaction. You do not pass a transaction object around.

The function can return a value:

int? id = await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  return actor.id;
});

To use a named connection, pass connection:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, connection: 'mysql');

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE are saved right away, so a rollback can not undo them.

docs.title: Nested transactions
docs.text:
Sometimes one part of the work may fail, and you still want to keep the rest. A transaction inside another transaction uses a savepoint, so if the inner function throws, only its work is undone:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'});
  try {
    await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
      await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bad row'});
      throw StateError('stop');
    });
  } on StateError {
    // only 'Bad row' is undone
  }
});
// 'John Wick' is saved

If you catch the error, the outer transaction goes on and can still commit. If you do not catch it, the outer transaction rolls back too. The inner work is saved only when the outer transaction commits.

This works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite, and you can nest many levels. Run nested transactions one after another, not at the same time (for example in Future.wait), because they share one connection.

docs.title: Handling deadlocks
docs.text:
Two transactions can wait for each other's rows. The database then stops one of them with a deadlock error. Often one more run works, so attempts runs the whole function again, up to that many runs in all:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, attempts: 3);

It runs again only on a deadlock or a lock / serialization failure. Other errors are thrown at once. When the last run fails too, its error is thrown. The default is 1, so one run and no retry.

The function runs again from the start. So keep work that is not in the database, like a mail or a call to another service, out of it. Or put that work in afterCommit().

docs.title: Begin and commit by hand
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.transaction() is the simple way, so use it when you can. If the work can not fit in one function, begin the transaction by hand:

DatabaseTransaction tx = await QueryBuilder.beginTransaction();
try {
  await tx.run(() async {
    User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
    await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => sendWelcomeMail(user));
  });
  await tx.run(() => QueryBuilder.table('audit').insert(<String, dynamic>{'event': 'signup'}));
  await tx.commit();
} finally {
  await tx.rollBack(); // does nothing after commit
}
  • Only code inside tx.run() uses the transaction. Other queries, and queries of other requests, never join it.
  • Await each run() before commit().
  • commit() saves the work, then runs the afterCommit() functions. It throws a StateError if the transaction is already closed.
  • rollBack() undoes the work. It does nothing if the transaction is already closed, so it is safe in a finally.
  • tx.isOpen is true until commit(), rollBack() or the timeout.
  • connection: picks a named connection, like in transaction().

The transaction holds one connection until you close it. If it is still open after timeout (default 1 minute), it is rolled back so the connection is free again. After that, run() and commit() throw a StateError and the work is lost. You can set your own timeout:

QueryBuilder.beginTransaction(timeout: const Duration(seconds: 10))

On Postgres, a database error inside run() breaks the whole transaction, so call rollBack() then. A commit() saves nothing and gives no error, because the server answers COMMIT with ROLLBACK. A plain QueryBuilder.transaction() works the same way if you catch a database error inside it.

docs.title: Run code after the commit
docs.text:
Some work must only happen when the data is saved, like sending a mail or a queue job. QueryBuilder.afterCommit() runs a function after the transaction commits:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => sendWelcomeMail(user));
});
  • The function runs after the outermost transaction commits, so the data is saved and other connections can see it.
  • If the transaction rolls back, the function does not run.
  • Outside a transaction, the function runs at once.
  • The functions run one by one, in the order you added them. They can be async, and the QueryBuilder.transaction() call waits for them.

If a function throws, the data stays saved and the other functions still run. Then the QueryBuilder.transaction() call throws the first error.

To wait for a transaction of a named connection, pass the same connection::

await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => notify(order), connection: 'mysql');

Queue jobs use this with dispatch(afterCommit: true).

docs.title: Row locks
docs.text:
A row lock stops two requests from changing the same row at the same time.

Think of a stock count. Two requests read stock = 5 at the same time. Each one takes 1 and saves 4, but the right value is 3. A lock makes the second request wait until the first one is done. This example has an int? stock column field on a Product model:

Future<void> buy(int productId, int quantity) async {
  await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
    // read the row and lock it
    Product product = await Product().lockForUpdate().findOrFail(productId);

    if (product.stock! < quantity) {
      throw BadRequestException(message: 'Not enough stock');
    }

    // change it and save it while the lock is held
    product.stock = product.stock! - quantity;
    await product.save();
  });
  // the lock ends here, when the transaction commits
}

lockForUpdate() adds FOR UPDATE to the select, so other transactions that lock or change these rows wait. sharedLock() adds a shared lock: other transactions can still read the rows, but they wait to change them.

Use a lock only inside a transaction. A lock lasts until the transaction ends, and outside a transaction each query commits right away, so the lock ends at once.

Locks work with find(), findOrFail(), getFirst(), firstOrFail(), get(), all() and pluck(). count(), sum() and the other aggregates do not lock.

Database lockForUpdate() sharedLock() Postgres FOR UPDATE FOR SHARE MySQL, MariaDB FOR UPDATE LOCK IN SHARE MODE SQLite nothing nothing

SQLite has no row locks. But a Dox transaction on SQLite starts with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, which takes the write lock of the whole database. So the same code is safe on SQLite too.

For one number column, increment() is simpler. It changes the value in one query, so it needs no lock.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Deadlock retries
docs.text:
• There is no wait between the runs. 0 and below also run once.
  • Only the outermost transaction runs again. A nested transaction gives the error to the outer one.
  • afterCommit() functions of a failed run are dropped. An error after the commit (for example in an afterCommit() function) never runs it again.
  • DatabaseTransaction.isConcurrencyError(error) tells you if an error counts, for your own checks. These errors count:
Database Errors Postgres SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure), 40P01 (deadlock) MySQL, MariaDB error 1213 (deadlock), 1205 (lock wait timeout), 1020 (record changed), SQLSTATE 40001 SQLite SQLITE_BUSY and SQLITE_LOCKED ("database is locked")

docs.title: Transactions by hand
docs.text:
• Nested QueryBuilder.transaction() calls (savepoints) and afterCommit() work inside run().
  • rollBack() also drops the afterCommit() functions.
  • beginTransaction() throws a StateError inside a transaction of the same connection. Use QueryBuilder.transaction() for nested work.
  • Use the transaction only in the code that began it: the same request, job or test.
  • On SQLite, other queries of the isolate wait until the transaction ends or times out. This includes a QueryBuilder.transaction() outside run(). So do not await them while it is open.

docs.title: After commit
docs.text:
• A function added in a nested transaction waits for the outermost commit. If that nested transaction rolls back, its functions are dropped, even if the outer one commits.
  • A function can open a new transaction, or call afterCommit() again.
  • With connection:, the function waits only for a transaction of that connection. With no connection, it uses the default connection.
  • A transaction opened with the default connection's own name (like connection: 'main') uses another driver than no name. So afterCommit() with no name runs at once there. Pass the same connection: to both, or no name to both.
  • Code can outlive its transaction, like a Timer or a future that you did not await. If it calls afterCommit() after the transaction ended, the function runs at once if the transaction committed, and is dropped if it rolled back. If such a late function throws, the error goes to the Future that afterCommit() returns, so await it or catch it.
  • A driver has it too: driver.afterCommit(() => ...). A custom DBDriver that does not use the afterCommitZone() and runAfterCommit() helpers runs the functions at once.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• On MySQL and MariaDB, a CREATE, ALTER or DROP TABLE inside a nested transaction saves the outer work and ends the savepoint. Do not change the schema there.
  • Postgres does not allow a lock with groupBy(), distinct(), or on the nullable side of a left join. The database throws an error then.
  • Postgres and MySQL use a connection pool (size: maxConnectionCount in extra). A transaction uses one connection of the pool, and other queries use the other connections. SQLite has one connection per isolate.
  • When a model has more than one relation to load (preload or eager), the relation queries run at the same time outside a transaction. Inside a transaction they run one after another on its connection.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A model is a Dart class for one database table, used to read, create, change and delete its rows.

Each model maps to one table, and each object of the model is one row. A model also has all the query builder methods, so you can query the table through it.

docs.title: Generating models
docs.text:
Use make:model to make a new model. The -m option also makes a migration for the table:

dox make:model Blog      # only the model
dox make:model Blog -m   # the model and a migration for the table `blogs`
dox make:model Blog -a   # the model, a migration, a factory, a seeder and a resource controller

This makes lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart. Other options are -c (controller), -r (resource controller), --api (resource controller without create and edit), -f (factory) and -s (seeder). You can join them, like -mfs. See the CLI reference.

A model uses a generated class (BlogGenerator), so you must run the generator after you make or change a model:

dart run build_runner build

If you want it to run again each time you save a file, use dart run build_runner watch.

docs.title: Defining models
docs.text:
A model is a class with @DoxModel(). Each @Column() field is one column of the table:

lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'blog.model.g.dart'; // (1)!

@DoxModel() // (2)!
class Blog extends BlogGenerator { // (3)!
  @Column() // (4)!
  String? title;

  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug) // (5)!
  String? slug;

  @Column()
  String? status;

  @Column(name: 'body') // (6)!
  String? description;

  @Column(name: 'user_id')
  int? userId;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}
  1. build_runner writes this file. It holds the generated BlogGenerator class.
  2. Marks the class as a model. The options, like table and softDelete, go here.
  3. The generated class gives the model id, createdAt and updatedAt, and the query builder methods.
  4. The column name is the field name in snake_case. Digits stay as they are: address2 is address2.
  5. beforeSave runs this static function before a save. See Changing values on save and read.
  6. Use name when the column name is not the snake_case of the field. The name is used exactly as written.

Make every column field nullable (String?, int?), because a new model has no values yet.

docs.title: Table names
docs.text:
The default table name is the class name in snake_case and singular: Blog uses blog, and BlogPost uses blog_post. With the pluralTableNames flag it is plural. If your table has another name, set table:

@DoxModel(table: 'blogs')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

dox make:model Blog always sets table: 'blogs' for you, and the migration from -m uses the same table.

docs.title: Primary keys
docs.text:
The primary key is id by default. If your key has another name, set primaryKey. The field name is the key in camelCase, so blog_id becomes blogId:

@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uid')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The key field is int? by default. If your key is a UUID string, set primaryKeyType:

@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uuid', primaryKeyType: String)
class Device extends DeviceGenerator {}

Device device = Device();
device.uuid = '0b6f2c1e-1a2b-4c3d-8e9f-001122334455';
await device.save(); // insert

save() inserts a new model, even when you set the key yourself.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text:
save() sets created_at and updated_at to the current UTC time. You read them with blog.createdAt and blog.updatedAt. If your columns have other names, set them:

@DoxModel(createdAt: 'created', updatedAt: 'modified')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

If the table has no timestamp columns, turn them off. To turn off only one, set it to null, like @DoxModel(updatedAt: null):

@DoxModel(timestamps: false)
class Setting extends SettingGenerator {}

docs.title: Column types
docs.text:
The field type tells Dox how to read the value:

Field type Column String? text, varchar int? integer types double? float, double. MySQL also gives DECIMAL as double. Postgres gives numeric as String. bool? boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false) DateTime? date, datetime, timestamp Map<String, dynamic>? or List<dynamic>? JSON an enum, like Status? text with the enum name

For other types, use a cast.

docs.title: Changing values on save and read
docs.text:
Sometimes a column needs a small change when you save or read it. beforeSave and beforeGet take a static function of the model. The function gets a map and returns the value:

  • beforeSave gets the model values (column name => value) and returns the value to save.
  • beforeGet gets the row from the database and returns the value for the field.
@DoxModel()
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  // beforeSave: make the slug from the title
  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug)
  String? slug;

  // beforeGet: old rows have no status, show them as draft
  @Column(beforeGet: readStatus)
  String? status;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }

  static String? readStatus(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['status'] as String? ?? 'draft';
  }
}

docs.title: Retrieving models
docs.text:
A model has all the query builder methods, so you read rows with them:

Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);

docs.title: Starting a new query
docs.text:
A model object keeps the parts of its query (where, orderBy, ...). If you want to start another query from it, use query(). It gives a new, empty model:

Blog blog = Blog();
List<Blog> active = await blog.where('status', 'active').get();

// a new query, without the where above
List<Blog> deleted = await blog.query().where('status', 'deleted').get();

docs.title: Refreshing models
docs.text:
Sometimes the row changed in the database after you read it. refresh() reads the row again into this model, and loads its relations again. fresh() gives a new model of the row and leaves this one as it is:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.refresh();          // this model now has the values of the table
Blog? now = await blog.fresh(); // a new model, or null when the row is gone

docs.title: Inserts
docs.text:
To add a row, make a new model, set its fields and call save():

Blog blog = Blog();
blog.title = 'My first blog';
await blog.save();
print(blog.id); // the new id

Fields that are null are not sent, so the database default is used.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
save() also updates a model that was read from the table or saved before. Only the fields that changed are sent:

Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
found?.title = 'New title';
await found?.save();

To clear a column, set the field to null and save:

found?.status = null;
await found?.save(); // status is now NULL in the database

model.exists tells you if save() will insert or update. save() returns false when a model event cancels it.

docs.title: Creating from a map
docs.text:
create() makes a new row from a map and returns the model as it is in the table. The model needs fillable, see Mass assignment:

Blog created = await Blog().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'title': 'My first blog',
  'status': 'draft',
});

create() works like save() on a new model: it saves only the @Column fields, runs beforeSave, sets the timestamps and fires the model events.

To change some columns of a loaded model from a map, use blog.update(<String, dynamic>{...}). It changes only that row and sets updated_at, but it fires no model events.

docs.title: Mass assignment
docs.text:
create(), insert(), update(), upsert() and the find or create methods take their keys from a map. If they took every key, User().create(req.body) with {"is_admin": 1} would make an admin. So a model is guarded by default, and you must say which keys may come from a map:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  // only these keys are taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email'];

  // or: every key but these is taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get guarded => <String>['is_admin'];
}
  • With fillable, other keys are dropped.
  • A model with no fillable (and the default guarded) throws a MassAssignmentException when it gets a map with keys.
  • Fields you set in code and save with save() are always saved.

If you want to take every key, set guarded to an empty list. This is not safe with user input:

@override
List<String> get guarded => const <String>[];

docs.title: Skip the fillable check
docs.text:
Sometimes your own code must set a guarded column, like is_admin. These methods ignore fillable and guarded, so never pass user input like req.body to them.

forceCreate() creates a row with every key of the map:

User admin = await User().forceCreate(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann', 'is_admin': true});

forceUpdate() updates the rows of a query with every key of the map:

await User().where('id', 1).forceUpdate(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});

forceFill() sets fields on a model. It does not save, so call save() after it:

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user!.forceFill(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true}).save();

Model.unguarded() turns the check off for everything inside the callback. Other requests that run at the same time still use fillable. Await everything inside the callback, because work that finishes later also runs with the check off:

await Model.unguarded(() async {
  await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob', 'is_admin': true});
  await User().where('id', 2).update(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});
});

docs.title: Find or create
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a row if it exists, and a new one if it does not. These methods find a row by the first map. When there is no row, they use both maps.

firstOrCreate() finds the row, or creates it:

User user = await User().firstOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'},
);

firstOrNew() finds the row, or makes a new model that is not saved yet:

User other = await User().firstOrNew(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'bob@example.com'});
if (!other.exists) {
  await other.save();
}

updateOrCreate() updates the row, or creates it:

User updated = await User().updateOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann Lee'},
);

firstOrCreate() and updateOrCreate() fire the model events. firstOrNew() does not save, so no event fires. See also the query builder.

docs.title: Incrementing and decrementing
docs.text:
If you want to add to a number column, like a view count, use increment() and decrement(). They change the column in one query, and the model field gets the new value too:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.increment('views');      // views + 1
await blog.increment('views', 5);    // views + 5
await blog.decrement('views');       // views - 1
print(blog.views);

They return the number of changed rows. They fire no model events and do not set updated_at.

docs.title: Touch and replicate
docs.text:
touch() sets updated_at to now. Give a column name to set another column. It fires the save events, and touchQuietly() does the same with no events:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.touch();               // updated_at = now
await blog.touch('published_at');  // published_at = now

replicate() makes an unsaved copy of a model. It has no primary key and no timestamps, so save() inserts a new row. Relations are not copied:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
Blog copy = blog!.replicate()..title = 'Copy of ${blog.title}';
await copy.save();

If you do not want some columns in the copy, list them. They are set to null:

Blog other = blog.replicate(<String>['slug']);

docs.title: Checking changed columns
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to know what changed before or after a save. A model tracks this. The names are column names, like user_id, not the Dart field names:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
blog!.title = 'New title';

blog.isDirty();                     // true
blog.isDirty('title');              // true
blog.isDirty(<String>['body']);     // false
blog.isClean('body');               // true
blog.getDirty();                    // {title: New title}
blog.getOriginal('title');          // the old title

After a save, wasChanged() and getChanges() tell you what the last save changed:

await blog.save();
blog.wasChanged('title');           // true
blog.getChanges();                  // {title: New title, updated_at: ...}

docs.title: Deleting models
docs.text:
Call delete() on a model to delete its row. It returns the number of deleted rows: 1, or 0 when the row was not there or a model event cancelled it:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
int count = await blog!.delete(); // deletes only this record

A model with no primary key value throws a StateError and runs no query, so Blog().delete() can not delete every row by mistake. To delete the rows of a query, add a where, like Blog().where('status', 'draft').delete(). A global scope counts as a where. To delete every row on purpose, see write every row.

docs.title: Soft deleting
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to keep deleted rows, so you can bring them back later. Turn on softDelete:

@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The table needs a nullable deleted_at column. In a migration, add table.softDeletes();.

Now delete() sets deleted_at to the current time and keeps the row. Queries leave out soft deleted rows. Use withTrash() to get them too, or onlyTrashed() to get only them.

trashed() tells you if a model is soft deleted, and restore() brings it back:

Blog? blog = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
if (blog!.trashed()) await blog.restore();

To really remove a soft deleted row, use forceDelete():

Blog? trashed = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await trashed?.forceDelete(); // deletes the row, also with softDelete

docs.title: Converting to a map or JSON
docs.text:
toMap() gives all columns and computed values. toJson() gives the same without hidden fields:

Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);

Map<String, dynamic>? map = blog?.toMap();  // all columns and computed values
Map<String, dynamic>? json = blog?.toJson(); // the same, without hidden fields
Map<String, dynamic>? row = blog?.toMap(original: true); // the raw database row

jsonEncode(blog) uses toJson(), so you can return a model, or a list of models, from a controller.

docs.title: Hide fields
docs.text:
You should never send fields like a password to the client. Put them in hidden, and toJson() leaves them out. Use the column names:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password', 'remember_token'];
}

If you prefer a list of the fields to keep, use visibleFields. When it is empty (the default), every field is kept:

@override
List<String> get visibleFields => const <String>['id', 'name'];

To change this for one model, or for a list of models, use makeHidden() and makeVisible(). makeVisible() also shows a field that is in hidden:

return user.makeVisible(<String>['email']).toJson();
return users.makeHidden(<String>['phone']);

docs.title: Computed values
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a value in the JSON that is not a column, like a full name. Add @Computed() to a getter, then run dart run build_runner build:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column(name: 'first_name')
  String? firstName;

  @Column(name: 'last_name')
  String? lastName;

  @Computed() // json key: full_name
  String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

  @Computed(name: 'initials') // custom json key
  String get shortName => '${firstName?[0]}${lastName?[0]}';
}

User? user = await User().find(1);
print(user?.toJson());
// {id: 1, first_name: John, last_name: Wick, ..., full_name: John Wick, initials: JW}

The key is the getter name in snake_case, or the name you give. A computed value is never read from or written to the database. hidden also hides it, by its json key. The getter runs each time toJson() or toMap() is called, so keep it fast.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
A model can load related models. See HasOne, HasMany, BelongsTo, ManyToMany, HasManyThrough and Polymorphic.

The relationship pages use these tables:

erDiagram
    user ||--o| user_info : "HasOne"
    user ||--o{ post : "HasMany"
    user ||--o{ comment : "BelongsTo, from comment"
    artist ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    song ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    user {
        int id PK
        string name
    }
    user_info {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string address
    }
    post {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string title
    }
    comment {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string content
    }
    artist_song {
        int id PK
        int artist_id FK
        int song_id FK
    }

docs.title: Preloading nested relations
docs.text:
A dot path also loads the relations of the loaded rows. It runs one query for each level:

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts.comments').get();

docs.title: Filtering a preload
docs.text:
If you want only some related rows, give a callback. It adds conditions to the query of the relation. With a dot path, it is for the last relation:

await User().preload('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

// all posts, and only the approved comments of each post
await User().preload('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('approved', true);
}).get();

docs.title: Saving through a relation
docs.text:
These methods save a related model and set the foreign key for you. They work with @HasMany, @HasOne, @MorphMany and @MorphOne:

Blog blog = (await Blog().find(1))!;
Comment c = await blog.createRelated<Comment>('comments', <String, dynamic>{'body': 'hi'});
await blog.saveRelated('comments', Comment()..body = 'hi');
await blog.saveManyRelated('comments', <Comment>[c1, c2]);

createRelated() uses create(), so fillable, events and timestamps work. The foreign key does not need to be in fillable.

For a @BelongsTo, comment.associate('blog', blog) sets the key and comment.dissociate('blog') sets it to null. Call save() after them.

docs.title: Debugging queries
docs.text:
If you want to see the SQL of a model, use debug(true). It prints the SQL in the terminal:

Blog blog = Blog();
blog.debug(true);
blog.title = 'John Wick';
await blog.save();

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: All options
docs.text:
All options go in @DoxModel(...).

Option Default What it does table class name in snake_case The table name. primaryKey 'id' The primary key column. primaryKeyType int The Dart type of the primary key, like String for a UUID. createdAt 'created_at' The column that keeps the create time. updatedAt 'updated_at' The column that keeps the last update time. timestamps true false turns off createdAt and updatedAt. softDelete false delete() sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
• create() can write NULL for a key that is null in the map, with the createWritesNull flag.
  • On update, a field is compared to its value from the last load or save. A Map or List field is always sent, because it can change in place.
  • On update, a field is set to NULL only when it had a value before. Fields that were not loaded, for example with select(), are not changed.
  • When nothing changed, save() runs no query and updated_at stays as it is. It still fires updating and updated, unless the skipCleanUpdateEvents flag is on.
  • When you set updatedAt yourself, save() keeps your value.
  • getChanges() and wasChanged() also count update(), increment(), decrement(), touch(), restore() and a soft delete on the model as a save.
  • A soft delete and restore() also set updated_at when the model has timestamps.

docs.title: Mass assignment
docs.text:
• forceFill() skips a key that is not a column. A value of the wrong type throws an ArgumentError.
  • Model.unguarded() also covers timers, futures that are not awaited and stream listeners that start inside the callback.
  • A query update() keeps the check, so update(req.body) stays safe.
  • Model events that fire inside forceCreate() and forceUpdate() also run with the check off. So a create() or update() inside such a hook skips fillable too.

docs.title: Increment, touch and replicate
docs.text:
• A third argument to increment() sets other columns in the same query: increment('views', 1, <String, dynamic>{'status': 'hot'}). Keys that fillable and guarded do not allow are dropped.
  • touch() returns the number of changed rows. It returns 0 when the model has no updated_at column and you give no column, or when a hook throws CancelModelEvent.
  • replicate() copies deleted_at, so a copy of a soft deleted model is soft deleted too. A column in its list that can not be null, or that is not a column, throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Rows with no primary key
docs.text: update(), increment(), decrement(), touch() and delete() on a model with no primary key value and no where throw a StateError. This happens on a model that was never saved, or that was read without its key.

docs.title: Refreshing
docs.text:
• refresh() and fresh() read by primary key from the write database. They find a soft deleted row too, and skip global scopes.
  • refresh() throws a StateError on a model that is not in the table, and a ModelNotFoundException when the row is gone.

docs.title: Relations after a reload
docs.text: await user.reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. A to-one field that can be null becomes null. A to-many field becomes []. A to-one field that can not be null keeps its old value.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• create:model is another name for make:model.
  • Computed values of loaded relations are in the nested JSON too. toMap(original: true) has no computed values.

docs.title: Attribute casts
docs.text:
A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart, for example to read JSON text as a map or to save an enum by its name.

Casts work the same on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. A cast runs when a row is read (get(), find() and others), when the model is saved, and in toJson().

docs.title: Defining casts
docs.text:
Set a cast with cast on @Column(), then run dart run build_runner build:

enum Status { draft, live }

enum Level { low, mid, high }

@DoxModel()
class Item extends ItemGenerator {
  @Column(cast: JsonCast())
  Map<String, dynamic>? meta;

  @Column(cast: ListCast<String>())
  List<String>? tags;

  @Column()
  bool? active; // gets BoolCast()

  @Column()
  Status? status; // gets EnumCast(Status.values)

  @Column(cast: EnumCast<Level>(Level.values, byIndex: true))
  Level? level;
}

A bool field gets BoolCast() and an enum field gets EnumCast(values) by itself, so you do not need cast for them. DateTime fields need no cast either.

A cast does not change a where() value, so use the database value there:

where('status', Status.live.name)

docs.title: Built-in casts
docs.text: Cast Dart value Database value JsonCast() a map or a list JSON, or JSON in a text column ListCast<E>() a typed list, like List<String> JSON, or JSON in a text column BoolCast() bool boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false), or the text 1, 0, true, false, t, f EnumCast<E>(E.values) an enum text with the enum name EnumCast<E>(E.values, byIndex: true) an enum a number, the enum index

docs.title: Custom casts
docs.text:
If no built-in cast fits, write your own. Extend Cast<T>: get() gets the database value and returns the Dart value, and set() gets the Dart value and returns the value to save. The class needs a const constructor:

class Money {
  final int cents;
  const Money(this.cents);
}

class MoneyCast extends Cast<Money> {
  const MoneyCast();

  @override
  Money? get(dynamic value) => value == null ? null : Money(value as int);

  @override
  dynamic set(Money? value) => value?.cents;
}

@DoxModel()
class Product extends ProductGenerator {
  @Column(cast: MoneyCast())
  Money? price;
}

A cast can take const arguments, like EnumCast does. The generator copies the cast code into the generated file, so the names in it must be imported in the model file.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: • A column with beforeGet does not use its cast.

docs.title: Counting relations
docs.text:
withCount() adds the number of related rows to each model, without loading the rows.

This is useful when a page shows "3 posts" next to each user. It adds a subquery to the select, so you get the counts with the same query.

docs.title: Counting related rows
docs.text:
Give withCount the relation name (the field name). Then read the count with countOf:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

List<User> users = await User().withCount('posts').get();

users.first.countOf('posts'); // 3
users.first.toJson();         // {..., "posts_count": 3}

In JSON, the key is the relation name in snake_case and _count, like posts_count.

It works with hasOne, hasMany, hasOneThrough, hasManyThrough, manyToMany, morphOne and morphMany relations. It is not for belongsTo relations, and there it throws an UnsupportedError.

docs.title: Counting only some rows
docs.text:
Sometimes you only want to count some related rows, like the published posts. Give a function with conditions, and use as to give the count its own key:

List<User> users = await User()
    .withCount('posts')
    .withCount('posts as published_count', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .get();

users.first.countOf('posts');               // all posts
users.first.aggregate('published_count');   // published posts

The global scopes and soft deletes of the related model are used in the count.

docs.title: Counting and loading together
docs.text:
withCount() works with where(), orderBy(), find(), getFirst(), paginate(), and with preload() or eager relations:

User? user = await User().preload('posts').withCount('posts').find(1);
user?.posts;              // the posts
user?.countOf('posts');   // the number of posts

docs.title: Sum, average, min and max
docs.text:
If you need a total of one column, like all views of a user's posts, use withSum(), withAvg(), withMin() or withMax(). They work like withCount(). Read the value with aggregate. It is null when there is no related row:

User? user = await User()
    .withSum('posts', 'views')
    .withAvg('posts', 'views')
    .withMin('posts', 'views')
    .withMax('posts', 'views')
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_sum_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_avg_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_min_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_max_views');

docs.title: Checking if related rows exist
docs.text:
If you only need to know whether there is a related row, use withExists(). It adds <relation>_exists, which is true when there is at least one related row. It takes a function and as, like withCount():

User? user = await User()
    .withExists('posts')
    .withExists('posts as has_published', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_exists');   // true or false
user?.aggregate('has_published');  // true or false

If you want to keep only the rows that have related rows, use whereHas() or has() instead. See Query by relations.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: • It works for a relation to the same table, like the children of a category.

docs.title: Model events
docs.text:
A model fires events when you save, delete or restore it, so you can run your own code at these moments.

There are two ways to listen:

  • Hooks are methods in the model class. Use them for code that belongs to the model, like filling a value.
  • Observers are separate classes. Use them for code that needs other services, like a mailer.

Events fire only on one model object. A query write like Post().where('draft', true).update({...}), Post().where(...).delete(), insertMultiple(), upsert(), increment(), decrement() or Post().where(...).touch() runs one query and fires no events.

docs.title: Defining hooks
docs.text:
Override an on... method in the model, then run dart run build_runner build. The hooks must be in the model class itself, because the generator looks there:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? slug;

  @override
  Future<void> onSaving() async {
    slug = title?.trim().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}

Post post = Post()..title = 'Hello World';
await post.save(); // onSaving runs first, so slug is 'hello-world'

Hooks come in pairs. A before hook runs before the query, so you can change values or cancel the operation. An after hook runs after the query, when the row is written and a new model has its id. Use it for side effects.

Before hook After hook Runs on onSaving onSaved every save(): a new or a loaded model onCreating onCreated save() or create() on a new model (INSERT) onUpdating onUpdated save() on a loaded model (UPDATE) onDeleting onDeleted delete() onForceDeleting onForceDeleted forceDelete(): really removes a soft-deleted row onRestoring onRestored restore(): brings back a soft-deleted row

onTrashed runs after onDeleted when a soft delete changed the row. It has no before hook.

docs.title: Setting a value only on create
docs.text:
If a value should be set once, when the row is new, use onCreating. Updates do not run it:

@override
Future<void> onCreating() async {
  status ??= 'draft';
  publicId = Uuid().v4(); // from package:uuid
}

docs.title: Doing something after a change
docs.text:
After hooks are good for side effects, because the row is already in the database:

@override
Future<void> onSaved() async {
  await Cache().forget('post:$id'); // the next read gets the new data
}

@override
Future<void> onDeleted() async {
  if (coverPath != null) {
    await Storage().delete(coverPath!); // remove the file of the post
  }
}

docs.title: Cancelling an operation
docs.text:
Sometimes a save or delete must not happen. Throw CancelModelEvent in a before hook, and the query does not run:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@override
Future<void> onDeleting() async {
  if (status == 'published') {
    throw CancelModelEvent('unpublish the post first');
  }
}

The caller sees the cancel in the return value. save() and restore() return false, and delete() and forceDelete() return 0:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
Future<Map<String, String>> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  Post? post = await Post().find(id);
  if (post == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();

  int deleted = await post.delete();
  if (deleted == 0) {
    throw BadRequestException(message: 'Unpublish the post first');
  }
  return <String, String>{'message': 'deleted'};
}

create({...}) returns the unsaved model, so its id is null. Any other error from a hook is thrown to the caller.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
An observer is a class that listens to one model. Use it when the code needs other objects, like a mailer, or when you do not want the code in the model.

Extend ModelObserver<T> and override only the methods you need. They have the same names as the hooks, and each one gets the model:

lib/app/observers/user.observer.dart
class UserObserver extends ModelObserver<User> {
  final Mailer mailer;

  UserObserver(this.mailer);

  @override
  Future<void> onCreated(User model) async {
    await mailer.sendWelcome(model.email!);
  }
}

A before method, like onCreating(T model), can also cancel the operation with CancelModelEvent.

docs.title: Registering observers
docs.text:
Add the observer in the setup() of a provider. Observers live in memory, and each isolate has its own memory, so this must run in every isolate. A provider does this for you:

lib/providers/observer_provider.dart
class ObserverProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.observe<User>(UserObserver(Mailer()));
  }
}

Dox finds ObserverProvider by itself, like every DoxProvider. Run dart run build_runner build after you add it. You can add more than one observer to a model.

docs.title: Listening to soft deletes
docs.text:
If you want to know when a row is soft deleted, add the TrashedObserver mixin and override onTrashed(T model):

class PostObserver extends ModelObserver<Post> with TrashedObserver<Post> {
  @override
  void onTrashed(Post post) => print('trashed ${post.id}');
}

docs.title: Saving without events
docs.text:
Sometimes you do not want the events to run, for example in imports, seed data or tests. saveQuietly() saves one model with no events:

await user.saveQuietly(); // save without events

Model.withoutEvents() turns off events for everything inside the callback:

await Model.withoutEvents(() async {
  await user.save();
  await post.delete();
});

docs.title: Events and transactions
docs.text:
save() does not start a transaction, so if an after hook throws, the row stays written. If you want to undo the row when a hook fails, wrap the call in a transaction:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await user.save(); // if onCreated() throws, the INSERT is rolled back
});

docs.title: Order of events
docs.text:
Call Events, in order save() on a new model saving → creating → INSERT → created → saved save() on a loaded model saving → updating → UPDATE → updated → saved create({...}) the same as save() on a new model firstOrCreate(), updateOrCreate() the same as save() when they create or update a row delete() deleting → DELETE or soft delete → deleted (→ trashed after a soft delete) forceDelete() forceDeleting → deleting → DELETE → deleted → forceDeleted restore() restoring → UPDATE deleted_at = NULL and updated_at → restored touch() saving → updating → UPDATE updated_at → updated → saved (touchQuietly() fires none)

The model hook runs first. Then the observers run, in the order you added them.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• save() on a loaded model with no changes fires the same events, but runs no UPDATE. A model with a Map or List field is always sent, because the field can change in place.
  • With the skipCleanUpdateEvents flag, a save with no changes fires only saving and saved. With this flag on, a save with changes runs beforeSave two times, and a save with no changes runs it one time.
  • When a model has events, create({...}) saves only the @Column fields.
  • Model.forgetObservers<User>() removes the observers of User. Model.forgetObservers() removes all.
  • A model with no hooks and no observers does no event work.

docs.title: Query by relations
docs.text:
whereHas(), whereDoesntHave() and has() keep the rows of a query by their related rows.

For example, you may want only the users that have a post. These methods do not load the related rows. They add a subquery to the where part, so it is still one query. If you also want to load the related rows, use preload(). See HasMany.

The examples on this page use these models:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? published;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;

  @HasMany(Comment)
  List<Comment> comments = <Comment>[];
}

Use the relation name (the field name), like 'posts'. Start the query with a model, like User(). A query from QueryBuilder.table() throws a StateError.

docs.title: Rows that have a relation
docs.text:
whereHas keeps the rows that have at least one related row:

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts').get();
// WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE ...)

If only some related rows should count, give a function with conditions. This keeps the users that have at least one published post:

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

docs.title: Rows that do not have a relation
docs.text:
whereDoesntHave keeps the rows that have no related row. It also takes a function:

List<User> users = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();
// WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE ...)

List<User> noDrafts = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', false);
}).get();

docs.title: Joining with or
docs.text:
orWhereHas and orWhereDoesntHave do the same, but they join the condition with OR:

List<User> users = await User()
    .where('name', 'Ann')
    .orWhereHas('posts')
    .get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR EXISTS (...)

await User().where('name', 'Ann').orWhereDoesntHave('posts').get();

docs.title: Counting related rows
docs.text:
Sometimes you need a number of related rows, like "three posts or more". has takes an operator and a number. The default is '>=' and 1, so at least one related row:

// at least one post
await User().has('posts').get();

// three posts or more
await User().has('posts', '>=', 3).get();

// no post
await User().has('posts', '=', 0).get();

// more than one published post
await User().has('posts', '>', 1, (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

The operator must be one of =, !=, <>, <, >, <= or >=. Any other operator throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Relations of relations
docs.text:
If you want to check a relation of a relation, use a dot. The function is for the last relation (comments):

// users that have a post with a comment
await User().whereHas('posts.comments').get();

// users that have a post with a comment by user 1
await User().whereHas('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('user_id', 1);
}).get();

// users that have no post with a comment
await User().whereDoesntHave('posts.comments').get();

With has(), the count is for the last relation of one row. So has('posts.comments', '>=', 2) keeps the users that have a post with two comments or more.

docs.title: A relation to the same table
docs.text:
It also works for a relation to the same table, like a Category with a parent Category:

// categories that have at least one child category
List<Category> parents = await Category().whereHas('children').get();

// categories whose parent is named 'Books'
List<Category> books = await Category()
    .whereHas('parent', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('name', 'Books');
    })
    .get();

In the function, write the column without the table name: name, not categories.name. With the table name, the column points to the parent row, not to the related row.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• It works with hasOne, hasMany, hasOneThrough, hasManyThrough, belongsTo, manyToMany, morphOne and morphMany relations. A morphTo relation throws an UnsupportedError.
  • Soft deleted related rows do not count. To count them, set q.withTrashed = true in the function.
  • The global scopes and the onQuery function of the relation are used.
  • It works with where(), count(), paginate(), withCount() and the other query methods.
  • A name that is not a relation of the model throws an ArgumentError.
  • For a relation to the same table, the subquery gives the table its own name, so each row is not compared with itself.

docs.title: Query scopes
docs.text: A scope is a query part that you use again and again, like "only active users", written once in the model and called like a query method.

docs.title: Local scopes
docs.text:
Add a static method with @Scope() to the model. It takes the query first and returns the query. Then run dart run build_runner build:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? active;

  @Column()
  int? age;

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> isActive(QueryBuilder<User> q) {
    return q.where('active', true);
  }

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> olderThan(QueryBuilder<User> q, int age) {
    return q.where('age', '>', age);
  }
}

The generator adds each scope as a method on the query of the model, so you can chain it with other query methods:

List<User> users = await User().isActive().get();

List<User> adults = await User()
    .where('name', 'like', 'a%')
    .isActive()
    .olderThan(18)
    .get();

A scope can take more arguments: required, optional ([...]) and named ({...}). The generated method takes the same arguments, without the query.

The scope name must not be a field or a method of the model. For example, a scope active next to a field active does not work, so name it isActive. A scope named like a query method (count, get) is never called.

docs.title: Global scopes
docs.text:
Sometimes every query of a model needs the same condition, like "leave out archived posts". Use @Scope(global: true) for this:

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? archived;

  /// every query leaves out archived posts
  @Scope(global: true)
  static QueryBuilder<Post> notArchived(QueryBuilder<Post> q) {
    return q.where('archived', false);
  }
}

await Post().get(); // ... WHERE ("archived" = false)

The scope is added to every query: get(), find(), all(), count(), paginate(), query updates and deletes, and relation queries. The scope goes in brackets, so an orWhere() in your query can not skip it.

A global scope counts as a where, so Post().delete() deletes only the rows in the scope.

docs.title: Removing global scopes
docs.text:
If one query needs the rows outside the scope, remove the scope by its method name with withoutGlobalScope(). To remove all of them, use withoutGlobalScopes():

await Post().withoutGlobalScope('notArchived').get();
await Post().withoutGlobalScopes().find(1);

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• save(), delete() and restore() on a model object work on that one row. They do not use the global scopes.
  • A query write with withoutGlobalScopes() and no where throws a StateError.
  • Soft deletes are not a global scope. Use withTrash() for them.

docs.title: BelongsTo
docs.text:
Use BelongsTo when this table keeps the foreign key to another table.

For example, a comment belongs to a user, so the comment table has the column user_id. BelongsTo is the other side of HasOne and HasMany.

docs.title: Defining the relation
docs.text:
Add a field with @BelongsTo(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, and it is nullable:

lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? content;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}

The related model needs nothing special:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text:
By default the foreign key is the class name of the related model in snake_case and _id, so User gives user_id. This is also true when the table is users. It is not taken from the field name, so a field named author still uses user_id. In that case, set foreignKey:

@BelongsTo(User, foreignKey: 'author_id', localKey: 'id')
User? author;

docs.title: Loading the relation
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name ('user') as the relation name.

docs.title: Preloading
docs.text:
Use preload when you load the models with a query. It runs one query for all comments, not one query per comment:

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
for (Comment comment in comments) {
  print(comment.user?.name);
}

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst. Each user is read once, also when it has many comments. Comments of the same user get the same User object.

docs.title: Loading on a model you have
docs.text:
If you already have the model, use $getRelation. Do not call it in a loop over many models, because it runs one query each time. Use preload for a list:

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
await comment?.$getRelation('user');
print(comment?.user?.name);

docs.title: Querying the relation
docs.text:
Sometimes you need more conditions on the related row. related gives you a query for it. It does not set comment.user:

Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
User? activeUser = await comment
    ?.related<User>('user')
    ?.where('status', 'active')
    .getFirst();

docs.title: Always loading the relation
docs.text:
If every query of Comment should load the relation, set eager: true. Then you do not call preload:

@BelongsTo(User, eager: true)
User? user;

docs.title: Filtering by the relation
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the comments by a user that matches. It does not load the users:

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().whereHas('user', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('name', 'Ann');
}).get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Changing the relation query
docs.text:
Sometimes the relation should only load some rows. Give onQuery a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it:

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User, onQuery: onlyActive)
  User? activeUser;

  static QueryBuilder<User> onlyActive(User q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: All options
docs.text: Option Default What it is foreignKey {related model}_id, like user_id The column in this table that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of the related model The column in the related table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• The belongsToKeyFromRelation flag takes the default foreign key from the relation name (author_id). The model generator does not pass the relation name yet, so set foreignKey when it is not the class name.
  • A relation with eager: true is always in toJson(). A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user.
  • reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.
  • The load runs one query like this:
SELECT * FROM "user"
  WHERE "user"."id" IN (@userid_p0, ...)

docs.title: HasMany
docs.text:
Use HasMany when one row of this table has many rows in another table.

For example, a user has many posts. The other table keeps the foreign key (post.user_id).

docs.title: Defining the relation
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasMany(...) to the model. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

The related model has the foreign key column:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text:
By default the foreign key is the class name in snake_case and _id, so User gives user_id. This is also true when the table is users. If your columns have other names, set foreignKey and localKey:

@HasMany(Book, foreignKey: 'author_code', localKey: 'code')
List<Book> books = <Book>[];

docs.title: Loading the relation
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name ('posts') as the relation name.

docs.title: Preloading
docs.text:
Use preload when you load the models with a query. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them. A user without posts gets an empty list:

User? user = await User().preload('posts').find(1);
print(user?.posts.length);

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst.

docs.title: Loading on a model you have
docs.text:
If you already have the model, use $getRelation:

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('posts');
print(user?.posts.length);

docs.title: Querying the relation
docs.text:
Sometimes you need more conditions on the related rows. related gives you a query for them. It does not set user.posts:

User? user = await User().find(1);
List<Post> activePosts = await user
        ?.related<Post>('posts')
        ?.where('status', 'active')
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .get() ??
    <Post>[];

docs.title: Always loading the relation
docs.text:
If every query of User should load the relation, set eager: true. Then you do not call preload:

@HasMany(Post, eager: true)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

docs.title: Filtering by the relation
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the users that have a post. whereDoesntHave() keeps the users with no post. has() counts the posts. They do not load the posts:

List<User> writers = await User().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('status', 'active');
}).get();

List<User> noPosts = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();
List<User> busy = await User().has('posts', '>=', 10).get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Changing the relation query
docs.text:
Sometimes the relation should only load some rows, or load them in an order. Give onQuery a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

You can have two fields for the same model with different queries:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasMany(Post, onQuery: onlyActive)
  List<Post> activePosts = <Post>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Post> onlyActive(Post q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active').orderBy('id', 'desc');
  }
}

docs.title: All options
docs.text: Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson(). A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case.
  • reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.
  • The load runs one query like this:
SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "post" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: HasOne
docs.text:
Use HasOne when one row of this table has one row in another table.

For example, a user has one user info row. The other table keeps the foreign key (user_info.user_id).

docs.title: Defining the relation
docs.text:
Add a field with @HasOne(...) to the model. The field type is the related model, and it is nullable:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user_info/user_info.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasOne(UserInfo)
  UserInfo? userInfo;
}

The related model has the foreign key column:

lib/app/models/user_info/user_info.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user_info.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class UserInfo extends UserInfoGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? address;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text:
By default the foreign key is the class name in snake_case and _id, so User gives user_id. This is also true when the table is users. If your columns have other names, set foreignKey and localKey:

@HasOne(UserInfo, foreignKey: 'owner_id', localKey: 'id')
UserInfo? userInfo;

docs.title: Loading the relation
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name ('userInfo') as the relation name.

docs.title: Preloading
docs.text:
Use preload when you load the models with a query. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them:

User? user = await User().preload('userInfo').find(1);
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst.

docs.title: Loading on a model you have
docs.text:
If you already have the model, use $getRelation:

User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('userInfo');
print(user?.userInfo?.address);

docs.title: Querying the relation
docs.text:
Sometimes you need more conditions on the related row. related gives you a query for it. It does not set user.userInfo:

User? user = await User().find(1);
UserInfo? info = await user
    ?.related<UserInfo>('userInfo')
    ?.where('address', '!=', '')
    .getFirst();

docs.title: Always loading the relation
docs.text:
If every query of User should load the relation, set eager: true. Then you do not call preload:

@HasOne(UserInfo, eager: true)
UserInfo? userInfo;

docs.title: Filtering by the relation
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the users that have a user_info row. whereDoesntHave() keeps the users without one. They do not load the UserInfo:

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('userInfo').get();

List<User> inParis = await User().whereHas('userInfo', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('address', 'Paris');
}).get();

List<User> noInfo = await User().whereDoesntHave('userInfo').get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Changing the relation query
docs.text:
Sometimes the relation should only load some rows. Give onQuery a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasOne(UserInfo, onQuery: onlyActive)
