  UserInfo? userInfo;

  static QueryBuilder<UserInfo> onlyActive(UserInfo q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}

docs.title: All options
docs.text: Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like user_id The column in the related table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• A relation with eager: true is always in toJson(). A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: user_info.
  • reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.
  • The load runs one query like this:
SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "user_info" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0)

docs.title: ManyToMany
docs.text:
Use ManyToMany when rows on both sides can have many rows on the other side.

For example, an artist has many songs, and a song has many artists. The link is kept in a third table, the pivot table. It has one foreign key to each side.

docs.title: Tables
Defining the relation
docs.text:
Add a field with @ManyToMany(...) to each model that needs it. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list:

lib/app/models/artist/artist.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../song/song.model.dart';

part 'artist.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @ManyToMany(Song)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
}
lib/app/models/song/song.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../artist/artist.model.dart';

part 'song.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Song extends SongGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @ManyToMany(Artist)
  List<Artist> artists = <Artist>[];
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text:
If your pivot table or columns have other names, set them:

@ManyToMany(
  Song,
  pivotTable: 'artist_song',
  pivotForeignKey: 'artist_id',
  pivotRelatedForeignKey: 'song_id',
  localKey: 'id',
  relatedKey: 'id',
)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

docs.title: Loading the relation
docs.text: The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name ('songs') as the relation name.

docs.title: Preloading
docs.text:
Use preload when you load the models with a query. For a list of models, it runs one query for all of them. A model without links gets an empty list:

Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
print(artist?.songs.length);

List<Song> songs = await Song().preload('artists').get();

preload works with find, get, all and getFirst.

docs.title: Loading on a model you have
docs.text:
If you already have the model, use $getRelation:

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
await artist?.$getRelation('songs');
print(artist?.songs.length);

docs.title: Querying the relation
docs.text:
Sometimes you need more conditions on the related rows. related gives you a query for them. It does not set artist.songs.

The query joins the pivot table, so write table.column for column names:

Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
List<Song> songs = await artist
        ?.related<Song>('songs')
        ?.orderBy('song.title')
        .get() ??
    <Song>[];

docs.title: Always loading the relation
docs.text:
If every query of Artist should load the relation, set eager: true. Then you do not call preload. Do not set eager: true on both sides, because each side would load the other side again and again:

@ManyToMany(Song, eager: true)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

docs.title: Reading pivot columns
docs.text:
The pivot table can have more columns, like a role. List them in withPivot:

@ManyToMany(Song, withPivot: <String>['role'])
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

Then read them with pivot on each related model:

Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
for (Song song in artist!.songs) {
  print(song.pivot['role']);
}

pivot also has the two pivot keys, like artist_id and song_id. It is filled when the rows are loaded by the relation: with preload, $getRelation, eager or related('songs')!.get(). A model that was not loaded by the relation has an empty pivot.

docs.title: Pivot timestamps
docs.text: If you want created_at and updated_at on the pivot rows, set withTimestamps: true. The pivot table needs both columns (table.timestamps()). Then attach(), sync() and toggle() set them, and updateExistingPivot() sets updated_at.

docs.title: Changing the links
docs.text:
These methods add and remove rows in the pivot table. The first argument is the relation name, like 'songs'. Save the model first, because a model without an id throws a StateError.

The ids can be:

  • one id: 1
  • a model: song
  • a list of ids or models: [1, 2, song]
  • a map of id => pivot values: {1: {'role': 'singer'}, 2: {}}

Each id is used once, so [1, 1, '1'] adds one row.

docs.title: Attaching
docs.text:
attach adds a pivot row for each id. The third argument has the pivot values for every new row:

await artist.attach('songs', 1);
await artist.attach('songs', <int>[2, 3], <String, dynamic>{'role': 'singer'});
await artist.attach('songs', <int, Map<String, dynamic>>{
  4: <String, dynamic>{'role': 'writer'},
});

attach does not check for a row that is already there. If the row may be there, use sync or syncWithoutDetaching.

docs.title: Detaching
docs.text:
detach deletes the pivot rows of the ids and returns how many rows it deleted. With no ids argument, it deletes every pivot row of the model. The songs stay in the song table:

await artist.detach('songs', <int>[1, 2]);
await artist.detach('songs');

docs.title: Syncing
docs.text:
sync makes the pivot rows match the ids. It adds a row for each new id, deletes the rows of the ids that are not in the list, and sets changed pivot values on the rows that are already there.

It returns a PivotSyncResult with the ids of each change:

PivotSyncResult result = await artist.sync('songs', <int>[1, 2, 3]);
print(result.attached); // ids that got a new row
print(result.detached); // ids whose row was deleted
print(result.updated);  // ids whose pivot values changed

If you only want to add links and never delete, use syncWithoutDetaching:

await artist.syncWithoutDetaching('songs', <int>[4]);

docs.title: Toggling
docs.text:
toggle adds a row for each id that has none, and deletes the row of each id that has one. It returns a PivotSyncResult with attached and detached:

await artist.toggle('songs', <int>[1, 2]);

docs.title: Updating pivot values
docs.text:
updateExistingPivot sets pivot values on the rows of one id or a list of ids. It returns how many rows changed:

await artist.updateExistingPivot('songs', 1, <String, dynamic>{'role': 'writer'});

docs.title: Filtering by the relation
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the artists that have a song. It checks the pivot table artist_song for you, and it does not load the songs:

List<Artist> artists = await Artist().whereHas('songs', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('title', 'Yesterday');
}).get();

List<Artist> noSongs = await Artist().whereDoesntHave('songs').get();

See Query by relations.

docs.title: Changing the relation query
docs.text:
Sometimes the relation should only load some rows. Give onQuery a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it. Write table.column, because the query joins the pivot table:

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @ManyToMany(Song, onQuery: onlyPublished)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Song> onlyPublished(Song q) {
    return q.where('song.status', 'published');
  }
}

docs.title: All options
docs.text:
The examples are for @ManyToMany(Song) in the Artist model.

Option Default Example value What it is pivotTable the two model names in A-Z order, joined with _ artist_song The pivot table. pivotForeignKey {this model}_id artist_id The pivot column that points to this model. pivotRelatedForeignKey {related model}_id song_id The pivot column that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of this model id The column in artist that pivotForeignKey points to. relatedKey the primary key of the related model id The column in song that pivotRelatedForeignKey points to. withPivot none ['role'] Extra pivot columns to read. See Reading pivot columns. withTimestamps false true Read and set created_at and updated_at in the pivot table. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Null and unsaved ids
docs.text:
• null means no ids. So attach('songs', null) and detach('songs', null) change nothing, and sync('songs', null) deletes every link, like sync('songs', []).
  • In a list, a null id or a model that is not saved is skipped by attach, detach, toggle, syncWithoutDetaching and updateExistingPivot.
  • sync throws an ArgumentError for one, before it changes anything, because it would delete every other link.

docs.title: How ids match
docs.text:
• Two texts only match when the text is the same. So on a text key column, '007' and '7' are two ids.
  • When one id is a number, Dart reads the other one as a number too. So on a number key column, '01' matches song 1.
  • A bool id is 1 or 0. A whole double like 2.0 is sent as the int 2. A BigInt that fits is an int.
  • Other doubles (like 1.5), a text number at or past ±2^53, a BigInt that does not fit, and any other type throw an ArgumentError. sync checks every id before its first write.
  • In PivotSyncResult, a number id is an int, also when you gave '3'. A text like '03' stays text.
  • On a text key that ignores case (MySQL and MariaDB by default, SQLite with COLLATE NOCASE), sync and toggle also ask the database about text ids that Dart did not match. So with a stored 'ABC', sync('songs', ['abc']) keeps that row.
  • Text ids are sent to the database as they are. The database may read some texts in its own way, for example '0x1'.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• toJson() of a model loaded by a ManyToMany relation has a pivot key. Dates are ISO text. Put 'pivot' in hidden to leave it out. If the model has its own pivot column, the key keeps the column value.
  • A relation with eager: true is always in toJson(). A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: songs.
  • reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.
  • The load runs one query like this. With withPivot or withTimestamps, it also selects those pivot columns, like "artist_song"."role" as "_pivot_role":
SELECT "song".*, "artist_song"."artist_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "song"
  LEFT JOIN "artist_song" on "artist_song"."song_id" = "song"."id"
  WHERE "artist_song"."artist_id" IN (@artist_songartist_id_p0, ...)

docs.title: Polymorphic
docs.text:
Use a polymorphic relation when one model can belong to more than one other model.

For example, a comment can belong to a photo or to a video. The comment table does not have a photo_id and a video_id. Instead it has two columns:

  • commentable_id: the id of the photo or the video.
  • commentable_type: the type, like photo or video.

commentable is the morph name. You pick it.

docs.title: Tables
The morph map
docs.text:
The morph map gives each model a type name. The type name is the value in the commentable_type column.

Set it in the setup() of a provider. Dox runs providers in every isolate, before the first request. The map is kept per isolate, so setting it only in main() is not enough:

class MorphMapProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.morphMap(<String, Model<dynamic> Function()>{
      'photo': Photo.new,
      'video': Video.new,
    });
  }
}

A queue worker or a CLI command that reads these relations must call it too.

You should always use a morph map, because without it the class name is stored, like Photo. The class name changes when you rename the class or build with --obfuscate, and then the old rows do not match. For the same reason, do not change a type name later. @MorphTo needs the map and throws without it.

docs.title: Has many
docs.text:
A photo has many comments. Use @MorphMany. The second argument is the morph name:

lib/app/models/photo/photo.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../comment/comment.model.dart';

part 'photo.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Photo extends PhotoGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @MorphMany(Comment, 'commentable')
  List<Comment> comments = <Comment>[];
}

docs.title: Has one
docs.text:
A photo has one cover image. Use @MorphOne. It works like @MorphMany, but the field is one model:

@MorphOne(Image, 'imageable')
Image? cover;

When there are many rows, it keeps the last row the query returns. Add an orderBy in onQuery to pick the row, like with HasOne.

docs.title: The other side
docs.text:
A comment belongs to a photo or a video. Use @MorphTo. The field type is Model<dynamic>?, and the morph name is the field name in snake_case: commentable.

The commentable_id and commentable_type columns must be @Column fields, or the relation is always null:

lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? body;

  @Column()
  int? commentableId;

  @Column()
  String? commentableType;

  @MorphTo()
  Model<dynamic>? commentable;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Saving a row
docs.text:
There is no associate(), so set the two columns yourself. Use Model.morphTypeOf() for the type, so it is the same as the morph map:

Comment comment = Comment()
  ..body = 'Nice'
  ..commentableId = photo.id
  ..commentableType = Model.morphTypeOf(photo);
await comment.save();

docs.title: Loading the relation
docs.text:
Load it like the other relations: with preload, $getRelation, related or eager. On a @MorphTo field, check the type of the loaded model:

Photo? photo = await Photo().preload('comments').find(1);
print(photo?.comments.length);

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('commentable').get();
for (Comment c in comments) {
  if (c.commentable is Photo) {
    print((c.commentable as Photo).title);
  }
}

A comment with a type that is not in the morph map throws a StateError. A comment with no type, or an empty type '', gets null.

docs.title: Filtering by the relation
docs.text:
whereHas(), whereDoesntHave() and withCount() work with @MorphMany and @MorphOne:

List<Photo> photos = await Photo().whereHas('comments').get();
List<Video> videos = await Video().withCount('comments').get();

They do not work with @MorphTo. It throws an UnsupportedError.

docs.title: Morph map helpers
docs.text:
Two helpers read the map:

String type = Model.morphTypeOf(Photo()); // 'photo'
Model<dynamic> model = Model.morphModel('video'); // a new Video()

Model.morphMap(map, merge: false) removes the names you set before.

docs.title: Options of @MorphMany and @MorphOne
docs.text:
The examples are for @MorphMany(Comment, 'commentable') in the Photo model.

Option Default Example value What it is name (2nd argument) commentable The morph name. typeColumn {name}_type commentable_type The type column in comment. idColumn {name}_id commentable_id The id column in comment. localKey the primary key of this model id The column in photo that idColumn points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Options of @MorphTo
docs.text: Option Default Example value What it is name the field name in snake_case commentable The morph name. typeColumn {name}_type commentable_type The type column in this table. idColumn {name}_id commentable_id The id column in this table. ownerKey the primary key of the related model id The column in the related table that idColumn points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query of each type. It runs for every type, so it takes and returns Model<dynamic>. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• @MorphMany and @MorphOne run one query for all models, with where commentable_type = 'photo'. @MorphTo runs one query for each type in the list.
  • related<Photo>('commentable') on one comment gives the query of its photo.
  • A relation with eager: true is always in toJson(). A relation loaded with preload is in toJson() of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: comments, commentable.
  • reload() and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See Relationships.

docs.title: HasManyThrough
docs.text:
Use HasManyThrough to read rows that are two steps away, through a model in the middle. HasOneThrough is the same, but it gives one row.

For example, a country has many users, and a user has many posts. So a country has many posts through its users.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: Table Columns country id, name user id, country_id post id, user_id, title

docs.title: Defining the relation
docs.text:
Add the field to the first model. The through option is the model in the middle:

lib/app/models/country/country.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';
import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'country.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Country extends CountryGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasManyThrough(Post, through: User)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasOneThrough(Post, through: User, onQuery: newest)
  Post? latestPost;

  static Model<Post> newest(Post q) {
    q.orderBy('post.id');
    return q;
  }
}

With HasOneThrough, when several rows match, the last row of the query wins. So newest orders by post.id from low to high, and the highest id is the last row.

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relationship.

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text:
If your columns have other names, set the four keys:

@HasManyThrough(
  Post,
  through: User,
  foreignKey: 'home_country_id', // on user, points to the country
  localKey: 'id', // on country
  throughForeignKey: 'author_id', // on post, points to the user
  throughLocalKey: 'id', // on user
)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

docs.title: Loading the relation
docs.text:
It loads like the other relations. preload runs one query for all countries. withCount, whereHas, whereDoesntHave and has work too:

Country? country = await Country().preload('posts').find(1);
print(country?.posts.length);

List<Country> countries = await Country().withCount('posts').get();
List<Country> active = await Country().whereHas('posts').get();

See Counting relations and Query by relations.

Soft deleted rows are left out, in the middle table and in the far table.

docs.title: Writing column names
docs.text:
The query joins the two tables, and a column like title can be in both. So in onQuery and in a whereHas function, write the table in front of the column:

List<Country> countries = await Country().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('post.title', 'Hello');
}).get();

docs.title: All options
docs.text: Option Default What it is foreignKey {this model}_id, like country_id The column in the middle table that points to this model. localKey the primary key of this model The column in this table that foreignKey points to. throughForeignKey {middle model}_id, like user_id The column in the far table that points to the middle model. throughLocalKey the primary key of the middle model The column in the middle table that throughForeignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.

docs.title: Broadcasting
docs.text:
Broadcasting sends server events to browsers and apps over Socket.IO, on public, private and presence channels.

Many apps need live pages: an order status that changes, a chat, or a list of who is online. With broadcasting, a client subscribes to a channel, your code sends an event to the channel, and every client in it gets the event. You do not need to poll the server.

Broadcasting is part of the dox_socketio package. It is off by default.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Do the Socket.IO setup first. Then turn on broadcasting in the config:

lib/config/socketio.dart
SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  broadcasting: true,
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace()],
);

docs.title: Channel rules
docs.text:
Private and presence channels need a rule that says who may join. Rules are kept per isolate, so add them where every isolate runs them. A provider is a good place:

lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build, so the generated container finds the provider. Without it, no rule is added, and every private subscribe gets Forbidden. See Authorizing channels for how rules work.

docs.title: The auth route
docs.text:
A client that has not logged in its socket gets a token from the auth route. Add the route with your own auth middleware:

lib/routes/api.dart
@override
void register() {
  Broadcast.routes(middleware: <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()]); // POST /api/broadcasting/auth
}

The router prefix is added to the path. This router has the prefix api, so the path is /api/broadcasting/auth. Pass path: to use another path.

The route runs the channel rule with req.auth, and answers {"auth": "<token>"} or 403. The token is signed with a key made from APP_KEY, so broadcasting needs APP_KEY. A token works for one socket, one channel and one minute.

docs.title: Channel types
docs.text:
There are three kinds of channels:

Channel Name Who can subscribe Channel('news') news any client PrivateChannel('orders.5') private-orders.5 a client that passes the rule PresenceChannel('chat.lobby') presence-chat.lobby a client that passes the rule. Members see each other

docs.title: Defining broadcast events
docs.text:
An event is a class with the ShouldBroadcast mixin:

class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcast {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() => <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  String broadcastAs() => 'order.shipped'; // default: the class name

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() => <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}
  • broadcastOn gives the channels. It is required.
  • broadcastAs gives the event name. The default is the class name.
  • broadcastWith gives the payload. It must be JSON. The default is an empty map.

Do not give an event a name that starts with client-, because that prefix is for client events.

docs.title: Authorizing channels
docs.text:
Broadcast.channel(pattern, rule) adds a rule for private and presence channels. The pattern has no private- or presence- prefix. A {name} part matches any text with no dot.

The rule gets the user, then one string for each {name} part. It can be async.

  • A private rule returns true to allow. Anything else refuses.
  • A presence rule returns a map with the member info, with an id. Anything else refuses.
  • A rule that throws refuses, and the error goes to stderr.

This presence rule lets any logged in user join a chat room:

Broadcast.channel('chat.{room}', (Object? user, String room) {
  User u = user as User;
  return <String, Object?>{'id': u.id, 'name': u.name};
});

One rule serves both kinds, so orders.{id} checks private-orders.1 and presence-orders.1. When more than one pattern matches, the first one added wins.

docs.title: Broadcasting events
docs.text:
Use broadcast to send an event. Broadcast.event does the same:

await broadcast(OrderShipped(order));
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order)); // the same

docs.title: Only to others
docs.text:
Sometimes the user who made a change should not get the event again, because their page already shows it. Use toOthers to skip their socket. The client sends its socket id in the X-Socket-ID header, and Broadcast.socketId(req) reads it:

await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order), toOthers: Broadcast.socketId(req));

docs.title: Receiving broadcasts
docs.text:
On the client, use socket.io-client. A public channel needs no token.

Subscribe inside the connect handler. A subscription belongs to one socket, and after a reconnect the client has a new socket with no channels. The connect handler runs again after each reconnect, so it subscribes again:

import { io } from 'socket.io-client';

const socket = io('https://app.example.com', { transports: ['websocket'] });

socket.on('order.shipped', (channel, payload) => console.log(channel, payload));
socket.on('connect', () => {
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'news' }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});

Events arrive as (channel, payload), under the name from broadcastAs.

docs.title: Private and presence channels
docs.text:
For a private or presence channel, get a token from the auth route first, then send it in subscribe. A token works for one socket id only, so ask for a new one in the connect handler:

socket.on('connect', async () => {
  const res = await fetch('/api/broadcasting/auth', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', authorization: `Bearer ${apiToken}` },
    body: JSON.stringify({ socket_id: socket.id, channel_name: 'private-orders.5' }),
  });
  const { auth } = await res.json();
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'private-orders.5', auth }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});

Send the token as a string in auth, like above.

A socket that is already logged in with SocketAuth needs no token. The server runs the rule with socket.user.

docs.title: Leaving a channel
docs.text: Use socket.emit('unsubscribe', { channel }, ack) to leave a channel.

docs.title: Subscribe errors
docs.text:
The ack of subscribe and unsubscribe is {ok: true} or {ok: false, error}:

error Why channel is missing no channel name channel name is too long over Broadcast.maxChannelLength too many channels over Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket already subscribing the same channel is still being checked Forbidden the rule refused, or the token is missing, wrong or old unsubscribed an unsubscribe came while it was subscribing presence is not available another server did not answer in time

docs.title: Presence channels
docs.text:
A presence channel tells its members who else is in it. The client gets three events:

Event Arguments When presence:subscribed (channel, members) to the new socket, with all members presence:joining (channel, member) to the others, when a member joins presence:leaving (channel, member) to the others, when a member leaves

A member is {user_id, user_info}. user_info is the map from the rule.

socket.on('presence:subscribed', (channel, members) => console.log(members));
socket.on('presence:joining', (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_info.name));
socket.on('presence:leaving', (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_id));

A user with two sockets is one member. presence:joining is sent for the first socket, and presence:leaving for the last one. The member list covers all isolates and servers that share the adapter.

docs.title: Queued broadcasting
docs.text:
Sometimes you do not want the request to wait while the event is sent. A queued broadcast goes through your queue instead.

dox_socketio does not depend on dox_queue, so you connect them with a hook and a small job. Follow these steps.

docs.title: 1. Mark the event
docs.text:
Use ShouldBroadcastQueued in place of ShouldBroadcast:

class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcastQueued {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() => <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() => <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}

await broadcast(OrderShipped(order)); // goes to the queue

docs.title: 2. Write the job
docs.text:
The worker runs this job. It sends the saved broadcast to the clients:

lib/app/jobs/broadcast.job.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

/// Sends one queued broadcast to the clients.
@Job()
class BroadcastJob extends DoxJob {
  BroadcastJob({required this.payload});

  final Map<String, dynamic> payload;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await Broadcast.deliver(BroadcastPayload.fromJson(payload));
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build. It adds the job to lib/generated/jobs.g.dart, which the queue needs to save and load the job. See queue setup. Make sure jobs: jobRegistry is set in your queue config.

docs.title: 3. Set the hook
docs.text:
The hook gets the broadcast and puts it on the queue. Add it to the setup() of the BroadcastProvider from Channel rules, next to the rules:

lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

import '../app/jobs/broadcast.job.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });

    // puts ShouldBroadcastQueued events on the queue
    Broadcast.useQueue(queueBroadcast);
  }

  static Future<void> queueBroadcast(BroadcastPayload payload) async {
    await Queue.dispatch(BroadcastJob(payload: payload.toJson()));
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Use the Redis adapter
docs.text:
The worker is its own process. It starts your providers, so it gets its own Socket.IO server, but that server has no clients. So the worker must reach the clients of the web server through Redis.

Set the Redis adapter in SocketIoConfig. The web server and the worker use the same config, so both use the same Redis. A Broadcast.emitter does not help here, because Broadcast.deliver sends through the worker's own Socket.IO server first.

docs.title: 5. Run the worker
docs.text:
dart run bin/queue.dart

Deploy the worker together with the web app. See run the worker.

If no hook is set (Broadcast.useQueue is not called), a ShouldBroadcastQueued event is sent at once, like a normal one. So tests and small apps work without a queue.

docs.title: Broadcasting from other processes
docs.text:
A command has no Socket.IO server. Set an emitter, so Broadcast.event can send through Redis:

Redis redis = Redis(RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379));
Broadcast.emitter = SocketIoEmitter(redis);

await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order));

The servers must use the Redis adapter. When the emitter is for another namespace than /, use SocketIoEmitter(redis).of('/chat').

If the process has no Socket.IO server and no emitter, Broadcast.event throws a StateError. To send from a queue job, use queued broadcasting.

docs.title: Client events
docs.text:
Sometimes a client wants to tell the other members something small, like "is typing". You do not need server code for this: a client event (a whisper) goes from one client to the other members of a private or presence channel. The server only passes it on.

It is off by default, because clients can then message each other with no code of yours in between. Turn it on in the config:

SocketIoConfig(broadcasting: true, whisper: true);

The client sends client event with {channel, event, data}. The event name must start with client-. The other sockets in the channel get the event with (channel, data):

socket.emit('client event', {
  channel: 'presence-chat.lobby',
  event: 'client-typing',
  data: { name: 'Alice' },
}, (ack) => console.log(ack)); // the ack is optional

socket.on('client-typing', (channel, data) => console.log(channel, data));
  • Only a socket that subscribed to the channel can whisper, and only on private and presence channels.
  • The sender does not get its own whisper. Its other sockets do.
  • It works across isolates and servers with the Redis adapter.
  • When a whisper is refused, the ack is {ok: false, error}, for example not subscribed or data is too big.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Broadcast.fake() keeps the events and sends nothing:

test('shipping an order broadcasts', () async {
  BroadcastFake fake = Broadcast.fake();

  await shipOrder(order);

  fake.assertBroadcasted<OrderShipped>();
  fake.assertBroadcastedOn<OrderShipped>('private-orders.${order.id}');
  fake.assertBroadcastedTimes<OrderShipped>(1);
});
Method Passes when assertBroadcasted<T>([test]) an event of type T was sent. With test, one of them passes it assertBroadcastedOn<T>(name) T was sent on the channel name, with its private- or presence- prefix assertBroadcastedTimes<T>(n) T was sent exactly n times assertNotBroadcasted<T>() no T was sent assertNothingBroadcasted() no event was sent
  • A failed assert throws an AssertionError.
  • fake.eventsOf<T>() gives the events, and fake.clear() forgets them.
  • The fake keeps queued events too. Check them with fake.assertQueued<OrderShipped>(). fake.delivered holds the payloads that deliver got.
  • Broadcast.restore() turns the fake off.
  • Broadcast.reset() forgets the rules, the emitter and the fake. Call it in tearDown.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Broadcast.maxChannelLength 200 the longest channel name a client may subscribe to Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket 100 the most channels for one socket Broadcast.tokenLifetime 1 minute how long a token from the auth route works Broadcast.presenceTimeout 2 seconds how long a presence join or leave waits for other servers Broadcast.maxWhisperSize 10 KB the biggest data of a client event, in bytes of JSON. A bigger one is dropped

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• Turn broadcasting on for one namespace only. With two namespaces, both accept subscribe, but Broadcast.event sends only through the last one.
  • An object of headers in auth is refused with Forbidden.
  • A presence subscribe is refused when a server does not answer in time. A leave still sends presence:leaving.
  • Presence joins and leaves of one channel run one after another in each isolate. During a Redis outage, each one waits up to presenceTimeout, so keep it short.
  • When two sockets of one user join or leave at the same moment on two isolates or servers, presence:joining or presence:leaving can be missed or sent twice.
  • The queued payload is JSON: {channels, event, data, except}. except is the toOthers socket id.
  • Normal ShouldBroadcast events never use the queue hook.
  • Broadcast.deliver throws a StateError when the worker has no way to send, which is when broadcasting is off and there is no Broadcast.emitter.
  • deliver prints a warning once when it sends through an in-memory adapter with no clients, because the clients of the web server do not get that broadcast.
  • With client events off, a client event is ignored, with no ack.
  • The event names and the whisper format match the Echo client, so channel.whisper('typing', data) and listenForWhisper('typing', ...) use the same names. But Echo sends auth as an object of headers, so it can not join a private or presence channel on its own. Log the socket in with SocketAuth, or send your own subscribe with the token, as in Private and presence channels.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Cache() keeps data that is slow to make, so the next request can read it fast.

Some work takes a long time, like a big database query or a call to another service. If the result does not change often, you can keep it in the cache and read it from there. The cache runs on dox_cache, which is built into dox_core.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A new project already has lib/config/cache.dart, with a file store and a memory store. CACHE_STORE in .env picks the default store. It is file when it is not set.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
A new app already has the cache. In an older app, run dox add cache:

dox add cache

It writes lib/config/cache.dart, adds it to lib/config/app.dart and adds the CACHE_STORE key. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

To pick another default store, add --store=redis (or memory, database). redis also adds the REDIS_* keys. database also adds dox_cache_database, its provider and the cache table migration, and it needs dox add orm first.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
A store uses one driver. The driver decides where the data is kept:

Driver Where the data is Shared between isolates file files in a folder (default storage/cache) yes, on the same machine memory a map inside the isolate no redis a Redis server yes, also between machines database a table in your database, from dox_cache_database yes, also between machines null nowhere. It stores nothing -

Dox runs one isolate per CPU core, and each isolate has its own memory store. So a value you put in one isolate is missing in the others. If all isolates and servers must see the same data, use redis or database.

Sessions on a memory store are the exception. They live in the main isolate, so every isolate sees them. See Session.

docs.title: Adding a Redis store
docs.text:
To add a store, edit lib/config/cache.dart. This example adds a redis store:

lib/config/cache.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

CacheConfig cache = CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: env.cacheStore,
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache'},
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory', 'max_size': 10000},
    'redis': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'redis',
      'host': env.redisHost,
      'port': env.redisPort,
      'prefix': 'app_cache:',
    },
  },
);

Redis needs two env keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to lib/config/env.dart, then run dart run build_runner build:

lib/config/env.dart
  String get redisHost => '127.0.0.1';

  int get redisPort => 6379;

lib/config/app.dart already passes the config to AppConfig(cache: cache). All options of each driver are in Store options.

docs.title: Retrieving items
docs.text:
Use get to read a value. It gives null when the key is missing. The second argument is the default, which you get instead of null:

await Cache().get('foo');            // 'bar', or null when missing
await Cache().get('foo', 'default'); // 'default' when missing

docs.title: Checking if an item exists
docs.text:
The has method returns true when the key is in the cache:

if (await Cache().has('foo')) {
  // ...
}

docs.title: Retrieving many items
docs.text:
The many method reads many keys at once. A missing key gives null:

await Cache().many(<String>['a', 'b', 'c']); // {a: 1, b: 2, c: null}

docs.title: Retrieve and store
docs.text:
Often you want to read a value, and make it when it is missing. The remember method does this. If the key is missing, the function runs and its result is stored for the given time:

List<dynamic> posts = await Cache().remember(
  'posts',
  Duration(minutes: 5),
  () async => (await Post().all()).map((Post p) => p.toJson()).toList(),
);

The value is stored as JSON, so return maps, lists, strings and numbers, not models. To keep the value with no expiry, use rememberForever(key, fn).

remember has two options:

  • decode: turns the stored JSON back into your type on a hit, like decode: (j) => (j as List).cast<String>(). Without it, use JSON types like List<dynamic>.
  • lock: true lets only one caller on all isolates and servers run the function. The others wait for its value. Use it when the function is slow and many requests could run it at once.

docs.title: Serving stale values
docs.text:
Sometimes an old value is fine for a while, but you do not want a user to wait while it is made again. The flexible method serves the value as it is for fresh. Then, until stale more has passed, it still serves the old value at once and runs the function once in the background:

Map<String, dynamic> stats = await Cache().flexible(
  'stats', Duration(minutes: 1), Duration(minutes: 5), loadStats,
);

After fresh + stale, the value is gone and the next call waits for the function.

If an old value is always better than no value, pass null as stale. Then the value stays until a refresh replaces it. This is good for data from a service that can be down: when the function fails, callers still get the last good value:

Map<String, dynamic> rates = await Cache().flexible(
  'rates', Duration(minutes: 10), null, fetchRates,
);

docs.title: Retrieve and delete
docs.text:
The pull method reads a value and removes it in one step:

dynamic code = await Cache().pull('login_code');

docs.title: Retrieving raw JSON
docs.text:
If you only send the cached value back as a response, you do not need to decode it and encode it again. getRaw gives the stored JSON text as it is:

String? json = await Cache().getRaw('posts');
if (json != null) {
  return response(json).contentType(ContentType.json);
}

A missing key gives null. A stored String comes back as JSON, with its quotes: "bar".

docs.title: Storing items
docs.text:
Use put to store a value. Pass a duration to make it expire. With no duration, the value stays forever:

await Cache().put('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

await Cache().put('foo', 'bar');

A value must be a JSON type: Map, List, String, num, bool or null. A Map comes back as Map<String, dynamic>, and a List comes back as List<dynamic>.

docs.title: Storing an item forever
docs.text:
The forever method stores a value with no expiry:

await Cache().forever('settings', <String, dynamic>{'theme': 'dark'});

docs.title: Storing if not present
docs.text:
The add method stores a value only when the key is missing. It returns true when the value was stored:

bool stored = await Cache().add('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

docs.title: Storing many items
docs.text:
The putMany method stores many values at once:

await Cache().putMany(<String, Object?>{'a': 1, 'b': 2});

docs.title: Incrementing and decrementing
docs.text:
The increment and decrement methods change an integer. A missing key starts at 0:

await Cache().increment('visits');
await Cache().decrement('stock', 5);

docs.title: Changing the expiry
docs.text:
The touch method gives a key a new expiry. It returns false when the key is missing:

await Cache().touch('foo', duration: Duration(hours: 1));

docs.title: Removing items
docs.text:
The forget method removes one key. The flush method removes all items of the store:

await Cache().forget('foo');

await Cache().flush();

docs.title: Using another store
docs.text:
By default, Cache() uses the default store. If you want another store from the config, use store:

await Cache().store('redis').put('foo', 'bar');

store() changes the Cache it is called on. The flag cacheCopies makes store() and tags() give a new Cache instead. See Core flags.

docs.title: Cache tags
docs.text:
Tags let you group items, so you can remove only the items of one group. Put items under a tag with tag, then call flush on the tag:

await Cache().tag('users').put('u1', 'Ann');
await Cache().tag('users').flush(); // removes only the items of this tag

To use many tags, call tags(['a', 'b']).

docs.title: Atomic locks
docs.text:
Sometimes only one request (or one server) may run some code at a time, like building a report. A lock does this. The memory, file, redis and database stores support locks:

CacheLock lock = Cache().store('redis').lock('report', Duration(seconds: 30));
if (await lock.get()) {
  try {
    await buildReport();
  } finally {
    await lock.release();
  }
}

get() tries once. It is true when you got the lock. The lock is freed after its time (30 seconds here), even if you never call release().

The memory lock works inside one isolate only, and the file lock works for all isolates on one machine. If many servers must share the lock, use redis or database.

docs.title: Waiting for a lock
docs.text:
block tries again and again until the time is over. It gives false when the time is over:

if (await lock.block(Duration(seconds: 5))) {
  // ...
}

If you pass a callback, block runs it while it holds the lock, then frees the lock. It returns the result of the callback, and throws a LockTimeoutException when it could not get the lock in time:

await lock.block(Duration(seconds: 5), buildReport);

With the flag CacheFlags(lockThrows: true), block with no callback throws a LockTimeoutException instead of giving false. See CacheConfig.

To free a lock, whoever holds it, use forceRelease().

docs.title: Encrypting the cache
docs.text:
By default the cache keeps plain JSON. So anyone who can read the cache files or the Redis database can read the values. To hide them, add 'encrypt': true to a file or redis store:

'file': {'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache', 'encrypt': true},

The values are encrypted with your APP_KEY. When the key changes, old entries count as a miss and the cache fills again. Old keys in previousKeys can still read old entries.

Encryption only stops people from reading values. Cache keys and tag names are not encrypted. On Redis, a plain int stays plain text, so increment still works. To keep a secret number encrypted, store it as a String.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: To use a memory store in tests, see Testing.

docs.title: Store options
docs.text:
Driver Options file path (default storage/cache), prefix, encrypt memory max_size: the most items. When it is full, the item used least recently is removed. No limit by default. Also prefix. redis host (default 127.0.0.1), port (default 6379), username, password, db (default 0), tls (true/false), pool_size (default 10), max_value_bytes (no limit by default), prefix, encrypt
  • A redis store with no prefix gets <app name>_cache: from APP_NAME, like my_shop_cache:. So two apps on one Redis do not share keys. The other drivers use dox_cache:.
  • To set any other ioredis option, see Redis options.
  • You rarely need pool_size. The cache sends no blocking commands, so each isolate uses about one Redis connection.
  • Each store is made once per isolate, the first time you use it.
  • The memory driver removes expired items when they are read, and in a sweep after many writes (at least 1000). It also keeps JSON text, so get decodes on every hit.
  • repository gives the dox_cache CacheStore. See dox_cache for custom drivers.

docs.title: Redis options
docs.text:
To set an option that Store options does not have, like a command timeout, give the redis store a RedisOptions. It is used as it is. prefix, max_value_bytes and encrypt still work next to it.

Do not set host, port, username, password, db, tls or pool_size with it. That throws an ArgumentError.

The client uses the ioredis defaults, not the pool_size default of the store. For example, commandTimeout is 10 seconds.

lib/config/cache.dart
'redis': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'redis',
  'options': RedisOptions(
    host: env.redisHost,
    port: env.redisPort,
    commandTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  ),
},

Sessions and the rate limit use the same store, so they get these options too.

RedisOptions, RedisTimeoutError and RedisQueueFullError come with package:dox_core/dox_core.dart. You need no ioredis import.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
• encrypt must be true or false. Any other type, like 'true', throws an ArgumentError.
  • A CacheManager you build yourself needs encrypter:, for example const CryptCacheEncrypter(). The normal Dox().cache has it set for you.
  • A memory or null store does not encrypt, because its values never leave the process. The option still needs an encrypter, or building the store throws.
  • On a file store, the whole file is encrypted, also the expiry time. Lock files are not encrypted, because they hold no values. prune deletes files that can not be decrypted.
  • Tag counters are int values, so on Redis they stay plain too.
  • Old plain values read as a miss after you turn the option on. Only an int on Redis still reads as a value.
  • A value is not tied to its key. So someone who can write to Redis or the cache folder can copy an encrypted value to another key.
  • max_value_bytes is checked on the plain JSON size. The encrypted text is about a third bigger.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

When your app is ready, you build it into a native binary, copy the binary to a server or a Docker image, and put a proxy in front of it for HTTPS.

Never run production with dart run

dart run (and dox serve) uses the JIT compiler, which is made for development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for production.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Run dox build to build your app for production:

dox build

It makes a build/bundle/ folder:

File What it is build/bundle/bin/server the native binary. No Dart SDK needed to run it build/bundle/bin/queue the queue worker, when bin/queue.dart exists build/bundle/bin/schedule the scheduler, when bin/schedule.dart exists build/bundle/lib/ native libraries from build hooks (eg. SQLite) build/bundle/db/ your db/ folder (migrations, seeders). SQLite database files are left out build/bundle/.env.example copy it to build/bundle/.env, or use env variables

Keep bin/ and lib/ together, because the binary loads the native libraries from ../lib.

dox build exits with code 1 when a step fails, so CI can stop.

docs.title: Starting the server
docs.text:
Start the binary from the bundle folder:

cd build/bundle
./bin/server

The binary reads .env and db/ from the folder you start it in. A real environment variable wins over the .env file.

A new Dox app runs the migrations in bin/server.dart, before the server starts. So the database is up to date when the first request comes in.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
A new Dox app has this multi-stage Dockerfile. The final image is FROM scratch: only the Dart AOT runtime, the bundle, db/, libgcc_s and an empty /tmp.

FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# The dox CLI. `dox build` runs build_runner, then AOT-compiles
# bin/server.dart, bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart with
# `dart build cli`. It puts all of them in build/bundle/bin, the native
# libraries in build/bundle/lib and the migrations in build/bundle/db.
# The queue worker and the scheduler run as their own processes:
# `/app/bin/queue work` and `/app/bin/schedule work`.
ARG DOX_VERSION=^3.2.0
RUN dart pub global activate dox "$DOX_VERSION"
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# Lay out the final file tree:
# /app/bin/server, /app/bin/queue, /app/bin/schedule, /app/lib (native
# libraries), /app/db/migration, /app/storage and a writable /tmp
# (uploads bigger than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Minimal serving image: the AOT runtime files from the dart image
# (`/runtime/`) plus our bundle. No Dart SDK, no source code.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file,
# so secrets stay out of it.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

The image has no .env file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass config as environment variables:

docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env -e DB_HOST=... my-app

docs.title: Docker compose
docs.text:
A new app also has a docker-compose.yml. It runs the app, a queue worker and Postgres, and reads .env with env_file: .env:

docker compose up -d --build
  • A new .env uses SQLite. The compose services set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and DB_NAME=dox themselves. To use the compose Postgres with dox s, set the same two values in .env.
  • A new app skips the Postgres driver in pubspec.yaml, because it uses SQLite. Remove the dox_postgres_native skip lines before you run the compose app. See Skip unused drivers.
  • The database port listens on 127.0.0.1 only.

See Docker for a health check in the image.

docs.title: Running the queue worker and scheduler
docs.text:
One build has three binaries. Run each one as its own process:

Process Command web server /app/bin/server (the default CMD) queue worker /app/bin/queue work scheduler /app/bin/schedule work

The image is FROM scratch, so it has no shell. Start the other binaries with --entrypoint:

docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env my-app
docker run -d --env-file .env --entrypoint /app/bin/queue my-app work
docker run -d --env-file .env --entrypoint /app/bin/schedule my-app work

In compose, use command: ["/app/bin/queue", "work"]. The worker service of a new app does this.

Without Docker, run ./bin/queue work and ./bin/schedule work in build/bundle, for example as two more systemd services.

Only the server runs the migrations when it starts, so start the server first.

For a small app, you can skip the extra processes. QueueConfig(inProcess: true) runs the jobs inside the server, and ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true) runs the schedule there. But heavy jobs then slow down requests. See Running jobs in the web server.

docs.title: HTTPS: put a proxy in front
docs.text:
Dox serves plain HTTP only, because its native server has no TLS. So run Dox on a private port, and put Caddy or nginx in front of it. The proxy does TLS, HTTP/2 and gzip.

By default Dox listens on all network interfaces. When the proxy runs on the same machine, set APP_HOST=127.0.0.1, so the app port can not be reached from outside.

flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|HTTPS| X["Caddy or nginx"]
    X -->|HTTP| D["Dox"]
    D --> DB[("Database")]

Dox runs one isolate per core, and they share one database pool. The migrations run once, before the server starts.

docs.title: Trusting the proxy
docs.text:
Behind a proxy, every request comes from the proxy. Tell Dox to trust the proxy, so req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client:

AppConfig(
  /// the proxy's IP, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8', or '172.16.0.0/12' for docker
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
  • req.ip() reads X-Forwarded-For. Dox walks the list from the right and skips your proxies, so a fake value from the client is ignored.
  • req.scheme() reads X-Forwarded-Proto (http or https). req.isSecure() is true for https.
  • trustedProxies is empty by default. Then Dox ignores those headers, because any client can send them.
  • ['*'] trusts any direct client. Only use it when the app port can not be reached from outside. If you have two proxies in a row, list their IPs or ranges instead.

docs.title: Caddy
docs.text:
Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. Websockets work with no extra config.

example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}

docs.title: Nginx
docs.text:
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

docs.title: Pass the real Host header
docs.text:
The proxy must pass the real Host header to Dox, like proxy_set_header Host $host; above. Some checks compare the request with this header:

  • the WebSocket origin check (allowedOrigins on Route.websocket, or AppConfig.webSocketAllowedOrigins)
  • back(), which only goes back to a page of the same host
  • allowedOrigins of socket.io

If the proxy sends its own host (like localhost:3000) instead, your own pages look like another site. Then their sockets get 403, and back() goes to the fallback.

docs.title: Behind a load balancer
docs.text:
A load balancer keeps idle connections to Dox open and sends new requests on them. Dox closes a connection after 30 seconds with no request. If the balancer keeps it longer, it may send a request on a connection Dox just closed, and the client gets 502.

To fix this, set idleTimeout longer than the idle timeout of the balancer. AWS ALB keeps idle connections for 60 seconds, so use 65 seconds:

AppConfig(
  // ...
  idleTimeout: Duration(seconds: 65),
)

docs.title: Keep it running
docs.text:
When a worker isolate dies, Dox starts it again. But when the main isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code (see Isolate). So let a supervisor restart it: restart: unless-stopped in Docker compose, or Restart=always in systemd.

# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
When the platform stops your app, you want open requests to finish first. Dox does this on SIGTERM (docker stop, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, Fly, systemd) and on SIGINT (Ctrl+C), in every isolate:

  1. It stops taking new connections at once.
  2. Open requests can finish. Each keep-alive connection closes after its current answer.
  3. After shutdownTimeout (default 8 seconds), it closes the connections that are still open.
  4. It runs shutdown() of every provider (see Providers). The ORMProvider of a new project closes the database connections here.
  5. It closes the cache stores of Cache(), eg. the Redis connections.
  6. The process exits with code 0.

A second SIGINT or SIGTERM stops the process at once.

Set the timeout in lib/config/app.dart:

AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
  ...
)

Keep it shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

Platform Waits Change it with docker stop 10 seconds docker stop -t 30, or stop_grace_period in compose Kubernetes 30 seconds terminationGracePeriodSeconds Cloud Run 10 seconds can not be changed Fly.io 5 seconds kill_timeout in fly.toml systemd 90 seconds TimeoutStopSec

In code, await Dox().stop() does steps 1 to 5 and does not exit.

docs.title: Many processes or machines
docs.text:
One Dox process already uses every core. You only need more processes to run on more machines, or to restart one process without downtime. Run each one on its own port (or machine), and list them in the proxy:

upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

Socket.IO rooms then need a shared adapter (like Redis), because each process has its own memory.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• dox build runs build_runner (when your app uses it), then dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build. It builds bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart the same way, when they exist.
  • Do not use dart compile exe. dox_orm bundles SQLite with a build hook, and dart compile exe does not run build hooks, so it stops with an error. dart build cli is the same AOT compiler and runs the hooks.
  • With trustedProxies: ['*'], req.ip() is the right-most X-Forwarded-For hop, the one your proxy added.

docs.title: Dox CLI
docs.text:
The dox CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Run dox help to see all commands, or dox help <command> for one command. Many make:* commands also answer to a create:* name. Every command is in the table at the end.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the CLI with dart pub:

dart pub global activate dox

If your shell can not find dox, add the pub bin folder to your PATH. Put this line in ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

docs.title: Updating the CLI
docs.text:
dox update installs the newest version with the same major version as your CLI. To pick the version yourself, run the install command again.

dox update

To remove the CLI, run dart pub global deactivate dox.

docs.title: Creating a project
docs.text:
Use dox create to start a new project:

dox create new_blog

It copies the dox-sample template from GitHub and makes .env from .env.example, with a new APP_KEY. The folder name is the project name in snake case, so NewBlog makes new_blog.

Then run cd new_blog, dart pub get and dox serve.

By default it uses the newest template release with the same major version as the CLI. To pick a release, pass --version:

dox create new_blog --version <release tag>

docs.title: Running the dev server
docs.text:
dox serve (or dox s) starts your app for development:

dox serve

When a file in lib/app/ changes, it hot reloads the new code into the running server. This takes about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds. When routes, providers, config, bin/, db/ or generated files change, it restarts the server instead. It also runs build_runner watch, so generated files stay up to date.

Hot reload does not run code again that already ran once. So a changed static or global value keeps its old value until a restart.

The server prints the VM service link. Open it in a browser to get DevTools, the debugger and the profiler.

If you do not want hot reload, or you run build_runner yourself, use these options:

dox s --no-reload             # restart on every change, no hot reload
dox s --ignore-build-runner   # do not run build_runner watch

See dox serve for all details.

docs.title: Building for production
docs.text:
dox build builds a native (AOT) bundle into build/bundle. Run the server from there:

dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server

See Deployment.

docs.title: Creating files
docs.text:
The make:* commands write new files with the right names and folders. Names keep their word breaks, so BlogPost makes blog_post.controller.dart with the class BlogPostController.

After make:controller or make:dto, run dox build_runner:build, or keep dox serve running. See Validation.

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
make:controller writes a controller in lib/app/http/controllers:

dox make:controller Blog        # lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart

If you want a controller for all actions of a resource, add -r (or --resource). It adds the methods index, create, store, show, edit, update and destroy. For an API, --api adds the same methods without create and edit. To use a model in it, add --model:

dox make:controller Blog -r
dox make:controller Blog --api
dox make:controller Blog --model=Post

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
make:model writes a model. The options also make the files that belong to it:

dox make:model Blog -m          # model and a create_blogs_table migration
dox make:model Blog -mcr        # model, migration and a resource controller
dox make:model Blog -a          # model, migration, factory, seeder and a resource controller

The options are -m migration, -c controller, -r resource controller, --api resource controller without create and edit, -f factory, -s seeder and -a for all of them. You can join them, like -mfs. See CLI reference.

The table of a model is its name in plural snake case. So BlogPost gets @DoxModel(table: 'blog_posts').

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
make:migration writes a Dart migration. Add --sql for a .sql file:

dox make:migration create_blogs_table
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql

docs.title: Mail and views
docs.text:
make:mail writes a mailable in lib/app/mail and its view. If you want a plain text body, add --no-view. make:view writes a .dox.html view:

dox make:mail Welcome           # lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart and resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html
dox make:mail Invoice --no-view # the mail only, with a plain text body
dox make:view pages/about       # resources/views/pages/about.dox.html

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
make:test writes a test that starts the app with DoxTestClient. Add --unit for a plain test:

dox make:test Ping              # test/ping_test.dart
dox make:test Math --unit       # test/math_test.dart

docs.title: Other files
docs.text:
dox make:middleware Auth        # lib/app/http/middleware/auth.middleware.dart
dox make:dto CreateBlog         # lib/app/dtos/create_blog/create_blog.dto.dart
dox make:serializer Blog        # lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart
dox make:provider Cache         # lib/providers/cache_provider.dart
dox make:command send_report    # lib/app/commands/send_report_command.dart, run it with dox app:send-report

docs.title: Listing routes
docs.text:
dox route:list prints every route of the app, without starting the server. Add --json for JSON output:

dox route:list

See dox route:list.

docs.title: Running migrations
docs.text:
The migration commands read the database settings from .env and the real environment. A real environment variable wins over .env:

.env
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password

DB_CONNECTION defaults to sqlite. If DATABASE_URL is set, it wins over all the DB_* keys. All keys are in the Env reference.

Use migration:run (or migrate) to run new migrations, and migration:status to see which ones ran:

dox migration:run
dox migration:status

A failed migration stops the run, and the CLI exits with code 1. On MySQL, statements like CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. So when a migration fails half way, these changes are not undone.

docs.title: Rolling back migrations
docs.text:
migration:rollback undoes the last batch. Use --step to undo the last N migrations, or --batch to undo only one batch:

dox migration:rollback
dox migration:rollback --step=2
dox migration:rollback --batch=3

docs.title: Resetting the database
docs.text:
migration:reset undoes all migrations. migration:refresh undoes all, then runs them again. migration:fresh drops all tables, then runs all migrations:

dox migration:reset
dox migration:refresh
dox migration:fresh

If you also want to run the seeders, add --seed to migration:run, migration:refresh or migration:fresh.

The migrate:* names also work, like migrate:rollback and migrate:fresh.

docs.title: All commands
docs.text: Command What it does dox create <name> [--version <v>] create a new project dox serve (or dox s) start the dev server with hot reload and build_runner watch dox build build the native (AOT) bundle into build/bundle dox build_runner:watch / dox build_runner:build run the code generator dox make:controller <name> [-r] [--api] [--model=<model>] create a controller dox make:middleware <name> create a middleware dox make:dto <name> create a DTO (typed, checked input) dox make:serializer <name> create a serializer dox make:provider <name> create a provider in lib/providers dox make:command <name> create a command in lib/app/commands and add it to the commands list dox make:mail <name> [--no-view] create a mailable in lib/app/mail, and its view unless you pass --no-view dox make:view <name> create a .dox.html view in resources/views dox make:test <name> [--unit] create a test in test/ that uses DoxTestClient, or a plain one with --unit dox route:list [--json] list every route of the app, without starting the server dox make:model <name> [-m] [-c] [-r] [--api] [-f] [-s] [-a] create a model, and with the options its migration, controller, factory and seeder dox make:migration <name> [--sql] create a Dart migration, or a .sql one with --sql dox migration:run (or dox migrate) run new migrations dox migration:rollback [--step=N] [--batch=N] undo the last batch, the last N migrations, or only batch N dox migration:reset undo all migrations dox migration:refresh undo all, then run all again dox migration:fresh (or migrate:fresh) drop all tables, then run all migrations dox migration:status show which migrations ran, and their batch dox make:factory <model> create a model factory in db/factories, see Factories dox make:seeder <name> create a seeder in db/seeders (and bin/seed.dart), see Seeders dox db:seed [--class=<name>] run DatabaseSeeder, or another seeder dox make:job <name> create a queue job in lib/app/jobs (and bin/queue.dart) dox queue:work [--queue=a,b] [--concurrency=N] [--once] [--tries=N] [--timeout=S] [--sleep=S] [--stop-when-empty] [--timeout-grace=S] run the queue worker dox queue:failed list the failed jobs dox queue:retry <id\|all> put a failed job (or all) back on the queue dox queue:forget <id> delete one failed job dox queue:flush delete all failed jobs dox queue:clear [queue] delete the jobs of a queue dox queue:restart stop the running workers after their current jobs dox queue:prune-failed [--hours=N] delete failed jobs older than N hours (default 24) dox queue:table create a migration for the jobs, failed_jobs and job_batches tables (from the dox_queue_database package) dox auth:tokens-table create a migration for the auth_access_tokens table (from the dox_auth package) dox schedule:work run the scheduler and keep it running dox schedule:run run the tasks that are due now, once dox schedule:list list the scheduled tasks dox schedule:test <name> run one scheduled task now dox schedule:clear-cache remove the withoutOverlapping() locks left by a crash dox key:generate [--show] [--force] make a new APP_KEY. --show prints a key and writes nothing. In production it asks first, --force skips dox env:generate make lib/config/env.dart (the typed env class) from .env.example, see Environment Variables dox env:check check the env against lib/config/env.dart. Prints every missing or bad key (exit code 1) dox openapi:generate [dir] run bin/openapi.dart to write openapi.json and openapi.yaml (default storage/openapi). A new project has no bin/openapi.dart yet, see OpenAPI dox update update the CLI dox version (or dox -v) show the CLI version dox help [command] show help

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• DB_CONNECTION must be sqlite, postgres or mysql. Any other value is an error. The default port is 5432 for postgres and 3306 for mysql.
  • DB_DATABASE works too, in place of DB_NAME.
  • In .env, a # after a space starts a comment, the same as in the app. The migration commands do not expand ${VAR} and do not read .env.testing.
  • dox serve runs dart run bin/server.dart. A failed hot reload restarts the server. One save gives one restart.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Declare your env keys once, in a typed class, and read them as normal Dart values.

Your app needs different settings on each machine. For example, the database password on your laptop is not the one in production. You keep these values in environment variables or in a .env file, not in your code.

Dox reads them through a typed class. So env.appPort is an int, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup, not in the middle of a request.

docs.title: Defining env keys
docs.text:
A new project already has lib/config/env.dart. Its keys are listed in the Env reference. Each getter in the class is one env key. This example shows the kinds of getters you can write:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

Run dart run build_runner build after each change to the class. It writes env.g.dart.

docs.title: Key names
docs.text: The key is the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. appName reads APP_NAME. A run of capitals is one word, so dbURL reads DB_URL. If you want another name, use @EnvKey('X').

docs.title: Default values
docs.text:
The getter body is the default. It runs only when the key is missing. It can be any expression, like Platform.numberOfProcessors.

A default can use another env getter, and it gets the loaded value. Write the getter directly (appPort), not env.appPort, because the global env is not ready while it loads:

String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:$appPort';

This getter is still a key: it reads APP_URL, and when APP_URL is set, it wins over the body.

docs.title: Required and optional keys
docs.text:
• A getter with no body is required. A missing key stops the app.
  • A nullable getter with no body, like String? get s3Bucket;, is optional. It is null when the key is missing.
  • An empty value (or the text null) counts as missing.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type Value in .env String any text int, double, num 3000, 0.5 bool true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off (any case) Uri https://dox.dev Duration a number and a unit: 500ms, 30s, 5m, 2h, 1d. A plain number is seconds: 300 is 5 minutes. an enum the name of a value, any case: debug List<String> comma separated: a, b, c. Empty items are dropped.

Any other type is a build error.

docs.title: Missing or bad keys
docs.text:
When the app starts, AppEnv.load() reads and checks every key. If something is wrong, it throws one EnvException that lists every missing or bad key:

EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int

The error names the key, never the value, because a value may be a secret and this text goes to logs and CI output.

docs.title: Reading env values
docs.text:
Import the config file and use env anywhere:

import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);

Keep only plain keys in the env class. A computed value, like "is this development", does not go there. Use appConfig.isDevelopment from the app config instead. It is true when APP_ENV is development.

docs.title: Where values come from
docs.text:
Dox reads values from these places. The first one that has the key wins:

  1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
  2. In tests only: the .env.testing file. See Testing: a test database.
  3. The .env file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

So you can keep a .env file for development and use real environment variables in production.

docs.title: The .env file
docs.text:
The .env file has one KEY=value per line:

.env
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
DB_PORT=5432
  • Quotes around a value are removed, so APP_NAME="My app" gives My app. Use ", ' or `.
  • A line that starts with # is a comment. A # after a space also starts a comment: APP_PORT=3000 # dev gives 3000.
  • A # with no space before it, or inside quotes, is kept: COLOR=#fff gives #fff.
  • KEY= (empty) gives the default value, the same as a missing key.
  • export KEY=value works too.
  • A value can not go over more lines. For a multi-line PEM key, keep the key in a file and put the file path in the env. Or turn on envExpand (below) and write it on one line with \n.

docs.title: Use one value in another
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to build a value from other values, like APP_URL from HOST and PORT. Turn on CoreFlags.envExpand for this. It is off by default.

.env
HOST=localhost
PORT=3000
APP_URL=http://${HOST}:${PORT}
GREETING="Hello\nWorld"
  • ${OTHER} works in an unquoted value and in a "..." value. It does not work in '...'.
  • Dox looks for a real environment variable first, then for a key above this line. A name it does not find stays as ${OTHER}.
  • In a "..." value, \n, \t, \", \\ and \$ become a new line, a tab, ", \ and $.

docs.title: Turning on envExpand
docs.text:
The .env file is read before AppConfig exists. So you set the flags in two places: in AppConfig, and in Env.flags at the very top of main(), before any env value is read:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

const CoreFlags flags = CoreFlags(envExpand: true);

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  appKey: Env.get('APP_KEY', ''),
  flags: flags,
  // ...
);
bin/server.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

void main() async {
  Env.flags = flags;
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Dox().startServer();
}

my_app is the name in your pubspec.yaml.

A test does not run bin/server.dart. So set Env.flags = flags; at the top of main() in each test file too:

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  Env.flags = flags;
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });
  // ...
}

If you forget it, ${OTHER} stays as written, and Dox prints a warning.

docs.title: Generating the env class
docs.text:
If you have a .env.example, dox env:generate makes lib/config/env.dart from it:

dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
  • Digits become an int with that default: APP_PORT=3000 gives int get appPort => 3000;.
  • true/false become a bool with that default.
  • An empty value becomes an optional String?.
  • Any other value becomes a required String. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
  • # comment lines above a key become its doc comment.

It does not overwrite an existing lib/config/env.dart. Run dox build_runner:build after it.

docs.title: Checking the env
docs.text:
dox env:check loads the env and prints every missing or bad key. It exits with code 1 when a key is wrong, so you can use it in CI or before a deploy:

dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key

docs.title: The app key
docs.text:
Dox needs APP_KEY to encrypt and sign data. Make one with dox key:generate.
