When APP_KEY is missing, not 32 characters, or a public sample key, Dox().startServer() stops with an error. When APP_ENV is development, local, test or testing, it only logs a warning.

docs.title: Reading a key by name
docs.text:
Sometimes you only know the key name at run time. Use Env.get() for this. For normal config, use the typed class.

Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

  • String gives ''.
  • String? and dynamic give null. Env.get('KEY') with no type is dynamic.
  • int, num, double and bool throw an ArgumentError with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

Env.get() looks up and converts the value on every call, so do not call it on a hot path.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: To pass your own values in a test, see Testing.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• The builder only reads getters of the @DoxEnv() class itself. Getters from a superclass or a mixin are not read from the env. A field (final String x = ...;) is a build error.
  • If a default reads the global env, the app stops at startup with a StateError: "A default of AppEnv reads the global env. Use the getter directly".
  • After startup, env.dbPort is a plain field read.
  • A = inside a value is kept: TOKEN=a=b gives a=b.
  • With envExpand, .env.testing also sees the keys of .env.
  • The first env read (like Env.get() or env.appName) loads .env with the flags of that moment. The file is not read again. If Env.flags was not set yet, Dox().initialize prints a warning.
  • The server isolates follow the main isolate, so you set nothing for them. When the flag is on in AppConfig but .env was read without it, Dox prints a warning at start, once in each isolate.

docs.title: File Storage
docs.text:
Storage() saves and reads files on a disk: a local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), or memory.

You use the same methods for every disk. So you can keep files in a local folder in development and on S3 in production, and your code stays the same.

It is in the dox_storage package. A new project already has it.

import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
If your project does not have storage yet, add it with the CLI:

dox add storage

It writes lib/config/storage.dart, the provider, the storage folder and the STORAGE_DISK=local key. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

Add --disk=s3 to also add an s3 disk and the AWS_* keys. STORAGE_DISK stays local, so the app starts before you fill in the keys. Fill them in, then set STORAGE_DISK=s3.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The disks are in lib/config/storage.dart. A new project has one local disk in the storage folder. STORAGE_DISK in .env picks the default disk.

To add disks, edit the file. This example adds a url to the local disk, an s3 disk and a memory disk:

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': 'https://app.test/files', // for signedUrl(); url() gives /storage/<path> without it
    },

    /// only when AWS_BUCKET is set
    if (env.awsBucket != null)
      's3': <String, dynamic>{
        'driver': 's3',
        'bucket': env.awsBucket,
        'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
        'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
        'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
        'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
      },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);

Each driver takes these options:

Driver Options local root (default storage), url, app_key (default: your APP_KEY), visibility, atomic_writes, permissions s3 bucket, region, key, secret, token, endpoint, path_style (MinIO), url (CDN), visibility, acl, batch_delete, unsigned_payload memory none. For tests

The provider of a new project sets up these disks in every isolate. It is in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it:

lib/providers/storage_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}

docs.title: The S3 disk
docs.text:
The s3 disk reads five keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to lib/config/env.dart and run dart run build_runner build. They are nullable, and the s3 disk is only added when AWS_BUCKET is set, so the app starts without them:

lib/config/env.dart
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;

The s3 disk needs bucket, key and secret. If one is missing, the app stops at start with an ArgumentError that names the setting.

docs.title: Skipping the body hash
docs.text:
To save CPU on big uploads, add unsigned_payload to the s3 disk. The upload then skips the hash of the body. Only use it over HTTPS:

's3': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 's3',
  'bucket': env.awsBucket,
  // ... region, key, secret, endpoint
  'unsigned_payload': true,
},

docs.title: Using another disk
docs.text:
Storage() uses the default disk. Use disk to pick another one:

await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports/2026.pdf', bytes, exact: true);

docs.title: Storing files
docs.text:
The putFile method saves a file in a folder with a new uuid name, and returns the path. It takes a RequestFile or bytes. For bytes, Dox finds the extension from the bytes, or you pass extension::

// save with a new uuid file name, returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().putFile('images', file);  // a RequestFile
Uint8List bytes = Uint8List.fromList(<int>[1, 2, 3]);
String path2 = await Storage().putFile('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path3 = await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png'); // like putFile

docs.title: Storing with your own name
docs.text:
If you want to pick the file name, use putFileAs. It replaces an old file with the same name:

String path4 = await Storage().putFileAs('avatars', file, 'user-1.png'); // your own name

Do not use the file name from the client here, because the name is used as it is. Make your own name, like user-1.png.

docs.title: Storing at an exact path
docs.text:
Use put with exact: true to write to an exact path. It replaces an old file there and returns the path. It takes a String, a List<int> or a Stream<List<int>>:

// save to this exact path. String, List<int> or Stream<List<int>>
await Storage().put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);

docs.title: Storing uploaded files
docs.text:
An uploaded file can store itself. store gives it a new uuid name, like putFile. storeAs uses your name, like putFileAs. Both take disk::

RequestFile file = req.input('image');
String path = await file.store('images');
String onS3 = await file.store('images', disk: 's3');
String avatar = await file.storeAs('avatars', 'user-1.png');

putFile and store take the extension from the file name. But if the bytes are a known format (png, jpg, pdf, zip, ...) that does not match the name, the extension of the bytes is used. So a png sent as a.html is saved as .png, and it is never served as a web page.

docs.title: Prepending and appending
docs.text:
Use append and prepend to add text to the end or the start of a file. A missing file is made:

await Storage().append('logs/app.log', 'new line');    // a missing file is made
await Storage().prepend('logs/app.log', 'first line');

They add a new line between the old and the new text, if the file is not empty. Change it with separator.

docs.title: Retrieving files
docs.text:
The get method returns the bytes of a file, or null when the file is missing:

Uint8List? found = await Storage().get(path);  // null when missing

docs.title: Checking if a file exists
docs.text:
exists checks for a file. missing is the opposite:

bool exists = await Storage().exists(path);           // files only
bool gone = await Storage().missing(path);            // not exists()

docs.title: File metadata
docs.text:
size gives the size in bytes, and lastModified gives the time of the last change. Both throw FileNotFoundException when the file is missing:

int size = await Storage().size(path);                 // throws when missing
DateTime changed = await Storage().lastModified(path); // throws when missing

docs.title: Downloading files
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to send a stored file to the browser. stream shows it in the browser, and download makes the browser save it as a file:

Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));    // shown in the browser
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf'); // saved as a file
});

Both read the file as a stream, so a big file is never loaded into memory. A missing file answers 404.

download names the file after the last part of the path. Pass name: to pick another name:

Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf', name: 'Invoice 42.pdf');
});

If you want to add headers, put the download in a response():

Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) async {
  DownloadableFile file = await Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf');
  return response(file).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
});

docs.title: File URLs
docs.text:
The url method gives the URL of a file. On a local disk with no url option, it gives /storage/<path>:

String url = await Storage().url(path);         // /storage/<path> when the disk has no `url`

Dox only serves that URL when you add Storage.route('storage', signed: false). See Serving local files.

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
Sometimes a file should only be open for a short time, like a private invoice. Use signedUrl for this. temporaryUrl is the same method:

String signed = await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));
String same = await Storage().temporaryUrl(path); // the same as signedUrl()

On a local disk, signedUrl needs the disk url option. Set it to the full URL of the route, like https://app.test/files.

docs.title: Serving local files
docs.text:
A local disk needs a route, so the browser can open its files. Storage.route adds one:

// lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk than the default
Storage.route('uploads', download: true);  // every file is a download

With a signed route, the URL looks like this:

String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...
  • A missing, wrong or expired signature answers 403.
  • Signed URLs work only on a local disk, and only on the route of their own disk. For another disk, use signed: false.
  • An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script does not run on your site.
  • Every file has X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

docs.title: Copying and moving files
docs.text:
copy and move replace an old file at the new path:

await Storage().copy('notes/a.txt', 'backup/a.txt');
await Storage().move('backup/a.txt', 'old/a.txt');

On S3 the copy runs inside S3, so the bytes do not pass through your app. A missing source file answers 404.

docs.title: Deleting files
docs.text: await Storage().delete(path);

docs.title: Directories
docs.text:
files gives the files in a folder. allFiles also gives the files in sub-folders. directories gives the sub-folders. All paths start with /, like the paths from putFile:

List<String> files = await Storage().files('images');         // direct files only
List<String> all = await Storage().allFiles('images');        // in sub-folders too
List<String> folders = await Storage().directories('images'); // direct sub-folders

Use directoryExists to check for a folder. On S3 and memory disks, a folder exists when a file is under it:

bool folder = await Storage().directoryExists('images');

makeDirectory makes a folder. It only works on a local disk. On other disks it does nothing:

await Storage().makeDirectory('reports');              // local disk only

deleteDirectory deletes a folder and every file in it. A missing folder is not an error:

await Storage().deleteDirectory('old');                       // the folder and its files

It refuses the root ('' or /) with InvalidKeyException, so a wrong path can not empty the disk. To empty a whole disk on purpose, use Storage().use().deleteAll().

docs.title: File visibility
docs.text:
A file can be public or private. Use setVisibility and getVisibility:

await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private);
Visibility visibility = await Storage().getVisibility(path);
  • On S3, setVisibility sets the ACL, because acl is on by default. With 'acl': false (R2 and similar), it does nothing, and getVisibility gives the disk visibility.
  • On a local disk, setVisibility does nothing by default, and getVisibility gives the disk visibility. Turn on permissions to use file modes.

docs.title: Visibility on a local disk
docs.text:
If you want visibility to be the file mode on a local disk, add 'permissions': true to the disk. Then setVisibility runs chmod, and getVisibility reads the mode of the file:

'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'permissions': true},

The modes are: public file 0644, private file 0600, public folder 0755, private folder 0700. To change them, see Custom file modes. On Windows, permissions does nothing, because there is no chmod.

docs.title: Full disk API
docs.text: Storage().use('s3') returns the dox_storage Disk. It has more methods, like listAll with pages, getMetaData, putStream, deleteAll and write options. See dox_storage.

docs.title: Custom drivers
docs.text:
Implement DriverContract from package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart. Register it in a provider, so every isolate has it:

Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: To swap a disk with a memory disk in tests, see Testing.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Signature and the body
docs.text: unsigned_payload is off by default. The signature then does not cover the body, so only use it over HTTPS.

docs.title: S3 part size
docs.text: multipartPartSize is the size of one part of a big upload. It is a field of S3DriverConfig, not a key of the disk map. The default is 8 MiB. See Storage. S3 needs 5 MiB to 5 GiB. With another size, Dox prints one warning to stderr. It does not throw.

docs.title: Atomic writes
docs.text:
A local disk writes a file in place by default. Add 'atomic_writes': true to write to a temp file and rename it when the write is done. Then a failed upload never leaves a partial file, and the old file stays:

'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'atomic_writes': true},

The rename makes a new file. So the folder must be writable, the file gets the default mode and owner, a hard link keeps the old content, and a symlink is replaced.

docs.title: Custom file modes
docs.text:
Give permissions a map with a file and a dir key. Each has a public and a private mode. A mode you leave out keeps its default. Dart has no octal numbers, so write the modes in hex: 0x1a0 is 0640, 0x1e8 is 0750:

'private': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage-private',
  'visibility': 'private',
  'permissions': <String, dynamic>{
    'file': <String, int>{'public': 0x1a4, 'private': 0x1a0},
    'dir': <String, int>{'public': 0x1ed, 'private': 0x1e8},
  },
},

Each mode must be an int from 0 to 0x1ff (0777). Anything else, like the string '0644', throws ArgumentError when the disk is made. Other keys are ignored.

docs.title: How file modes work
docs.text:
• The mode is set before the content is written, so a private file is never readable by others, not even for a moment.
  • A new file gets the visibility of the write, or the disk visibility.
  • An overwrite, append, prepend and move keep the mode of the file, unless the call gives a visibility.
  • A copy gets the visibility of the call, or else the mode of the source.
  • Folders that a write creates get the folder mode. Folders that were there before, and the disk root, keep their mode.
  • getVisibility reads the real mode. The private mode is private. Any other mode is public.
  • getVisibility and setVisibility of a symlink throw UnsupportedOperationException.
  • If the chmod fails, a file that the write created is removed.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• append and prepend read the file and write it back, so two writers at the same time can lose a write. They keep the visibility and content type of the file.
  • putFile with a RequestFile on a local disk moves the upload temp file, so it does not read the file into memory.
  • directoryExists('') is always true: the empty path is the root.
  • getVisibility and setVisibility of a missing file answer 404. With 'acl': false on S3, getVisibility gives the disk visibility, also for a missing file.
  • On a local disk, a copy or move of a missing file makes no folders. A local copy writes a temp file and renames it. Listings hide that temp file.
  • Any download name is safe in the header. Quotes are escaped, a new line becomes _, and a name like résumé.pdf is also sent as filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.pdf.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text:
A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

The load balancer calls the route every few seconds. If the answer is not 200, it stops sending traffic to this server, or it restarts it.

docs.title: Adding the route
docs.text:
Add Route.health in register() of a router:

lib/routes/web.dart
@override
void register() {
  Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);
  Route.health('/health');
}

GET /health answers 200 with:

{"status": "ok"}

The route gets the middleware of its router and the global middleware. So put Route.health in a router with no auth middleware, or the health check gets 401.

docs.title: Checking the database and the cache
docs.text:
The app may run, but its database may be down. To check this, give named checks. Each check is a function:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);

When all checks pass, the answer is 200:

{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}

When one check fails, the answer is 503 Service Unavailable:

{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}

A check fails when it throws an error, returns false, or takes longer than the timeout. The checks run at the same time.

HealthCheck.cache() writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. HealthCheck.cache('redis') checks the store with that name. Any other check is your own function, like a call to another API.

docs.title: Changing the timeout
docs.text:
A check fails after 5 seconds by default. Use timeout to change it:

Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

docs.title: Seeing why a check failed
docs.text:
The error of a failed check goes to exceptionHandler.report(), so you see it in your logs.

The answer has the error text (in errors) only when APP_ENV is development or local. In other envs the text is left out, because it can show hosts or user names.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Docker for a health check in the image
  • Deployment

docs.title: Isolate
docs.text:
Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads) at once, so it can use every CPU core.

Each isolate runs its own native server on the same port, and the operating system spreads the connections between them. You write your app once, and Dox starts a copy of it in every isolate.

flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See How Dox works.

docs.title: Setting the number of isolates
docs.text:
By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU core (Platform.numberOfProcessors). You may want fewer when the same machine also runs the database or other heavy work.

Set totalIsolate in the app config. A new app reads it from APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate ?? Platform.numberOfProcessors,
);

You can also set it in code, before startServer(). This wins over the config:

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
Isolates do not share memory. This matters when you keep state in your code:

  • A static value or a singleton exists once per isolate. If you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. See Cache.
  • To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

If you need to know which isolate runs your code, use Dox().isolateId. The first isolate is 1:

int id = Dox().isolateId;

docs.title: Sending a message to the other isolates
docs.text:
Sometimes one isolate needs to tell the others that something changed, for example "forget this cache key". Use IsolateBus for this. It sends a message from one isolate to all the others in the same process.

Listen on a channel in a provider's setup(), and publish from anywhere:

IsolateBus.instance.on('users').listen(onMessage); // in a provider's setup()
IsolateBus.instance.publish('users', <Object>['changed', 42]);

A listener only gets the messages of its own channel, and an isolate never gets its own message. A message must be something a SendPort can send: null, bool, num, String, typed data, and lists and maps of those.

The bus works inside one process only. For many servers, use Redis. Socket.IO uses the bus to share broadcasts, see Socket.IO.

docs.title: What each isolate does at start
docs.text:
Dox copies the AppConfig, the providers and the routes you added before startServer() to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

  1. runs setup() of each provider (for example, it opens the database pool),
  2. registers the routes of your routers,
  3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
  4. runs boot() of each provider,
  5. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in setup(). See Providers.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
Dox keeps your app running when code fails:

  • An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a 500 and keeps going.
  • An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is passed to the report method of the exception handler. The isolate keeps running.
  • If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints [server] isolate N exited, restarting to stderr and starts a new isolate after 1 second.

If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. So let a supervisor start it again, like Docker restart: or systemd Restart=always. See Deployment.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Linux gives each isolate its own socket (SO_REUSEPORT). On macOS the isolates share one socket. On Windows only one isolate serves HTTP.
  • Dox().isolateCount is the number of running isolates. IsolateBus.instance.size is the number of isolates that listen on the bus, this one included. size can be old for a short time after an isolate joins or leaves.
  • publish throws an ArgumentError for a value a SendPort can not send, and then no isolate gets the message. In the main isolate it only throws when another isolate listens.
  • publish never waits. A slow listener keeps the messages in a queue in its memory.
  • A message only reaches the isolates that listen at that moment. An isolate that calls on() later does not get older messages.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
The dox_mailer package sends email from your app with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark or sendmail.

You write a Message and call Mail.send(), and a transport sends it. You pick the transport in a config file, so you can change providers with no code change. Slow emails can go through the queue, so the request does not wait.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the package with the dox CLI. Add --transport=smtp (or resend, mailgun, postmark, ses) to pick a transport. log is the default:

dox add mailer

It adds the package, writes the mail config and the provider, and adds MAIL_MAILER, MAIL_FROM and the keys of the transport to .env. If the app has dox_view, it also makes the resources/views/emails folder. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

If you want to set it up by hand, add the package and write the two files below yourself:

dart pub add dox_mailer

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A mailer is a name and a transport. defaultMailer is the one that Mail.send() uses:

lib/config/mail.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  /// the mailer of Mail.send()
  defaultMailer: Env.get('MAIL_MAILER', 'log'),

  /// for messages with no from address
  from: Address(Env.get('MAIL_FROM', 'hello@example.com'), 'My app'),

  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'smtp': SmtpTransport(
      host: Env.get('MAIL_HOST', 'localhost'),
      port: Env.get<int>('MAIL_PORT', 587),
      username: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_USERNAME'),
      password: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    ),

    /// prints emails, sends nothing
    'log': LogTransport(),
  },
);

Env.get() reads the .env file and the real environment. You can also add the keys to the AppEnv class of your app and use env.mailHost.

.env
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_FROM=hello@example.com
MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=me
MAIL_PASSWORD=secret
Option Default What it does defaultMailer log the mailer of Mail.send() mailers a log mailer each mailer name and its transport from none the from address of a message that has none replyTo none the reply-to addresses of a message that has none

docs.title: The mail provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up the mailers in every isolate. Put it in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it:

lib/providers/mail_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

import '../config/mail.dart';

/// Sets up the mailers. Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);
}

When the server stops, the provider closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients.

docs.title: Sending mail
docs.text:
Make a Message and pass it to Mail.send():

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

await Mail.send(
  Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann Lee')],
    subject: 'Welcome',
    text: 'Hello Ann, welcome!',
    html: '<p>Hello Ann, <b>welcome</b>!</p>',
  ),
);

A message needs a from address, at least one recipient, and a text or HTML body. If the message can not be sent, send() throws a MailException. It has the statusCode and the body of the server's answer.

docs.title: Using another mailer
docs.text:
If you want to send with a mailer that is not the default, use Mail.mailer():

await Mail.mailer('ses').send(message);

docs.title: Short ways to send
docs.text:
For a quick plain text email, use Mail.raw():

await Mail.raw('Your code is 1234', to: 'ann@example.com', subject: 'Your code');

Mail.to() starts an email with chained calls. to(), cc() and bcc() take an Address, an email text, or a list of these. send() takes a mailable, and the recipients are added to the ones of the mailable:

await Mail.to('ann@example.com')
    .cc('Bob Lee <bob@example.com>')
    .bcc(<String>['audit@example.com'])
    .send(WelcomeMail(user));

queue() and later() work here too, like Mail.to(email).queue(WelcomeMail(user)).

docs.title: The message
Attachments
docs.text:
Add files with attachments. The content type comes from the file extension, or you can pass contentType:

Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Your invoice',
  text: 'The invoice is attached.',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment(pdfBytes, 'invoice.pdf'),
    Attachment.fromFile('storage/terms.pdf'),
  ],
);

To attach a file from a storage disk, like S3, read its bytes first. This works with every disk:

Uint8List? pdf = await Storage().disk('s3').get('invoices/42.pdf');
Attachment(pdf!, 'invoice.pdf');

docs.title: Inline images
docs.text:
To show an image inside the HTML, give the file a cid and use it with cid::

Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Hello',
  html: '<img src="cid:logo.png"> Hello!',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment.fromFile('assets/logo.png', cid: 'logo.png'),
  ],
);

Mailgun uses the file name as the cid. So for Mailgun, use a cid with the file extension, like logo.png.

docs.title: HTML from a view
docs.text:
With views, you can render a template to HTML:

String html = View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
await Mail.send(Message(to: to, subject: 'Welcome', html: html));

docs.title: Mailables
docs.text:
A mailable is one kind of email in its own class, for example the welcome email. It keeps the address, the subject, the template and the data in one place.

To make one, run dox make:mail. It writes lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart and the view resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html. Add --no-view for a mail with a plain text body. See dox make:mail.

dox make:mail Welcome

Override the getters you need:

class WelcomeMail extends Mailable {
  WelcomeMail(this.user);

  final User user;

  @override
  List<Address> get to => <Address>[Address(user.email, user.name)];

  @override
  String get subject => 'Welcome';

  @override
  String? get view => 'emails/welcome';

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> get data => <String, Object?>{'name': user.name};
}
Getter What it is to, cc, bcc, replyTo the addresses from the sender. Null: the from of the mail config subject the subject html, text the body as text, when there is no template view a dox_view template for the HTML body textView a dox_view template for the plain text body markdown a dox_view template with Markdown, see Markdown mail data the variables of the templates attachments the files mailer the mailer name, eg. ses. Null: the default mailer

docs.title: Sending a mailable
docs.text:
Call send() on the mailable, or put it on the queue with queue() or later():

await WelcomeMail(user).send();
await WelcomeMail(user).queue();
await WelcomeMail(user).later(Duration(minutes: 10));

queue() and later() render the templates at once, so the worker sends the finished email. They take the same options as Mail.queue().

docs.title: Changing the message
docs.text:
toMessage() gives the email as a Message. If you want to set more, like headers or tags, override it:

@override
Message toMessage() {
  return super.toMessage().copyWith(tags: <String>['welcome']);
}

docs.title: Markdown mail
docs.text:
You can write the email in Markdown. From one template you get a simple HTML email with a layout (a white card on a grey page) and a plain text part. The Markdown is CommonMark with tables.

resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html
# Hi {{ name }}

Thanks for joining. Here is what you can do next:

- Fill in your profile
- Invite your team

[Open your profile]({{ profileUrl }})

<a href="https://example.com/dashboard" class="button">Open the app</a>

Then point the markdown getter to it:

@override
String? get markdown => 'emails/welcome';

<a class="button"> shows as a button. In the text body it stays an <a> tag, so the link is still there.

Do not indent the Markdown inside @if or @each, because Markdown makes a line that starts with 4 spaces into a code block.

{{ }} escapes HTML and Markdown, so a user's name like [click](https://evil.example) shows as text and does not become a link. Links with an unsafe URL, like javascript:, lose their URL. Raw HTML in the template, like <a href="{{ url }}">, is not checked, so only put full URLs that your app builds there. For links, write [text]({{ url }}) instead. To put Markdown from a value into the email, pass a SafeString.

docs.title: Custom layout
docs.text:
To use your own look, override layout(). It gets the HTML of the Markdown and returns the full page. Put it in a base class to use it for all your mailables:

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart'; // View, SafeString

abstract class AppMail extends Mailable {
  @override
  String layout(String body) {
    return View.render('emails/layout', <String, Object?>{'body': SafeString(body)});
  }
}

docs.title: A simple email with no template
docs.text:
Sometimes you only need a few lines and a button. MailMessage is a mailable for this. It needs no template and uses the Markdown layout:

await (MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid', to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')])
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/1')
      ..line('Thank you!'))
    .send();
  • cc: in the constructor adds cc addresses.
  • attach(Attachment(...)) adds a file.
  • error() makes the buttons red, for a message about a problem.
  • The email starts with greeting (default Hello!) and ends with salutation (default none). Set them to null to leave them out.

Lines can use Markdown, like **bold**. HTML in a line shows as text. action() throws an ArgumentError for an unsafe URL.

To send one email on more than one channel, see Notifications.

docs.title: Queue an email
docs.text:
Sending an email can take a second or more. With a queue, the request does not wait, because a queue worker sends the email later:

await Mail.queue(message);

To send it later, use Mail.later(). Both methods return the job id:

await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message);

You can pick another mailer and another queue:

await Mail.mailer('ses').queue(message, queue: 'emails');

This uses dox_queue, so you need its QueueProvider and a worker. The mail jobs come with dox_mailer, and build_runner adds them to lib/generated/jobs.g.dart. The worker (bin/queue.dart) must run your MailProvider too, because the job sends with your mail config. Without it, the job fails with "Mail is not set up".

The message is checked at once, so a bad message fails in the request and not in the worker. The worker sends with the same mailer you picked.

Option Default What it does queue default the queue name encrypt false save the job data encrypted with the app key. The worker needs the same key

The whole email, with every attachment, is saved in Redis or in the jobs table. So keep attachments small, a few MB at most. For a big file, write your own job that saves the file path, and build the email in handle().

An email has personal data. If other people can read Redis or the jobs table, use encrypt: true.

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text:
'smtp': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'smtp.example.com',
  port: 587,
  username: Env.get('MAIL_USERNAME'),
  password: Env.get('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.starttls,
),
Option Default What it does host required the server port 465 for tls, 587 for starttls, 25 for none the port username, password none the login. No username: no login encryption starttls none, starttls (switch to TLS after connect) or tls (TLS from the start) allowInsecure false accept a self-signed TLS certificate. Only for test servers auth PLAIN, or LOGIN when the server has no PLAIN SmtpAuth.plain, SmtpAuth.login or SmtpAuth.xoauth2 localDomain localhost the name of this machine, for EHLO timeout 30 seconds the time to connect, and to wait for each reply keepAlive false keep the connection open for the next message

With starttls, the send fails if the server does not offer STARTTLS, so your password is never sent in plain text by mistake.

For Gmail or Outlook with OAuth 2, use auth: SmtpAuth.xoauth2. The username is the email and the password is the access token.

If you send many emails, use keepAlive: true, so one connection sends them one by one.

For local work, Mailpit catches all emails:

'mailpit': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 1025,
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.none,
),

docs.title: Amazon SES
docs.text:
There are two classes, and both send the same MIME message with attachments and inline images. SesTransport uses SES API v1 (SendRawEmail), and SesV2Transport uses SES API v2 (SendEmail with raw content):

'ses': SesV2Transport(
  key: Env.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
  secret: Env.get('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
  region: Env.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1'),
),
Option Default What it does key required the AWS access key id secret required the AWS secret access key sessionToken none for temporary keys, eg. from a role region us-east-1 the AWS region of SES configurationSet none the SES configuration set, to track events endpoint https://email.<region>.amazonaws.com/ another API address

No AWS SDK is needed.

docs.title: Azure Communication Services
docs.text:
'azure': AzureTransport(
  endpoint: 'https://my-app.europe.communication.azure.com',
  accessKey: Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_KEY'),
),

Or use the connection string of the Azure portal:

'azure': AzureTransport.fromConnectionString(
  Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_CONNECTION_STRING'),
),
Option Default What it does endpoint required the address of your resource accessKey required the access key of the resource apiVersion 2023-03-31 the API version disableTracking false turn off open and click tracking

Inline images need a newer apiVersion that supports them.

docs.title: Resend
docs.text: 'resend': ResendTransport(apiKey: Env.get('RESEND_API_KEY')),

docs.title: Mailgun
docs.text:
'mailgun': MailgunTransport(
  apiKey: Env.get('MAILGUN_API_KEY'),
  domain: 'mg.example.com',
  region: MailgunRegion.eu,
),

region is MailgunRegion.us (the default) or MailgunRegion.eu. Use the region of your Mailgun domain.

docs.title: Postmark
docs.text:
'postmark': PostmarkTransport(
  serverToken: Env.get('POSTMARK_TOKEN'),
  messageStream: 'outbound',
),

messageStream is optional. Without it, Postmark uses the default stream of the server.

docs.title: sendmail
docs.text:
This sends with the sendmail program of the server (Postfix, Exim, msmtp and others):

'sendmail': SendmailTransport(
  path: '/usr/sbin/sendmail',
  mode: SendmailMode.smtp,
),
Mode Command How it works SendmailMode.smtp (default) sendmail -bs speaks SMTP on stdin and stdout SendmailMode.pipe sendmail -t -i pipes the message in. sendmail reads the recipients from the headers

docs.title: Log
docs.text:
The log transport prints each email and sends nothing, so it is good for local work:

'log': LogTransport(),

Pass output to print somewhere else, eg. LogTransport(output: stderr.writeln) (from dart:io). To show both the text and the HTML body, set bothBodies: true. When it is off, only the text body is shown:

'log': LogTransport(bothBodies: true),

docs.title: Array
docs.text:
The array transport keeps each email in a list and sends nothing. See Testing.

'array': ArrayTransport(),

docs.title: Failover
docs.text:
If one provider is down, you may want to try another. FailoverTransport tries each transport in order, until one sends the email. If every transport fails, it throws the error of the last one:

SesV2Transport ses = SesV2Transport(key: '...', secret: '...');
SmtpTransport smtp = SmtpTransport(host: 'smtp.example.com');

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  defaultMailer: 'main',
  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'main': FailoverTransport(<Transport>[ses, smtp]),
  },
);

To see why the first ones failed, pass onError. It gets the error of each transport that fails.

docs.title: Tags and metadata
docs.text:
Each provider has its own way to group and mark emails. This is what each transport does with tags and metadata:

Transport tags metadata SES not used message tags Resend tags with the value true tags Mailgun o:tag variables (v:name) Postmark the first tag metadata Azure, SMTP, sendmail not used not used

For SMTP and sendmail, use headers instead.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to run code before or after each email is sent, for example to log it. Use Mail.onSending and Mail.onSent.

Each isolate has its own hooks, also the queue worker. So add them in setup() of your mail provider, after super.setup(). A hook added in main() does not reach queued emails.

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Mail.clearHooks(); // a second setup() does not add each hook twice
    Mail.onSending((Message message) {
      print('sending "${message.subject}" to ${message.to}');
    });
    Mail.onSent((SentMessage sent) {
      print('sent ${sent.messageId}');
    });
  }
}

Hooks run for every mailer, for queued emails and with Mail.fake(). If an onSending hook throws, the email is not sent and send() throws that error. If an onSent hook throws, the error is only logged, because the email is already sent.

docs.title: Sending all mail to one address
docs.text:
On a staging server, you want every email to go to your own inbox, so real users get nothing. Use Mail.alwaysTo(). Like hooks, call it in setup() of your mail provider, so every isolate gets it:

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'staging') {
      Mail.alwaysTo('qa@example.com');
    }
  }
}

The to of each email becomes that address, and cc and bcc are cleared. This counts for queued emails too. Mail.alwaysTo(null) turns it off.

docs.title: Custom transports
docs.text:
If your provider is not in the list, extend Transport and add it to mailers:

class MyApiTransport extends Transport {
  @override
  Future<SentMessage> send(Message message) async {
    // call your API here
    return SentMessage(message, messageId: 'id from the API');
  }
}

The message is already checked, and has a from address, when it gets to send(). For a provider that takes raw MIME, MimeBuilder().build(message) gives the MIME text.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_mailer also works on its own. Call Mail.configure() once at start, and Mail.close() at the end. The rest of this page works the same way:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

  Mail.configure(MailConfig(
    defaultMailer: 'smtp',
    from: Address('hello@example.com', 'My app'),
    mailers: <String, Transport>{
      'smtp': SmtpTransport(
        host: env['MAIL_HOST'] ?? 'localhost',
        username: env['MAIL_USERNAME'],
        password: env['MAIL_PASSWORD'],
      ),
    },
  ));

  await Mail.send(Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    subject: 'Hello',
    text: 'Hello Ann!',
  ));

  // closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients
  await Mail.close();
}

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Mail.fake() sends every mailer to one ArrayTransport, so nothing goes out. Then you check what was sent:

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late ArrayTransport mail;

  setUp(() {
    mail = Mail.fake();
  });

  tearDown(() {
    Mail.restore();
  });

  test('sign up sends a welcome email', () async {
    await signUp('ann@example.com');

    expect(mail.messages, hasLength(1));
    Message message = mail.messages.single;
    expect(message.to.single.email, 'ann@example.com');
    expect(message.subject, 'Welcome');
  });
}

The fake works with or without a config, and it stays on when MailProvider sets up the config again.

docs.title: Testing queued mail
docs.text:
The fake also catches queued emails: Mail.queue(), Mail.later(), the queue() and later() of a mailable, and notifications with shouldQueue. They go to mail.queued, not to the job queue, so you need no queue setup:

await Mail.queue(message);

mail.assertQueued((Message m) => m.subject == 'Welcome');
mail.assertNothingSent();

Each item in mail.queued is a QueuedMessage with mailer, message, id, delay, queue and encrypt.

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
Method Checks assertSent([test]) an email was sent. With test, one of them passes it assertSentCount(count, [test]) exactly count emails were sent. With test, count emails pass it assertNotSent(test) no sent email passes test assertNothingSent() no email was sent assertQueued([test]) an email was queued. With test, one of them passes it assertNotQueued(test) no queued email passes test assertNothingQueued() no email was queued

test is a bool Function(Message). A failed check throws a StateError. mail.clear() forgets the sent and the queued emails, and Mail.restore() stops the fake.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Sending
docs.text:
• send() gives a SentMessage. Its messageId is the id of the provider, or the Message-ID header for SMTP and sendmail.
  • A subject or header with a line break is an error, so user input can not add headers. FailoverTransport throws this MailException at once, and no transport tries it.
  • In FailoverTransport, an error thrown by onError is ignored and the next transport is still tried. An async onError is not awaited.
  • {{ }} in a template escapes HTML. In the plain text body of textView and markdown, the escape is undone, so Tom & Jerry stays Tom & Jerry.
  • With keepAlive: true, if the server closed the connection, the next send opens a new one.
  • SES requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4. Azure requests are signed with the access key (HMAC-SHA256).
  • The package has its own SMTP client, AWS signer and MIME builder.

docs.title: Markdown safety
docs.text:
• The escaped characters are backslash, backtick, *, [, ], # and |. A _ is not changed, so _word_ can still be italic. In @if, a value with one of these characters is not equal to the same text written in the template.
  • Escaping covers text values in data, in its maps, lists and sets, and in objects with toJson(). Values from View.global() and from functions are not changed.
  • Only http, https, mailto, tel, cid and relative URLs are kept. The same check runs on the lines of MailMessage. Email apps can not open a relative link like /dashboard, so use full URLs.
  • [text]({{ url }}) and <{{ url }}> keep the URL as it is, with & and %XX. Entity text inside a URL is decoded, so ?q=<b> reaches the browser as ?q=<b>.
  • A bare URL does not become a link, but most email apps make it a link anyway.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
• The default from and reply-to addresses are added when the email is queued.
  • The worker flags --tries and --timeout work for queued emails, like for other jobs.
  • With the sync queue driver, the email is sent at once, and later() does not wait.
  • Attachments are saved as base64, so they take about 4/3 of their size. MySQL and MariaDB refuse a job bigger than max_allowed_packet (by default 64 MB in MySQL 8, 16 MB in MariaDB). Redis keeps every job in memory.
  • With encrypt: true, a send error is encrypted too. The plain text of the error is only its type and code, like RedactedMailError: MailException (code 550). Details are encrypted: .... The encrypted part holds at most the first 64K characters (UTF-16 code units). To read it, take a FailedJob from Queue.driver.failed() and call RedactedMailError.decrypt(job.error). It works with the app key or any key in AppConfig.previousKeys.
  • To use another queue than dox_queue, call Mail.useQueue(queue). null goes back to the dox_queue queue.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
• If an onSent hook throws, a queue worker does not try the job again, so the email is not sent twice. The other onSent hooks still run.
  • Mail.clearHooks() removes all hooks. Call it first in setup(), and in tests.

docs.title: Native server
docs.text:
Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package dox_http_native.

You do not need to set anything. Every app uses it, also an app with WebSocket or Socket.IO routes. Rust owns the sockets and parses HTTP, but all your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware and the ORM. It gets about 5 times more requests than the dart:io server on one or two cores. See Performance.

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your system when you build the app.

docs.title: Using it without Dox
docs.text:
dox_http_native also works on its own, in any Dart app. Add the package:

dart pub add dox_http_native

Then bind a server and listen for requests. The API is the same as the dart:io HttpServer:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_http_native/dox_http_native.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(3000);
  server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
    req.response.write('Hello World');
    await req.response.close();
  });
}

With no address, the server listens on all interfaces. To listen on one host, pass address:

NativeHttpServer.bind(3000, address: '127.0.0.1');

If the port is open to the internet, set maxConnections. At the limit, the server stops accepting new connections until one closes. There is no limit by default:

NativeHttpServer.bind(3000, maxConnections: 10000);

close() waits for open requests. close(force: true) closes every connection at once.

The rest of this page is the same with or without Dox.

docs.title: Writing handlers
docs.text:
Because the server has the same API as dart:io, req.httpRequest, HttpResponse and code written for dart:io keep working.

Each isolate runs the server on its own thread. So a slow synchronous handler holds all the sockets of its isolate until it is done. await is fine, because it gives the isolate back.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
If the native library can not load, Dox stops at start, before any isolate runs. The error says why and how to fix it:

Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...

<reason> is for example native library ABI 8, expected 9. This means the library on disk is from another version of the package. See Troubleshooting.

You must build with dox build or dart build cli, because dart compile exe does not run build hooks, so it has no library. See Deployment.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
Rust also does the WebSocket upgrade and the WebSocket protocol. Your route, middleware and the Origin check run first, like for any request. If they give a normal answer (like 403), the upgrade is refused.

In your own code, use NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request). It gives a dart:io WebSocket:

WebSocket socket = await NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request);

A message over the size limit closes the socket with code 1009. Set the limit with maxMessageSize of NativeWebSocket.upgrade. Socket.IO uses maxHttpBufferSize.

To find clients that vanished with no close (like a phone that lost its network), set pingInterval. When the client sent nothing for that long, the server sends a ping. When it still sends nothing for one more interval, the socket closes with 1001. It is off by default:

socket.pingInterval = Duration(seconds: 30);

On a graceful stop (SIGTERM), every open WebSocket gets close code 1001.

docs.title: Streaming a response
docs.text:
To send a body in parts, like server-sent events, write with add() and call flush(). The first flush() sends the status, the headers and the bytes so far. Later writes go out at once:

import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
  req.response.headers.contentType = ContentType('text', 'event-stream');
  req.response.add(utf8.encode('data: hello\n\n'));
  await req.response.flush();
});

NativeResponse.headSent is true once the status and headers went out. After that, an error page can not be sent any more. The response can only end. req.response is an HttpResponse, so cast it to read the flag:

bool sent = (req.response as NativeResponse).headSent;

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• On the internet, run it behind a reverse proxy like Caddy or nginx. The proxy does HTTPS, buffers slow clients and caps connections.
  • Set maxConnections when the app port is open to the internet.
  • Another process of the same OS user can bind the same port. So do not run untrusted code as the user of the app.
  • req.uri resolves .. in the path. Never build a file path from the raw path. Use the storage helpers.

docs.title: Where the library comes from
docs.text:
The build hook of dox_http_native (hook/build.dart) picks the first one that works:

  1. A path you give in the root pubspec.yaml of your app:

    hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_http_native:
      lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so

  2. A local build in native/target/release of the package (for work on the package itself).

  3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
  4. A build from source with cargo, when Rust is installed.

For a git or path dependency, step 4 comes before step 3, because the source can be newer than the release.

When none works, the app still builds, but it stops at start with the error above. Install Rust and run it again, so step 4 works.

docs.title: Working on the native code
docs.text:
dox_http_native lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-http-native. The Rust code is in its native folder:

cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, or to release the package, see Contribute.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The server runs on the thread of the isolate, in a loop:

  1. Dart calls Rust (one FFI call).
  2. Rust writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them back to Dart as one batch.

  3. Dart runs your handlers and calls Rust again with their answers.

  4. Under load there is no other thread, so a request never waits for a thread to wake up. When the isolate has nothing to do, a small helper thread watches the sockets and wakes the isolate once when a request comes.

  5. A second helper thread does gzip, only with compress: true. Under load both helper threads sleep.
  6. The loop gives the event loop a turn after a few batches, so timers and database answers still run on time.
  7. Each isolate runs its own server on the same port. See Isolate. The OS spreads connections, not requests, so a keep-alive connection stays on one isolate. A few busy connections (like from one proxy) can keep some isolates idle, so use more connections than isolates.
  8. WebSocket: Rust sends the 101 answer, answers pings, does the close handshake, checks that text is UTF-8 and checks the size of each frame. Dart gets whole messages in the same batches as requests.
  9. Compression (permessage-deflate) is never agreed, because a small compressed message could grow very big in memory.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The request line plus headers can be at most 16 KB. Bigger gets 431. A bad request gets 400.
  • A multipart form over maxMultipartSize, or any other body over maxBodySize, gets 413 from Rust. With Expect: 100-continue, the 413 comes before the body is sent. Else Rust reads and drops the body first, so the client sees the 413.
  • A client that sends no body bytes for 120 seconds gets 408. A slow but steady upload is fine.
  • Accepted sockets get TCP keep-alive. After 60 seconds with no traffic, the OS checks the client every 10 seconds, and a client that misses 6 checks (about 2 minutes) is closed. A live client always answers.
  • A client that closed its side while the handler has not answered is closed when nothing was written for idleTimeout (30 seconds by default). Set it with the idleTimeout argument of NativeHttpServer.bind. In a Dox app, set AppConfig.idleTimeout.
  • A request head must arrive within 30 seconds. A keep-alive connection with no request for 30 seconds is closed. A client that does not read its answer for 30 seconds is cut off.
  • A request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding: chunked gets 400. A transfer encoding other than chunked gets 501.
  • At most 64 requests of one connection wait for an answer, and at most 1 MB of answers waits to be sent. Then the server stops reading that connection until the answers go out.
  • A streamed response with a contentLength must send exactly that many bytes. add() throws when the body passes it, and close() fails when it is shorter.
  • A streamed response over 64 KB goes out in parts, and at most 1 MB of it waits in memory. Dart reads more of a file only when the client has read what was sent, and stops when the client leaves.
  • A request body of 64 KB or more goes to Dart without a copy.
  • compress: true in AppConfig gzips on a helper thread. A streamed response is not compressed.
  • WebSocket: one turn reads at most 256 KB of one socket, so one busy client can not hold the isolate. While more than 256 KB waits to be sent to a client, the server stops reading its frames.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
A notification tells a user about something, like "your invoice is paid", by email or by any channel you write.

One notification can go out on more than one channel, like email, a database table or SMS. Each notification is a class, so the text and the channels live in one place.

Notifications are in the dox_mailer package. Set up mail first.

docs.title: Creating notifications
docs.text:
A notification extends Notification. The via method picks the channels, and toMail builds the email:

class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  InvoicePaid(this.invoiceId);

  final int invoiceId;

  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Mailable toMail(Object notifiable) {
    return MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid')
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/$invoiceId');
  }
}

toMail() can return any mailable, so a WelcomeMail with a template works too.

docs.title: Making a model notifiable
docs.text:
The class that gets notifications, usually the user model, needs the Notifiable mixin. Its routeNotificationFor method tells each channel where to send. For the mail channel, it returns the email address:

class User extends Model<User> with Notifiable {
  @override
  Object? routeNotificationFor(String channel) {
    return channel == 'mail' ? Address(email!, name) : null;
  }
}

The mail route can be an Address, an email text like Ann <ann@example.com>, or a list of these. If the mailable has its own to address, that address is used and the route is not.

docs.title: Sending to one user
docs.text:
Call notify on the model:

await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));

docs.title: Sending to many users
docs.text:
Use Notification.send with a list:

await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));

docs.title: Sending to an address with no user
docs.text:
Sometimes the person has no user row, like a guest. Pass an Address:

await Notification.send(<Object>[Address('ann@example.com')], InvoicePaid(1));

docs.title: Handling errors
docs.text:
If one channel throws, the other channels and the other notifiables still get the notification. At the end, Notification.send() throws a NotificationException. Its errors list says which notifiable and channel failed, and why.

The error text of a NotificationException has no email addresses and no error messages, so it is safe for logs. Read errors for the details.

With one notifiable and one error, like in user.notify(), the error is thrown as it is. So on MailException catch (e) still works there.

docs.title: Queueing notifications
docs.text:
Sending an email can be slow, so you may want to send it in the background. Override shouldQueue. The mail channel then puts the email on the job queue, like Mail.queue(). This needs a queue:

@override
bool get shouldQueue => true;

The email is rendered at once, and the worker sends the finished email.

You can set the queue options with these getters. They work like the options of Mail.queue():

Getter Default What it does queue null (default) the queue name delay null the worker sends the email after this wait encrypt false save the job data encrypted with the app key

shouldQueue and these options only change the mail channel. Your own channels still run at once. To queue them, dispatch a job in the channel.

docs.title: Custom channels
docs.text:
If you want to send a notification another way, like to a database table, write your own channel. A channel implements NotificationChannel. It gets the data of the notification from toArray():

import 'dart:convert';

class DatabaseChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  @override
  Future<void> send(Object notifiable, Notification notification) async {
    // only a user has a row. An Address or an email text has none.
    if (notifiable is! User) return;
    AppNotification row = AppNotification()
      ..userId = notifiable.id
      ..data = jsonEncode(notification.toArray(notifiable));
    await row.save();
  }
}

Then add the channel to via(), and give the data in toArray():

class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel(), DatabaseChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toArray(Object notifiable) {
    return <String, Object?>{'type': 'invoice_paid', 'invoice_id': invoiceId};
  }

  // ...
}

dox_mailer has no database channel of its own, so it does not need the ORM.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Mail.fake() also catches the emails of the mail channel:

ArrayTransport mail = Mail.fake();
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
expect(mail.messages.single.subject, 'Invoice paid');

With shouldQueue, the email goes to mail.queued, not to mail.messages, and it does not reach the job queue. Check it with mail.assertQueued(). See Mail.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Each item of NotificationException.errors has the notifiable and the channel. When via() throws, the channel is null. The error text has one line per failure: the place and the type of the notifiable, the channel, and the error type.
  • When shouldQueue is false, the queue options do nothing.

docs.title: Package commands
docs.text:
A package can add its own dox commands.

Your app can add its own commands too. You do not write a bin file, and you do not register anything, because the dox CLI finds the commands by itself. For example, dox queue:table comes from the dox_queue_database package, and dox auth:tokens-table comes from the dox_auth package.

docs.title: Using a package command
docs.text:
Add the package and run dart pub get. Then run the command:

dart pub add dox_queue_database
dox queue:table

dox help lists the commands of each package, under the package name.

docs.title: Add a command to your package
docs.text: A package command needs three things: the command class, a list of commands, and a key in pubspec.yaml.

docs.title: 1. Write the command
docs.text:
A command extends Command from package:dox_core/command.dart. The run method gets the words after the command name as args:

lib/src/commands/hello_command.dart
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

class HelloCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:say';

  @override
  String get description => 'Say hello';

  /// optional, shown by `dox help`. The default is the name.
  @override
  String get usage => 'hello:say <name>';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    print('Hello ${args.join(' ')}');
  }
}

So dox hello:say Ann calls run(['Ann']).

A package that does not use dox_core imports package:dox_annotation/command.dart instead.

docs.title: 2. List the commands
docs.text:
Make one library with a top-level commands list:

lib/commands.dart
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

import 'src/commands/hello_command.dart';

final List<Command> commands = <Command>[HelloCommand()];

docs.title: 3. Name the library in pubspec.yaml
docs.text:
Add the dox: commands: key. Its value must be a library of the package itself:

pubspec.yaml
dox:
  commands: package:my_package/commands.dart

That is all. An app that depends on your package now has dox hello:say.

docs.title: Add a command to your app
docs.text:
It works the same way. The easy way is dox make:command:

dox make:command send_report

It writes lib/app/commands/send_report_command.dart, adds the command to lib/app/commands/commands.dart, and sets the dox: commands: key in your pubspec.yaml. The command name is app:send-report. See dox make:command.

If you write it by hand, put the command in lib/ of your app and add the key to the app's own pubspec.yaml:

pubspec.yaml
dox:
  commands: package:my_app/commands.dart

docs.title: Failing a command
docs.text:
When run ends, dox exits with code 0. If something went wrong, set exitCode from dart:io, or throw:

exitCode = 1;

A thrown error is printed with its stack trace, and the exit code is 1. The exit code of the command is the exit code of dox, so scripts and CI see it.

docs.title: Writing a migration
docs.text:
Some packages need a table, so their command adds a migration file. Use MigrationFile for this. The file gets the same name as dox make:migration makes, like 2026_10_21_120000_create_queue_tables.dart:

String? path = MigrationFile().create('create_queue_tables', source);
if (path == null) {
  print('A create_queue_tables migration is already in db/migration.');
  exitCode = 1;
}

create returns null and writes nothing when a migration with this name is already there. The next dox migrate runs the new file.

docs.title: Ship an install command
docs.text:
dox add <x> adds the package dox_x, then runs its <x>:install command. So if your package needs setup (config files, .env keys, a provider), ship an <x>:install command.

Use Installer from package:dox_annotation/install.dart. Each step is safe to run twice, because it never overwrites a file and never adds a key twice:

lib/src/commands/hello_install_command.dart
import 'package:dox_annotation/command.dart';
import 'package:dox_annotation/install.dart';

class HelloInstallCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:install';

  @override
  String get description => 'Set up dox_hello in this app';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    Installer installer = Installer();
    String app = installer.appName;
    installer.writeFile(
      'lib/config/hello.dart',
      "import 'package:$app/config/env.dart';\n",
    );
    installer.addEnvGetter("String get helloName => 'world';");
    installer.addEnv('HELLO_NAME', 'world');
    await installer.buildRunner();
    installer.printSummary(<String>['Restart the server.']);
  }
}
Method What it does writeFile(path, content) Writes the file only when it is not there. makeFolder(path) Makes the folder when it is not there. addEnv(key, value) Adds KEY=value to .env.example and .env when the key is missing. A key that is there is never changed. addEnvGetter(getter) Adds a getter to AppEnv in lib/config/env.dart when the class has no member with that name. When it can not find the class, it changes nothing and prints a hint. addDependency(package, dev: false) Runs dart pub add when the app does not have the package. buildRunner() Runs dart run build_runner build. note(line) Adds your own line to the summary, like added hooks to pubspec.yaml. printSummary(nextSteps) Prints what was done and the next steps. Sets exit code 1 when a step failed.

Some tips for a good install command:

  • Read the options from args, like --driver=postgres. Give a good default, so dox add <x> with no options works.
  • Test it on an app made without your package. Run it twice and check that nothing changes the second time.
  • Add dox add <x> to the skill of your package (skills/<name>/SKILL.md), so AI agents set it up the same way.

dox_orm has an example: orm:install.

docs.title: Name clashes and errors
docs.text:
• A built-in command always wins. If a package has a command with the same name as a built-in one, dox runs the built-in one, and dox help marks the package command as not used.
  • If two packages have a command with the same name, dox <name> prints an error with both package names and exits with code 1.
  • A bad dox: commands: key (not a library of the package, or a missing file) prints a warning with the package name. The commands of the other packages still work.
  • The key path may use only letters, digits, _, -, . and /, and no ...
  • An unknown command prints Could not find a command named "<name>", with a hint about the dox: commands: key.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• dox <name> first looks for a built-in command. Then it reads .dart_tool/package_config.json and the dox: commands: key of each package and of the app.
  • It writes .dart_tool/dox/commands.dart, which imports each commands library, and runs it with dart run. So the command code is always the newest.
  • It writes that file again only when .dart_tool/package_config.json or a pubspec.yaml changes. If a package had a warning, dox looks again on the next run.
  • dox help keeps the list in .dart_tool/dox/commands.json. If you change only a file that the commands library imports, dox help can show an old description. The command itself always runs the new code.
  • MigrationFile().create finds a migration with the same name and any time in its name. dox migrate writes db/migration/migrations.dart again before it runs, and makes bin/migrate.dart when it is missing.
  • An app inside a pub workspace works too, also when the workspace: list uses a glob like apps/*. dox finds the workspace root from .dart_tool/pub/workspace_ref.json.

docs.title: Performance mistakes
docs.text:
These are the mistakes that make a Dox app slow, with the fix for each one, and a strict mode that warns you about the worst of them while you develop.

Dart runs one thing at a time in each isolate. When one request does slow work without an await, every other request on that isolate waits. Most of the mistakes below come from this, or from using too much memory or too many connections. For server settings, see Performance.

docs.title: Heavy CPU work in a request
docs.text:
Hashing, building a PDF, resizing an image or parsing a huge JSON file keeps the CPU busy. Run it on a worker isolate with Dox().compute, so the server can answer other requests meanwhile:

Wrong
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return buildPdf(order.toJson()); // blocks the isolate
}
Right
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return renderPdf(order.toJson());
}

Future<List<int>> renderPdf(Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return Dox().compute(() => buildPdf(data));
}

The task runs in another isolate. So make it in a small top-level or static function, and pass only plain values (numbers, strings, lists, maps). Do not use a database connection, the container or a cache store inside it. To change the number of workers, set computeWorkers in AppConfig.

docs.title: Sync password hashing
docs.text:
Hash.make and Hash.verify run bcrypt on the isolate, and bcrypt is slow on purpose. In a handler, use the async methods. They run bcrypt on a worker:

Wrong
bool ok = Hash.verify(password, user.password);
Right
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync(password, user.password);
String hashed = await Hash.makeAsync(password);

docs.title: Sync file calls
docs.text:
A sync file call stops the isolate until the disk answers. Use the async call:

Wrong
String text = File('data/terms.txt').readAsStringSync();
Right
String text = await File('data/terms.txt').readAsString();

docs.title: Loading a whole table
docs.text:
all() and get() read every row into memory. On a big table, this is slow and can use all your memory. Read one page, or read the rows in parts:

Wrong
List<Order> orders = await Order().all();
Right
Pagination<Order> page = await Order().orderBy('id').paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 50);

To work on all rows, use chunk(), lazy() or cursor(). They keep only a few rows in memory:

await for (Order order in Order().orderBy('id').cursor(chunkSize: 500)) {
  // one row at a time
}

See Paginating results, Chunking results and Streaming results.

docs.title: A query inside a loop
docs.text:
This is the N+1 problem. One query loads the rows, then one more query runs for each row. 100 posts make 101 queries. Use preload() to load the relation for all rows in one extra query:

Wrong
List<Post> posts = await Post().all();
for (Post post in posts) {
  await post.$getRelation('author'); // one query per post
  User? author = post.author;
}
Right
List<Post> posts = await Post().preload('author').get();
for (Post post in posts) {
  User? author = post.author; // already loaded
}

docs.title: Awaiting independent work one by one
docs.text:
If two calls do not need each other, start both and wait for both. The total time is then the slowest call, not the sum:

Wrong
int users = await User().count();
int orders = await Order().count();
Right
(int, int) counts = await (User().count(), Order().count()).wait;

For a list of futures, use Future.wait(futures).

docs.title: A static Map as a cache
docs.text:
A static Map that you fill and never clean grows until the memory is full. Also, each isolate has its own copy, so the isolates do not agree. Use the cache with a time to live:

Wrong
static final Map<String, Object> _settings = <String, Object>{};
Right
Map<String, dynamic> settings = await Cache().remember(
  'settings',
  Duration(minutes: 10),
  loadSettings,
);

With the redis or database store, all isolates and servers share the same values.

docs.title: Forgetting await
docs.text:
If you call an async function without await, the work runs on its own. Its error is lost, and it can end after the response is sent. Await it:

Wrong
mailer.sendWelcome(user);
Right
await mailer.sendWelcome(user);

Turn on the unawaited_futures lint in analysis_options.yaml and the analyzer finds these for you. If you really want the client to answer first, use a queue job with dispatchAfterResponse.

docs.title: A new client for every request
docs.text:
An HTTP client or a Redis client opens connections. If you make one in each request, you open and close a connection every time. Make one client and share it:

Wrong
Future<String> rate(DoxRequest req) async {
  HttpClient client = HttpClient();
  // ...
}
Right
class RateService {
  RateService(this._client);

  final HttpClient _client;

  Future<String> rate() async {
    // use _client
  }
}

Register the client once in the container and inject it. Each isolate makes its own copy, which is fine.

docs.title: A long transaction
docs.text:
A transaction holds one database connection until it ends. If you call an outside API inside it, the connection waits for that API. When many requests do this, the pool runs out of connections. Do the slow call before or after the transaction:

Wrong
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
  await paymentApi.charge(order); // the connection waits here
});
Right
await paymentApi.charge(order);
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
});

docs.title: Reading a big file into memory
docs.text:
bytes loads the whole upload into memory. A big download read into a variable does the same. Stream both. See Request and Files and big responses:

Wrong
List<int> data = await file.bytes;
Right
Stream<List<int>> data = file.stream();

Keep maxBodySize and maxMultipartSize set, so a huge body gets 413 before Dart reads it. See Size limits.

docs.title: Timers and listeners that never stop
docs.text:
On a long connection, like server-sent events or a WebSocket, a Timer.periodic or a stream listener keeps running after the client leaves. Keep it and cancel it when the connection closes:

StreamSubscription<Event> subscription = events.listen(send);
// when the client disconnects
await subscription.cancel();

docs.title: Let Dox warn you
docs.text: Strict mode finds the worst mistakes while you develop. It writes a warning, and it never throws or changes the response. It is off by default, and when it is off it costs nothing.

docs.title: Strict mode in Dox
docs.text:
Set strict in AppConfig. Turn it on only in development:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  strict: StrictConfig(enabled: Env.appEnv == 'development'),
  // ...
);

Warnings go to stderr with a [strict] tag. blockLimit is how long code may block the isolate, 50 ms by default. To change it, use StrictConfig(enabled: true, blockLimit: Duration(milliseconds: 100)).

A route that blocks the isolate for too long warns once:

[strict] GET /invoices/{id} blocked the isolate for 180 ms (limit 50 ms). Other requests on this isolate had to wait. Move heavy CPU work (like bcrypt, PDF or image work) to await Dox().compute(...), and use Hash.makeAsync or Hash.verifyAsync for passwords.

Code that blocks the event loop, also after an await, warns at most once in 10 seconds. It cannot tell you which code did it:

[strict] The event loop of isolate 1 was blocked for about 120 ms (limit 50 ms). Some code ran that long without an await, so other requests had to wait. Move heavy CPU work to await Dox().compute(...).

Hash.make, Hash.verify and Hash.check in the web server warn once for each place in your code:

[strict] Hash.make ran in the web server at AuthController.register (package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth_controller.dart:21:18). It blocks the isolate while bcrypt runs, so other requests wait. Use await Hash.makeAsync(...) instead.

docs.title: Strict mode in the ORM
docs.text:
Set strict in DatabaseConfig:

lib/config/database.dart
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  // ...
  strict: OrmStrict(enabled: appConfig.isDevelopment),
);
