nPlusOneCount (default 5) is how many row by row loads of one relation in about one second make a warning. maxRows (default 1000) is how many rows get() or all() may read. The warnings are printed with a [db] tag:

[db] Strict mode: possible N+1 query. The relation "author" of Post was loaded row by row 5 times in a short time. Load it for all rows in one query with preload('author').

[db] Strict mode: table "orders" read 25000 rows into memory (the limit is 1000). Use paginate(), chunk(), lazy() or cursor() for big results.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

Dox is fast by default, so most apps only need to follow a few rules in production:

  1. Build with dox build and run the AOT binary. Never use dart run in production. See Deployment.
  2. Put Caddy or nginx in front, for HTTPS and gzip.
  3. Keep the default isolates, one per CPU core.
  4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

For the code mistakes that slow an app down, see Performance mistakes.

docs.title: Bodies, uploads and big responses
docs.text:
Big requests and responses can fill the memory of your server. Dox protects you from this by default, so you only need to keep these settings:

  • A body over maxBodySize or maxMultipartSize gets 413 from the native server, before Dart reads it. Set the same limit in the proxy. See Size limits.
  • An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file. See Request.
  • A File or Stream response is streamed, not loaded into memory. See Files and big responses.

docs.title: gzip
docs.text:
gzip saves bandwidth, but it costs CPU on every response. A proxy like Caddy or nginx does it better. So gzip in Dart is off by default. If there is no proxy, turn it on:

AppConfig(compress: true);

Only a body over 256 bytes is gzipped, and only when the client accepts gzip. Streamed responses are not compressed.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: LogMiddleware logs one line per request. If a proxy already writes access logs, turn LogMiddleware off, because writing logs costs time. A new project does this for you: enabled is false when APP_ENV is production or not set.

docs.title: Response handler
docs.text: Leave responseHandler unset if you do not need it. With no handler, a plain value (text, map, list) is sent without building a DoxResponse.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
This benchmark uses the rules of the-benchmarker/web-frameworks: each server answers GET / (empty body), GET /user/:id (the id) and POST /user (empty body). Dox is a full Dox app with these three routes. "Dox server only" is dox_http_native with no framework, to show what the framework costs.

This only measures the HTTP stack. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are smaller there. See App benchmark.

docs.title: 2 cores
docs.text:
2 cores: ahead of Rust hyper and Bun

GET /, 256 connections. Every server has one worker per core: Dox one isolate, Bun and Node one process, Go and Rust one thread.

req/s p99 RAM Doxfull app 626,655fastest 1.1 ms 21 MB Rusthyper 585,6581.07× slower 0.7 ms 13 MB BunBun.serve 501,5291.25× slower 1.0 ms 40 MB Nodenode:http 286,8472.2× slower 1.7 ms 200 MB Gonet/http 242,0432.6× slower 3.3 ms 36 MB dart:ioHttpServer 129,7964.8× slower 3.8 ms 75 MB

The Dox numbers are from the 3.2 patch release (2026-11-16). The other servers are from the run before, on the same Mac. See How it was run.

docs.title: Why it is fast
docs.text:
The server runs on the isolate's own thread. One FFI call writes the answers, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. Dart runs the handlers and calls again. A request never waits for another thread to wake up. A small helper thread only watches the sockets while the isolate has nothing to do. See Native server.

A profile with perf (4 server cores, 64 connections) shows the effect:

Dox Bun CPU time per request 4.85 µs 5.5 µs Context switches per request 0.08 0.035

docs.title: How it was run
docs.text:
• Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), linux/arm64.
  • One server at a time. The server and wrk run in two containers on different CPUs: the server on 2 CPUs, wrk on the other 6. Host network, keep-alive.
  • wrk 4.1, 64, 256 and 512 connections, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds per route.
  • Every server has as many workers as server CPUs.
  • Peak memory is the peak of the container (all workers).
  • Dart 3.13.6, AOT build with dart build cli (this is what dox build does). dox_core and dox_http_native as released when these numbers were measured. The Dox rows were measured again on 2026-11-16 for the 3.2 patch release (same Mac, a new Docker VM). The other servers are from the run before. Node 26.12, Bun 1.4.4, Go 1.26, Rust 1.99 with hyper 1.

docs.text:
A small real app, the same in each language: GET /json returns a map, GET /db reads one row by id from Postgres, GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows one after another. The table has 10,000 rows. Each app uses its database driver directly, with no ORM. Dox uses dox_postgres_native.

2 cores: one row from Postgres

GET /db, 256 connections. Requests per second, higher is better.

The same app on MySQL 8.4 (dox_mysql_native). The dart:io app has no MySQL version.

The Postgres Dox row was measured again on 2026-11-16 for the 3.2 patch release (same Mac, a new Docker VM). The other servers and the MySQL table are from the run before.

docs.title: Database drivers
docs.text:
One find-by-id query, AOT build (dart build cli), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

Database One query at a time Many queries in flight App CPU time per query Postgres 14 (4 connections) 60 µs 12.5 µs each (64 in flight) MySQL 8.4 (10 connections) 67 µs 11 µs each (32 in flight) 13.5 µs MariaDB 11 (10 connections) 63 µs 9.7 µs each (32 in flight) 12.4 µs
  • The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core.
  • Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
  • One query alone spends most of its time on the trip to the database. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

docs.title: Dart VM flags
docs.text: A bigger young generation (DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64 or 128) did not give a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise, and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set, and Dox never sets VM flags for you. DART_VM_OPTIONS is read by the AOT binary from dox build, so you can try your own.

docs.title: How logs are written
docs.text:
• Logger collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every 64 KB) in one write, because writing to stdout blocks the isolate.
  • A warn, warning, danger or error line is written right away, with the waiting lines before it, so the order stays.
  • The buffer is also written when the app stops. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of logs can be lost.

docs.title: What Dox does for you
docs.text:
• Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not on every request.
  • The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on every request.
  • JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with Content-Length set.
  • The native server gzips on a Rust thread, and the gzipped body still gets a Content-Length.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app when it starts, for example the database, auth or a Redis connection.

Dox runs your app on many isolates, and they do not share memory. So code that you run once in bin/server.dart only sets up the first isolate, and the others have, for example, no database connection. A provider fixes this, because each isolate runs it itself.

docs.title: Writing providers
docs.text:
To make a provider, run dox make:provider. It writes lib/providers/cache_provider.dart with an empty setup():

dox make:provider Cache

See dox make:provider.

docs.title: The setup method
docs.text:
A provider extends DoxProvider. Put your code in setup(). It runs when the app starts, and it can be async, because Dox waits for it:

lib/providers/orm_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}

Open connections in setup(), not in the constructor. A provider listed in AppConfig is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.

Keep setup() short, because it runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is also kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.

A package that does not use dox_core imports DoxProvider from package:dox_annotation/provider.dart.

docs.title: The boot method
docs.text:
Sometimes a provider needs other providers to be ready, for example to start a background worker. Use boot() for this. It runs after setup() of every provider is done:

class ReportProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {}

  @override
  Future<void> boot() async {
    // every provider has run setup() here
  }
}

The boots run one by one, in the provider order. boot() is optional.

The web server and the queue worker (bin/queue.dart) run boot(). The scheduler (bin/schedule.dart) and dox openapi:generate do not. They run only setup().

docs.title: Clean up on shutdown
docs.text:
When the app stops, you often want to close connections or flush data. Use shutdown() for this. On SIGTERM or SIGINT, Dox stops the server gracefully (see Deployment). After the open requests are done, it runs shutdown() of every provider, in every isolate:

lib/providers/redis_provider.dart
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}

shutdown() is optional. The ORMProvider of a new project already closes the database here. Dox closes the cache stores (like Redis) by itself, after the providers.

An error in shutdown() goes to the report method of the exception handler. The other providers still run.

docs.title: Registering providers
docs.text:
You do not need to register a provider. Dox finds every class that extends DoxProvider. Run dart run build_runner build, and the provider is then in lib/generated/container.g.dart.

Each isolate makes its own instance from the container, so its constructor can ask for other classes of the container. See Dependency injection.

docs.title: Choosing the order
docs.text:
Providers run in the order of their file path. If one provider must run first, list it in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);

A listed provider runs first, then the others run. No provider runs twice.

docs.title: Adding a provider in code
docs.text:
You can also add a provider in bin/server.dart, before startServer():

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Example: auth
docs.text:
This provider sets up authentication:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}

The class is named AppAuthProvider, because dox_auth already has a class named AuthProvider (it finds the user model).

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• In each isolate, Dox runs setup() of each provider one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container. Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a provider set up. See What each isolate does at start.
  • dox openapi:generate also runs setup() of every provider, because it needs the routes.
  • The queue inProcess worker starts in boot(), so it does not run in the scheduler process.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
A queue runs slow work in the background, so the request can answer at once.

Some tasks take too long to do during a request, like sending an email, calling a slow API, making a report or resizing an image. You put these tasks on a queue as jobs. A worker process then takes each job and runs it.

The dox_queue package gives you jobs, retries, delays and a worker. It has a redis driver and a sync driver. The database driver is in the dox_queue_database package.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app from dox create already has the queue. In other apps, run:

dox add queue

The default driver is database. Add --driver=redis or --driver=sync to pick another one. The command adds the package and writes the config, the provider, bin/queue.dart and a sample job. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

With database, it also adds dox_queue_database and the migration for the jobs tables, so run dox add orm first. With redis, it adds the REDIS_* keys.

The sections below show the files it writes. Check them, and change the driver if you want. To set it up by hand, run dart pub add dox_queue and write the same files.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The queue config picks the driver and lists your jobs:

lib/config/queue.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../generated/jobs.g.dart';

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  /// sync, database or redis
  driver: 'database',

  /// every @Job class, from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart
  jobs: jobRegistry,
);

jobRegistry holds every job class of your app. dart run build_runner build writes it, because the job builder is in dox_builder, which your app already runs. See All options for the other settings.

Dox has three drivers:

  • sync: dispatch() runs the job at once and waits for it. There is no worker, no retry and no delay. Use it for tests and local work.
  • database: jobs are rows in the jobs table. It needs dox_queue_database, and Postgres, MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+ or SQLite.
  • redis: jobs are kept in Redis.

Keep retryAfter bigger than your longest job

retryAfter (default 90 seconds) is how Dox finds the job of a crashed worker. A job that runs longer than retryAfter looks crashed, so a second worker runs it again.

docs.title: The provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up the queue in every isolate. Put it in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it:

lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

/// Sets up the queue. Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class AppQueueProvider extends QueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

docs.title: The worker file
docs.text:
The worker runs from bin/queue.dart. It starts the providers of your app (database, cache, queue), but not the HTTP server:

bin/queue.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

/// run queued jobs: `dart run bin/queue.dart [work] [flags]`.
/// the `dox` CLI runs this file for its queue commands.
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await QueueWorker(app: appConfig).run(args);
}

docs.title: Database driver
docs.text:
The database driver, job batches and dispatching after the commit are in the dox_queue_database package. If you use only Redis or sync and none of these, skip this step.

dart pub add dox_queue_database

Then make your queue provider extend DatabaseQueueProvider in place of QueueProvider. This turns the package on. Without it, QueueConfig(driver: 'database') throws an ArgumentError that names the package.

lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends DatabaseQueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

The database driver needs the jobs and failed_jobs tables. Batches need the job_batches table, with every driver. dox queue:table writes a migration in db/migration that makes all three:

dox queue:table
dox migrate

The migration looks like this, so you can also write it by hand:

db/migration/2026_10_25_000000_create_queue_tables.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

/// The jobs, failed_jobs and job_batches tables of dox_queue_database.
class CreateQueueTables extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.up(schema);
    await QueueTables.upBatches(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.downBatches(schema);
    await QueueTables.down(schema);
  }
}

To keep the jobs in another database connection of config/database.dart, use QueueConfig(connection: 'postgres').

docs.title: Adding the pop indexes to an old table
docs.text:
A new jobs table has the indexes a worker needs to find the next job fast. A table you made earlier works too, but a poll can read every waiting job. To add the indexes, write a new migration. It adds only the indexes the table does not have, so you can run it more than once:

db/migration/2026_11_20_000000_add_queue_pop_index.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class AddQueuePopIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.popIndex(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {}
}

On MySQL and MariaDB it does nothing, because the index on queue is enough.

docs.title: Redis driver
docs.text:
Set the driver to redis and give the Redis server:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(host: env.redisHost, port: 6379),
);

A Redis command that gets no reply in 10 seconds fails with RedisTimeoutError, and the client reconnects. This stops a Redis outage from hanging every request. Change it with commandTimeout. null turns it off. Blocking commands and subscriber connections never time out.

To cap the commands that wait for a connection, set maxQueuedCommands. One more fails at once with RedisQueueFullError. It is off by default:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(
    host: env.redisHost,
    port: 6379,
    commandTimeout: Duration(seconds: 5),
    maxQueuedCommands: 1000,
  ),
);

You can also read the Redis server from the env with QueueConfig.redisFromEnv():

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: QueueConfig.redisFromEnv(),
);

It reads REDIS_URL, like rediss://user:password@host:6380/0, where rediss turns on TLS. If REDIS_URL is not set, it reads REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_USERNAME, REDIS_PASSWORD and REDIS_TLS. A key that is not set keeps the default of RedisOptions.

docs.title: Generating job classes
docs.text:
dox make:job makes a new job file in lib/app/jobs/:

dox make:job SendWelcomeEmail

docs.title: Class structure
docs.text:
A job is a class with @Job() that extends DoxJob. The worker calls its handle() method:

lib/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

@Job()
class SendWelcomeEmail extends DoxJob {
  SendWelcomeEmail({required this.userId});

  final int userId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    MailService mail = Dox().ioc.get<MailService>();
    await mail.sendWelcome(userId);
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add or change a job. It writes lib/generated/jobs.g.dart, which knows how to save and load each job.

docs.title: Job data
docs.text:
The parameters of the unnamed constructor are saved with the job. Each parameter needs a field or getter with the same name. These types work:

  • int, double, num, String, bool
  • DateTime
  • enums (saved by name)
  • List and Map<String, ...> of these, also nested
  • dynamic and Object (the value must be JSON)
  • nullable versions of all of them

Any other type stops the build with a clear message.

Save an id, not an object

Do not save a User. Save the userId, and load the user in handle(). The user may change between dispatch and run, so the id gives you fresh data.

docs.title: Using services in a job
docs.text:
A job is made again from its saved data, so it can not get services in its constructor. Get them in handle() from the Dox container:

UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();

The worker runs registerContainer, so every @Inject() class of your app is there.

docs.title: Setting the number of tries
docs.text:
By default a job runs once. If you want the worker to try again when handle() throws, set tries. Use backoff to wait between the tries:

/// run up to 3 times
@override
int get tries => 3;

/// wait 10 seconds before the 2nd try, 60 seconds before the 3rd
@override
List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[
  Duration(seconds: 10),
  Duration(seconds: 60),
];

The last backoff entry is used for all later tries. With no backoff, the retry happens at once.

There are three more settings for retries:

  • retryUntil retries until a time, in place of a number of tries. It is read once, when the job is dispatched.
  • maxExceptions fails the job after this many tries that threw an error. A timeout does not count.
  • failOnTimeout fails the job at once when a try times out, with no retry.

docs.title: Setting a timeout
docs.text:
timeout is the max run time of one try. The default is the worker --timeout, which is 60 seconds:

/// stop a try after 30 seconds
@override
Duration? get timeout => const Duration(seconds: 30);

docs.title: Choosing the queue
docs.text:
Jobs go on the default queue. You can give a job its own queue, so a worker can run it first or apart:

/// the queue of this job
@override
String get queue => 'emails';

docs.title: Handling failed jobs
docs.text:
failed() runs once, after the last try failed. Use it to tell someone, or to clean up:

/// runs once, after the last try failed
@override
Future<void> failed(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  // tell someone, or clean up
}

docs.title: Encrypting job data
docs.text:
If a job holds private data, add the ShouldBeEncrypted mixin. Then a person who can read Redis or the jobs table can not read the data:

@Job()
class ChargeCard extends DoxJob with ShouldBeEncrypted {
  // ...
}

The data is encrypted with the app key (AppConfig.appKey), so the worker needs the same key, or one of AppConfig.previousKeys. The job name, the queue and the id stay plain text.

docs.title: Renaming a job class
docs.text:
The class name is saved with each job. So when you rename a class, queued jobs with the old name can not be found. Keep the old name with name:

@Job(name: 'SendWelcomeEmail')

docs.title: Dispatching jobs
docs.text:
Call dispatch() to put a job on the queue. It returns the job id:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch();

Queue.dispatch() does the same:

await Queue.dispatch(SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id));

docs.title: Delayed dispatching
docs.text:
Sometimes a job should wait before it runs. Use delay. You can also pick another queue here:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delay: Duration(minutes: 10),
  queue: 'emails',
);

To wait until a fixed time, use delayUntil. Give delay or delayUntil, not both:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delayUntil: DateTime.utc(2030, 1, 1, 9),
);

docs.title: Conditional dispatching
docs.text:
dispatchIf dispatches only when the condition is true, and dispatchUnless only when it is false. They return null when the job was not dispatched:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchIf(user.wantsEmail);
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchUnless(user.isBlocked);

docs.title: Synchronous dispatching
docs.text:
dispatchSync runs the job now, in this process, with no queue:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchSync();

docs.title: Dispatching after the response
docs.text:
Sometimes a job is short, but the client should not wait for it. dispatchAfterResponse runs the job in this process after the answer is sent:

SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchAfterResponse();

Do not await it, because it returns nothing. The job does not go on the queue, so it has no job id and no retry. If the job throws, its failed() runs and the error goes to the exception handler, never to the client. If the server stops before the job runs, the job is lost.

docs.title: Dispatching after the commit
docs.text:
If you dispatch a job inside a database transaction, it is pushed at once. Then a worker can run it before the transaction commits, or after it rolls back. So the job reads data that is not saved yet, or is never saved.

Use afterCommit: true to wait for the commit. This needs dox_queue_database:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch(afterCommit: true);
});
  • The job is pushed after the outermost transaction commits.
  • If the transaction rolls back, the job is not pushed.
  • Outside a transaction, the job is pushed at once.
  • dispatch() still returns the job id at once.

To do this for every dispatch, set QueueConfig(afterCommit: true). Then afterCommit: false on one dispatch pushes that job at once. Chains and batches take afterCommit too. See Dispatch after the commit details for special cases.

docs.title: Queueing an email
docs.text:
You do not need a job class to send an email later. With dox_mailer, call Mail.queue():

await Mail.queue(message);
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message, queue: 'emails');

The mail jobs are part of dox_mailer, so the queue provider and a worker run them.

docs.title: Running the worker
docs.text:
Start a worker to run the jobs:

dart run bin/queue.dart

Use --queue to pick the queues. The first one goes first. Use --concurrency to run more jobs at once:

dart run bin/queue.dart work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4

--concurrency runs jobs as async tasks on one thread. It helps for jobs that wait, like email, HTTP or database calls. For CPU heavy jobs, run more worker processes. See Worker flags for all flags.

The dox CLI runs the same file, with the same flags: dox queue:work, dox queue:failed, dox queue:retry <id|all>, dox queue:forget <id>, dox queue:flush, dox queue:clear [queue], dox queue:restart and dox queue:prune-failed.

docs.title: Stopping the worker
docs.text: Press Ctrl+C, or send SIGTERM (docker stop does it). The worker takes no new job, waits for the running jobs, then stops. A second signal stops it at once.

docs.title: Restarting after a deploy
docs.text:
The worker keeps your code in memory. So restart it after each deploy, or it runs the old code:

dart run bin/queue.dart restart

This tells every running worker to stop after its current jobs, and your process manager starts them again with the new code. It works through the app cache, so the workers and the command must use the same cache store, like file on one machine, or redis. The memory store does not work for it.

docs.title: Running the worker in production
docs.text:
In production, run the binary, not dart run. dox build makes build/bundle/bin/queue, next to the server. It takes the same commands and flags:

cd build/bundle
./bin/queue work --concurrency=4

Run the worker as its own process, next to the web server. For example, with Docker Compose and the image of the project Dockerfile:

services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/server
  worker:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/queue work --concurrency=4

You can also use systemd, Supervisor or a second Fly.io process. Set it to restart when it stops.

docs.title: Running jobs in the web server
docs.text:
A small app can skip the worker process. Set inProcess: true, and the first isolate of the web server runs jobs too:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  inProcess: true,
);

When the server stops, it waits for the running jobs. Only the web server runs this worker, not the scheduler process (bin/schedule.dart).

Heavy jobs slow down your API

The jobs share the isolate with web requests, so a long or CPU heavy job makes requests on that isolate slow. Use a worker process when your jobs are heavy or many.

docs.title: Dealing with failed jobs
docs.text:
When handle() throws, the worker waits the backoff time and tries again, up to tries times. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and failed() runs. A timeout counts as a failed try.

A timeout does not stop the code

Dart can not stop a running Future. After a timeout the try counts as failed, but handle() keeps running in the background until it ends. So write jobs that are safe to run twice.

If you want the worker to wait for the old run, start it with --timeout-grace=SECONDS (or set workerTimeoutGrace for the in-process worker). Keep timeout plus the grace time below retryAfter.

When a worker crashes, its job stays reserved. After retryAfter, another worker takes it, and this counts as a try.

docs.title: Retrying failed jobs
docs.text:
Failed jobs are kept until you retry or delete them. List them with failed, and put one or all of them back on their queue with retry:

dart run bin/queue.dart failed
dart run bin/queue.dart retry 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart retry all

docs.title: Deleting failed jobs
docs.text:
forget deletes one failed job, and flush deletes all of them:

dart run bin/queue.dart forget 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart flush

prune-failed deletes failed jobs older than --hours=N (default 24):

dart run bin/queue.dart prune-failed --hours=48

docs.title: Controlling the job from handle()
docs.text:
Sometimes the job itself knows what should happen next. For example, an API is busy, so the job should try again later. Add the InteractsWithQueue mixin, then call one of these in handle():

Call What it does attempts() how many times a worker took the job. The first run gives 1 release(delay) put the job back on its queue. It runs again after delay fail(error) fail the job now, with no retry. failed() runs delete() delete the job, with no retry and no failed() 
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with InteractsWithQueue {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    ReportApi api = Dox().ioc.get<ReportApi>();
    if (await api.isBusy()) {
      release(Duration(seconds: 30));
      return;
    }
    if (!await api.hasReport(reportId)) {
      delete();
      return;
    }
    await api.send(reportId);
  }
}

release() counts as a try. Because the default tries is 1, set tries above 1 (or retryUntil) when a job calls release(). If not, the job fails on its next pickup.

docs.title: Clearing jobs from a queue
docs.text:
clear deletes all jobs of a queue, also the running ones. The default queue is default:

dart run bin/queue.dart clear emails

docs.title: Job middleware
docs.text:
Job middleware wraps handle() of a job. Use it for rules that many jobs share, like a rate limit. Add the HasMiddleware mixin and list the middleware. The first one runs first:

@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with HasMiddleware {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  List<JobMiddleware> get middleware => <JobMiddleware>[
    RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
  ];

  // ...
}

The built-in middleware keeps its counts and locks in the default cache store. So all workers must use the same store: file on one machine, or redis for several servers. The memory store is per process, so the limit would not work.

A middleware that puts the job back counts as a try. So give these jobs tries above 1, or a retryUntil.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
RateLimited(key, max, per) runs at most max jobs of key in each per window. The other jobs go back on the queue until the window ends:

RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),

docs.title: Preventing job overlaps
docs.text:
WithoutOverlapping(key) runs only one job of key at a time:

WithoutOverlapping(
  'report-$reportId',
  releaseAfter: Duration(seconds: 30),
  expireAfter: Duration(minutes: 10), // longer than the longest report run
),
  • releaseAfter is when the other jobs go back on the queue. The default is zero, so at once. With releaseAfter: null, they are dropped.
  • expireAfter frees the lock after this time, also while a job still runs. The default is no expiry. Set it longer than the longest run of the job, so a crash can not hold the lock forever.
  • The key has no class name in it, so job classes with the same key share one lock. Put the class name in the key if they should not.

docs.title: Throttling exceptions
docs.text: ThrottlesExceptions(key, maxAttempts:, decay:, retryAfter:) is for jobs that call a service that is down. After maxAttempts errors (default 10), jobs of key wait until decay is over (default 10 minutes). A job that threw goes back after retryAfter (default zero).

docs.title: Writing your own middleware
docs.text:
Extend JobMiddleware. Call next() to go on. If you do not call it, the job is skipped and counts as done. Call release(job, delay) to put the job back on the queue:

class SkipAtNight extends JobMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<void> handle(DoxJob job, JobNext next) async {
    if (DateTime.now().hour < 6) {
      release(job, Duration(hours: 1));
      return;
    }
    await next();
  }
}

docs.title: Unique jobs
docs.text:
Some jobs should wait in the queue only once, like "rebuild the search index of product 5". Add the ShouldBeUnique mixin. While a job with the same class and uniqueId waits or runs, dispatch() pushes nothing and returns '':

@Job()
class UpdateSearchIndex extends DoxJob with ShouldBeUnique {
  UpdateSearchIndex({required this.productId});

  final int productId;

  @override
  String get uniqueId => '$productId';

  @override
  Duration? get uniqueFor => Duration(hours: 1);

  // ...
}
  • uniqueId is the key next to the class. The default is empty, so only one job of the class at a time.
  • uniqueFor ends the lock after a time, also when the job never ran. You should set it, because the lock of a crashed worker never ends without it.
  • The worker frees the lock when the job is done, deleted or failed for good. A release or a retry keeps it.
  • The lock is in the default cache store, so the web app and the workers must use the same store, like redis.

If a new job may be queued while the old one runs, use ShouldBeUniqueUntilProcessing in place of ShouldBeUnique. It frees the lock when a worker starts the job.

docs.title: Job chaining
docs.text:
A chain runs jobs one after the other. The next job is pushed only when the job before it is done. If a job fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped and the catch job runs:

await Queue.chain(<DoxJob>[
  ResizeImage(imageId: 1),
  UploadImage(imageId: 1),
  TellUser(imageId: 1),
]).catchError(TellAdmin(imageId: 1)).dispatch(queue: 'images');

The rest of the chain is saved in the job that runs now, so the chain works across worker processes and restarts. dispatch() returns the id of the first job. queue and connection count for every job, but delay counts for the first job only.

Each job carries the data of the jobs after it. So keep chains short, and save ids in the jobs, not big data. Give chain jobs more than one try, and make them safe to run twice.

docs.title: Handling chain failures
docs.text:
A function can not be saved in the queue. So the catch handler is a job too, of a class in jobRegistry. Add the CatchesError mixin to read the error:

@Job()
class TellAdmin extends DoxJob with CatchesError {
  TellAdmin({required this.imageId});

  final int imageId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await alertAdmin('image $imageId failed: $caughtError');
  }
}

The catch job runs once, in the worker where the job failed, with no queue and no retry. An error in it is logged. For slow work, dispatch a new job from it.

queue:retry of the failed job brings the chain back. When the job is then done, the chain goes on.

docs.title: Job batching
docs.text:
A batch runs many jobs and acts when they are all done. Batches need dox_queue_database and the job_batches table, with every driver. Without the package, Queue.batch() throws a StateError.

Batch batch = await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[
  ImportRows(from: 0),
  ImportRows(from: 1000),
  ImportRows(from: 2000),
])
    .name('import')
    .then(ImportDone())
    .catchError(ImportFailed())
    .whenComplete(CleanUpImport())
    .dispatch(queue: 'imports');

print(batch.id);

The batch is saved in the job_batches table of the QueueConfig.connection database, also with the Redis and sync drivers.

docs.title: Batch callbacks
docs.text:
These callbacks run at the steps of a batch:

Callback Runs before(job) once, at dispatch(), before the jobs are pushed progress(job) each time a job is done. With allowFailures(), also when one fails then(job) once, when every job is done catchError(job) once, when the first job fails for good whenComplete(job) once, when every job ran, done or failed

A function can not be saved in the queue, so each callback is a job of a class in jobRegistry. It runs once, with no queue and no retry. An error in a callback is logged. Add Batchable to read the batch, and CatchesError to read the error:

@Job()
class ImportFailed extends DoxJob with Batchable, CatchesError {
  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    await alertAdmin('import ${batch?.name} failed: $caughtError');
  }
}

docs.title: Defining batchable jobs
docs.text:
Add the Batchable mixin to a job to read its batch. batchId is the id, and batch() reads the batch as it is now. For example, a job can skip its work when the batch was cancelled:

@Job()
class ImportRows extends DoxJob with Batchable {
  ImportRows({required this.from});

  final int from;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    if (batch?.cancelled ?? false) return;
    await importRows(from);
  }
}

docs.title: Inspecting batches
docs.text:
A Batch has these fields:

Field What it holds id, name the id and the name totalJobs how many jobs the batch has pendingJobs how many jobs are not done. It also counts failed jobs, because they can be retried failedJobs how many jobs failed processedJobs how many jobs are done. Failed jobs are not counted progress the percent of done jobs, from 0 to 100 finished true when every job ran, or the batch was cancelled cancelled true after cancel(), or after a first failure

A Batch shows the state at the time it was read. To read it again, use Queue.findBatch(id). It gives null when there is no such batch.

docs.title: Cancelling batches
docs.text: The first job that fails for good cancels the batch. If you want the batch to go on, add allowFailures(). You can also cancel a batch yourself with cancel(). This does not stop the jobs: they still run and count, so a Batchable job should read cancelled to skip its work.

docs.title: Adding jobs to a batch
docs.text: add(jobs) adds jobs to a batch, for example from a job of the batch. They go on the queue and connection of the batch. It throws a StateError when the batch is finished, cancelled or deleted.

docs.title: Chains in a batch
docs.text:
Use chain(jobs) to put a chain in a batch. Its jobs run one after the other, and the batch counts the chain as one job:

await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[ImportUsers()])
    .chain(<DoxJob>[ImportOrders(), SumOrders()])
    .dispatch();

When a job of the chain fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped, and the batch counts one failed job.

docs.title: Pruning batches
docs.text:
Old batch rows stay in the table until you delete them. prune-batches deletes batches that finished, or were cancelled, more than --hours ago (default 24). Add --unfinished to also delete batches that never finished and were made more than that many hours ago:

dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48 --unfinished=168

In code, use Queue.pruneBatches(before, unfinishedBefore:).

docs.title: Queue events
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to log or count jobs. Listen to the steps of a job:

Queue.before((QueueEvent event) => print('start ${event.name} ${event.id}'));
Queue.after((QueueEvent event) => print('done ${event.name}'));
Queue.failing((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.name, event.error));
Hook When Queue.queued dispatch() pushed a job Queue.before a worker starts a job Queue.after a worker finished a job and deleted it Queue.released a worker put a job back (release() or a retry) Queue.exceptionOccurred handle() threw and the job will be tried again Queue.failing a job failed for good Queue.looping a worker is about to take the next job Queue.stopping a worker stops

Listeners are per isolate. So register them where the app starts, like in a provider. Then the web app and each worker have them. A listener can be async, and a listener that throws is only logged. See Event details for the fields of QueueEvent.

docs.title: Batch events
docs.text:
A batch has its own events. In them, event.batch is the batch after the step:

Queue.batchProgress((QueueEvent event) {
  Batch batch = event.batch!;
  print('${batch.name}: ${batch.progress}%');
});
Queue.batchFailed((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.batch!.id, event.error));
Hook When Where it fires Queue.batchDispatched the batch was saved, before its jobs are pushed the process that called dispatch() Queue.batchProgress a job (or a chain) of the batch is done. With allowFailures(), also when one failed the worker that counted it Queue.batchFailed the first job failed for good. event.error is its error the worker that counted it Queue.batchCancelled the batch was cancelled: cancel(), the first failure without allowFailures(), or a push that threw the process that cancelled it Queue.batchFinished every job ran, done or failed the worker that counted the last job

Each event fires once per step, also with many workers. When one failure cancels the batch, batchFailed fires first, then batchCancelled.

docs.title: Queue connections
docs.text:
Sometimes one app needs more than one queue store. The config is the main connection. Add more in connections, by name:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  connections: <String, QueueConfig>{
    'database': QueueConfig(driver: 'database'),
  },
);

Pick a connection when you dispatch. With no connection, the job goes to the main connection. An unknown name throws an ArgumentError:

await SendReport(reportId: 1).dispatch(connection: 'database');

Run a worker for each connection. Every command of bin/queue.dart takes --connection:

dart run bin/queue.dart work
dart run bin/queue.dart work --connection=database
dart run bin/queue.dart failed --connection=database
  • An entry uses only driver, redis, prefix, connection (the dox_orm one), retryAfter, serializeSync and failedAtTimestamp. The jobs of the main config count for all connections.
  • The in-process worker (inProcess) runs the jobs of the main connection only.
  • Two database connections on the same dox_orm connection share the jobs and failed_jobs tables. So give each one its own dox_orm connection.

docs.title: Using the queue without Dox
docs.text:
dox_queue also works in a plain Dart app. Add build_runner and dox_builder, so it writes lib/generated/jobs.g.dart:

dart pub add dox_queue dox_core
dart pub add dev:build_runner dev:dox_builder

Write your jobs as in Creating jobs, and run dart run build_runner build. Then set up the queue and run a worker yourself:

import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:my_app/jobs/resize_image.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // the worker logs with the Dox logger, so it needs an AppConfig
  Dox().initialize(AppConfig(appKey: 'not-used'));

  Queue.configure(QueueConfig(
    driver: 'redis',
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    redis: RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379),
  ));

  await ResizeImage(path: 'photo.png').dispatch();

  Worker worker = Worker(
    driver: Queue.driver,
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    options: WorkerOptions(queues: <String>['default'], concurrency: 4),
  );

  // Ctrl+C: finish the running jobs, then stop
  StreamSubscription<ProcessSignal> signal =
      ProcessSignal.sigint.watch().listen((_) => worker.stop());
  await worker.run();
  await signal.cancel();
  await Queue.close();
}
  • WorkerOptions takes the same settings as the flags of work: queues, concurrency, once, tries, timeout, sleep and stopWhenEmpty.
  • The database driver needs dox_queue_database. There are no providers here, so call QueueDatabase.register() before Queue.configure(). It uses the default dox_orm connection, so set that up first with SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(...).
  • No services are in the Dox container, so make the services of a job in handle().

docs.title: Running jobs in tests
docs.text:
Use the sync driver. dispatch() then runs the job at once, so you can check the result right after:

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUp(() {
    Queue.configure(QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry));
  });

  test('sends the welcome email', () async {
    await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch();
    // check the email was sent
  });
}

A job that uses Dox() (for example Dox().ioc or Logger) needs the app config. Call Dox().initialize(appConfig) in setUpAll.

The sync driver runs the job object as it is. So a job that is not in jobRegistry, or a field that is not JSON, works here and fails later in the worker. Set serializeSync: true to save the job and read it back before it runs, the way a worker gets it. Then dispatch() throws for such a job:

Queue.configure(
  QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry, serializeSync: true),
);

To test a job alone, call handle():

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).handle();

docs.title: Faking the queue
docs.text:
If you only want to check that your code dispatched a job, without running it, use Queue.fake(). It records every dispatch() in a list, and needs no Queue.configure():

late QueueFake queue;

setUp(() {
  queue = Queue.fake();
});

tearDown(Queue.restore);

test('signing up queues the welcome email', () async {
  await signUp(userId: 1);

  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>();
  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>(
    (SendWelcomeEmail job) => job.userId == 1,
  );
  queue.assertPushedTimes<SendWelcomeEmail>(1);
  queue.assertNotPushed<SendInvoice>();
});
Method Checks assertPushed<T>([test]) a T job was pushed. With test, one of them passes it assertPushedTimes<T>(n) exactly n T jobs were pushed assertNotPushed<T>() no T job was pushed assertNothingPushed() no job was pushed at all assertChained(<Type>[A, B]) a chain of exactly these job classes, in this order, was dispatched assertBatched([test]) a batch was dispatched. With test, one of them passes it. test gets a PendingBatch assertBatchedChain(<Type>[A, B]) a batch has a chain of exactly these job classes, in this order assertBatchCount(n) exactly n batches were dispatched

To read the jobs, use queue.pushed. Each item has the job, the queue name and the delay. queue.jobsOf<T>() gives the T jobs, queue.clear() forgets them, and Queue.restore() stops the fake.

The fake does not encode the job. So a job that is missing from QueueConfig.jobs, or has data that is not JSON, passes a faked test but fails for real.

docs.title: Testing the queue itself
docs.text:
To test the real queue, use the database driver of dox_queue_database with SQLite :memory:. Then run a worker that stops when the queue is empty:

await Worker(
  driver: Queue.driver,
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  options: WorkerOptions(stopWhenEmpty: true),
).run();

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: All options
docs.text: Option Default What it does driver sync sync, database (needs dox_queue_database) or redis jobs empty jobRegistry from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart redis 127.0.0.1:6379 RedisOptions(host: ..., port: ..., password: ...) for the redis driver. QueueConfig.redisFromEnv() reads it from the env prefix dox_queue: the start of every Redis key connection default the dox_orm connection name, for dox_queue_database retryAfter 90 seconds when a worker does not finish a job in this time, another worker can take it inProcess false run a worker inside the web server, see Running jobs in the web server workerQueues ['default'] the queues of the in-process worker workerConcurrency 1 jobs at once in the in-process worker workerTimeoutGrace none the --timeout-grace wait of the in-process worker serializeSync false the sync driver saves the job and reads it back before it runs connections none more queue connections by name, see Queue connections afterCommit false push jobs that are dispatched inside a transaction only after it commits (needs dox_queue_database) failedAtTimestamp false the failed_at column is a timestamp, not a number, see The failed_at column

docs.title: Worker flags
docs.text:
Flag Default What it does --queue=high,default default the queues to work. The first one goes first --concurrency=4 1 jobs at once in this process --once off run one job, then stop --tries=3 1 tries of a job that does not set tries --timeout=60 60 max run time in seconds of a job that does not set timeout --sleep=3 3 seconds to wait when the queues are empty --max-sleep=30 off when the queues stay empty, double the sleep on each empty poll, up to this many seconds. A job sets it back to --sleep --stop-when-empty off stop when the queues are empty --timeout-grace=10 none after a timeout, wait up to this many seconds for the old run to end before the next try --backoff=1,5,10 none seconds to wait before each retry of a job that does not set backoff --max-jobs=1000 off stop after this many jobs --max-time=3600 off stop after this many seconds --memory=256 off stop when the process uses more than this many MB --connection=name main the queue connection to use

With --max-jobs, --max-time and --memory, the worker stops after its running jobs, so let your process manager start it again.

docs.title: Worker details
docs.text:
• The worker logs one warning when a job may run longer than retryAfter (the --timeout, the timeout of a job class, and the grace time all count). Then a second worker can take the job while the first one still runs it. Raise retryAfter or lower the timeout.
  • While the worker waits for --timeout-grace, it takes no other job. If timeout plus the grace time is above retryAfter, another worker can take the job while this one waits.
  • When a crashed worker's job has no tries left, it fails with a message that the worker did not finish.
  • restart writes a time to the app cache, and each worker reads it every 3 seconds.
  • With InteractsWithQueue, the worker does the call when handle() ends. When you call more than one, the last one wins. A call also wins over an error that handle() throws after it. When handle() times out, the call is dropped.
  • With dispatchSync(), dispatchAfterResponse() and the sync driver there is no queue. There attempts() is 1, release() and delete() do nothing, and fail() only runs failed().
  • In a test file, package:test has its own fail(). Inside a job class with InteractsWithQueue, write this.fail(...) to make it clear which one you call.
  • Job middleware also runs with the sync driver, dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse(). There is no queue there, so a release logs a warning and handle() does not run.
  • dispatchAfterResponse() works because QueueProvider turns on AfterResponse. Outside a request, the job runs soon.

docs.title: Dispatch after the commit details
docs.text:
• afterCommit needs dox_queue_database. Without it, a dispatch with afterCommit on throws a StateError.
  • A job that is not in the registry, or data that is not JSON, throws at dispatch(), not at the commit.
  • When the push fails after the commit, the QueryBuilder.transaction() call throws that error. The data stays saved.
  • It waits only for a transaction on the default dox_orm connection, opened with no connection: name. A transaction opened by name pushes the job at once.
  • The sync driver runs the job after the commit. A sync chain runs as a whole after the commit, and gets a new id.
  • A batch saves its job_batches row and pushes its jobs after the commit. A rollback drops it all. Before the commit, the returned Batch is not saved yet.
  • dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() do not wait for a commit.
  • Queue.fake() keeps the job when you call dispatch(), also when the transaction later rolls back.
  • It works through QueryBuilder.afterCommit() of dox_orm.

docs.title: Unique job details
docs.text:
• clear frees the locks of the jobs it deletes. retry of a failed job does not take the lock.
  • dispatchSync() ignores uniqueness.
  • With afterCommit inside a transaction, the lock is taken at the commit. dispatch() returns the id at once, also when the job is then skipped.
  • Queue.fake() keeps its own locks and needs no cache.

docs.title: Chain details
docs.text:
• A job that is released or retried keeps the chain. A job that ends with delete(), or that a middleware skips, counts as done, so the chain goes on.
  • The sync driver runs the jobs now, one after the other. When one throws, the catch job runs and dispatch() throws the error.
  • A ShouldBeEncrypted job stays encrypted inside the job before it.
  • A skipped unique job stops the chain, and the catch job runs with a StateError. When the first job is skipped, dispatch() returns '' and nothing runs.
  • A next job that can not be read, for example because its class was removed, stops the chain. The catch job runs with the error.
  • The worker pushes the next job before it deletes the job that is done. So a crash between the two can run the next job twice.
  • When the push of the next job fails, the try of the current job counts as failed, and the job is tried again.
  • The unique lock of a job is freed before the next job is pushed. So a next job with the same unique id is not skipped.

docs.title: Batch details
docs.text:
• A failed job that you retry with queue:retry is not counted again when it fails again. When it is done, pendingJobs and failedJobs both go down by one, so catchError can run again on a later failure.
  • An empty batch throws an ArgumentError, because it would never finish.
  • then and whenComplete run once, also with many workers, because each count changes in one atomic step.
  • A skipped unique job is taken out of the counts. When it was the last open job, then and whenComplete run. In a chain of a batch, a skipped first job takes the chain out of the counts, and a skipped later job fails the chain.
  • When a push fails in dispatch() or add(), the jobs that were not pushed are taken out of the counts. The batch is cancelled and the error is thrown. The jobs that were pushed still run.
  • A job that runs twice, for example when it runs longer than retryAfter, can be counted twice. failedJobs never goes below 0.
  • The batch is marked finished before then and whenComplete run, so add() from a callback throws a StateError. add() takes jobs only, not chains.
  • When a worker crashes after a job is done and before it counted the job, the batch keeps that job as pending, and then never runs. Delete such batches with prune-batches --unfinished.
  • The sync driver runs the jobs at dispatch() and counts them. A job that throws counts as failed, and dispatch() does not throw.
  • In Queue.fake(), chains are in queue.chains and batches in queue.batches, and the chains of a batch in PendingBatch.chains. Nothing is saved or run. In a faked batch, add() adds to the batch, cancel() does nothing and Queue.findBatch() gives null.

docs.title: Event details
docs.text:
A listener gets a QueueEvent:

Field What it holds type the kind of event job the job. null for looping and stopping, and when the worker can not read the job name the job name of the registry id the job id queue the queue name attempts the try number. 0 for queued, looping and stopping error, stack the error and its stack trace, for exceptionOccurred and failing. batchFailed has error only delay the wait, for queued and released batch the Batch, for the batch events. null for other events
  • The sync driver, dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() fire no job events. The sync driver does fire the batch events, all in the process that called dispatch().
  • Queue.fake() fires no events.
  • Queue.forgetListeners() removes all listeners, for example between tests.

docs.title: Fake details
docs.text:
• dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() still run the job under the fake. Their jobs are in queue.dispatchedSync and queue.dispatchedAfterResponse, not in queue.pushed.
  • Queue.fake() keeps the connection name in PushedJob.connection.
  • The fake also catches Mail.queue() on the default queue, but only when Mail.fake() is off. It does not catch a custom queue set with Mail.useQueue(). See Mail.

docs.title: How the drivers store jobs
docs.text:
• Database: jobs are rows in jobs, failed jobs are rows in failed_jobs. On Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB a worker takes a job with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so many workers do not wait on each other. On SQLite a worker takes a job with one UPDATE ... RETURNING. SQLite runs one write at a time, so this is safe for small apps.
  • Redis: each queue has a list of ready jobs, a sorted set of delayed jobs and a sorted set of reserved jobs. A Lua script takes a job, so two workers never get the same one. Failed jobs are in the hash dox_queue:failed.
  • failed_jobs.connection has the name of the queue connection, or NULL for the main one. A table without this column works too, but then the name is not saved, and failed --connection=X lists all failed jobs of the table. A worker checks for the column once, so restart the workers after you add it:
await schema.table('failed_jobs', (Table table) {
  table.string('connection').nullable();
});

docs.title: The failed_at column
docs.text:
failed_jobs.failed_at is the time the job failed. By default it is a big integer with unix time in milliseconds. If you want a UTC timestamp, pass failedAtTimestamp: true to QueueTables.up in the migration, and set it in the queue config too:

await QueueTables.up(schema, failedAtTimestamp: true);

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  failedAtTimestamp: true,
);

FailedJob.failedAt is the same DateTime with both types. Each entry of connections has its own failedAtTimestamp.

The setting and the column must match

A worker reads the column type once, when it first uses failed_jobs. If the setting does not match the column, fail, failed, retry, forget and prune-failed throw a StateError, and nothing is written. A job that fails all its tries is NOT moved to failed_jobs, and its failed() does not run. It stays in jobs and runs again after retryAfter, until the setting matches.

If the type can not be read (for example, the connection dropped), the worker tries again on the next call. With the setting off, it logs a warning and goes on. With the setting on, the call throws.

Database Column How the time is kept SQLite TIMESTAMP ISO text in UTC, with milliseconds Postgres TIMESTAMP (without time zone) the UTC time, with milliseconds MySQL, MariaDB TIMESTAMP whole seconds, in UTC. The queue writes it with FROM_UNIXTIME() and reads it with UNIX_TIMESTAMP(), so the session time zone does not change the time. A MySQL and MariaDB TIMESTAMP can not hold a time after 2038-01-19

To change an existing integer column to a timestamp:

  1. Stop all workers, on every server. Stop the app too when it has inProcess: true. A worker that still runs writes numbers into the timestamp column, and on SQLite this gives no error.
  2. Run the SQL for your database below, in a new migration (await schema.driver.execute('...'); for each line) or in a database client.
  3. Set failedAtTimestamp: true in the queue config.
  4. Start the workers again.

SQLite (3.35 or newer). The new column allows NULL, because SQLite can not add a NOT NULL column without a default. The queue never writes NULL there:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%fZ', failed_at / 1000.0, 'unixepoch');
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs RENAME COLUMN failed_at_utc TO failed_at;

Postgres:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ALTER COLUMN failed_at TYPE TIMESTAMP USING to_timestamp(failed_at / 1000.0) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';

MySQL and MariaDB:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP NULL;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = FROM_UNIXTIME(failed_at DIV 1000);
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs CHANGE failed_at_utc failed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL;

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
dox_scheduler runs your tasks on a schedule, so you do not need a cron line for each task.

You write the whole schedule in Dart, in one file, and each task is a plain function. One small process runs the schedule. A task runs only once per tick, even when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the package with the dox CLI. A new app from dox create already has it:

dox add scheduler

It adds the package and writes three files. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

  • lib/config/schedule.dart: your tasks and the ScheduleConfig. See Defining tasks.
  • bin/schedule.dart: the program that runs the schedule. See Running the scheduler.
  • lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart (optional): runs the schedule inside the server. See Run inside the server.

If you want to set it up by hand, add the package and write these files yourself:

dart pub add dox_scheduler

docs.title: Defining tasks
docs.text:
Put your tasks in the schedule function in lib/config/schedule.dart. Use s.call(name, function) to add a task, then chain a frequency:

lib/config/schedule.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}

The name must be unique, because it is used in the logs and in the lock keys. A task with no frequency runs every minute.

docs.title: Scheduling queued jobs
docs.text:
If a task is slow, you can put a queue job on the queue instead. Wrap the dispatch in a function, so the task only adds the job and a queue worker runs it:

s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();

To use another queue connection, pass connection: to dispatch():

s.call('prune', () => PruneFiles().dispatch(connection: 'redis')).hourly();

docs.title: Scheduling shell commands
docs.text:
Use exec to run a program. A non-zero exit code fails the task:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['-f', 'backup.sql', 'mydb']).daily();

No shell is used, so |, > and * are plain text. If you need a shell, run it yourself:

s.exec('sh', args: <String>['-c', 'pg_dump mydb | gzip > backup.sql.gz']).daily();

docs.title: Scheduling dox commands
docs.text:
Use command to run a dox command of your app. It runs as the process dox <command> <args>:

s.command('queue:prune', args: <String>['--hours=48']).hourly();

The task name is the command line, like dox queue:prune --hours=48, and it shows in the logs and in list. So if args holds a secret, give the task your own name:

s.command('sync', args: <String>['--token=$token'], name: 'sync');

The output of exec and command tasks is dropped. Use the output hooks to keep it.

docs.title: Frequency options
docs.text:
Chain one of these methods to say how often a task runs:

Method Runs everySecond() every second. Also everyTwoSeconds, everyFiveSeconds, everyTenSeconds, everyFifteenSeconds, everyTwentySeconds, everyThirtySeconds everyMinute() every minute (the default) everyTwoMinutes() every 2 minutes everyThreeMinutes() every 3 minutes everyFourMinutes() every 4 minutes everyFiveMinutes() every 5 minutes everyTenMinutes() every 10 minutes everyFifteenMinutes() every 15 minutes everyThirtyMinutes() at minute 0 and 30 hourly() at minute 0 of every hour hourlyAt(17) at minute 17 of every hour everyTwoHours() every 2 hours at minute 0. Also everyThreeHours, everyFourHours, everySixHours. Pass a minute: everyTwoHours(15) everyOddHour() at 01:00, 03:00 ... 23:00. Pass a minute: everyOddHour(30) daily() every day at 00:00 dailyAt('13:00') every day at 13:00 twiceDaily(1, 13) every day at 01:00 and 13:00 twiceDailyAt(1, 13, 15) every day at 01:15 and 13:15 at('13:00') same as dailyAt('13:00') weekly() every Sunday at 00:00 weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00') every Monday at 08:00 monthly() the 1st of every month at 00:00 monthlyOn(15, '12:00') the 15th of every month at 12:00 twiceMonthly(1, 16, '13:00') the 1st and 16th of every month at 13:00 lastDayOfMonth('15:00') the last day of every month at 15:00 quarterly() January, April, July and October 1st at 00:00 quarterlyOn(4, '14:00') January, April, July and October 4th at 14:00 yearly() January 1st at 00:00 yearlyOn(6, 1, '17:00') June 1st at 17:00 cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5') any 5 field cron expression

docs.title: Day constraints
docs.text:
If a task should run only on some days, add a day method:

Method Runs weekdays() Monday to Friday weekends() Saturday and Sunday mondays() ... sundays() only on that day of the week days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday]) only on these days 
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');

A day method and a time method like dailyAt() can come in any order.

docs.title: Sub-minute tasks
docs.text:
A task with a seconds method, like everyFiveSeconds(), repeats inside each due minute. You can still limit the minutes with a frequency, days or filters. Call the seconds method first, because it also sets the task to every minute:

s.call('poll', poll).everyFiveSeconds().between('09:00', '17:00');

docs.title: Cron expressions
docs.text:
cron() takes the standard 5 fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

Field Values minute 0-59 hour 0-23 day of month 1-31 month 1-12 or JAN-DEC day of week 0-7 or SUN-SAT (0 and 7 are Sunday)

Each field takes *, a number 5, a range 1-5, a list 1,15, and a step */15 or 0-30/10.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The schedule uses UTC by default. Use timezone() to read the time of a task in another zone:

s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');

The name is an IANA name, like Europe/London or America/New_York. An unknown name throws an ArgumentError when the schedule starts.

To use one zone for every task, set it in the config. A task's own timezone() still wins:

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');

docs.title: Between times
docs.text:
Use between to run a task only in one time of day. Use unlessBetween to skip a time of day. Both ends are included, and a range can cross midnight:

s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00');
s.call('quiet', quiet).hourly().unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00');

docs.title: Truth tests
docs.text:
Sometimes a task should run only when a condition is true. when runs the task when the function gives true, and skip skips it when the function gives true. The function can give a bool or a Future<bool>:

s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Use environments to run a task only when APP_ENV is one of the names. When APP_ENV is not set, the task does not run:

s.call('emails', sendEmails).daily().environments(<String>['production']);

docs.title: Preventing task overlaps
docs.text:
A slow task may still run when its next minute comes. If it must not run twice at the same time, use withoutOverlapping. The task is then skipped while the last run still runs:

s.call('report', sendReport).everyFiveMinutes().withoutOverlapping();

The lock expires after 24 hours, in case the process dies. You can pass another expiry: withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1)). After a crash, remove the lock at once with clear-cache.

docs.title: Running tasks on one server
docs.text:
A task runs only once per tick across all isolates and servers. This is on by default (onOneServer()). Before a task runs, the scheduler takes a lock named after the task and the minute. The first process to get it runs the task, and the others skip it.

The locks live in a cache store. If many servers run the schedule, use a shared store like Redis, because a memory or file store is not shared between servers:

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis');

If a task should run on every process instead, use onEveryServer():

s.call('clear-tmp', clearTmp).hourly().onEveryServer();

docs.title: Background tasks
docs.text:
Tasks of the same minute run one after another. If a long task should not hold back the next one, use runInBackground:

s.call('export', export).daily().runInBackground();

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Use timeout to count a run as failed when it takes too long. The failure hooks then run:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().timeout(Duration(minutes: 5));

For an exec() or command() task, the process is killed at the timeout. A Dart function can not be stopped, so its work may go on after the timeout.

docs.title: Running the scheduler
docs.text:
bin/schedule.dart runs your schedule. With app, the runner starts your app providers first (like the database), and it stops them at the end:

bin/schedule.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

The dox CLI runs the same file. For example, dox schedule:work is the same as dart run bin/schedule.dart work.

docs.title: Running the worker
docs.text:
work is a long running process. It wakes at each full minute and runs the due tasks. Run it next to your server, with the same deploy tool (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes):

dox schedule:work

On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM it starts no new task and waits for the running ones. A second signal stops it at once.

docs.title: Running from cron
docs.text:
If you would rather use the system cron, run runs the tasks of this minute once, waits for them, and exits. Add one line to the crontab:

* * * * * cd /path/to/app/build/bundle && ./bin/schedule run

./bin/schedule is the binary that dox build makes in build/bundle. It starts fast and needs no Dart SDK. Do not use dart compile exe, because it can not build apps with native libraries like SQLite. The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

docs.title: Listing tasks
docs.text:
list shows each task, its schedule and its next run time:

dox schedule:list

Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon

docs.title: Running one task now
docs.text:
test runs one task now, with its hooks. It does not check the schedule, the filters or the locks:

dox schedule:test cleanup

docs.title: Clearing overlap locks
docs.text:
If the process crashed while a task ran, its withoutOverlapping() lock stays in the store, so the task is skipped until the lock expires. clear-cache removes these locks:

dox schedule:clear-cache

Only run it when the task does not really run on another process or server. Otherwise that task could start a second time.

docs.title: Run inside the server
docs.text:
For a small app, you can run the schedule inside your Dox server instead of a work process. Add a provider that extends SchedulerProvider:

lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleProvider extends SchedulerProvider {
  ScheduleProvider() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}

Then turn it on in the config, and run dart run build_runner build so the generated container finds the provider:

lib/config/schedule.dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);

Only the first isolate of the web server runs the tasks, and the other isolates only serve requests. A bin/queue.dart worker, a test or the work process does not start this in-process schedule. The work process runs the tasks on its own. In a test of the in-process schedule, set Dox().isWebServer = true; first. With many servers, each server runs the loop, and the once-per-tick lock makes each task run once. Use a Redis store for this. When the server stops, it waits for the running tasks.

The tasks use the CPU of the server, so they can slow down requests on the first isolate. A separate work process can be deployed, scaled and restarted on its own. So use work for heavy tasks.

docs.title: Logging the schedule
docs.text:
By default the scheduler prints its own plain [schedule] lines. To send them through the app Logger instead, turn on loggerLines:

lib/config/schedule.dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(
  flags: SchedulerFlags(loggerLines: true),
);

The lines get the tag [scheduler], for example [scheduler] ran cleanup in 12ms. They follow LoggerConfig.enabled, level and prettyPrint. SchedulerFlags.all() turns on every flag.

docs.title: Task output
docs.text:
These hooks keep the output (stdout and stderr) of an exec() or command() task. They do nothing on a function task.

Use sendOutputTo to write the output to a file. It replaces the file each run:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().sendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');

Use appendOutputTo to add the output to the end of the file:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().appendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');

Use onOutput to get the output in code after the process ends. It holds the whole output in memory, so do not use it for a very large output:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().onOutput((String output) {...});

docs.title: Task hooks
docs.text:
Hooks run code around a task, for example to log it or to alert your team when it fails:

s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
Hook Runs before before the task. If it throws, the task does not run and counts as failed onSuccess after the task worked onFailure after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace after after the task, always

An error in a task is logged, and the next task still runs.

docs.title: Pinging URLs
docs.text:
You can send a GET request to a URL around a task, for example to a health check service:

s
    .call('backup', backup)
    .daily()
    .pingBefore('https://health.example.com/backup/start')
    .pingOnSuccess('https://health.example.com/backup')
    .pingOnFailure('https://health.example.com/backup/fail');

thenPing(url) pings after the task, always. Each ping method also has an If form that takes a bool first, like pingOnFailureIf(isProduction, url). A failed ping is logged, but it never fails the task.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_scheduler also works in a plain Dart app. Leave out app:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old files, ...
}

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule).run(args);
}

With no app, no providers start, and the locks use a memory store. For many servers, pass a shared CacheStore from dox_cache, like SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule, store: myRedisStore). The commands are the same.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Scheduler runs the tasks. Give it a fake clock, so you can test a schedule with no waiting:

import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule(timezone: scheduleConfig.timezone);
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});

To check a schedule without running anything, use ScheduledTask.isDue(time) and ScheduledTask.nextRun(time). To replace the ping request in tests, set ScheduledTask.sendPing = (Uri url) async {...};.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Frequencies
docs.text:
• The day methods, weekly(), weeklyOn() and cron() all set the day of the week. The last call wins: .mondays().weekly() runs on Sundays.
  • weekly() and weeklyOn() also set the time (00:00 unless you pass one). So .dailyAt('09:00').weekly() runs at 00:00, but .weekly().dailyAt('09:00') runs at 09:00.
  • A day of the month and a day of the week join with OR, like standard cron: monthlyOn(15).fridays() and 0 0 1 * MON run on that date and on every such weekday. When one day field of a cron expression starts with *, both must match.
  • lastDayOfMonth() runs only on the last day of the month, whatever day methods you add. list shows it as 28-31, but the next run time is right.
