  • yearlyOn() with a day the month never has, like yearlyOn(2, 30), throws.
  • A seconds method called last undoes the frequency before it: .everyFiveSeconds().hourly() repeats in minute 0 of each hour, but .hourly().everyFiveSeconds() repeats in every minute.
  • With a sub-minute task, when() and skip() are checked before each repeat. A run that takes longer than its step skips the steps it missed. run from cron then stays until the end of the minute, and work also wakes inside the minute.
  • With summer time (DST), a time that does not exist that day does not run, and a time that happens twice runs once. hourly() and other "every" frequencies keep running every real hour.
  • The zone data comes from the timezone package.

docs.title: Filters and locks
docs.text:
• environments() ignores case and spaces around the names. It is read at run time. An empty list or a blank name throws.
  • With loggerLines on, the plain [schedule] line is left out on stdout and stderr when the Logger printed it. So the lock store warning goes to stdout, not to stderr. Other sinks (like a StringBuffer) still get every plain line.
  • The once-per-tick lock is not released, so a late server can not run the same minute again. It expires after 10 minutes. When the store is null, the scheduler uses a memory store.
  • At start, the scheduler prints one warning to stderr when a task uses onOneServer() and the lock store is memory, file or null. It does not print when APP_ENV is development or local. With one server you can ignore it.
  • clear-cache removes only the withoutOverlapping() lock of each task, by its exact name. Other cache keys and the once-per-tick locks stay. It exits with 0, also when there was no lock. A memory store loses its locks with the process, so clear-cache is for file and Redis stores.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text:
• The stdin of an exec() or command() process is closed, so a program that waits for input ends at once.
  • At a timeout the process gets SIGTERM, and SIGKILL 5 seconds later (Schedule.processGrace). Only the process itself is killed, so the children of a shell (sh -c 'a | b') may live on.
  • A stop of work waits for the processes to end.
  • If dox is not on PATH, set its full path: Schedule.doxExecutable = '/usr/local/bin/dox';.
  • A name: also lets you add the same command line twice.

docs.title: Output and pings
docs.text:
• The file gets the output as it comes. Two runs at the same time write to the same file, so use withoutOverlapping() or appendOutputTo().
  • A file that can not be written fails the task, and so does a throwing onOutput hook. onOutput still gets the output first. When more than one thing fails, the error is the first of: a non-zero exit code, an onOutput error, a file error.
  • After a timeout, the file and onOutput finish a bit later, after the failure hooks ran. An error there is lost.
  • A ping fails after 10 seconds (ScheduledTask.pingTimeout), or on a status of 400 or more. A URL that is not http or https throws an ArgumentError when the schedule is made.
  • The next run time in list checks the frequency, between() and unlessBetween(). It does not check when(), skip() and environments().

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
This page shows how to test a Dox app with the test package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

Dox starts your real app inside the test, so you can send requests to it and check the answers. Helpers for the cache, storage and the database let each test start from a clean state.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app from dox create already has the test package. In another app, add it as a dev dependency:

dart pub add dev:test

Put your tests in the test/ folder and run them with dart test:

dart test

docs.title: Creating a test
docs.text:
Use dox make:test to make a test file. It writes test/ping_test.dart, which already starts the app with a DoxTestClient:

dox make:test Ping

If the test does not need the app, add --unit to get a plain test. See dox make:test.

docs.title: Test HTTP routes
docs.text:
DoxTestClient from package:dox_core/testing.dart starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it. Start it once in setUpAll and close it in tearDownAll:

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });

  test('POST /api/posts', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/posts',
      body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'My first post.'},
    );
    res.expectStatus(201).expectJson(containsPair('title', 'Hello'));
  });
}

DoxTestClient.start(appConfig) runs your providers and adds your routes, the same as a real start. client.close() stops the server and runs shutdown() of every provider, so for example the database is closed.

docs.title: Making requests
docs.text:
The client has get, post, put, patch and delete. The path can have a query, like '/api/users?page=2'. For any other method, use send:

await client.get('/api/users?page=2');
await client.send('OPTIONS', '/api/users');

A Map or List body is sent as JSON. A String or List<int> body is sent as it is.

Redirects are not followed, so you can check a 302 and its Location header.

docs.title: Sending headers
docs.text:
To send extra headers with one request, pass headers:. If every request needs them, use withHeaders. It gives a copy of the client that sends these headers each time:

await client.get('/api/me', headers: <String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});

DoxTestClient german = client.withHeaders(<String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});

docs.title: Log in as a user
docs.text:
If your API uses tokens, log in first, then use withToken. It gives a copy of the client that sends Authorization: Bearer <token>:

TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);

docs.title: Keep a session (cookies and CSRF)
docs.text:
Web pages with forms use a session cookie and a CSRF token. client.withSession() gives a client that works like a browser. It keeps the cookies of every response and sends them back. On POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE it sends the XSRF-TOKEN cookie in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header, so CsrfMiddleware lets the request in:

test('log in with a form', () async {
  DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();

  // the first page gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
  (await browser.get('/login')).expectStatus(200);

  (await browser.post(
    '/login',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
  )).expectStatus(303).expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');

  (await browser.get('/dashboard')).expectStatus(200);
});

Each withSession() call gives a new browser with no cookies. You can read and change the kept cookies in browser.cookies (name to raw value).

The normal client keeps no cookies. To send the cookies of one response once, use withCookies(res.cookies).

docs.title: Checking the response
docs.text:
A TestResponse has the status, body and headers:

int status = res.status;
String body = res.body;
dynamic json = res.json; // the body read as JSON
String? type = res.header('content-type'); // any case

res.headers has all headers, with lower case names.

The expect methods fail the test when the response is not right. They return the response, so you can chain them:

res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});

docs.title: Checking the status
docs.text:
expectStatus fails when the status is another one. The message shows the body, so you can see what went wrong:

res.expectStatus(200);

docs.title: Checking JSON
docs.text:
expectJson takes a value or a matcher. Use a Map for the whole body, or a matcher to check only one part:

res.expectJson(containsPair('id', 1));

docs.title: Checking the body
docs.text:
expectBody checks the body as text:

res.expectBody('pong');

docs.title: Checking a header
docs.text:
expectHeader takes a header name and a value or matcher. Use isNull to check that a header is not there:

res.expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');
res.expectHeader('set-cookie', isNull);

docs.title: Test the cache
docs.text:
Tests should not write cache files or need Redis. So replace Dox().cache with a memory store. Cache() uses Dox().cache, so your code then uses the memory store:

setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});

Because the new CacheManager is made in setUp, each test starts with an empty cache. See Cache.

docs.title: Test file storage
docs.text:
If your code saves files, you do not want the test to write to S3 or your disk. Storage.manager.fake(name) from dox_storage swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. restore(name) puts the real disk back:

setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .putFile('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Storage.manager.restore('s3');
});

Call Dox().initialize() first. Without the StorageProvider, Storage.manager has only the local disk.

Storage() paths start with /, but a Disk key does not. So remove the first / when you ask the Disk directly.

A disk also has assertExists(key) and assertMissing(key). They throw a StateError when the check fails:

await fake.assertExists('reports/a.pdf');

See File Storage.

docs.title: Use a test database with .env.testing
docs.text:
Your tests should never use the database with your real data. Put the values for tests in a .env.testing file, next to .env:

.env.testing
DB_NAME=my_app_test
CACHE_STORE=memory

When the app runs its tests (dart test, or APP_ENV=testing), Dox reads .env first and then .env.testing. A key in .env.testing wins over the same key in .env. Keys that are only in .env stay.

A real environment variable still wins over both files. So CI can run DB_NAME=ci_test dart test. Outside tests, .env.testing is never read.

docs.title: Test the database
docs.text:
A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations once in setUpAll. Then empty the tables before each test with refreshDatabase() from package:dox_orm/testing.dart:

test/user_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM provider
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}

refreshDatabase() empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. The tables stay, and the rows of the migrations table (dox_db_migration) are kept. It works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Use a separate test database, set in .env.testing. Never run refreshDatabase() on a database with real data.

docs.title: Keeping some tables
docs.text:
If a table holds data that every test needs, like a list of countries, pass it in keep:

refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries']);

See Testing with a database for a full example with SQLite.

docs.title: Running test files one by one
docs.text:
dart test runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, they can break each other. So run them one by one:

dart test --concurrency=1

docs.title: Test the env
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to test code that reads the env, or test that the app stops on a bad env. Pass your own values to AppEnv.load(). Then nothing is read from the shell or the .env file:

AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);

A missing or bad key throws an EnvException. See Environment Variables.

Only the getters read through the EnvReader. A getter default that calls Env.get() or Platform.environment reads the real env. So in a default, use other getters, like appEnv == 'development'.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• The test server listens on 127.0.0.1 on a free port. So it does not clash with dox serve, and many test files can run at the same time.
  • It runs on one isolate. serverPort and totalIsolate of the config are not used. Because of this, a Route.get(...) you add inside a test works right away.
  • The session client removes a cookie when the response deletes it (an empty value, Max-Age=0 or an old Expires). A copy made from it, for example with withHeaders, shares its cookies.
  • Without the server, you can set the disks yourself with Storage.manager = StorageDiskFactory().create(storageConfig);, and start the ORM with SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig).
  • refreshDatabase() turns off foreign key checks while it empties the tables.
  • .env.testing is also read by the typed AppEnv.load(), not only by Env.get().

docs.title: Add a package
docs.text:
dox add adds a Dox package to your app and sets it up.

Many packages need config files and .env keys. dox add writes them for you, so you do not set up each package by hand:

dox add orm

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
dox add orm does three steps:

  1. Runs dart pub add dox_orm. orm is short for dox_orm. The full name works too.
  2. Runs dart pub get.
  3. Runs the setup command of the package, dox orm:install.

The setup command writes the config files, adds the keys to .env and .env.example, and runs build_runner when the package needs it. At the end it prints what it did and the next steps.

A package with no setup command is only added, and dox add says so.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Words after the name go to the setup command, for example to pick a driver:

dox add orm --driver=postgres

--dev adds the package as a dev dependency.

docs.title: Safe to run twice
docs.text: The setup command never overwrites a file and never changes a .env key that is already there. So you can run dox add again, and it only adds what is missing.

docs.title: Packages with a setup command
docs.text:
These packages have a setup command:

Command What it sets up dox add orm [--driver=sqlite\|postgres\|mysql] The ORM and migrations. See Database. dox add queue [--driver=database\|redis\|sync] Queued jobs and bin/queue.dart. database is the default and needs dox add orm first. See Queue. dox add scheduler Scheduled tasks and bin/schedule.dart. See Scheduler. dox add mailer [--transport=log\|smtp\|resend\|mailgun\|postmark\|ses] Mail. log is the default. See Mail. dox add cache [--store=file\|redis\|memory\|database] Cache stores. database needs dox add orm first. See Cache. dox add auth Access token auth. Needs dox add orm and a User model first. See Authentication. dox add storage [--disk=local\|s3] File storage. See File storage. dox add socketio [--broadcasting] Socket.IO, and broadcasting with the flag. See Socket.IO. dox add view Views and resources/views/. See Views. dox add inertia The server side of Inertia. It prints the Vite steps. See Inertia. dox add mcp An MCP server with a sample tool. See MCP.

The first dox add orm can download (or build) the Postgres and MySQL drivers once, also the one you do not use. After that, pubspec.yaml skips the unused drivers, so later builds do not get them.

To add a setup command to your own package, see Package commands.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page shows how to install the Dox CLI, make a new project and start the server.

Dox needs Dart 3.13 or newer.

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
The dox CLI makes projects, runs the server and makes files for you. Install it with pub:

dart pub global activate dox

Check that it works:

dox version

dox: command not found

The shell can not find the CLI, because the pub bin folder is not in your PATH. Add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

docs.title: Create a new project
docs.text:
Use dox create with the name of your app:

dox create new_blog

It downloads the newest release of dox-sample, the starter project. To get one exact release, add --version with a release tag of dox-sample.

It also makes your .env file from .env.example, with a new random APP_KEY. Then get the packages:

cd new_blog
dart pub get

The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install. The file db/dox.sqlite is created at the first start. To use Postgres or MySQL instead, change DB_CONNECTION and the DB_* values in .env. See Database.

Add Dox to an existing Dart project

If you already have a Dart project, add the packages you need with dart pub add:

dart pub add dox_core dox_orm dox_migration
dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Start the server in dev mode:

dox s

dox s does two things:

  • It runs dart run bin/server.dart. When you change a file in lib/app/, it hot reloads the new code, so no restart is needed. For routes, providers, config and other start-up code, it restarts the server.
  • It runs dart run build_runner watch, so generated files stay up to date.

At each start it also runs the new migrations in db/migration. The server uses the port in APP_PORT in the .env file (3000 by default). Check that it works:

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

These options change dox s:

  • dox s --ignore-build-runner skips the builder.
  • dox s --no-reload turns hot reload off.

To start the server without the CLI, run dart run bin/server.dart.

docs.title: Start the server with Docker
docs.text:
The starter project has a Docker setup. This starts the app, a queue worker and a Postgres database:

docker compose up -d --build

The app and the worker always use the Postgres service. They set DB_CONNECTION and DB_NAME themselves. The database port is open on this machine only (127.0.0.1), not on the network.

If you want only the database in Docker, and the app with dox s, run docker compose up -d postgres. Then set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and DB_NAME=dox in .env.

Production

Do not use dox s or dart run in production. Build a native binary with dox build. See Deployment.

docs.title: Run the code generator
docs.text:
Dox makes code for models and DTOs with build_runner. dox s already runs it. To run it alone:

dox build_runner:watch   # runs again on every file change
dox build_runner:build   # runs once

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text:
If you use an AI coding agent, it should know the real API of each package. The Dox packages ship skills for this. Install them in your app, after dart pub get:

dart run skills@ get

It finds the skills of your dependencies and installs them for your agent. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot and others. Run it again after you add a package or update one.

It only reads the packages listed in your own pubspec.yaml. To get the skill of a package that comes in through another one (like ioredis), add it to pubspec.yaml. See skills for the options.

The starter project also has an AGENTS.md file with the rules of the project.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Dox is split into packages, so you add only what you need:

Package What it does dox the CLI dox_core HTTP server, routing, requests, responses, validation dox_orm query builder and models dox_migration database migrations dox_auth Login with access tokens, JWT or sessions dox_builder, dox_annotation code generation for models, DTOs and the container dox_validation typed validation schemas dox_openapi OpenAPI docs dox_storage file storage: local, S3 dox_cache cache: memory, file, Redis dox_cache_database cache in a database table dox_socketio Socket.IO server dox_queue background jobs dox_queue_database queue in a database table dox_scheduler scheduled tasks dox_mailer send email dox_view HTML views dox_inertia Inertia.js pages dox_http_native native HTTP server (Rust) dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native native drivers for Postgres and MySQL/MariaDB

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Each guide solves one job from start to end: you copy the files, run the commands and check the result.

The guides are short on theory. If you want to know more about one part, follow the links to the reference pages.

Guide What you get File upload Accept an image, check its size and type, save it, return its URL. Pagination A list route with page and per_page, and the JSON shape it returns. JWT authentication Register, log in, protect routes, read the user, log out. Custom errors Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. Background work Run work after the response, on another thread, in a queue job, or on a schedule. Static files and SPA Serve a folder or a single page app, with cache headers. CORS for a browser front-end The CORS setup that works with a React, Vue or Flutter web app. Environments Dev, staging and production config, .env files, secrets and APP_KEY. Testing with a database Tests on SQLite or a test Postgres, with migrations and cleanup. Share code with Flutter One DTO package that the server and the Flutter app both use to check input. API docs with OpenAPI A docs page for your API, made from your routes, DTOs and models. Docker A small production image, Postgres in Docker Compose, env and a health check. Deploy to a Linux server Your own server with systemd, and Caddy in front for HTTPS. Deploy to Fly.io Fly.io from your Dockerfile, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres. Deploy to Google Cloud Run Cloud Run from your Dockerfile, with Cloud SQL and Secret Manager.

docs.title: The example apps
docs.text:
Most guides use the app that dox create my_app makes, so the package name is my_app. Change it to your own package name in the imports.

The OpenAPI guide and the deploy guides use the blog API of the tutorial. Its package name is blog.

All the code is on GitHub:

  • the app guides: examples/guides
  • the blog API: examples/blog-api

CI builds both apps and runs their tests on every push, so the code on these pages keeps working.

docs.title: API docs with OpenAPI
docs.text:
Turn on OpenAPI docs for the blog API, open the docs page, and make the docs better with annotations.

API docs show every route on one page, so a front-end team can see what to send and what comes back. Dox builds the docs from your code, so they never get out of date.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.
  • build_runner and dox_builder. A new app has both. dox_core already has dox_openapi, so you add no package.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
A new app already serves the docs pages, but each route shows only its path and method. To get the full docs, give Dox what the builder found in your code.

build_runner writes lib/generated/openapi.g.dart. Its openApiRegistry holds your routes, controllers, DTOs and models. Pass it to an OpenApiConfig:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:blog/generated/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Add it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  /// OpenAPI docs (config/openapi.dart)
  openApi: openApi,
);

docs.title: 2. Build and start
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

The docs routes are on, because .env has APP_ENV=development.

docs.title: 3. Open the docs page
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:3000/docs. It is a Scalar page with every route and "Try it" buttons.

The app now has three new routes:

Route What it gives GET /docs the Scalar docs page (HTML) GET /openapi.json the OpenAPI 3.1 document as JSON GET /openapi.yaml the same document as YAML

docs.title: 4. Read the JSON
docs.text:
curl http://localhost:3000/openapi.json

This is the output for the blog API, shortened. The top level:

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {"title": "Blog API", "version": "1.0.0"},
  "paths": {
    "/api/ping": {},
    "/api/posts": {},
    "/api/posts/{id}": {},
    "/api/auth/register": {},
    "/api/auth/login": {},
    "/api/auth/user": {},
    "/ping": {}
  },
  "components": {
    "schemas": {"Post": {}, "SavePost": {}, "RegisterUser": {}, "LoginUser": {}, "User": {}, "ValidationError": {}},
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {"type": "http", "scheme": "bearer"}
    }
  }
}

This is POST /api/posts. You wrote no docs code for it:

{
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "POST /api/posts",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "requestBody": {
    "required": true,
    "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/SavePost"}}}
  },
  "responses": {
    "200": {"description": "Successful response"},
    "401": {
      "description": "Not logged in",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"code": {"type": "string"}, "message": {"type": "string"}}}}}
    },
    "422": {
      "description": "Validation failed",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/ValidationError"}}}
    },
    "500": {"description": "Server error"}
  },
  "security": [{"bearerAuth": []}],
  "x-dox-middleware": ["LogMiddleware", "AuthMiddleware"]
}

Where each part comes from:

Part Comes from tags: ["Post"] the class name PostController, without Controller summary no @Summary here, so the first line of the /// comment: /// POST /api/posts requestBody the argument SavePost body of store 401 and bearerAuth AuthMiddleware on the route 422 the route has a request class 200 with no body store returns DoxResponse, so the builder can not see the body. Step 6 fixes this x-dox-middleware the middleware of the route: the global LogMiddleware and AuthMiddleware

Other routes get error answers in the same way. The Can middleware or a req.authorize(...) call gives 401 and 403. The GuestMiddleware and ValidateSignature middleware give 403. A req.validateSchema(...) call gives 422.

docs.title: 5. See how a DTO becomes a schema
docs.text:
Dox turns each DTO into a schema, so the docs show the rules of every field. This is the SavePost DTO of the tutorial:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

And this is its schema in /openapi.json:

"SavePost": {
  "type": "object",
  "title": "SavePost",
  "properties": {
    "title": {"type": "string", "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100},
    "body": {"type": "string", "minLength": 10}
  },
  "required": ["title", "body"]
}
In the DTO In the schema String title (not nullable) "type": "string" and title in required @Length(min: 3, max: 100) "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100 @MinLength(10) "minLength": 10 @Email() (in RegisterUser) "format": "email" @Describe('...') or /// A comment "description". @Describe wins over the comment @Trim(), @Lowercase(), @Unique(...) nothing. They change or check the value on the server only

A model becomes a schema too. Post has id, the @Column fields title and body, and created_at and updated_at. Keys in hidden are left out, so User has no password.

When you change a rule, run build_runner again, and the docs change with it.

docs.title: 6. Make the docs better
docs.text:
The builder can not guess everything. For example, it can not see the body of a DoxResponse. Add annotations to a controller method to fill the gaps: @Summary, @Description, @Tags and @Response (from dox_core). A /// comment on the method also works for the summary and the description.

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
@Inject()
class PostController {
  @Summary('List all posts')
  @Description('Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.')
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  @Summary('Create a post')
  @Tags(<String>['Posts'])
  @Response(201, Post, description: 'The new post')
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  // ...
}

Run dart run build_runner build again and restart the app. The result:

"get": {
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "List all posts",
  "description": "Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.",
  "operationId": "PostController.index",
  "responses": {
    "200": {
      "description": "Successful response",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"type": "array", "items": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}}}}
    },
    "500": {}
  }
},
"post": {
  "tags": ["Posts"],
  "summary": "Create a post",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "responses": {
    "201": {
      "description": "The new post",
      "content": {"application/json": {"schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}}}
    },
    "401": {},
    "422": {},
    "500": {}
  }
}
  • @Response(201, Post) replaces the empty 200. The docs now match the real status code.
  • @Tags(['Posts']) moves the route to the group "Posts" in the docs page.
  • @Summary('...') and @Description('...') set the text. A /// comment gives the same result. When a method has both, the annotation wins.
  • @ApiIgnore() leaves a method (or a whole controller) out of the docs.

See OpenAPI: describe a route for all annotations.

docs.title: 7. Turn it off in production
docs.text:
You do not need to do anything here. enabled is null by default, so the docs routes are on only when APP_ENV is development or local. With APP_ENV=production all three routes give 404:

curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/docs           # 404
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/openapi.json   # 404

To turn the docs on in production, set enabled: true. See OpenAPI: turn the docs on in production.

To build the document at build time and serve the files in production, see OpenAPI: production setup.

If you want the docs on staging too, but never in production, set enabled yourself:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:blog/config/env.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: env.appEnv != 'production',
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Warning

enabled: true in production shows every route of your API to anyone. Only do it for a public API.

To give the document to a front-end team without a running server, write it to files with dox openapi:generate. See OpenAPI: write the files.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl -s http://localhost:3000/openapi.json | head -n 5

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "Blog API",
    "version": "1.0.0"

Open http://localhost:3000/docs, find "Create a post" under "Posts", and send a request with "Try it".

docs.text:

  • Validation rules for the rules and their JSON Schema keys
  • Environments for APP_ENV

docs.title: Background work
docs.text:
Answer the request now and do the slow work later: after the response, on another thread, in a queue, or on a timer.

Some work is too slow to do while the user waits, like sending an email or building a report. You should answer the request first and do that work in the background.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the queue (dox_queue) and the scheduler (dox_scheduler) set up.

docs.title: Pick the right tool
docs.text:
Dox gives you four ways to run work in the background. Pick one by how slow the work is and if it may get lost:

You want Use Runs where Lost when the process stops small I/O work after the response (a log line, a cache update) a Future you do not await the same isolate, between requests yes CPU work (resize an image, parse a big file, compute) Isolate.run() a new thread yes work that must not get lost (an email, a payment call), with retries a queue job the queue worker process no work every N minutes (cleanup, sync) a scheduled task the schedule process it runs again at the next tick

docs.title: 1. Work after the response
docs.text:
For small I/O work, start the future and return without waiting for it. unawaited tells the linter you did this on purpose. If the future throws, the error goes to the report method of the ExceptionHandler in AppConfig.

This file has the code of steps 1, 2 and 3:

lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart';

@Inject()
class ReportController {
  /// POST /api/reports
  /// Answers at once. The work runs after the response, in this isolate.
  Map<String, String> store(DoxRequest req) {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    unawaited(_build(id));
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// POST /api/reports/queued
  /// Saves a job in the jobs table and answers at once.
  /// The queue worker (`dox queue:work`) runs it, and tries again when
  /// it fails. The job is not lost when the server stops.
  Future<Map<String, String>> queue(DoxRequest req) async {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    String jobId = await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'job': jobId, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// I/O work (database, HTTP calls, email) is fine here. It shares the
  /// event loop with the requests, so it must not block the CPU.
  Future<void> _build(String id) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print('report $id is ready');
  }

  /// GET /api/primes/{limit}
  /// CPU work runs on another thread with `Isolate.run`.
  /// The request waits for the result, but other requests are not blocked.
  Future<Map<String, int>> primes(int limit) async {
    int count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit));
    return <String, int>{'limit': limit, 'primes': count};
  }
}

/// Must be a top level or static function with plain arguments.
/// The new isolate has no Dox, no database and no providers.
int countPrimes(int limit) {
  List<bool> sieve = List<bool>.filled(limit + 1, true);
  int count = 0;
  for (int i = 2; i <= limit; i++) {
    if (!sieve[i]) continue;
    count++;
    for (int j = i * i; j <= limit; j += i) {
      sieve[j] = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}

Do not block the event loop

_build shares the thread with the requests of this isolate, so a long loop makes them all wait. Put a long loop in Isolate.run.

docs.title: 2. CPU work on another thread
docs.text:
Heavy CPU work blocks the requests, so run it on another thread. Isolate.run runs the function on a new isolate and sends the result back. Pass plain data in (an int, a String, bytes) and get plain data out. Save the result in the request isolate.

primes above waits for the result. If you do not want to wait, combine both patterns:

unawaited(Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit)).then(saveResult));

docs.title: 3. A job that must not get lost
docs.text:
A future you do not await is gone when the server stops, and it does not retry. So for work that must happen, use a queue job. dispatch() saves the job in the database. A worker process takes it and runs handle(), and tries again if it fails.

Make the job:

dox make:job BuildReport
lib/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

/// Builds a report in the queue worker.
/// Dispatch it: `await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();`
@Job()
class BuildReport extends DoxJob {
  BuildReport({required this.reportId});

  final String reportId;

  /// try 3 times, wait 10 seconds between tries
  @override
  int get tries => 3;

  @override
  List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[Duration(seconds: 10)];

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Logger.info('report $reportId is ready');
  }
}

The fields of the job (reportId) are saved with it, so use plain values like String, int, bool, DateTime, lists and maps. Save an id, not a model, and load the model in handle().

Run dart run build_runner build after you add or change a job. It updates lib/generated/jobs.g.dart.

The queue method of the controller above dispatches it. dispatch() returns the id of the job.

A new app keeps the jobs in the database (the database driver in lib/config/queue.dart). The jobs tables come from a migration in db/migration/, which the server runs at start.

Start the worker next to the server, in a second terminal:

dox queue:work

dox queue:failed lists the jobs that failed every try. dox queue:retry all puts them back on the queue. See Queue for Redis, delays and all worker flags.

docs.title: 4. Work on a timer
docs.text:
Some work must run again and again, like a cleanup every hour. Put the task in lib/config/schedule.dart. A new app has this file with an empty schedule function.

lib/config/schedule.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

/// `inProcess: false`: run `dox schedule:work` next to the server.
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

/// The tasks. `dox schedule:list` shows them.
void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanupUsers).hourly();
}

/// Removes the users that were soft deleted more than 30 days ago.
Future<void> cleanupUsers() async {
  DateTime limit = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 30));
  List<User> old = await User()
      .withTrash()
      .where('deleted_at', '<', limit)
      .get();
  int removed = 0;
  for (User user in old) {
    removed += await user.forceDelete();
  }
  print('cleanup: removed $removed users');
}

Start the scheduler next to the server, in a third terminal:

dox schedule:work

dox schedule:list shows each task and its next run. dox schedule:test cleanup runs the task now.

The scheduler runs each task once per tick, even when many processes run the schedule. If you have many servers, use a Redis cache store for the lock (ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis')). For a small app, you can run the schedule inside the server. See Scheduler: run inside the server.

docs.title: 5. Add the routes
Check it
docs.text:
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports

The answer comes at once:

{"id":"1792677668393002","status":"queued"}

Two seconds later, the server prints report 1792677668393002 is ready.

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports/queued

{"id":"1792677670112345","job":"9f2c4e1a7b3d5f60a1c2e3f4a5b6c7d8","status":"queued"}

The terminal of dox queue:work shows a log line with report 1792677670112345 is ready. If you stop the worker first, the job waits in the jobs table until the worker runs again.

curl http://localhost:3000/api/primes/100000

{"limit":100000,"primes":9592}

docs.title: CORS for a browser front-end
docs.text:
Let a web app on another origin (http://localhost:5173 in development, https://my.app in production) call your API.

A browser blocks a page from calling an API on another origin, unless the API says it is allowed. CORS headers tell the browser which origins may call. You need this when your front-end and your API run on different hosts or ports.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A front-end that runs on its own origin, like Vite, Next.js or Flutter web.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
A new app already has lib/config/cors.dart, but with enabled: false. Replace the whole file with this one:

lib/config/cors.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

/// `enabled` is true by default, so every route sends the headers.
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  /// One origin, or a list of origins. Set CORS_ORIGIN to the real
  /// front-end URL in production.
  origin: env.corsOrigin,

  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],

  /// the request headers the front-end sends
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],

  /// the response headers the front-end may read
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],

  /// true only when the front-end sends cookies. Not needed for a
  /// `Authorization: Bearer` token.
  credentials: false,

  /// the browser keeps the preflight answer for 10 minutes
  maxAge: 600,
);

AppConfig in lib/config/app.dart already passes it on with cors: cors.

docs.title: 2. Set the origin per environment
docs.text:
The front-end URL is different in each environment, so read it from a new key, CORS_ORIGIN. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then set the value in .env:

.env
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173

In staging and production, set CORS_ORIGIN as a real environment variable, like https://my.app. The origin is the scheme, host and port only, with no path and no / at the end.

docs.title: 3. Choose credentials
docs.text:
The right origin and credentials depend on how the front-end logs in:

Your front-end sends origin credentials a token in Authorization: Bearer (see JWT authentication) your front-end URL false cookies (fetch(url, {credentials: 'include'})) your front-end URL, never * true nothing, a public API '*' false

Two or more front-ends

Set origin to a list, like ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']. Dox sends back only the origin that matches the request. If none matches, the browser blocks the call.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Before a POST with JSON or a custom header, the browser first sends an OPTIONS request, called a preflight. Dox answers it by itself, so you do not need an OPTIONS route:

curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization'

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type,Authorization
access-control-expose-headers: Content-Disposition
access-control-allow-credentials: false
access-control-max-age: 600

A normal request gets the origin header too:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' | grep -i access-control-allow-origin

access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173

In the browser, open the front-end and call the API with fetch. The console shows no CORS error.

docs.title: When it still fails
docs.text: The console says The fix No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header CORS_ORIGIN does not match the page origin exactly. Check http or https, and the port. The value of ... header is 'a.com,b.com' origin is one text with commas. Use a List<String> instead. Request header field x-foo is not allowed Add the header to headers. credentials mode is 'include' with * Set origin to the front-end URL and credentials: true.

docs.title: Turning CORS off for some routes
docs.text:
CORS only matters for browsers. A webhook from Stripe or a call from another server ignores these headers. So you can turn CORS off for such routes, to send fewer headers:

Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.text:
• CORS for every option
  • JWT authentication

docs.title: Custom errors
docs.text:
Give your app its own exception classes, send every error in one JSON shape, and log the unexpected ones.

A client is easier to write when every error has the same shape. You also want to know when something breaks on the server, without showing the details to the client.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: How Dox handles an error
docs.text:
First, see what Dox does when a controller or a middleware throws:

Error Status What Dox does an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code sends {"code": ..., "message": ...}. Does not call report a validation error (bad DTO input) 422 sends the field errors: {"field": "message"}. Does not call report any other Exception or Error 500 sends {"code":"server_error","message":"Server Error"}. When APP_ENV is development or local, it sends the error text. Calls report

report is a method of the exception handler. Every response goes through the responseHandler of AppConfig last, so this guide sets the error shape there.

docs.title: 1. Write your own exceptions
docs.text:
For a quick error, use abort(403) or abort(409, 'The email is taken'). See HTTP exceptions.

If you throw the same error in many places, write a class for it. Extend IHttpException, and set code (the HTTP status), errorCode (a short text for the client) and message:

lib/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// 409. Thrown when the row already exists or was changed by someone else.
class ConflictException extends IHttpException {
  ConflictException({String message = 'Conflict'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.conflict;
    super.errorCode = 'conflict';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

Throw them anywhere in a controller, a middleware or a service:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users/{id}
  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    if (user == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /// DELETE /api/users/{id}
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(int id) async {
    if (id == 1) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException(message: 'The first user can not be deleted');
    }
    User user = await show(id);

    /// 0 rows: the user was deleted after show() found it
    if (await user.delete() == 0) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return <String, bool>{'deleted': true};
  }
}

docs.title: 2. One JSON shape for every error
docs.text:
The response handler sees every response before it is sent. For an error, the content is the exception object, so you can turn it into your shape here:

lib/app/http/response_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Gives every error the same JSON shape:
/// `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`.
/// A validation error (422) also has `"errors": {field: message}`.
class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    dynamic content = res.getContent();

    if (content is ValidationException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': 'The input is not valid',
        },
        'errors': content.message,
      });
    }

    if (content is IHttpException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': content.message.toString(),
        },
      });
    }

    // any other exception: hide the details from the client
    if (content is Exception || content is Error) {
      return res.statusCode(HttpStatus.internalServerError).content(
        <String, dynamic>{
          'error': <String, String>{
            'code': 'server_error',
            'message': 'Something went wrong',
          },
        },
      );
    }

    return res;
  }
}

The last if gives a 500 your shape too, in every environment. Without it, the client gets the default body, which in development or local is the error text. That text can show a SQL query or a file path.

docs.title: 3. Log unexpected errors
docs.text:
You want to know about unexpected errors, so log them. The report method of the exception handler runs for every 500, and for errors outside a request, like a future nobody awaited or a timer:

lib/app/error_handler.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Dox calls [report] for every unexpected error (a `500`, or an error
/// outside a request). It does not run for `IHttpException` errors
/// like `404` or `422`, because those are expected.
/// One JSON line per error. Send it to Sentry or Datadog from here.
class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    print(
      jsonEncode(<String, String>{
        'timestamp': DateTime.now().toIso8601String(),
        'status': 'error',
        'message': error.toString(),
        'error': <String, String>{'stack': stackTrace.toString()},
      }),
    );
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Register both
docs.text:
Add both handlers to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/app/error_handler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/response_handler.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  responseHandler: ResponseHandler(),
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Add a route that throws, only for this check:

Route.get('/boom', (DoxRequest req) => throw StateError('boom'));
Request Status Body GET /api/users/999 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"User 999 not found"}} GET /api/users/abc 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}} DELETE /api/users/1 403 {"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"The first user can not be deleted"}} POST /api/auth/register with {} 422 {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"The input is not valid"},"errors":{"name":"The name is required", ...}} GET /api/boom 500 {"error":{"code":"server_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}

After GET /api/boom, the server prints one line:

{"timestamp":"2026-10-22T14:01:12.000Z","status":"error","message":"Bad state: boom","error":{"stack":"#0  ApiRouter.register.<anonymous closure> (package:my_app/routes/api.dart:41:44) ..."},"source":"error"}

Remove the /boom route when you are done.

A URL with no route

A URL that matches no route is a NotFoundHttpException. It goes through the response handler too, so it gets the same JSON shape: {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"GET /nothing not found"}}.

docs.title: Deploy to Google Cloud Run
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Cloud Run from the Dockerfile of your project, with Postgres on Cloud SQL and secrets in Secret Manager.

Cloud Run is a good fit when you want Google to run and scale the containers for you. You give it an image, and it gives you an HTTPS URL.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Google Cloud project with billing, and the gcloud CLI (gcloud auth login, gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Docker for how that file works.
  • A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a database and a user. See step 3.

docs.title: Choosing the port
docs.text: Cloud Run tells the container which port to use with the PORT env variable. It is 8080 by default, or the --port value. Dox listens on APP_PORT, or on PORT when APP_PORT is not set. So do not set APP_PORT on Cloud Run. If you do set it, pass the same port with --port.

docs.title: 1. Turn on the APIs
docs.text:
Cloud Run, Cloud Build, Artifact Registry, Secret Manager and Cloud SQL are all off in a new project. Turn them on once:

gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com sqladmin.googleapis.com

docs.title: 2. Save the secrets in Secret Manager
docs.text:
You should keep APP_KEY and the database password out of the plain env variables, because anyone who can see the service can read those. Save them in Secret Manager:

openssl rand -hex 16 | tr -d '\n' | gcloud secrets create blog-app-key --data-file=-
printf '%s' '<the database password>' | gcloud secrets create blog-db-password --data-file=-

Let the Cloud Run service account read them. By default this is the Compute Engine service account, PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com:

for s in blog-app-key blog-db-password; do
  gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding "$s" \
    --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"
done

docs.title: 3. Reach Cloud SQL
docs.text:
Cloud Run can reach Cloud SQL by a Unix socket or by a private IP. Dox can use both. This guide uses the socket, because it needs no VPC:

  1. Find the connection name of the instance: gcloud sql instances describe INSTANCE --format='value(connectionName)'. It looks like PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE.
  2. Deploy with --add-cloudsql-instances <connection name> (step 4). Cloud Run then makes the socket in /cloudsql/<connection name>.
  3. Give the service account the roles/cloudsql.client role.
  4. Set DB_HOST=/cloudsql/<connection name>. A host that starts with / is a Unix socket. See Unix socket.

The same with one url: DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:<password>@/blog?host=/cloudsql/<connection name>.

For Cloud SQL for MySQL, use the same DB_HOST with DB_CONNECTION=mysql. Leave out DB_PORT. Or use one url: DATABASE_URL=mysql://blog:<password>@/blog?socket=/cloudsql/<connection name>.

To use the private IP instead: give the instance a private IP on your VPC network, deploy with Direct VPC egress (--network default --subnet default --vpc-egress private-ranges-only), and use the private IP as DB_HOST.

Do not use SQLite on Cloud Run. Each instance has its own file system in memory, so the data is lost when the instance stops.

docs.title: 4. Deploy from source
docs.text:
The easiest way to deploy is from source. --source . uploads the folder, and Cloud Build builds the image with your Dockerfile. The image is saved in Artifact Registry, in the repository cloud-run-source-deploy.

gcloud run deploy blog \
  --source . \
  --region europe-west1 \
  --port 3000 \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --cpu 1 --memory 512Mi \
  --min-instances 1 \
  --add-cloudsql-instances PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE \
  --set-env-vars APP_ENV=production,APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1,DB_CONNECTION=postgres,DB_HOST=/cloudsql/PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE,DB_PORT=5432,DB_NAME=blog,DB_USERNAME=blog \
  --set-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:1,DB_PASSWORD=blog-db-password:1
Flag Why --port 3000 the port Cloud Run sends requests to. It also sets PORT=3000, and Dox listens on PORT. See Choosing the port --min-instances 1 keeps one instance warm, so the first request does not wait for a cold start. The default is 0. An idle instance still costs money --add-cloudsql-instances makes the Cloud SQL Unix socket in /cloudsql/... --set-env-vars config that is not secret --set-secrets ENV_NAME=SECRET:VERSION. Cloud Run reads the secret when an instance starts. Pin a version number, not latest APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1 one isolate per CPU. Set it to the --cpu value

If you want to build the image yourself, push it to Artifact Registry and deploy it with --image:

docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 .
docker push europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1
gcloud run deploy blog --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 --region europe-west1 --port 3000 ...

Use the same other flags as above.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
gcloud run deploy prints the service URL at the end.

curl https://blog-xxxxxxxx-ew.a.run.app/api/ping

pong

gcloud run services logs read blog --region europe-west1 --limit 20
gcloud beta run services logs tail blog --region europe-west1   # live, needs the log-streaming component

The first log lines after the first start:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 1 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"},"source":"server"}

If the deploy fails with "the container did not listen on the port", the app listens on a different port than --port. Check APP_PORT and --port.

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Cloud Run handles HTTPS and sends plain HTTP to the container. You want req.ip() and req.scheme() to show the real client, so set trustedProxies. Only the Cloud Run front end can reach the container port, so ['*'] is safe here:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Updating the app
docs.text:
To ship a new version, deploy again:

gcloud run deploy blog --source . --region europe-west1
  • Cloud Run keeps the flags of the last revision. You only pass what changes.
  • A new revision starts, runs new migrations, and takes the traffic when it listens on the port. The old one then stops.
  • If many instances start at the same time, each one runs the migrations. So keep migrations safe to run twice, or run one instance during a deploy with a migration.
  • A new secret version: create it with gcloud secrets versions add, then deploy with the new number in --update-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:2.

docs.text:

  • Docker for a health check binary and Docker Compose
  • Cloud Run docs: container contract, deploy from source, secrets, minimum instances, Cloud SQL

docs.title: Deploy to Fly.io
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Fly.io from the Dockerfile of your project, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres.

Fly.io runs your container on small machines close to your users. You give it a Dockerfile and a fly.toml, and it builds and runs the app.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Fly.io account and the fly CLI (fly auth login).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Docker for how that file works.

docs.title: 1. Make the app on Fly.io
docs.text:
In the project folder:

fly launch --no-deploy

fly launch finds the Dockerfile, asks for an app name and a region, and writes fly.toml. --no-deploy stops before the first deploy, so you can set the config first.

docs.title: 2. Write fly.toml
docs.text:
fly.toml holds the app config for Fly.io. Replace the file with this one, and change app and primary_region to your values:

fly.toml
app = "blog-api"
primary_region = "ams"
# Dox waits up to 8 seconds for open requests on stop. Fly waits 5 by default.
kill_timeout = 10

[build]
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"

# config that is not secret. Secrets come from `fly secrets set`.
[env]
  APP_ENV = "production"
  APP_PORT = "3000"
  DB_CONNECTION = "sqlite"
  DB_NAME = "/data/blog.sqlite"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 3000
  force_https = true
  # one machine, always on: the SQLite file is on its volume
  auto_stop_machines = "off"
  auto_start_machines = true
  min_machines_running = 1

  [[http_service.checks]]
    grace_period = "10s"
    interval = "30s"
    method = "GET"
    timeout = "5s"
    path = "/api/ping"

# the volume with the SQLite file
[mounts]
  source = "blog_data"
  destination = "/data"

[[vm]]
  memory = "256mb"
  cpu_kind = "shared"
  cpus = 1
  • internal_port is the port the app listens on. Dox reads it from APP_PORT (or PORT when APP_PORT is not set). Keep the two the same.
  • Values in [env] must be strings, so write "3000", not 3000.
  • [[vm]] wins over fly scale vm. Each fly deploy sets the machine to these values.
  • Keep kill_timeout above shutdownTimeout of AppConfig, so open requests can finish on stop. See Graceful shutdown.

docs.title: 3. Set the secrets
docs.text:
Secrets like APP_KEY should not be in fly.toml, because that file goes into git. Set them with fly secrets:

fly secrets set APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

A secret is an environment variable on every machine of the app. fly secrets list shows the names, not the values. A secret with the same name as an [env] key wins.

docs.title: SQLite on a volume
docs.text:
SQLite is the simplest choice for a small app. Make the volume that [mounts] asks for, in the same region:

fly volumes create blog_data --region ams --size 1

A volume is attached to one machine only, and Fly.io does not copy the data between volumes. So with SQLite, run exactly one machine.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
Use Postgres if you want more than one machine. Create a Managed Postgres cluster with fly mpg create, and attach it to the app:

fly mpg attach <cluster-id> --app blog-api

This sets the secret DATABASE_URL. It wins over the DB_* keys, for the app and the migrations. See DATABASE_URL.

Then delete DB_CONNECTION and DB_NAME from [env], and delete the [mounts] section. If the database asks for TLS, add ?sslmode=require to the url with fly secrets set DATABASE_URL=....

docs.title: 5. Deploy
docs.text:
fly deploy

fly deploy builds the image, makes the machine and starts it. The app runs the migrations at start. Then check that there is one machine:

fly scale show

If the count is more than 1 and you use SQLite, run fly scale count 1.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl https://blog-api.fly.dev/api/ping

pong

fly status    # the machines and their state
fly logs      # the app logs, live

The first log lines after the first start:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 1 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"},"source":"server"}

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Fly.io handles HTTPS and sends plain HTTP to port 3000. force_https = true sends HTTP visitors to HTTPS.

You want req.ip() and req.scheme() to show the real client, so set trustedProxies in AppConfig. Only the Fly.io proxy can reach the app port, so ['*'] is safe here:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Scaling the app
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU core it sees. On cpus = 1 that is one isolate.

You want Do this more speed on one machine raise cpus in [[vm]] (and memory), then fly deploy. Dox uses the new cores by itself more machines use Postgres, then fly scale count 2. With SQLite, stay at one machine a fixed number of isolates set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in [env]

Each machine is its own process. Socket.IO rooms and the memory cache are not shared between machines.

docs.title: Updating the app
docs.text:
To ship a new version, deploy again:

fly deploy
  • Change config in [env] and run fly deploy again.
  • fly secrets set restarts the machines with the new value. With --stage it only saves the value, and the next deploy uses it.
  • The app runs new migrations at start.
  • With one machine there is a short gap while it restarts.

docs.text:

  • Environments for all env keys and APP_KEY
  • Docker for a health check binary and Docker Compose
  • Fly.io docs: fly.toml, secrets, volumes, Managed Postgres

docs.title: Deploy to a Linux server
docs.text:
Run the blog API on your own Linux server (a VPS), with systemd to keep it running and Caddy in front for HTTPS.

A VPS gives you full control and a fixed monthly price. systemd starts the app and starts it again after a crash. Caddy gets the TLS certificate and sends the requests to the app:

flowchart LR
  client[Browser or app] -- "HTTPS :443" --> caddy[Caddy]
  caddy -- "HTTP 127.0.0.1:3000" --> dox["/opt/blog/bin/server (systemd)"]

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux server (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with SSH and sudo.
  • A domain name. Its A (and AAAA) record points to the server.
  • Docker on your machine, to build a Linux binary.
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.

docs.title: 1. Build the bundle for Linux
docs.text:
dox build makes a native binary for the system it runs on, so a binary built on macOS does not run on Linux. Build it inside the dart:stable image instead, which is Debian:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/app -w /app dart:stable sh -c \
  'dart pub get && dart pub global activate dox && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build'

The result is build/bundle/:

build/bundle/
  bin/server                         the AOT binary
  lib/dox_http_native-linux-*.so     the native HTTP server
  lib/dox_postgres_native-linux-*.so the native Postgres driver
  lib/dox_mysql_native-linux-*.so    the native MySQL driver
  lib/libsqlite3.so                  SQLite
  db/                                the migrations
  .env.example

Keep bin/ and lib/ together, because the binary loads the libraries from ../lib. See Deployment.

Match the CPU of the server

Docker builds for the CPU of your machine. On a Mac with Apple silicon that is arm64, but most VPS plans are x86_64. For them, add --platform linux/amd64 after docker run. Check the server with uname -m.

The container writes Linux paths into your .dart_tool/. So run dart pub get on your machine again before you use dox serve.

docs.title: 2. Make a user and the folders
docs.text:
You should not run the app as root. Run this on the server to make a user dox, which can not log in:

sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin dox
sudo mkdir -p /opt/blog
sudo install -d -o dox -g dox /opt/blog/storage
Path What it holds Owner /opt/blog the bundle (bin/, lib/, db/) root /opt/blog/storage files the app writes (uploads, file cache) dox /var/lib/blog the SQLite file. systemd makes it (see step 5) dox /etc/blog.env config and secrets root, mode 600

docs.title: 3. Copy the bundle to the server
docs.text:
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server 'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

docs.title: 4. Write the env file
docs.text:
/etc/blog.env
APP_NAME=blog
APP_ENV=production
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=/var/lib/blog/blog.sqlite

sudo chown root:root /etc/blog.env
sudo chmod 600 /etc/blog.env

systemd reads this file as root before it starts the app, so the user dox does not need to read it.

For Postgres, set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and add DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_NAME. Or set one DATABASE_URL, like postgres://app:secret@localhost:5432/blog. It wins over the DB_* keys. systemd gives it to the app as a real environment variable. See DATABASE_URL. See Environments for all keys.

Do not put a .env file in /opt/blog. The values of /etc/blog.env are real environment variables, so they win over a .env file anyway, and one place is easier to check.

docs.title: 5. Write the systemd unit
docs.text:
The systemd unit starts the app at boot and starts it again after a crash:

/etc/systemd/system/blog.service
[Unit]
Description=Blog API (Dox)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=dox
Group=dox
# the binary reads db/ and .env from this folder
WorkingDirectory=/opt/blog
EnvironmentFile=/etc/blog.env
ExecStart=/opt/blog/bin/server
# start again after a crash, and after `kill`
Restart=always
RestartSec=2
# makes /var/lib/blog, owned by the user dox
StateDirectory=blog
# small safety settings
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=full

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now blog
systemctl status blog
  • When the main isolate dies, the process exits and Restart=always starts it again. See Deployment: keep it running.
  • The app runs the migrations at start, before it takes requests.
  • Dox starts one isolate per CPU core. Set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in /etc/blog.env to change it.

docs.title: 6. Close the app port
docs.text:
Only Caddy should talk to the app. Caddy runs on the same machine, so let Dox listen on 127.0.0.1 only. Add this line to /etc/blog.env:

/etc/blog.env
APP_HOST=127.0.0.1

Now only programs on this machine can reach port 3000. Also turn on a firewall, so that only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are open:

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

docs.title: 7. Put Caddy in front
docs.text:
Install Caddy from its install page. The Debian package runs Caddy with systemd and reads /etc/caddy/Caddyfile.

/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
api.example.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 {
        # while the app restarts, wait up to 10s for it instead of failing
        lb_try_duration 10s
        lb_try_interval 250ms
    }
}

sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo systemctl reload caddy
  • Caddy gets a TLS certificate for api.example.com by itself. Ports 80 and 443 must be open.
  • reverse_proxy sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.

docs.title: 8. Trust Caddy in the app
docs.text:
Dox ignores X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto until you list the proxy in trustedProxies. Caddy talks to the app from the same server, so list the local addresses:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);

Now req.ip() is the real client IP and req.scheme() is https. Build and copy again after this change (steps 1 and 3). See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
curl https://api.example.com/api/ping

pong

Read the logs. In production the app writes one JSON line per log.

journalctl -u blog -f                     # follow new lines
journalctl -u blog --since "1 hour ago"   # the last hour
journalctl -u blog -b                     # since the last boot

The first lines after the first start look like this:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 2 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"},"source":"server"}

(native) means the native HTTP server loaded. When it does not load, the app stops at start and the error says why.

Check that the app port is closed. From your machine:

curl -m 5 http://api.example.com:3000/api/ping   # must time out

docs.title: Updating the app
docs.text:
1. Build a new bundle (step 1).

  2. Copy it to the server (step 3). Keep the old one first, so you can go back:

    ssh you@server 'sudo rm -rf /opt/blog.prev && sudo cp -a /opt/blog /opt/blog.prev'
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server 'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

  3. Restart the app. It runs new migrations at start.

    ssh you@server 'sudo systemctl restart blog'

  4. Read the logs (journalctl -u blog -n 20) and run the check.

To go back: copy /opt/blog.prev to /opt/blog and restart. A migration that already ran is not undone.

A restart is short, but not zero

A restart takes about one second. New requests do not fail, because lb_try_duration makes Caddy wait for the app. If you need a real zero-downtime update, run two copies on two ports and list both in Caddy. See Deployment: many processes.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for dox build, Docker, nginx and many processes
  • Environments for config per environment and APP_KEY
  • Docker to run the app and Postgres with Docker Compose
  • Native server

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Build a small production image with dox build, and run it with Postgres in Docker Compose, with a health check.

A Docker image runs the same way on your laptop and on any server. The image in this guide holds only the compiled app, so it is small and starts fast.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app with a database.
  • Docker with Compose.

docs.title: 1. Add a health route
docs.text:
Docker needs a way to know if the app works. Add a health route that it can ask. The route answers 503 when the database does not answer.

Put it in register() of WebRouter. QueryBuilder comes from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

See Health check for more checks.

docs.title: 2. Add the health check binary
docs.text:
The final image has no shell and no curl, so the health check is a second small Dart binary:

bin/health.dart
import 'dart:io';

/// Docker health check. The final image has no shell and no curl,
/// so this small binary asks the app itself. Exit 0 = healthy.
Future<void> main() async {
  String port = Platform.environment['APP_PORT'] ?? '3000';
  HttpClient client = HttpClient()
    ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 3);
  try {
    HttpClientRequest request = await client.getUrl(
      Uri.parse('http://127.0.0.1:$port/health'),
    );
    HttpClientResponse response = await request.close();
    exit(response.statusCode == 200 ? 0 : 1);
  } catch (_) {
    exit(1);
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Write the Dockerfile
docs.text:
The Dockerfile has two stages. The first stage builds the AOT bundle. The second stage holds only the Dart runtime and the bundle, so the final image is small: about 17 MB for the blog API.

Dockerfile
# Stage 1: build the AOT bundle with the Dart SDK and the dox CLI.
FROM dart:stable AS build

WORKDIR /app

# Resolve dependencies first, so Docker caches this layer.
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# `dox build` runs build_runner, then `dart build cli`.
# The bundle is in build/bundle: bin/server, lib/, db/, .env.example
# (and bin/queue, bin/schedule when the app has them)
RUN dart pub global activate dox \
  && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# The health check binary. Plain dart:io, so `dart compile exe` is fine.
RUN dart compile exe bin/health.dart -o build/bundle/bin/health

# Lay out the final file tree. /tmp must be writable: uploads bigger
# than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file.
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/app/public /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r public/. /out/app/public/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Stage 2: the Dart AOT runtime and the bundle only. No SDK, no source.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file.
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["/app/bin/health"]
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

Delete the public lines if your app has no public folder.

When the container starts, check the start log. It must end with (native):

[server] Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

The libgcc_s lines are needed. Without them the native HTTP server does not load, and Dox stops at start with dox_http_native did not load.

dox build, not dart compile exe

dox_orm bundles SQLite with a build hook. dart compile exe does not run build hooks and stops with an error. dox build runs dart build cli, which does. It puts the native libraries in build/bundle/lib, next to bin/server.

Keep the build context small with a .dockerignore:

.dockerignore
.dart_tool/
.git/
.github/
.idea/
build/
storage/
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
pubspec_overrides.yaml

docs.title: 4. Write the compose file
docs.text:
Docker Compose runs the app and Postgres together. env_file: .env gives the app your .env. The lines under environment win over the file, so the app always talks to the postgres service:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    # secrets and config come from .env, never from the image
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      APP_ENV: production
      APP_PORT: 3000
      DB_CONNECTION: postgres
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      # uploads survive a new image
      - uploads:/app/storage
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-dox}
    volumes:
      - postgres:/var/lib/postgresql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-q", "-U", "${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres:
  uploads:
  • depends_on with service_healthy starts the app after Postgres answers. This matters because the app runs the migrations at start.
  • ${DB_PASSWORD:?...} stops compose with a clear message if .env has no password.
  • When the main isolate dies, the process exits and restart: unless-stopped starts it again.

docs.title: 5. Write the .env
docs.text:
.env
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=production
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
APP_PORT=3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=<a real password>

.env is in .dockerignore and .gitignore. It never goes into the image or into git.

The app now uses Postgres, so the build needs the Postgres driver. A new app skips it in pubspec.yaml, so remove the dox_postgres_native skip lines. See Skip unused drivers.

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose ps

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
docker compose ps

NAME             STATUS
my_app-app-1       Up 30 seconds (healthy)
my_app-postgres-1  Up 35 seconds (healthy)

curl http://localhost:3000/health

{"status":"ok","checks":{"database":"ok"}}

To see the health check work, stop Postgres with docker compose stop postgres. After about 45 seconds, docker compose ps shows the app as unhealthy.

docs.title: HTTPS
