docs.text: Do not add TLS to the app itself. Put Caddy or nginx in front, and set trustedProxies in AppConfig. See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Deployment for dox build, the bundle layout and systemd
  • Environments for dev, staging and production config
  • Migration: run on server start

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Run the same app in development, staging and production with different config, and keep secrets out of git and out of the image.

Your app needs different values in each place it runs: another database, another log format, another front-end URL. You should not put these values, and above all your secrets, in the code. So Dox reads them from the environment.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • build_runner for the typed env class (a new app has it).

docs.title: How Dox reads config
docs.text:
Dox looks for each key in two places:

  1. A real environment variable (from the shell, Docker or systemd). This one wins.
  2. The .env file in the folder where the app starts.

So use a .env file on your machine, and real environment variables on a server. On a server the .env file is optional.

docs.title: 1. The typed env class
docs.text:
A new project already has lib/config/env.dart. Its AppEnv class lists every key, with its type and its default. In this guides app, corsOrigin and appUrl are added keys. The rest comes with a new project.

lib/config/env.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

/// The env of the app, typed. Made by `dox env:generate`.
/// -------------------------------
/// Each getter reads one key: `appName` reads `APP_NAME`.
/// A getter body is the default. A nullable getter is optional.
/// Other getters are required: the app stops at startup when one is missing.
/// Run `dart run build_runner build` after you change this class.
@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  /// reads and checks every key once
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName => 'dox';

  /// development, staging or production. Not set: production.
  String get appEnv => 'production';

  int get appPort => 3000;

  /// required: used to sign tokens and encrypt cookies
  String get appKey;

  /// isolates (threads) of the HTTP server. Null: one per CPU core.
  int? get appTotalIsolate;

  String get logLevel => 'info';

  /// memory, file or redis
  String get cacheStore => 'file';

  /// local, s3 or memory
  String get storageDisk => 'local';

  /// sqlite, postgres or mysql
  String get dbConnection => 'sqlite';

  /// the database name. For SQLite: the file path.
  String get dbName => 'db/dox.sqlite';

  String get dbHost => 'localhost';

  /// null: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL
  int? get dbPort;

  String get dbUsername => 'postgres';

  String get dbPassword => '';

  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

Each getter reads the key with the same name in UPPER_SNAKE case, so dbPort reads DB_PORT. The getter decides if the key is needed:

  • A getter with a body has a default: int get appPort => 3000;.
  • A nullable getter with no body is optional: int? get dbPort; is null when the key is not set.
  • Any other getter with no body is required: String get appKey;.

If a required key is missing, the app stops at start and lists all the problems. build_runner makes the part file env.g.dart.

docs.title: 2. Add a key
docs.text:
When your app needs a new value, add a getter for it. For example, if the app needs a mail host, add this getter to AppEnv:

  /// the SMTP server for mails
  String get mailHost => 'localhost';

Then run build_runner again:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

Now env.mailHost reads MAIL_HOST. Add MAIL_HOST to .env.example too, so other developers know the key exists.

docs.title: 3. Use it in the config files
docs.text:
The config files read the typed getters. If a setting must differ per environment, base it on APP_ENV, like prettyPrint and debug here:

lib/config/logger.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

LoggerConfig logger = LoggerConfig(
  name: env.appName,
  enabled: true,
  level: env.logLevel,
  // colors on your machine, one JSON line per log in staging and production.
  // Env.appEnv, not appConfig.isDevelopment: appConfig is built from
  // this logger, so reading appConfig here would loop.
  prettyPrint: Env.appEnv == 'development',
);
lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      // print every query on your machine only
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName,
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);

docs.title: 4. Write the env files
docs.text:
You should commit .env.example, because it shows every key with a safe value. Never commit .env, because it holds your real secrets.

.env.example
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=development
APP_PORT=3000
# run `dox key:generate`
APP_KEY=
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
LOG_LEVEL=debug

To start on a new machine, copy the example and make a key:

cp .env.example .env
dox key:generate   # writes a new APP_KEY into .env

Keep every .env file out of git, except the example:

.gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

This is where the values live in each environment:

Environment Where the values live APP_ENV your machine .env development staging real env variables (compose environment:, a secrets manager) staging production real env variables production

On a server you can also keep a .env file next to the binary, outside git, with chmod 600. systemd reads it with EnvironmentFile=. See Deployment.

docs.title: 5. APP_KEY
docs.text:
APP_KEY is your most important secret, because it encrypts cookies and signs JWT tokens and local signed URLs.

  • Make one key per environment with dox key:generate. Never share the production key with staging.
  • The key must be exactly 32 characters. dox key:generate makes a key of the right length.
  • In production a bad key stops the app at start. A bad key is empty, not 32 characters, or a public sample key. In development the app only logs a warning.
  • If you change the key, every cookie, token and signed URL stops working, so every user is logged out. Plan it.

docs.title: 6. Check the env before a deploy
docs.text:
You want to find a missing key before the deploy, not after it. dox env:check loads AppEnv with the real environment and .env, and prints every missing or bad key. If there is a problem, it exits with code 1, so CI stops.

dox env:check

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Start the app with a key missing:

APP_KEY= dart run bin/server.dart

Unhandled exception:
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing

Now start it as staging on another port. The real variables win over .env:

APP_ENV=staging APP_PORT=4000 dart run bin/server.dart

The app listens on 4000. env.appEnv is 'staging', and appConfig.isDevelopment is false.

docs.title: Things that differ per environment
docs.text:
These are the settings that most apps change between environments:

Setting Development Staging and production prettyPrint of the logger true false (one JSON line per log) debug of the database true false totalIsolate 1 or 2 is enough one per core (the default) CORS_ORIGIN http://localhost:5173 the real front-end URL the server dox serve (JIT) the dox build binary (AOT)

docs.title: Details
docs.text: • "Development" means an APP_ENV of development, local, test or testing. Any other value, or no value, counts as production.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Environment variables for all types and rules of the typed env class
  • Docker
  • Deployment

docs.title: File upload
docs.text:
Accept an image from a form, check its size and type, save it to a disk, and return its URL.

You should never trust an uploaded file: it can be too big, or it can be a different type than its name says. So this guide checks the file in a DTO first, and only then saves it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the dox_storage package, lib/config/storage.dart and lib/providers/storage_provider.dart.

docs.title: 1. Set up the disk
docs.text:
The local disk of a new app saves files in the storage folder. Give the disk a url, because Storage().url() uses it to build the public URL of a file:

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    /// uploads go to the `storage` folder.
    /// `url` is the public address of `Storage.route('files', ...)`.
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': '${env.appUrl}/files',
    },
  },
);

APP_URL is a new key, so add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';

Run dart run build_runner build to update env.g.dart. Then add APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 to your .env.

The provider of a new app sets up the disks. You do not need to change it:

lib/providers/storage_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}

docs.title: 2. Write the DTO
docs.text:
The DTO checks the file before your controller runs. If the check fails, Dox answers 422 and the controller never sees the file.

lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  /// jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp or bmp. Dox reads the first bytes of the
  /// file to find the real type. The file name is not trusted.
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}

If you want other file types, use @Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx']) in place of @Image().

docs.title: 3. Write the controller
docs.text:
The controller saves the file with putFile and returns its path and URL. putFile gives the file a new UUID name, and on the local disk it does not read the whole file into memory.

lib/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart';

@Inject()
class UploadController {
  /// POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data, field `image`)
  Future<Map<String, String>> store(UploadImage body) async {
    // saves the file as /images/<uuid>.<ext> on the default disk
    String path = await Storage().putFile('images', body.image);
    String url = await Storage().url(path);
    return <String, String>{'path': path, 'url': url};
  }
}

Save the file before you return

Dox deletes the uploaded temp file when the response is sent. So call putFile, store or moveTo inside the controller, not later.

docs.title: 4. Add the routes
docs.text:
You need two routes. One route takes the upload, and Storage.route serves the saved files at GET /files/{key*}:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/upload', (UploadController c) => c.store);
  }
}
lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // GET /files/{key*}, any file of the default disk
    Storage.route('files', signed: false);
  }
}

signed: false makes every file public. If the files are private, leave it out, so the route serves only signed URLs. Then use Storage().signedUrl(path) in place of Storage().url(path).

docs.title: 5. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. build_runner writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. You add it only once, so skip this step if your app.dart already has dtos: dtos.

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Upload a PNG:

curl -F image=@photo.png http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"path":"/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png","url":"http://localhost:3000/files/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png"}

Open the url in the browser. The image shows.

Now upload a text file. You get 422:

curl -F image=@notes.txt http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"image":"The image must be an image"}

If you send no file at all, you also get 422, with {"image":"The image is required"}.

docs.title: Bigger files
docs.text: A multipart/form-data body can be 100 MB by default. If you need more, change it in AppConfig(maxMultipartSize: ...). Set the same limit in your proxy too (client_max_body_size in nginx).

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• @Image() reads the first bytes of the file to find the real type. It does not trust the file name.
  • A file bigger than 1 MB is written to a temp file while it arrives. That is the file Dox deletes after the response.
  • On the local disk, putFile moves the temp file. With permissions on, it streams the file in place of a move.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Request: form data for RequestFile
  • Validation rules: files for @Image, @Mimes, @MimeTypes, @MaxSize, @MinSize, @Dimensions
  • File storage for S3 and signed URLs

docs.title: JWT authentication
docs.text:
Let users register and log in, give them a JWT token, protect routes with it, and read the user in a controller.

A JWT token is a good fit for an API that a mobile app or a single page app calls. The client gets the token at login and sends it with every request, so the server needs no session.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has a database (SQLite), a User model and a users table with name, email and password columns.
  • The dox_auth package. A new app does not have it. Add it:
dart pub add dox_auth

docs.title: 1. Hide the password in the model
docs.text:
The token holds user.toJson(), and anyone with the token can read it. So the password hash must be in hidden. The model of a new app already does this:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

docs.title: 2. Set up the auth provider
docs.text:
The provider tells Dox how to make and check tokens, and how to find the user:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              // APP_KEY signs the tokens. A new key logs every user out.
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              // a token stops working after this time
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

The secret must be at least 32 bytes. A key from dox key:generate has the right length. A shorter secret stops the app in production, and prints a warning in development.

You do not need to register the provider, because Dox finds it by itself. After dart run build_runner build it is in lib/generated/container.g.dart.

docs.title: 3. Write the DTOs
docs.text:
You need one DTO for register and one for login. @Unique makes sure the email is not taken yet. It comes from dox_orm, so hide the Schema class of dox_orm in the import.

lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  @Trim()
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

docs.title: 4. Write the controller
docs.text:
The controller makes the user, logs in, and returns the user of a token:

lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': user};
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/me (behind AuthMiddleware)
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/logout (behind AuthMiddleware)
  /// By default a JWT is not cancelled on the server. The client deletes
  /// the token, and it still works until `expiresIn` passes. To cancel it,
  /// turn on revocation and call `Auth().revokeToken(req)`.
  Map<String, String> logout(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, String>{'message': 'Delete the token on the client'};
  }
}

Hash.makeAsync makes a bcrypt hash of the password. At login, auth.attempt finds the user by email and checks the password against that hash. It returns null if the email or the password is wrong.

docs.title: 5. Add the routes
docs.text:
Register and login are open to everyone. Every other route goes inside AuthMiddleware. The middleware reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, checks the token and loads the user from the database. A missing or bad token stops the request with 401.

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
      Route.post('/auth/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
      // put every protected route here
    });
  }
}

docs.title: 6. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. build_runner writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. You add it only once, so skip this step if your app.dart already has dtos: dtos.

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 7. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Register a user. You get a token and the user:

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"...","updated_at":"..."}}

If you log in with a wrong password, you get 401:

{"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}}

Now log in and use the token:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login | jq -r .token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/auth/me

{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"...","updated_at":"..."}

Without the header, /api/auth/me gives 401 Authentication failed.

The {"error": ...} shape comes from the response handler in Custom errors. Without that handler, the 401 body is {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}.

docs.title: Logout and expiry
docs.text:
By default the server checks only the signature of a JWT, so it can not cancel one token. This is what you can do:

You want Do this Log out on this device The client deletes the token. That is all logout does. Limit the damage of a stolen token Keep expiresIn short, for example Duration(hours: 12). Log every user out at once Change APP_KEY. Every old token stops working. Block one user Delete the user. AuthMiddleware loads the user from the database on each request, so a deleted user gets 401.

If you need to cancel one token, or all tokens of a user, turn on revocation. See Revoke tokens. Or use access tokens, which you can revoke at any time.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Authentication for all options of AuthGuard, JwtAuthDriver and AuthProvider
  • Hashing
  • Middleware

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Make a list route that takes page and per_page from the query string and returns one page of rows.

A table can have many thousands of rows. You do not want to send them all in one response, because it is slow for the server and for the client. So the client asks for one page at a time.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has a database (SQLite), a User model and a users table.

docs.title: 1. Write the query DTO
docs.text:
The DTO reads page and per_page and checks them. Because it has source: Source.query, it reads the query string, not the body. The field perPage reads the key per_page, because keys are snake_case by default.

lib/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'list_users.dto.g.dart';

/// GET /api/users?page=2&per_page=10
@Dto(source: Source.query)
class ListUsers {
  @Min(1)
  final int page;

  @Range(1, 100)
  final int perPage; // query key: per_page

  const ListUsers({this.page = 1, this.perPage = 20});

  static const DtoSchema<ListUsers> schema = $ListUsersDto;
}

Both fields have a default, so the client can leave them out. @Range(1, 100) stops a client from asking for 10000 rows at once.

docs.title: 2. Write the controller
docs.text:
paginate() runs one count query and one select query, and returns a Pagination. The controller can return it as it is, because Dox sends its toJson().

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users?page=1&per_page=20
  Future<Pagination<User>> index(ListUsers query) async {
    return User()
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  }
}

You should always add an orderBy. Without it, the database may return the rows in a different order on each page, so a row can show up twice or not at all.

If you want to filter the rows, add a where before paginate: User().where('role', 'admin').orderBy('id').paginate(...).

docs.title: 3. Add the route
docs.text:
lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/users', (UserController c) => c.index);

docs.title: 4. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. build_runner writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. You add it only once, so skip this step if your app.dart already has dtos: dtos.

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 5. Build and run
docs.text:
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Ask for page 2, with 2 rows per page. With 3 users in the table, you get the last user:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=2&per_page=2'

{
  "total": 3,
  "per_page": 2,
  "last_page": 2,
  "current_page": 2,
  "data": [
    {"id": 1, "name": "User 1", "email": "user1@example.com", "created_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z", "updated_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z"}
  ]
}

The keys of the answer are:

Key Meaning total rows that match the query, on all pages per_page rows per page last_page the number of the last page current_page the page you asked for data the rows of this page, from toJson() of the model

If you ask for a page after the last one, data is an empty list.

Bad input gets 422 before the controller runs:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=0&per_page=500'

{"page":"The page must be greater than or equal 1","per_page":"The per_page must be between 1 and 100"}

docs.title: Change the shape of a row
docs.text:
Sometimes the model has fields you do not want to send. Then use a serializer for the rows. dox make:serializer User makes lib/app/serializers/user.serializer.dart. page.data gives the typed rows (List<User>), so you can pass them to the serializer:

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Query builder: paginate
  • DTOs: body and query string
  • Serializer

docs.title: Share code with Flutter
docs.text:
Put a @Dto class in a shared Dart package, so the Dox server and the Flutter app check input with the same rules and error messages.

You want to check a form in the app, so the user sees an error at once. But the server must check the same input again, because it can not trust the client. If you write the rules twice, they drift apart. So you write them once, in a shared package.

This works because the generated DTO code imports only dox_validation. It is pure Dart (no dart:io, no dart:mirrors), so it runs in Flutter and on the web.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create server). Here it is in the server folder.
  • A Flutter app (flutter create app). Here it is in the app folder.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
The three parts live next to each other in one folder:

my_blog/
  packages/
    blog_shared/     # the DTOs. Pure Dart.
  server/            # the Dox app
  app/               # the Flutter app

flowchart LR
    S[packages/blog_shared<br>SaveBlog + SaveBlog.schema] --> A[app: Flutter<br>checks the form]
    S --> B[server: Dox<br>checks the request]
    A -- "POST /api/blogs (JSON)" --> B

docs.title: 1. The shared package
docs.text:
Make a plain Dart package for the DTOs:

packages/blog_shared/pubspec.yaml
name: blog_shared
description: DTOs shared by the Dox server and the Flutter app.
version: 0.1.0
publish_to: none

environment:
  sdk: ^3.13.0

Add the packages:

cd packages/blog_shared
dart pub add dox_validation
dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner

dox_builder is a dev dependency, because it only runs when you generate code. So the Flutter app does not get it.

Now write the DTO. Import dox_validation, not dox_core, because dox_core does not run in Flutter:

packages/blog_shared/lib/src/save_blog.dart
import 'package:dox_validation/dox_validation.dart';

part 'save_blog.g.dart';

/// A new blog post. The server and the app check it with the same rules.
@Dto()
class SaveBlog {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 255)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String description;

  const SaveBlog({required this.title, required this.description});

  static const DtoSchema<SaveBlog> schema = $SaveBlogDto;
}

Export the DTOs. Also export dox_validation, so the app gets ParseResult and ValidationException from the same import:

packages/blog_shared/lib/blog_shared.dart
export 'package:dox_validation/dox_validation.dart';

export 'src/save_blog.dart';

Generate the code:

cd packages/blog_shared
dart pub get
dart run build_runner build

This writes two files:

  • lib/src/save_blog.g.dart: the checks, the converter and the JSON Schema of SaveBlog.
  • lib/generated/dtos.g.dart: the list of every DTO in this package. The server uses it.

Commit both files, so the Flutter app does not need to run the generator.

Rules that need the database stay on the server

@Unique and @Exists come from dox_orm. Do not use them in the shared package, because the app can not import dox_orm. Check them on the server, in the service or in a server-only DTO.

docs.title: 2. The Dox server
docs.text:
Add the shared package to the dependencies of the server:

server/pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  # ... the packages of the new app stay
  blog_shared:
    path: ../packages/blog_shared

Run dart pub get.

Dox finds a DTO in the dtos list of AppConfig. The server's own lib/generated/dtos.g.dart lists only the DTOs in the server, so add the list of the shared package too:

server/lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog_shared/generated/dtos.g.dart' as shared;
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:server/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  dtos: <DtoSchema<Object>>[...dtos, ...shared.dtos],
);

If the server has no DTOs of its own, its dtos list is empty, and the line above still works.

The controller asks for SaveBlog like any other DTO. Dox checks the body before the method runs, so bad input gets 422:

server/lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:blog_shared/blog_shared.dart' show SaveBlog;
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> store(SaveBlog body) async {
    // body.title is already trimmed and checked.
    return <String, dynamic>{'title': body.title, 'saved': true};
  }
}
server/lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.store);

Use show SaveBlog in server code, because dox_core and blog_shared both export a class named ValidationException. With show, the two names do not clash.

A bad request gets the errors as {"key": "message"}:

POST /api/blogs  {"title": "ab", "description": "short"}
422 {"title":"The title must be between 3 and 255 characters","description":"The description must be at least 10 characters"}

docs.title: 3. The Flutter app
docs.text:
Add the shared package to the app:

app/pubspec.yaml
name: app
publish_to: none

environment:
  sdk: ^3.13.0

dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  http: ^1.6.0
  blog_shared:
    path: ../packages/blog_shared

The app does not depend on dox_core.

The widget checks the form with SaveBlog.schema.safeParse(...), and it sends the request only when the input is good. result.errors has the same shape as the server's 422 body, so one _errors map shows both:

app/lib/new_blog_form.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:blog_shared/blog_shared.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

class NewBlogForm extends StatefulWidget {
  const NewBlogForm({super.key});

  @override
  State<NewBlogForm> createState() {
    return _NewBlogFormState();
  }
}

class _NewBlogFormState extends State<NewBlogForm> {
  final TextEditingController _title = TextEditingController();
  final TextEditingController _description = TextEditingController();
  Map<String, String> _errors = <String, String>{};

  Future<void> _submit() async {
    ParseResult<SaveBlog> result = SaveBlog.schema.safeParse(<String, dynamic>{
      'title': _title.text,
      'description': _description.text,
    });
    if (!result.success) {
      setState(() {
        _errors = result.errors;
      });
      return;
    }

    http.Response response = await http.post(
      Uri.parse('https://api.example.com/api/blogs'),
      headers: <String, String>{'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
      body: jsonEncode(SaveBlog.schema.toMap(result.value!)),
    );
    setState(() {
      _errors = response.statusCode == 422
          ? Map<String, String>.from(jsonDecode(response.body) as Map)
          : <String, String>{};
    });
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _title.dispose();
    _description.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(
      children: <Widget>[
        TextField(
          controller: _title,
          decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Title', errorText: _errors['title']),
        ),
        TextField(
          controller: _description,
          decoration: InputDecoration(labelText: 'Description', errorText: _errors['description']),
        ),
        ElevatedButton(onPressed: _submit, child: const Text('Save')),
      ],
    );
  }
}

docs.title: Other schema methods
docs.text:
The schema has more methods than safeParse:

  • parse throws a ValidationException when the input is bad.
  • toMap gives the JSON map to send.
  • toJsonSchema gives the JSON Schema of the DTO.

If the DTO has an async validate() method, use safeParseAsync or parseAsync.

See Validation and dox_validation for all rules and methods.

docs.title: Static files and SPA
docs.text:
Serve a folder of files, or a single page app (React, Vue, Flutter web), from the Dox app, with the right cache headers.

If your front-end is small, you can serve it from the same Dox app as your API. Then you have one server to run and no CORS setup.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A public folder with the built front-end (index.html, assets/...).
  • For the storage way and the controller below: the dox_storage package, with its provider. See File storage.

docs.title: Serve a folder: one line
docs.text:
If you only need to serve the files of a folder, Route.staticFiles does it in one line. Add it in register() of WebRouter:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');

Now GET /app.js sends public/app.js with the right Content-Type. If a route and a file have the same path, the route wins. A missing file answers 404.

The browser gets 304 when it already has the file, because Dox sends ETag and Last-Modified. If you want a Cache-Control header too, add maxAge:. See Routing: serve static files for all the rules.

For a single page app, add Route.fallback, so every URL with no route and no file gets index.html. See Routing: fallback route.

docs.title: Or serve a storage disk
docs.text:
You can also serve the folder as a storage disk. Storage.route serves every file of a disk. First add a public disk for the folder in lib/config/storage.dart:

lib/config/storage.dart
StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage'},

    /// the front-end files
    'public': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'public'},
  },
);

Then add the route in register() of WebRouter. Storage comes from package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart.

lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('static', disk: 'public', signed: false); // GET /static/{key*}

Now GET /static/app.js sends public/app.js with the right Content-Type. A missing file answers 404. The disk rejects .. in the path, so a client can not read files outside public.

This is enough for a few files, but it sends no Cache-Control header. For an SPA, read on.

docs.title: Serve an SPA
docs.text:
An SPA needs two things, and a small controller gives you both:

  • index.html for every URL the SPA router handles, with no cache.
  • The built assets with a long cache. Build tools put a hash in the file name (app.3f9c2b.js), so a new build has new names.

docs.title: 1. Write the controller
docs.text:
The controller has one method for the assets and one for index.html:

lib/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

@Inject()
class StaticController {
  /// GET /assets/{path*}
  /// Built files have a hash in the name, so the browser may keep them
  /// for one year. The `public` disk rejects `..` in the path.
  Future<DoxResponse> asset(String path) async {
    StreamFile file = await Storage().disk('public').stream(path);
    return response(file).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
  }

  /// GET / and GET /{path*}
  /// Every other URL gets index.html, so the router of the SPA can
  /// handle it. Never cache it, so a new deploy shows at once.
  /// An unknown API URL stays a 404, it does not get the page.
  DoxResponse index(DoxRequest req) {
    if (req.uri.path.startsWith('/api/')) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return response(File('public/index.html')).cache(Duration.zero);
  }
}

cache(duration) sets Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds>. Duration.zero gives max-age=0, so the browser asks again each time.

docs.title: 2. Add the routes
docs.text:
The catch-all route must come last, because it matches every URL. So put the API router before the web router in AppConfig:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // the SPA: assets with a long cache, every other URL gets index.html
    Route.get('/assets/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.asset);
    Route.get('/', (StaticController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.index);
  }
}
lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// the SPA catch-all route is in WebRouter, so it must come last.
  /// Listed routers come first, in this order.
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter(), WebRouter()],
  // ...
);

Keep the route for / too, because /{path*} does not match the start page.

docs.title: 3. Put the build in public
docs.text:
Build the front-end and copy the files to public:

# React (Vite)
npm run build && cp -r dist/. public/

# Flutter web
flutter build web && cp -r build/web/. public/

Vite puts the files in assets/. Flutter web puts them next to index.html. For Flutter, change the asset route to match, or serve everything with Storage.route and give index.html the catch-all.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The start page comes with no cache:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=0
content-type: text/html

Any other page also gets index.html, and an asset gets a cache of one year:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/settings/profile   # same answer: index.html
curl -i http://localhost:3000/assets/app.js

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=31536000
content-type: text/javascript

GET /assets/nope.js answers 404. GET /assets/..%2Fpubspec.yaml answers 404 too. GET /api/nothing answers 404, not the page.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
Put a proxy in front of Dox, and let it do gzip. See Deployment.

For a big site, serve public from the proxy or a CDN, and keep Dox for the API only.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Routing: serve storage files
  • Response: files and big responses
  • File storage

docs.title: Testing with a database
docs.text:
Run model tests against a real database: SQLite for fast local tests, or a test Postgres for the real thing.

A test with a real database finds bugs that a mock can not find, like a wrong column name or a broken query. In this guide the migrations run once, and every test starts with empty tables, so the tests do not change each other's data.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the User model, a users migration in db/migration and the test package.

docs.title: 1. Check the migration
docs.text:
The test builds its tables from your migrations. A new app has this one (its file name starts with another date). For a new table, run dox make:migration create_posts_table.

db/migration/2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.string('password');
      table.timestamps();
      table.softDeletes();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

db/migration/migrations.dart is the list of all migrations, and dox make:migration updates it. The test imports that list. Because a Dart migration works on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite, the same test runs on all of them.

docs.title: 2. Write the test (SQLite)
docs.text:
Start with SQLite, because it needs no server. The test makes its own database config, so your .env does not matter.

test/user_test.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

/// One SQLite file for this test file. No server, no Postgres.
const String dbFile = 'storage/test.sqlite';

DatabaseConfig testDatabase = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'sqlite',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: dbFile,
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);

Future<void> deleteDbFile() async {
  for (String suffix in <String>['', '-wal', '-shm']) {
    File file = File('$dbFile$suffix');
    if (await file.exists()) await file.delete();
  }
}

void main() {
  setUpAll(() async {
    await deleteDbFile();
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: testDatabase.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(testDatabase);
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await deleteDbFile();
  });

  test('saves and finds a user', () async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = 'Ann'
      ..email = 'ann@example.com'
      ..password = Hash.make('secret123');
    await user.save();

    User? found = await User().where('email', 'ann@example.com').getFirst();
    expect(found?.id, user.id);
    expect(found?.name, 'Ann');
    expect(Hash.verify('secret123', found!.password!), isTrue);
  });

  test('the tables are empty again', () async {
    expect(await User().count(), 0);
  });
}

This is what happens:

  1. setUpAll deletes an old database file, runs the migrations, and starts the ORM on the same file.
  2. setUp runs refreshDatabase() before each test. It empties every table (not the migrations table) and starts the ids at 1 again.
  3. tearDownAll deletes the file.

Put storage/test.sqlite in .gitignore. The test uses a file and not :memory:, because the migrator and the ORM each open their own connection. Two connections to :memory: are two different databases.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text: dart test test/user_test.dart

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
You see the migrations run, and then the tests pass. The migration names start with the dates of your files, and a new app also has the tables of the queue:

00:00 +0: (setUpAll)
Migrating: 2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_23_000000_create_queue_tables
Migrated: 2026_10_23_000000_create_queue_tables
00:00 +1: saves and finds a user
00:00 +2: the tables are empty again
00:00 +2: All tests passed!

docs.title: The same test on Postgres
docs.text:
SQLite is fast, but your app may run on Postgres in production. Then you should test on Postgres too. Use a separate database for tests, never the one you develop on, because the tests delete all rows.

Start a test database with Docker:

docker run -d --name my_app_test -p 5433:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -e POSTGRES_DB=my_app_test postgres:18

Change the config at the top of the test:

DatabaseConfig testDatabase = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 5433,
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'postgres',
      database: 'my_app_test',
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);

Delete deleteDbFile() and its two calls. The rest of the test stays the same. You can also read these values from the env, and run DB_PORT=5433 DB_NAME=my_app_test dart test.

docs.title: Many test files
docs.text:
Each test file runs in its own process, at the same time as the others. So two files that use the same table can break each other. To fix it, give each file its own SQLite file (storage/test_users.sqlite, storage/test_posts.sqlite), or run the files one by one:

dart test --concurrency=1

docs.title: Test a route with the database
docs.text:
You can also test a full route, from the request to the database. This test uses the GET /api/users route of the Pagination guide.

DoxTestClient starts the app inside the test. It runs the providers, so the ORM uses the config in lib/config/database.dart. So you pick the test database with env variables:

test/api_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/users has no rows', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/users');
    res.expectStatus(200);
    expect(res.json['data'], isEmpty);
  });
}

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite DB_NAME=storage/test.sqlite dart test test/api_test.dart

See Testing: test HTTP routes for all client methods.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Testing
  • Migration
  • Database: SQLite

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
dox_cache keeps data that is slow to make, so the next request can read it fast.

It is the cache behind Cache() in Dox. It has remember, tags, atomic locks and many drivers. This page shows the full API. For a shorter guide, see Cache.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
dox_core uses dox_cache and exports it, so there is nothing to install. A new app already has the cache config. If your app does not have it, run dox add cache. See Cache.

The stores are in lib/config/cache.dart, and lib/config/app.dart passes them to AppConfig(cache: cache). To add a store, like Redis, edit this file:

lib/config/cache.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

CacheConfig cache = CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: env.cacheStore, // CACHE_STORE in .env, default 'file'
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache'},
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory', 'max_size': 10000},
    'redis': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'redis', 'host': '127.0.0.1', 'prefix': 'app_cache:'},
  },
);

Then set CACHE_STORE=redis in .env. With no config at all, Dox has a file store (the default) and a memory store.

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
Driver What it is Shared between isolates memory a map in this isolate. Fast. Optional LRU size limit No file one JSON file per key in a folder Yes (same machine) redis Redis, with the ioredis package Yes null stores nothing. Use it to turn caching off - database a table in your database, from the dox_cache_database package. See Database store Yes

Dox runs many isolates, and each isolate has its own memory cache. So use redis or database when all isolates and servers must see the same data.

Sessions on a memory store are the exception. They live in the main isolate, so every isolate sees them. See Session.

docs.title: Store options
docs.text:
Driver Options every driver driver, prefix (default dox_cache:) memory max_size: the most items. When full, the least recently used item is removed. No limit when not set file path (default storage/cache). Each prefix gets its own sub folder. prune_every, see Pruning the file store. fsync (default true): sync each write to the disk redis host (default 127.0.0.1), port (default 6379), username, password, db, tls, pool_size (default 10), max_value_bytes (values bigger than this throw. No limit by default), options (a RedisOptions, replaces the connection keys. See Redis options)

The prefix is added to every key. Use different prefixes when two apps share one Redis database.

docs.title: Using another store
docs.text:
Cache() uses the default store. Use store to pick another one by name:

await Cache().store('memory').get('foo');

docs.title: Retrieving items
docs.text:
Use get to read a value. The second argument is the default, which you get when the key is missing or expired. The default can also be a function, which runs only on a miss:

String? foo = await Cache().get('foo');

String name = await Cache().get('name', 'none');

docs.title: Checking if an item exists
docs.text:
The has method returns true when the value is there and is not null:

if (await Cache().has('foo')) {
  // ...
}

docs.title: Retrieving many items
docs.text:
The many method reads many keys at once. A missing key gives null:

Map<String, dynamic> values = await Cache().many(<String>['a', 'b']);

docs.title: Retrieve or store
docs.text:
Often you want to read a value, or make it and cache it when it is missing. Use remember for this:

List<dynamic> posts = await Cache().remember(
  'posts',
  Duration(minutes: 5),
  () async => (await Post().all()).map((Post p) => p.toJson()).toList(),
);

If many calls ask for the same key at the same time, the function runs only once in one isolate. The others wait for it. Pass lock: true if callers in other isolates and servers should wait too. This needs a driver with locks.

rememberForever does the same, but the value never expires.

A cached value comes back as JSON, so a List is List<dynamic> and a Map is Map<String, dynamic>. If you want another type, pass decode. It turns the cached JSON into your type:

List<String> names = await Cache().remember<List<String>>(
  'names',
  Duration(minutes: 10),
  loadNames,
  decode: (Object? json) => List<String>.from(json as List<dynamic>),
);

docs.title: Stale while revalidate
docs.text:
Sometimes an old value is fine for a while, but you do not want callers to wait for a refresh. Use flexible. The value is fresh for the first time. After that it is stale for the second time: callers still get it right away, and one caller refreshes it in the background. After both times, the next call waits for the function:

int count = await Cache().flexible<int>(
  'users',
  Duration(minutes: 5),  // fresh
  Duration(minutes: 10), // stale
  countUsers,
);

It takes decode like remember. The driver must support locks.

docs.title: Retrieve and delete
docs.text:
The pull method reads a value and removes it, in one atomic step:

dynamic value = await Cache().pull('foo');

docs.title: Storing items
docs.text:
Use put to store a value. Without a duration, the value is kept forever. A zero or negative duration removes the key:

await Cache().put('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

Values must be JSON types: Map, List, String, num, bool or null. Other types throw. So for a model, store model.toJson(), not the model. A stored null reads as a miss.

docs.title: Storing if not present
docs.text:
The add method stores the value only when the key is missing. It returns true when it stored it:

bool added = await Cache().add('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

docs.title: Storing many items
docs.text: await Cache().putMany(<String, Object?>{'a': 1, 'b': 2});

docs.title: Storing items forever
docs.text: await Cache().forever('foo', 'bar');

docs.title: Incrementing and decrementing
docs.text:
Use increment and decrement for counters. A missing key starts at 0, and the ttl stays the same:

await Cache().increment('visits');
await Cache().decrement('stock', 5);

docs.title: Changing the expiry time
docs.text:
The touch method gives a key a new ttl and keeps the value. It returns true when the key was there:

await Cache().touch('foo', duration: Duration(hours: 1));

docs.title: Deleting items
docs.text:
The forget method removes one item. The flush method removes all items of the store:

await Cache().forget('foo');

await Cache().flush();

On Redis, flush deletes only the keys with the store prefix. It never runs FLUSHDB. So an empty prefix makes flush throw.

docs.title: Cache tags
docs.text:
Tags let you group items, so you can flush the group without touching other items:

await Cache().tag('users').put('u1', 'Ann');

await Cache().tag('users').flush(); // removes only the 'users' items

Use tags(<String>['users', 'admins']) for many tags. Tags work with every driver. A flushed item is not deleted at once. It is just not found any more, and it goes away when its ttl ends.

docs.title: Atomic locks
docs.text:
Sometimes only one worker may run a piece of code at a time, for example a report job. Use a lock:

CacheLock lock = Cache().lock('report', Duration(seconds: 10));
if (await lock.get()) {
  try {
    // only one worker runs this
  } finally {
    await lock.release();
  }
}

get() takes the lock and returns true, or returns false when someone else has it. The ttl frees the lock by itself if the worker crashes. Without a ttl, the lock stays until release().

docs.title: Waiting for a lock
docs.text:
block tries again every 50 ms until it gets the lock or the time is over. It returns false when the time is over:

bool got = await lock.block(Duration(seconds: 5));

If you give a callback, block runs it while it holds the lock, frees the lock and returns the result. It throws LockTimeoutException when the time is over:

String result = await lock.block(Duration(seconds: 5), () async => makeReport());

The memory, file, redis and database drivers support locks. A memory lock works inside one isolate only. A file lock works for all isolates on one machine.

docs.title: Encrypting the cache
docs.text:
By default the cache keeps plain JSON, so anyone who can read the cache files or the Redis database can read the values. To hide them, add 'encrypt': true to the store:

'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache', 'encrypt': true},

The values are then encrypted with your APP_KEY. Old keys in previousKeys can still read old entries. When the key changes and the old key is gone, the old entries count as a miss, and the cache fills again.

Cache keys and tag names are not encrypted. Encryption protects against reading only: someone who can write to the store can still copy an encrypted value to another key.

docs.title: Database store
docs.text:
The dox_cache_database package keeps the cache in a table of your database. All servers that use the same database share the cache, the locks and the sessions, with no Redis. It works on SQLite, Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB.

Install it and make the table:

dart pub add dox_cache_database
dox cache:table
dox migrate

dox cache:table writes a migration that calls CacheTables.up(schema). Give --table=<name> for another table name.

Register the driver when the app starts, before the first use of the store:

import 'package:dox_cache_database/dox_cache_database.dart';

Dox().cache.extend(
  'database',
  DatabaseCacheDriverFactory(Dox().cache.config.encrypter),
);

Then add a store to lib/config/cache.dart:

'database': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'database',
  'table': 'cache', // optional, default `cache`
  'connection': 'cache', // optional, default the default connection
  'prefix': 'app:', // optional
  'encrypt': true, // optional
},

Cache calls inside an app transaction on the same connection join that transaction, so their writes roll back with it. If you do not want this, give the store its own connection: a second connection with the same database settings.

An expired row reads as a miss, but it stays in the table, so the table keeps growing. To delete expired rows, set prune_interval on the store. It is in seconds. A write then starts a delete of expired rows in the background, at most once per that time. A read never starts it, and no call waits for it. Each server counts its own time. It is off by default:

'database': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'database', 'prune_interval': 3600},

On a very big table the first delete can be slow. On MySQL and MariaDB it can make writes wait for a short time.

You can also call prune() yourself from time to time, for example in a schedule:

int deleted = await (store.driver as DatabaseCacheDriver).prune();

A new cache table has an index on expires_at, so a prune reads only the expired rows. A table you made earlier does not have it. Add it with a migration:

await schema.table('cache', (Table t) => t.index('expires_at'));

An increment that goes past the 64-bit integer limit throws an error. The stored value does not change.

docs.title: Pruning the file store
docs.text:
A read never deletes a file, so an expired file stays until it is written again. The store cleans up by itself: at most once an hour, a write starts a light prune in the background. The first one can start on the first write that comes at least a minute after the first write of the app. It deletes expired files, temp files left by a crash, and lock files that are free. It keeps files it can not read or decrypt, because they can belong to another app in the same folder. It never touches files the cache did not make. Only one runs per hour, also with many isolates or servers on one folder, and also when the app restarts often.

To clean up more often, or to also delete broken files, call prune() yourself, for example in a schedule:

int deleted = await (store.driver as FileDriver).prune();

You can also set prune_every on the store. It runs prune() in the background once every that many writes, in place of the hourly prune. Each run reads every file of the store, so pick a big number:

'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache', 'prune_every': 1000},

docs.title: Faster writes with fsync: false
docs.text:
Each write syncs the file to the disk first. This keeps the newest value after a power cut, but it is slow. A cache can lose its last writes, so you can turn it off:

'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache', 'fsync': false},

A crash of the app alone loses nothing. Only a power cut or a crash of the machine can lose the last writes. A lost value reads as a miss. Keep it on for a store that holds sessions, if a power cut must not log users out.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_cache also works on its own:

dart pub add dox_cache

Make a CacheManager with your stores:

import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';

CacheManager cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: 'redis',
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory', 'max_size': 1000},
    'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache'},
    'redis': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'redis', 'host': '127.0.0.1', 'prefix': 'app:'},
  },
));

CacheStore store = cache.store();     // the default store
await cache.store('file').get('a');   // a named store

A CacheStore has the same methods as Cache(). The only difference is that the ttl is a normal argument, not a named one:

await store.put('a', 1, Duration(minutes: 5));

In a Dox app, Dox().cache is this CacheManager, and Cache().repository is the CacheStore. dox_core exports the same classes, so importing both packages is fine.

docs.title: Encryption without Dox
docs.text:
A CacheManager you build yourself needs an encrypter for stores with 'encrypt': true. Use const CryptCacheEncrypter() with Dox, or write your own class:

class MyEncrypter implements CacheEncrypter {
  @override
  String encrypt(String text) => myEncrypt(text);

  @override
  String decrypt(String text) => myDecrypt(text); // throw on bad input
}

CacheConfig(defaultStore: 'file', stores: stores, encrypter: MyEncrypter());

docs.title: Your own driver
docs.text:
Write a factory and register it with extend. Or add a ready driver with addStore:

class MyDriverFactory implements CacheDriverFactory {
  @override
  CacheDriver create(Map<String, dynamic> options) {
    return MyDriver(options);
  }
}

cache.extend('mine', MyDriverFactory()); // config: {'driver': 'mine'}
cache.addStore('ready', MemoryDriver());

MyDriver extends CacheDriver. It must implement prefix, get, put, add, increment, forget and flush. Override lock to support locks and close to close its connections. You can also override pull to make it atomic, and has and touch to make them faster.

docs.title: Closing the cache
docs.text: cache.close() closes the connections of every store that was built, like the Redis connections. It is safe to call twice. In a Dox app you do not call it, because Dox closes the stores on shutdown.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

  • getRaw(key) gives the stored JSON text with no decode, or null when it is missing.
  • pool_size is the most Redis connections one store opens in one isolate. A store uses about one, so you rarely change it.
  • On Redis, a prefix with no : at the end gets one, so app does not match the keys of app2.
  • release() frees a lock only for the owner that took it. forceRelease() frees it, whoever holds it.
  • block(timeout) with no callback throws LockTimeoutException instead of returning false when you set lock.throwOnTimeout = true or the flag CacheFlags(lockThrows: true). See CacheConfig.
  • The null driver throws UnsupportedError for locks.
  • On the file driver, add, increment, touch and prune() take a file lock on the key, so they are safe across isolates. A plain put takes no lock, so a put at the same moment as prune() can be lost. It is only a cache miss.
  • With encrypt, a whole cache file is encrypted, also the expiry time. Lock files hold no values and are not encrypted.
  • With encrypt on Redis, a plain int stays plain text, so increment and decrement still work. Tag counters are int values too. To keep a secret number encrypted, store it as a String.
  • memory and null stores do not encrypt, because the values never leave the process. The option still needs an encrypter.
  • 'encrypt' must be true or false. Another type, like 'true', throws an ArgumentError. A store with 'encrypt': true and no encrypter throws a StateError when it is built.
  • After you turn encrypt on, old plain values read as a miss (except an int on Redis).
  • On an encrypted file store, prune also deletes files that it can not decrypt.
  • max_value_bytes is checked on the plain JSON size. The encrypted text is about a third bigger.
  • On the database store, a full key (the prefix and the key) may have at most 255 characters. A longer key throws an ArgumentError.
  • The database store takes expiry times from the clock of each server, so keep the clocks in sync.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
dox_mcp serves your app's tools to AI clients like Claude, ChatGPT and IDE agents, with the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

A tool is an action the AI can call, like "add an expense". You write the tool in Dart, and dox_mcp serves it from a normal Dox route over the Streamable HTTP transport.

  • Tool arguments are dox_validation schemas. Clients see them as JSON Schema, and every call is checked before your code runs.
  • Session ids are signed with APP_KEY, so a session works on every isolate and after a restart. No store is needed.
  • Replies are plain JSON. No SSE stream is needed for tools.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run:

dox add mcp

It adds the package, lib/config/mcp.dart with an McpServer, and a sample tool in lib/app/mcp/echo.tool.dart. You add the route and the auth yourself. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

To set it up by hand, add the package:

dart pub add dox_mcp

docs.title: Writing tools
docs.text:
A tool extends McpTool. It has a name, a description for the model, an input schema, and a call method that does the work:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mcp/dox_mcp.dart';

class AddExpense extends McpTool {
  @override
  String get name => 'add_expense';

  @override
  String get description => 'Record an expense. Amount is in dollars.';

  @override
  ObjectSchema get input => v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
    'amount': v.num().positive().describe('Amount, like 12.50.'),
    'note': v.string().max(500).optional(),
  });

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> call(Map<String, dynamic> args, McpContext context) async {
    User user = context.authAs<User>();
    // ... save it
    return McpToolResult.text('Recorded ${args['amount']} for ${user.email}.');
  }
}

If the arguments are wrong, the client gets a tool result with isError: true that lists each problem, so the model can fix the call. If your tool throws, the client also gets a tool result with isError: true and the error text.

docs.title: Small tools
docs.text:
A small tool can be a function. Use McpTool.of:

McpTool.of(
  name: 'echo',
  description: 'Say the text back.',
  input: v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{'text': v.string()}),
  handler: (Map<String, dynamic> args, McpContext context) {
    return McpToolResult.text(args['text'] as String);
  },
);

docs.title: Tools that take a DTO
docs.text:
If you already have a @Dto class, a tool can use it as its input. Extend McpDtoTool<T>. The rules of the DTO (like @Length and @HexColor) are written once, and handle gets the typed object, not a map.

Use @Describe on a field to explain it to the model. It goes into the JSON Schema as description, and it does not change the checks:

@Dto()
class NewCategory {
  @Describe('The category name, like Food.')
  @Length(min: 1, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Describe('A color, like #1a2b3c.')
  @HexColor()
  final String color;

  const NewCategory({required this.name, required this.color});

  static const DtoSchema<NewCategory> schema = $NewCategoryDto;
}

class CreateCategory extends McpDtoTool<NewCategory> {
  @override
  String get name => 'create_category';

  @override
  String get description => 'Add a category.';

  @override
  DtoSchema<NewCategory> get dto => NewCategory.schema;

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> handle(NewCategory input, McpContext context) async {
    // ... save it
    return McpToolResult.text('Added ${input.name}.');
  }
}

The arguments are checked like a DTO in a controller, also with async rules like @Unique and @Exists. A bad call gets a text like this:

Input validation error: Invalid arguments for tool create_category: name: The name is required; color: The color must be a hex color like #1a2b3c

docs.title: Serving the tools
docs.text:
Make an McpServer with your tools, and call handle from a route. The MCP route has no auth of its own, so you must check who calls first. Find the user (from a token, a header or the URL) and pass it as auth. The scope ties each session to that user:

final McpServer mcp = McpServer(
  name: 'my-app',
  version: '1.0.0',
  tools: <McpTool>[AddExpense()],
);

Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp/{token}', (DoxRequest req) async {
  User? user = await User().where('mcp_token', req.param['token']).getFirst();
  if (user == null) return response('Invalid token').statusCode(401);
  return mcp.handle(req, auth: user, scope: 'user:${user.id}');
});

In a tool, context.authAs<User>() gives this user back.

A token in the URL ends up in proxy logs. So prefer a header when your clients can send one. If you want clients to sign in by themselves, use OAuth.

docs.title: Signing in with OAuth
docs.text:
With McpOAuth, you give the client only the address, like https://my.app/mcp. The client finds the rest and signs the user in. This is the sign-in the MCP spec asks for: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE.

dox_mcp does the OAuth part. Your app does three things:

  1. Tokens. Implement McpOAuthTokens. issue makes a token for a grant. verify gives what a token stands for (like a user), or null. You choose the table and how a token is revoked. Keep only a hash of the token.
  2. The consent page. Serve it at <issuer>/oauth/authorize, or set authorizePage. It reads client_id, redirect_uri, state, code_challenge, code_challenge_method and resource from the query. The person signs in there the way your app always does.
  3. The answer. Your page calls a route of your own, behind your own login. On yes, the route calls oauth.approve(subject: ...) and gives the page the address to send the browser to. On no, it calls oauth.deny(...).

Then add the routes and check the token on the MCP route:

final McpOAuth oauth = McpOAuth(
  issuer: 'https://my.app',
  tokens: MyTokens(),
  codes: Cache().store('file'), // all isolates must share it
);

class McpRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    oauth.routes(); // discovery, register and token
    Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp', handleMcp);
  }
}

Future<DoxResponse> handleMcp(DoxRequest req) async {
  Object? user = await oauth.authenticate(req); // reads Authorization: Bearer
  if (user == null) return oauth.unauthorized(); // 401 with WWW-Authenticate
  return mcp.handle(req, auth: user, scope: '$user');
}

Call oauth.routes() in a router with no prefix, because clients look for /.well-known/... at the root of the host. The codes store must be shared by all isolates: a file store on one host, or Redis on many.

docs.title: Keeping the consent page safe
docs.text:
The consent page decides who gets access, so keep these rules:

  • Put the answer route behind CSRF protection. Without it, another site can make a signed-in person say yes to a client without knowing it.
  • Use oauth.checkClient(...) to get the client for the page. It throws when the client or the redirect address is wrong. Then never send the browser anywhere.
  • Show the redirect host, so the person sees where the browser goes.
  • HTML-escape the client name before you print it. The client chose the name, so do not trust it.

There is no refresh token. To revoke a client, delete its token.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
SignedMcpSessions is the default. It makes ids like <random>.<signature>, signed with a key made from APP_KEY. So every isolate, and every server with the same APP_KEY, can check an id, and nothing is stored. A new APP_KEY ends every session, and clients start a new one by themselves.

Because nothing is stored, a signed id can not be ended. If you want DELETE to end a session, give a cache store that all isolates share (file or Redis, not memory):

SignedMcpSessions(ended: Cache().store('redis'))

For another kind of session, implement McpSessions.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The MCP route has no auth of its own. Check who calls before handle. McpOAuth is one way to do it.
  • Set allowedOrigins when the server runs on a local or private network. It stops browser pages on other sites (DNS rebinding). A request with an Origin that is not in the list gets 403.
  • Keep tokens out of logs.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: What the server answers
docs.text:
Request Answer POST initialize 200 with the server info and an Mcp-Session-Id header POST a request with a valid Mcp-Session-Id 200 with the JSON-RPC response (a list for a batch) POST only notifications or responses 202, no body POST with no session id 400 POST with an unknown session id, or one of another scope 404, so the client starts a new session POST with an ended session id 404, only when SignedMcpSessions has an ended store. Without it, the id still works POST with a body that is not valid JSON 400 with the JSON-RPC error -32700 POST with an empty batch, or a message that is not JSON-RPC 2.0 400 with the JSON-RPC error -32600 POST with initialize in a batch with other messages 400 with the JSON-RPC error -32600. Send initialize alone POST with an unsupported MCP-Protocol-Version header 400 POST with another Content-Type than JSON 415 Any request with an Origin header that is not in allowedOrigins 403 GET 405: there is no server-to-client stream DELETE with a valid session id 200. The session ends only if SignedMcpSessions has an ended store (see Sessions) DELETE with no session id 400 DELETE with an unknown session id, or one of another scope 404. An ended id also gets 404 when there is an ended store
  • Methods: initialize, ping, tools/list, tools/call. Others get -32601 Method not found.
  • An unknown tool is a JSON-RPC error (-32602).
  • tools/list sends the JSON Schema of a DTO tool (toJsonSchema()) as inputSchema.
  • onToolError gets the error of a tool that throws, for logs.
  • Protocol versions: 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26 and 2024-11-05. A client that asks for another one gets the newest.
  • The session signature is HMAC-SHA256 of the random part and the scope. The key is made from APP_KEY with the label dox:mcp.

docs.title: OAuth routes
docs.text:
oauth.routes() adds these routes:

Route What it does GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource (also with /mcp after it) Names the MCP address and the issuer. GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server Lists the endpoints. PKCE S256 only, authorization_code only, no client secret. POST /oauth/register Dynamic client registration. Nothing is stored. The client_id is the name and the redirect addresses, signed with APP_KEY. POST /oauth/token Swaps a code for a token. The body is a form or JSON. The code works once, for codeTtl (1 minute). The client, the redirect address and the PKCE verifier must all match. An unknown client_id gets 401 with invalid_client.
  • The discovery file gives <issuer>/oauth/register and <issuer>/oauth/token as full addresses. Under a router prefix the routes move but these addresses do not, so clients can not find them.
  • A redirect address must be https, or http on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]. It has no #fragment. It has at most 2048 characters (McpOAuth.maxRedirectUriLength).
  • A code_verifier must be 43 to 128 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ (RFC 7636). Other verifiers get invalid_request. A code_challenge must be 43 base64url characters.
  • Each code is taken under a lock, so two isolates can not both swap it.
  • These routes answer any origin (CORS *) and read no cookie. They skip the CORS list of the app.
  • issue may throw McpOAuthException, like access_denied when a person has too many clients. The client gets it from the token endpoint.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
Dox makes OpenAPI 3.1 docs for your API from your routes, controllers and request classes.

You get three URLs:

  • /docs: a Scalar page with every route and "Try it" buttons.
  • /openapi.json: the OpenAPI document as JSON.
  • /openapi.yaml: the same document as YAML.

The docs come from your code: the routes (method, path, middleware), the @Dto request classes, and the controller methods (annotations, arguments and return type). So you write very little by hand.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
An app made with dox create already serves /docs while APP_ENV is development. But each route only shows its path and method, because the config has no openApiRegistry yet. Do these steps to get the full docs from your code.

  1. Write the config, and pass the generated openApiRegistry to it:

    lib/config/openapi.dart
    import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

    The import of generated/openapi.g.dart shows an error until the builder runs in step 3.

  2. Add it to AppConfig:

    lib/config/app.dart
    import 'package:my_app/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  openApi: openApi,
  // ...
);

  3. Run the builder:

    dart run build_runner build      # or: dox build_runner:build

    It reads your code and writes lib/generated/openapi.g.dart. Run it again after you change routes, controllers, request classes or models. dox build_runner:watch does this for you while you work.

  4. Make sure .env has APP_ENV=development. Then start the app and open http://localhost:3000/docs.

The docs are on only when APP_ENV is development or local. If APP_ENV is not set, Dox treats the app as production, so /docs gives 404. Set APP_ENV=development in your .env and in CI.

docs.title: Describe a route
