docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
dox_auth lets you decide what a logged in user may do, with gates and policies.

Authentication tells you who the user is. Authorization tells you what this user may do. For example, a user may edit their own post, but not the post of another user.

There are two ways to write the rules:

  • A gate is one rule, written as a function.
  • A policy is a class with all the rules of one model, like Post.

docs.title: Registering the rules
docs.text:
Gates and policies are kept per isolate. Dox runs many isolates, so add them in the setup() of a provider, because it runs in every isolate:

lib/providers/gate_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/policies/post_policy.dart';

class GateProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
  }
}

Dox finds the provider by itself. Run dart run build_runner build to add it to lib/generated/container.g.dart.

docs.title: Writing gates
docs.text:
A gate gets the user and a subject, and gives true when the user may do it. The user and subject types come from the function, so a check with another type is denied:

Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);

If the gate needs no subject, use _ for the second parameter:

Gate.define('create-post', (User user, _) => user.verified == true);

A gate can also be async:

Gate.define('publish-post', (User user, Post post) async {
  return await user.canPublishIn(post.categoryId);
});

docs.title: Checking a gate
docs.text:
Use Gate.allows to check if the user may do something:

if (await Gate.allows(user, 'update-post', post)) {
  // the user may update the post
}

Gate.denies is the opposite:

if (await Gate.denies(user, 'create-post')) {
  // the user may not create a post
}

If you want to stop the request when the check fails, use Gate.authorize. It throws, and the client gets a 403:

await Gate.authorize(user, 'update-post', post);

To check many abilities at once, use Gate.any (at least one) or Gate.all (all of them):

await Gate.any(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
await Gate.all(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);

An ability with no gate and no policy is always denied.

docs.title: Giving a reason
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to tell the user why they may not do something. Return a GateResponse instead of a bool. The reason of GateResponse.deny becomes the message of the 403 answer:

Gate.define('delete-post', (User user, Post post) {
  if (post.published == true) {
    return GateResponse.deny('You can not delete a published post.');
  }
  return post.userId == user.id;
});

Gate.inspect gives you the full answer:

GateResponse response = await Gate.inspect(user, 'delete-post', post);
print(response.allowed);
print(response.message);

docs.title: Writing policies
docs.text:
When a model has many rules, put them in a policy. Write one method per ability. A method takes the user, and the model when the ability needs one. Then list the methods in abilities:

lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;

  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    'create': create,
    'update': update,
    'delete': delete,
  };
}

The abilities map is needed because compiled Dart apps can not find a method by its name.

Register the policy for its model:

Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());

Now a check with a Post as the subject uses the policy. For an ability with no model, like create, pass the type Post:

await Gate.allows(user, 'update', post);
await Gate.allows(user, 'create', Post);
await Gate.authorize(user, 'delete', post);

Each method must take (User user) or (User user, Post post). A method with another signature fails at Gate.policy, so you see the mistake when the app starts.

docs.title: Authorizing in a controller
docs.text:
In a controller, use req.authorize, req.can and req.cannot. They use the logged in user of req.auth, so put the route after AuthMiddleware:

Future<Post> update(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  await req.authorize('update', post);
  post.title = req.input('title');
  await post.save();
  return post;
}

req.can gives a bool, for example to tell the front end what the user may do:

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> show(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'post': post,
    'can_edit': await req.can('update', post),
  };
}

req.authorize answers 401 for a guest and 403 for a user who may not do it.

docs.title: Authorizing on a route
docs.text:
The Can middleware checks an ability before the controller runs. Put it after AuthMiddleware:

// a gate with no subject
Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('view-admin'), adminController.index]);

For a policy method with no model, pass the type with subject:

// a policy method with no model
Route.post('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('create', subject: Post), postController.store]);

For a policy method with a model, use param. The subject is then the value that Route.bind gives for that route param. When Route.bind finds nothing, the answer is 404:

// a policy method with the model of the route param
Route.bind<Post>('post', (String id) => Post().find(id));
Route.put('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('update', param: 'post'), postController.update]);

A guest who may not do it gets 401, and a logged in user who may not do it gets 403.

docs.title: Guest users
docs.text:
A guest has no user, so a gate or policy is denied for a guest. If you want a rule that also works for guests, make the user type nullable:

Gate.define('view-post', (User? user, Post post) {
  return post.published == true || post.userId == user?.id;
});

The same works in a policy:

class CommentPolicy extends Policy<User?, Comment> {
  bool view(User? user, Comment comment) => comment.visible == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{'view': view};
}

On a public route, use AuthMiddleware(optional: true). It loads the user when the login is good, and lets guests through. Without it, nothing loads the user, so a logged in user is a guest too:

Route.get('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), Can('view-post', param: 'post'), postController.show]);

docs.title: Before and after hooks
docs.text:
Sometimes one user may do everything, like an admin. Gate.before runs before every check. Return true or false to decide at once, or null to go on with the normal check:

Gate.before((User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null);

A hook runs only for users of its type, so a User hook does not run for guests.

Gate.after sees the answer of every check, for example to log it. It can not change the answer:

Gate.after((User user, String ability, GateResponse response) {
  print('${user.id} $ability ${response.allowed}');
});

A policy can have its own before. It runs before the methods of that policy:

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  @override
  bool? before(User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null;

  // ...
}

docs.title: Auth flags
docs.text:
Some behaviors are opt-in. Turn them on with flags: in AuthConfig. All flags are off by default:

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(forbidGuest: true, jsonNoRedirect: true),
);
  • forbidGuest: req.authorize and Can give a guest 403 with the gate message, not 401. AuthMiddleware still gives a guest 401.
  • jsonNoRedirect: AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login') gives a JSON or XHR client a 401, not a redirect. An Inertia request still gets the redirect.
  • endSessionsOnPasswordChange: a session login ends when the user's password changes. It also turns on logoutOtherDevices. See Ending sessions when the password changes.

AuthFlags.all() turns on every flag:

AuthConfig(defaultGuard: 'web', guards: guards, flags: const AuthFlags.all());

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Gate.flush() removes all gates, policies and hooks. Call it in setUp when each test adds its own rules.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• A JSON client is a request with a json Accept header, a JSON body, or X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest.
  • When a policy has no method for an ability, the gate with that name is used.
  • Policy methods are normal typed Dart methods, so you can also call them directly in a test.
  • The flags are part of AuthConfig, and Auth.initialize runs in every isolate, so every isolate gets the same flags.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
CORS headers let a web page on another domain call your API.

A browser blocks a request from https://my.app to https://api.my.app by default. The API must send CORS headers to allow it. Dox adds these headers from CORSConfig.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The config is in lib/config/cors.dart. A new app has this file with enabled: false, so it sends no CORS headers. Set origin to the URL of your front end, and set enabled: true:

lib/config/cors.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  enabled: true,
  origin: 'https://my.app',
  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],
  credentials: true,
  maxAge: 600,
);

Then pass it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  cors: cors,
  // ...
);

You do not need an OPTIONS route. Dox answers the browser's preflight OPTIONS request with 204 No Content and the CORS headers of the route the browser asks about.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Each option sets one response header. All options except enabled are null by default, and a null option sends no header. So with no origin, the browser blocks pages on other domains.

Option Header Value enabled - true adds the headers to every route. Default: true origin Access-Control-Allow-Origin one origin, a List<String> of origins, or '*' for all methods Access-Control-Allow-Methods a List<String> or a text like 'GET,POST'. '*' allows all headers Access-Control-Allow-Headers a List<String> or a text. '*' allows all exposeHeaders Access-Control-Expose-Headers the response headers the page may read credentials Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true lets the browser send cookies maxAge Access-Control-Max-Age how many seconds the browser keeps the preflight answer

docs.title: Allowing more than one origin
docs.text:
If your API has more than one front end, give origin a list. Do not put many origins in one text, because a text is sent as it is:

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  origin: <String>['https://my.app', 'https://admin.my.app'],
);

The header accepts only one origin, so Dox checks the Origin header of the request. When the origin is in the list, Dox sends back that one origin. When it is not, Dox sends no header, and the browser blocks the call.

docs.title: Sending cookies
docs.text:
If the front end sends cookies, set credentials: true. Then do not use origin: '*', because the browser blocks every call with cookies when the origin is *. Set origin to your real front end URL, or a list of URLs.

A page on an allowed origin can send requests with the cookies of your users, so list only sites you trust.

docs.title: CORS for some routes
docs.text:
enabled is the default for all routes. You can change it for a group of routes:

lib/routes/api.dart
// CORS headers only on these routes (use with enabled: false)
Route.enabledCors(() {
  Route.get('/public/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
});

// no CORS headers on these routes
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• For methods, headers and exposeHeaders, a list is joined with commas.
  • With an origin list, Dox also sends Vary: Origin, so caches know the answer depends on the origin. A list with '*' sends *.

docs.title: CSRF protection
docs.text:
CsrfMiddleware stops other sites from sending forms to your app in the name of your logged in users.

This attack is called cross site request forgery (CSRF). Another site makes the browser of your user send a form to your app. The browser sends your session cookie with it, so the request looks real.

To stop it, each session has a secret token. A request that changes data must send the token back. Another site can not read the token, so it can not send it.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The middleware needs a session, so put it right after SessionMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']),
  ],
  // ...
);

Now every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE request must send the token. A request with no token, or a wrong one, gets a 419 with {"code": "csrf_token_mismatch", "message": "CSRF token mismatch"}.

GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests are not checked, so never change data in a GET route.

docs.title: Sending the token
docs.text:
Dox reads the token from the _token field of the body, or from the X-CSRF-TOKEN or X-XSRF-TOKEN header. In your code the token is req.session.token.

Do not put the token in a URL, because URLs end up in logs and in the browser history. For the same reason, Dox does not read _token from the query string.

docs.title: HTML forms
docs.text:
Put the token in a hidden field. With views, @csrf writes this field for you:

<form method="POST" action="/posts">
  @csrf
  ...
</form>

@csrf must be alone on its line. In the middle of a line, use {{ csrfField() }}, which prints the same field. If you only need the token, for example for a <meta> tag, use csrfToken().

docs.title: axios and Inertia
docs.text:
Dox also sets an XSRF-TOKEN cookie with the token. It is not HttpOnly, so page scripts can read it. axios reads this cookie and sends it in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header by itself. Inertia uses axios, so it works with no code.

With fetch, read the cookie and send the header yourself:

const token = document.cookie
  .split('; ')
  .find((c) => c.startsWith('XSRF-TOKEN='))
  ?.split('=')[1];

fetch('/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hi' }),
});

docs.title: Excluding paths
docs.text:
Some routes can not send the token, like webhooks that other servers call, or APIs that use tokens. List them in except:

const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']);

A path that ends with * matches everything that starts with it, so /api/* matches /api/posts and /api/users/5. Any other path must match exactly.

Only skip paths that do not use the session login. A webhook should check its own signature instead.

docs.title: After login
docs.text: req.session.regenerate() also makes a new token, and Dox sends the new XSRF-TOKEN cookie with the same response. So after login, the client must use the new token.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• An excluded path is not checked and gets no XSRF-TOKEN cookie.
  • regenerate(keepToken: true) keeps the token, so forms open in other tabs keep working. Do not use it at login, because a token from before the login would stay valid.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Crypt and AESEncryptor encrypt and decrypt text with AES-256-GCM, so you can store or send data that nobody else can read or change.

Dox uses the same encryption for cookies and the cookie session driver, with your APP_KEY.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The key is the APP_KEY in .env. Make a new one with the CLI. It writes a random key of 32 letters and digits:

dox key:generate

Keep APP_KEY in .env or in the secrets of your host. Never put it in code or in git.

At startup Dox checks APP_KEY. When it is empty, not exactly 32 bytes, or a public sample key, the app stops. In development, local, test and testing it only prints a warning.

docs.title: Encrypting values
docs.text:
Crypt uses the APP_KEY of the app, so you do not pass a key. Use encryptString for text:

String secret = Crypt.encryptString('card-1234');

Use encrypt for any JSON value:

String data = Crypt.encrypt(<String, dynamic>{'id': 5}); // any JSON value

The result is base64 text. The same value gives a different result each time.

docs.title: Decrypting values
docs.text:
Use decryptString or decrypt to get the value back:

String card = Crypt.decryptString(secret); // 'card-1234'

Map<String, dynamic> map = Crypt.decrypt(data);

They throw a DecryptException when the text was changed or made with another key. The client then gets a 400. They also try the old keys in AppConfig.previousKeys, so values still work after you rotate the key.

docs.title: Using your own key
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a key that is not the APP_KEY. Use AESEncryptor and pass the key yourself:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

String secret = env.appKey;

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode('Hello world', secret);
String decoded = AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret); // 'Hello world'

decode throws a DecryptException when the text was changed or the key is wrong.

docs.title: One key per purpose
docs.text:
Dox does not use your key as it is. It makes a 32-byte key from it with HKDF-SHA256 and a label. The default label is dox:encrypt. You should pick your own label with purpose:, so a value made for one purpose can not be used for another. decode needs the same purpose:

AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, purpose: 'app:invoice')

Dox uses these labels for its own keys:

Label Used for dox:cookie encrypted cookies, and the cookie session driver dox:jwt the HMAC key of JwtAuthDriver (with a SecretKey) dox:encrypt AESEncryptor when you give no purpose dox:signed-url for signed URLs

docs.title: Encrypted cookies
docs.text:
DoxCookie encrypts its value with APP_KEY by default, and req.cookie(key) decrypts it:

return response().cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark'));  // encrypted

String? theme = req.cookie('theme');                    // decrypted

If you need a plain text cookie, turn encryption off. Read the raw value with decrypt: false:

DoxCookie('theme', 'dark', encrypt: false);             // plain text

String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);      // as sent

req.cookie(key) returns null when the cookie was changed, made with another APP_KEY, or made for another cookie name. The cookie name is bound to the value, so a value can not be copied from one cookie to another. To decrypt a raw cookie value yourself, use DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value).

docs.title: Rotating the key
docs.text:
You should change APP_KEY from time to time, or when someone who knew it leaves the team. If you just change it, old cookies and sessions can not be read, so every user is logged out, and JWT tokens signed with it stop working. With previousKeys, users stay logged in while you change it:

  1. Copy the current APP_KEY to APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS.

  2. Run dox key:generate. It writes a new APP_KEY. Now .env has both:

    .env
    APP_KEY=<the new key from dox key:generate>
APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=<the old APP_KEY>

  3. Read it in the env class, and give it to AppConfig:

    lib/config/env.dart
    List<String> get appPreviousKeys => <String>[]; // APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=a,b
    lib/config/app.dart
    AppConfig(
  appKey: env.appKey,
  previousKeys: env.appPreviousKeys,
)

  4. Deploy. Every instance must get the new env at the same time.

  5. Wait until the old cookies have expired: the session lifetime, and the maxAge of your own cookies.
  6. Remove the old key from APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS and deploy again.

APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS can hold more than one key, comma separated. Dox writes a cookie with the new key the next time it sends it, so a user who comes back during step 5 moves to the new key without noticing.

The old keys are used to read encrypted cookies, the cookie session driver, the CSRF token, Crypt.decrypt, and JWT tokens signed with APP_KEY. A JWT secret that is not APP_KEY needs its own previousSecrets, see Authentication. Your own AESEncryptor.decode calls read old keys only when you pass previousSecrets: Dox().config.previousKeys.

docs.title: When the key leaked
docs.text: Do not put a leaked key in previousKeys, because anyone who has it can still make cookies and JWT tokens that Dox accepts. Change APP_KEY with no previousKeys. Every user is logged out, and that is what you want.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• To store passwords, do not encrypt them. Hash them. See Hashing.
  • Crypt.encryptString(v) gives the same as AESEncryptor.encode(v, appKey).
  • The flag decryptServerError makes a DecryptException a reported 500 instead of a 400. See Core flags.
  • KeyDerivation.forAppKey(label) gives the 32-byte key of a label.
  • The work runs in Rust with the AES instructions of the CPU. One cookie takes about 1–2 µs.
  • Each message gets a new random 12-byte nonce. The output is base64 of nonce + encrypted text + tag. The 16-byte tag makes decode throw if one byte is changed.
  • encode and decode also take associatedData, like a cookie name. It is not in the output, but decode needs the same value.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
Hash turns a password into a bcrypt hash that you can store, and checks a password against it later.

A hash is one-way: you can not turn it back into the password. Hash uses bcrypt with a new random salt each time. It is in package:dox_core/dox_core.dart.

You do not need Hash for a normal login, because Auth().attempt() from dox_auth checks the password for you. See Authentication.

docs.title: Hashing passwords
docs.text:
Hash the password before you save it:

user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
await user.save();

makeAsync runs bcrypt in another isolate, so it does not block the server. The result looks like $2a$10$.... It holds the salt, so you only store this one string.

Never send the hash to the client. Put the column in the hidden list of the model.

docs.title: Verifying passwords
docs.text:
Use verifyAsync to check a password against a hash. It gives true when they match:

bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync('secret', user.password!);

It gives false when the password does not match, or when the hash is not a valid bcrypt hash, like an empty string.

Hash.make and Hash.verify do the same, but they block the request isolate while bcrypt runs. Use them only outside request handlers. Hash.check is the same as Hash.verify:

bool ok = Hash.verify('secret', user.password!);

docs.title: Changing the cost
docs.text:
Hash.rounds is the bcrypt cost for new hashes. The default is 10, and each step up doubles the time. The cost must be from 4 to 31. Do not go below 10:

Hash.rounds = 12;
String hash = Hash.make('secret', rounds: 12); // or per call

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still verify. If you change the cost, also set hashRounds on your auth driver to the same value. See Authentication.

docs.title: Long passwords
docs.text:
bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes. So Hash.make and Hash.makeAsync throw an ArgumentError for a longer password, and Hash.verify gives false. Limit the length in your DTO, like @Length(min: 8, max: 72).

@Length counts characters, but a letter outside ASCII can use up to 4 bytes. So such a password can still be too long. Catch the error and answer 422, or use a smaller max.

docs.title: Comparing secrets
docs.text:
To check an API key or a token, use Hash.equals(given, expected), not ==. == stops at the first wrong character, so the time can tell how much of the key was right. Hash.equals takes the same time for every value of the same length:

bool ok = Hash.equals(req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '', Env.get<String>('API_KEY'));

docs.title: Storing tokens
docs.text:
For a long random secret that you keep in the database, like an API key, store only Hash.sha256(token). Then find the row by the hash of what the client sends. SHA-256 gives the same hash for the same input, so a unique index works on it:

String stored = Hash.sha256(token);          // save this, never the token
Token? row = await Token().where('hash', Hash.sha256(given)).getFirst();

Never use Hash.sha256 for passwords. A password is short and can be guessed, so use bcrypt.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• The error text of a too long password does not hold the password, so it is safe in logs.
  • bcrypt is slow on purpose, so guessing is slow too. Do not hash in a loop on hot paths.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
RateLimit is a middleware that stops a client that sends too many requests.

You should use it on login, sign up and other routes that bots like to hammer.

docs.title: Limiting a route
docs.text:
Add RateLimit to the route. The defaults are max: 60 and per: Duration(minutes: 1):

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1)),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);

Now each client (by ip) can send 5 login requests per minute. The 6th request gets a 429:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 42
X-RateLimit-Limit: 5
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

{"code":"too_many_requests","message":"Too Many Requests"}

Retry-After is the number of seconds until the client can try again. Every answer, also a normal one, has the X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers. The error goes through your exception handler, so it has the same JSON shape as your other errors.

docs.title: Limiting every route
docs.text:
To limit all routes, put it in globalMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    RateLimit(max: 120),
  ],
  // ...
);

docs.title: Counting by user
docs.text:
By default each ip has its own count. Sometimes you want to count per user instead. Give a key function, which returns any String. For example, count by user id after AuthMiddleware:

Route.get('/reports', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  RateLimit(
    max: 100,
    key: (DoxRequest req) => '${req.auth?.user<User>()?.id ?? req.ip()}',
  ),
  (ReportController c) => c.index,
]);

Do not count by a raw header, like req.header('X-Api-Key'). A client can send a new value with each request and get a new count each time. Count by a value that you checked first, like the id of the logged in user.

docs.title: Two limits with the same settings
docs.text:
Two RateLimit with the same max and per share one count for the same client. If you want separate counts, give each one a name:

Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text: Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer, every request comes from the proxy ip, so all clients share one count. Add the proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, so req.ip() is the real client ip. See App config.

docs.title: IPv6 clients
docs.text:
A home or a server with IPv6 often gets a whole /64 block. That is 2^64 addresses. By default each address has its own count, so such a client can send from a new address each time and never hit the limit.

Turn on rateLimitIpv6Prefix in CoreFlags to count each IPv6 client by its /64 prefix:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  flags: CoreFlags(rateLimitIpv6Prefix: true),
  // ...
);

All clients in one /64 then share one count. An IPv4 address stays as it is. A key function you give is used as it is. To use the same rule in your own key, call RateLimit.ipBucket(req.ip()).

docs.title: Where the counts live
docs.text:
When the default cache store is Redis, the counts are in Redis, so all isolates and all servers share them. Use this when you run more than one server. To set a command timeout or other Redis options, see Redis options.

With any other default store, the counts are kept in the main isolate of each server. All isolates of one server share them, but each server has its own counts. So with 3 servers, a client can send up to 3 times max.

To use a store by name, pass store:

RateLimit(max: 10, store: 'redis')

docs.title: Sliding window
docs.text:
By default the count starts at 0 at the start of each window. So a client can send max requests at the end of one minute, and max more at the start of the next. That is fine for most apps.

If you want to stop this burst, set sliding: true:

RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1), sliding: true)

The count is then the count of this window, plus a part of the window before. That part gets smaller as the window goes on. It costs one more read per request.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• A blocked request still counts, so a client that keeps sending while it is blocked stays blocked.
  • In the main isolate mode, each limited request sends one small message to the main isolate.
  • In the main isolate mode, the counter keeps at most 100,000 clients (about 15 MB). When it is full, it first drops the expired counts, then the oldest ones. A dropped client starts again at 0. New clients are never turned away, so a flood of fake clients can not lock out real users.
  • A memory store named in store also counts in the main isolate. A store passed in cacheStore is used as it is.
  • Sliding window example: 4 requests last minute, 1 this minute, 15 seconds in: the count is 4 x 45/60 + 1 = 4. X-RateLimit-Remaining is max minus this count, rounded up. Each count is kept for 2 windows.

docs.text:

docs.title: Security headers
docs.text:
SecurityHeaders is a middleware that adds safe HTTP headers to every answer.

The browser reads these headers and blocks some common attacks, like showing your page in a frame on another site.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Put it first in globalMiddleware. Then an error from a later middleware, like a 419 or a 429, also gets the headers:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SecurityHeaders(),
  ],
  // ...
);

Every answer now has these headers:

Header Default value What it does X-Content-Type-Options nosniff The browser does not guess the file type. X-Frame-Options DENY No site can show your page in a frame. Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin Other sites only see your domain, not the full url. Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=() The page can not use the camera, the microphone or the location. Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin A page of another site that opens yours can not reach it. Strict-Transport-Security max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains The browser uses only https for one year. Sent only on https requests.

Content-Security-Policy is off by default, because a good policy depends on your pages.

docs.title: Changing a header
docs.text:
Each header has an option. Give a new value to change it, or null to remove it. Use extra for other headers:

const SecurityHeaders(
  frameOptions: 'SAMEORIGIN', // allow frames from your own site
  permissionsPolicy: null, // do not send this header
  contentSecurityPolicy: "frame-ancestors 'none'",
  extra: <String, String>{'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy': 'same-origin'},
)
Option Header contentTypeOptions X-Content-Type-Options frameOptions X-Frame-Options referrerPolicy Referrer-Policy permissionsPolicy Permissions-Policy crossOriginOpenerPolicy Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy strictTransportSecurity Strict-Transport-Security contentSecurityPolicy Content-Security-Policy xssProtection X-XSS-Protection (default '0') extra any other headers, name to value. A null value removes that header

docs.title: HSTS behind a proxy
docs.text:
Dox serves plain http, and a proxy (Caddy, nginx, a load balancer) does the https part. Dox sends Strict-Transport-Security only when the request came in over https. It knows this from the X-Forwarded-Proto: https header, but it only believes this header from a trusted proxy. So add your proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, or Dox never sends HSTS:

AppConfig(trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1']);

See App config.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Without this middleware, the server already sends X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and X-XSS-Protection: 0 on every answer. SecurityHeaders replaces them, and null also removes them.
  • X-XSS-Protection: 0 turns off the old XSS filter of browsers, because in old browsers it can make holes. Use Content-Security-Policy instead.
  • Middleware runs only for routes that exist. So a 404 for an unknown URL and a preflight OPTIONS answer get only the three server headers.

docs.text:

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
A signed URL has a signature in its query, so nobody can change the URL without your APP_KEY.

You need it for links in emails, like "unsubscribe" or "download your file", where the user is not logged in.

docs.title: Creating signed URLs
docs.text:
Give the route a name and add the ValidateSignature middleware:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');

Then make the URL with Route.signedUrl:

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'unsubscribe',
  params: <String, Object>{'user': 5},
);
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?signature=3f9a...

A URL with no signature, a wrong one, or a changed path or query gets 403 Forbidden.

docs.title: URLs that expire
docs.text:
Sometimes a link should work only for a while. Give expires. The URL then gets a signed expires query param, and after that time it gets a 403:

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'download',
  params: <String, Object>{'file': 12},
  expires: Duration(hours: 1),
);

docs.title: Relative URLs
docs.text:
By default the URL is absolute. Dox puts APP_URL in front, and the scheme and host are signed too. Give baseUrl: to use another one. The Host and the scheme of the request must match the URL it was made with: APP_URL, or the baseUrl.

If you want to sign only the path and the query, use absolute: false, and check it with ValidateSignature(absolute: false):

Route.get('/files/{id}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(absolute: false),
  (FileController c) => c.show,
]).name('files.show');

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'files.show',
  params: <String, Object>{'id': 3},
  absolute: false,
);
// /files/3?signature=...

Behind a proxy that ends TLS, add the proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, so Dox sees that the scheme is https.

docs.title: Checking in a controller
docs.text:
If you want to answer a bad link in your own way, use ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req). It gives true or false:

if (!ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)) {
  return redirect('/link-expired');
}

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• The signature is HMAC-SHA256 of the URL, with a key made from APP_KEY. Dox compares it in constant time.
  • URLs made with an old key still work when the old key is in AppConfig.previousKeys.
  • signature is a reserved query param. Any other param added to a signed URL makes it invalid.
  • The Host must match the host of APP_URL, with the same port.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
A controller holds the code that answers a route, so your route files stay short.

You could write all your code in route closures. But when an app grows, it is easier to group the code for one topic, like blogs, in one class. A controller can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

docs.title: Basic controllers
docs.text:
Make a controller with the CLI:

dox make:controller Blog

It writes lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart with an empty index method. Fill it in:

lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  String index(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'all blogs';
  }
}

Then point a route to the method:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);

@Inject() puts the controller in the container. Run dart run build_runner build after you add one. The constructor can ask for services and repositories. See Dependency injection.

docs.title: Static methods
docs.text:
If a controller needs nothing from the container, a static method also works:

class AppController {
  static String ping(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

Route.get('/ping', AppController.ping);

docs.title: Plain functions
docs.text:
A plain function works too:

String listBlog(DoxRequest req) {
  return 'all blogs';
}

Route.get('/blogs', listBlog);

docs.title: Resource controllers
docs.text:
Most models need the same routes: list, show, create, update and delete. A resource controller has the 7 methods that Route.resource uses, so one line of routes covers all of them.

Make one with -r:

dox make:controller Blog -r
lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  /// delete() gives the number of rows it deleted, so 0 is a 404:
  /// `if (await Blog().where('id', id).delete() == 0) throw NotFoundHttpException();`
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}
}

Register it with one route:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);

You can delete the methods you do not need, because Route.resource skips them. See Routing: resource routes.

docs.title: API resource controllers
docs.text:
An API has no form pages. So --api makes the resource controller without create and edit:

dox make:controller Blog --api

docs.title: Resource controllers for a model
docs.text:
If the controller works with one model, use --model. It fills the methods with model code:

dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog
lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().all();
  }

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  /// create() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().create(req.body);
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  /// Dox loads blog by the {id}. No row answers 404.
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  /// update() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.update(req.body);
    return blog;
  }

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.delete();
  }
}

show, edit, update and destroy take the model. Route model binding loads it by the {id}.

create() and update() take only the columns in the model's fillable list, so add your columns there first.

You can use --api and --model together. And dox make:model Blog -r makes the model and this controller in one step.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A controller method asks for what it needs by type, and Dox fills each parameter:

Route.put('/teams/{teamId}/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User> update(int teamId, int id, UpdateUser body) async { ... }
}

These types work:

Parameter type Dox gives DoxRequest the request a @Dto class the checked body or query. See Validation. String, int, double, num, bool the path params, in the order of the route the same types with ? an optional path param ({id?}). null when it is not in the URL. a @DoxModel class the model, loaded by the route param. See route model binding. an @Inject() class the instance from the container

You can put the parameters in any order. Path params are matched by position: the first path-param parameter gets the first {...} in the route. DoxRequest is not needed, so add it only when you use it.

There are a few rules:

  • At most one @Dto parameter.
  • Only positional parameters. Named and [optional] parameters are not supported.
  • A catch-all {path*} param is a String.
  • The same rules work for static methods and plain functions.

docs.title: Path param types
docs.text:
Dox converts the text from the URL to the type you ask for. If the text does not fit the type, the client gets 404 Not Found:

  • int: "42" is 42. "abc" or "4.5" answers 404.
  • double, num: "4.5" is 4.5.
  • bool: true or 1 is true. false or 0 is false. Any other text answers 404.

Path params are checked first. When one is wrong, the DTO is not checked.

docs.title: Returning a response
docs.text: Return a String, a Map, a model, a File and more. See Response.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Dox reads the parameter types once, at start. It does not use dart:mirrors.
  • The server does not start when a parameter type is not in the list above (did you run dart run build_runner build?), or when the method has more path-param parameters than the route has {...} params.

docs.title: Dependency injection
docs.text:
The Dox container makes your classes and gives each constructor what it needs, so you never wire classes by hand.

Put @Inject() above a class, and dox_builder adds it to the container. Then any class can ask for it in its constructor. Dox does not use dart:mirrors: all the wiring is generated code.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The builder writes lib/generated/container.g.dart. Give it to the app once:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/container.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  // ...
);

Run the builder again after you add a class:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: A full example
docs.text:
A common setup has three layers. A repository reads the database. A service holds the business logic. A controller answers the route. Each one asks for the one below it in its constructor.

The repository needs nothing:

lib/app/repositories/user.repository.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserRepository {
  Future<User?> find(int id) => User().find(id);
}

The service asks for the repository:

lib/app/services/user.service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart';

@Inject()
class UserService {
  UserService(this.users);

  final UserRepository users;

  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await users.find(id);
    if (user == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();
    return user;
  }
}

The controller asks for the service:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  UserController(this.service);

  final UserService service;

  Future<User> show(int id) => service.show(id);
}

And the route points to the controller:

lib/routes/api.dart
class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show);
  }
}

That is all. After dart run build_runner build, GET /api/users/5 makes the repository, the service and the controller, and calls show(5).

docs.title: Lifetime
docs.text:
By default, @Inject() makes one instance per isolate. It is made on first use, and every class that asks for it gets the same one.

If you want a new instance each time it is asked for, use singleton: false:

@Inject(singleton: false)
class ReportBuilder {}

Dox runs one server per isolate, and isolates do not share objects. So each isolate has its own instances. Do not keep state in a singleton that all isolates must see. Use the cache or the database for that.

docs.title: Constructor parameters
docs.text:
Each constructor parameter is found by its type. Positional and named parameters both work.

If the type is not in the container, an optional parameter keeps its default value, and a nullable parameter gets null. Any other parameter stops the build.

docs.title: Abstract types
docs.text:
A constructor parameter of an abstract type gets the one container class that implements it:

abstract class Mailer {}

@Inject()
class SmtpMailer implements Mailer {}

@Inject()
class SignupService {
  SignupService(this.mailer); // gets the SmtpMailer

  final Mailer mailer;
}

This works for constructor parameters only. c.get<Mailer>() and handler parameters still need the class itself.

docs.title: Routes to controller methods
docs.text:
Pass a function that picks the method. Dox finds the controller by the parameter type:

Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);

The controller comes from the container. Dox gets it once per isolate, at start, so a request does no extra work. .name(), groups and middleware lists work the same:

Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show).name('posts.show');
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.me]);

For resource routes, pass the class:

Route.resource('posts', PostController);

The method still gets its parameters as usual: DoxRequest, a @Dto, path params and bound models. See Controller: parameters.

docs.title: Handler parameters
docs.text:
A controller method (or a plain route function) can ask for any class of the container:

Route.get('/stats', (StatsService stats) => stats.today());

A singleton is read once, at start. A singleton: false class is made on each request.

docs.title: Route model binding
docs.text:
Often a route gets the id of a model, and the controller loads the model first. Dox can do this for you. Every @DoxModel class gets a binder, so when a handler has a parameter of a model type, Dox loads the model by its primary key:

Route.get('/posts/{post}', (PostController c) => c.show);

@Inject()
class PostController {
  Post show(Post post) => post;
}

Dox uses the route param with the name of the model: {post} for Post, {blogPost} for BlogPost. When there is no such param, it uses the next route param in order, like {id}.

A missing row answers 404. An int key that is not a number also answers 404, with no database call.

A binder from Route.bind wins over this one. See Routing: route model binding.

docs.title: Routers and providers
docs.text:
Routers and providers do not need @Inject(). Dox finds every class that extends Router and registers its routes at start. It finds every class that extends DoxProvider and runs its setup() at start, in every isolate. Their constructors get parameters from the container too.

They run in the order of their file path, then the order in the file. If you want to pick the order, list them in AppConfig:

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs first
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter()],       // registered first
);

A listed class comes first, and the others follow. No class runs twice. A listed provider is also the instance that the container gives.

A provider can add global middleware with Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(...) in setup(). See Middleware.

docs.title: Using the container in code
docs.text:
Sometimes you need a class in code that the container does not build, like a script. Dox().ioc is the container of the current isolate. Use get to read a class:

UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();

get throws when the class is not registered. Use has to check first:

if (Dox().ioc.has<UserService>()) {
  // ...
}

You can also add classes by hand. singleton makes one instance per isolate, on first use. factory makes a new instance on each get. instance uses the value you give, for example a config object:

Dox().ioc.singleton<Clock>((IocContainer c) => Clock());
Dox().ioc.factory<Report>((IocContainer c) => Report());
Dox().ioc.instance<MailConfig>(mailConfig);

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
In a test you often want a fake in place of a real class. Use override before the app starts, and clearOverrides at the end:

setUpAll(() async {
  Dox().ioc.override<UserRepository>(FakeUserRepository());
  client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
});

tearDownAll(() async {
  await client.close();
  Dox().ioc.clearOverrides();
});

Call override before DoxTestClient.start, because controllers get their objects once, at start. An override stays when the app registers its classes again.

docs.title: Build errors
docs.text:
The build stops with a clear message, with the file and line, when:

  • a required parameter has a type that is not in the container,
  • a parameter has an abstract type, and two or more classes in the container implement it,
  • classes need each other in a circle. The message shows the chain, like A -> B -> C -> A,
  • @Inject() is on an abstract class or a generic class,
  • a class has no unnamed constructor.

A private class (like _AdminRouter) is not put in the container. The build shows a warning for it. Remove the _ to add it.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Dox finds classes in lib/ only.
  • Two classes with the same name in two files both work. But use the typed route style (Route.get<C>(...)) for them. They can not be handler parameters, because Dox can not tell them apart by name.
  • A route without a parameter of the model type does not load the model.

docs.title: The generated file
docs.text:
lib/generated/container.g.dart has one function. Each class gets a factory that calls its constructor. Do not edit it.

lib/generated/container.g.dart
// GENERATED CODE - DO NOT MODIFY BY HAND
// Made by dox_builder. Run `dart run build_runner build`.
// ignore_for_file: type=lint

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart' as i1;
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart' as i2;
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart' as i3;
import 'package:my_app/providers/orm_provider.dart' as i4;
import 'package:my_app/routes/api.dart' as i5;
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart' as i6;

/// Puts every class of the app into the container: the
/// `@Inject()` classes, routers, providers and model binders.
/// Use it in `AppConfig(container: registerContainer)`.
void registerContainer(IocContainer c) {
  c.singleton<i1.UserController>(
    (IocContainer c) => i1.UserController(c.get<i3.UserService>()),
  );
  c.singleton<i2.UserRepository>((IocContainer c) => i2.UserRepository());
  c.singleton<i3.UserService>(
    (IocContainer c) => i3.UserService(c.get<i2.UserRepository>()),
  );
  c.provider<i4.ORMProvider>((IocContainer c) => i4.ORMProvider());
  c.router<i5.ApiRouter>((IocContainer c) => i5.ApiRouter());
  c.bindModel<i6.User>((String id) {
    int? key = int.tryParse(id);
    if (key == null) return null;
    return i6.User().find(key);
  });
}

docs.title: DTOs
docs.text:
A DTO is a typed Dart class that describes the input of a request, so your controller gets checked data instead of a raw map.

DTO means "data transfer object". You write a class with @Dto() and give each field a Dart type and some rules. When you ask for the class in a controller, Dox reads the request, converts the values to your types, and checks the rules. Your method gets a typed object. When the input is wrong, the client gets 422, and your method does not run.

You write the input shape once, and Dox uses it in many places: the request body, the query string, file uploads, the OpenAPI docs, MCP tools and even a Flutter app.

docs.title: Creating a DTO
docs.text:
Use the make:dto command. It writes a DTO with one name field to lib/app/dtos/<name>/<name>.dto.dart:

dox make:dto CreateUser

A DTO uses generated code, so run the generator after you create or change one. It writes a .dto.g.dart file next to the DTO:

dox build_runner:build

If dox serve or dox build_runner:watch is running, this happens for you on every save.

docs.title: Defining fields
docs.text:
Each field is a final field and a parameter of the constructor. Put rules on a field as annotations:

lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'create_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class CreateUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Email()
  final String email;

  @Min(18)
  final int? age; // nullable, so optional

  const CreateUser({required this.name, required this.email, this.age});

  static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema = $CreateUserDto;
}

Keep the part line and the static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema line. They connect the class to its generated code.

The Dart type decides if a field is required. A field that is not nullable and has no default is required. A nullable field, or a field with a default, is optional. See Required and optional fields.

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
These field types work:

Dart type JSON Query and form data String, int, double, num, bool the same JSON type text, converted DateTime an ISO 8601 string the same an enum the name, like "admin" the same RequestFile not allowed a file part a @Dto class an object bracket keys: address[city] List<T> an array tags=a&tags=b or tags[]=a Map<String, T> an object bracket keys: meta[color]

JSON is strict: "18" is not an int. Query and form data are text, so Dox converts them.

If a client sends numbers as text in JSON too, use @Dto(coerce: true). Then "18" is read as 18, "4.5" as 4.5, and "true", "1", "yes", "on" (and the opposites) as a bool. A bool also takes the numbers 1 and 0:

@Dto(coerce: true)
class UpdateStock {
  final int count; // {"count": "18"} gives 18
  final bool active; // {"active": 1} gives true

  const UpdateStock({required this.count, required this.active});
}

Every detail is in Types in detail.

docs.title: Nested objects and lists
docs.text:
Sometimes the input has an object inside it, or a list of objects. A field can be another @Dto class, or a list of them:

@Dto()
class CreateOrder {
  final Address address;

  @MinItems(1)
  final List<OrderItem> items;

  const CreateOrder({required this.address, required this.items});

  static const DtoSchema<CreateOrder> schema = $CreateOrderDto;
}

Address and OrderItem are @Dto classes too. An error in a nested value has a path key, like items.1.quantity.

docs.title: Input keys
docs.text:
The input key is the field name in snake_case, so firstName reads first_name. Use @Name to pick another key:

final String firstName; // key: first_name

@Name('emailAddress')
final String email; // key: emailAddress

To use the field names as they are, use @Dto(keyCase: KeyCase.field).

Unknown keys are dropped. If you want an unknown key to be an error, use @Dto(strict: true).

docs.title: Registering DTOs
docs.text:
Dox uses no reflection, so it needs a list of all your DTOs. The generator writes this list to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. Give it to the app config:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos, // from lib/generated/dtos.g.dart
  // ...
);

A new app already has this line. You only add it once, and new DTOs join the list when the generator runs. Without it, Dox throws an error that tells you to add it.

docs.title: Using a DTO in a controller
docs.text:
Add a parameter with the DTO type. Dox checks the request before your method runs:

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User> store(CreateUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email;
    await user.save();
    return user;
  }
}

You can mix it with other parameters, like DoxRequest and path params. A method can have at most one DTO parameter:

Future<User> update(DoxRequest req, int id, UpdateUser body) async { ... }

See Controller: parameters for the full rules.

docs.title: Validating inside the method
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to check the input later in the method, not before it. Use req.validate<T>(). It returns the object, or throws the 422 error:

CreateUser data = await req.validate<CreateUser>();

docs.title: Body and query string
docs.text:
Dox reads one source, and it never mixes the query and the body:

Request Dox reads GET, HEAD, DELETE the query string POST, PUT, PATCH the body (JSON, form or multipart)

So a DTO for a list page, like GET /users?page=2, reads the query string for you. To choose the source yourself, set source on the DTO, or on one call:

@Dto(source: Source.query) // on the DTO
class SearchUsers { ... }

await req.validate<SearchUsers>(source: Source.query); // for one call

Path params are not part of a DTO. Ask for them as controller parameters, like int id. See the Pagination guide for a full query DTO.

docs.title: Uploaded files
docs.text:
A RequestFile field reads a file from a multipart/form-data request. Add file rules to check its type and size:

@Image()
@MaxSize('2MB')
final RequestFile avatar;

@Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx'])
final List<RequestFile> documents;

Dox checks the real file type from its first bytes. It does not trust the file name or the client. To save the file, see Request: form data and the File upload guide.

docs.title: When validation fails
docs.text:
When the input is wrong, Dox answers 422 with one message per field, and your method does not run:

{
  "email": "The email is not a valid email"
}

On a form post with a session, Dox redirects back with the errors instead. To change the messages or add your own rules, see Validation.

docs.title: OpenAPI docs
docs.text: If you use dox_openapi, each DTO becomes a schema in the API docs. The field types and the rules (like @Length and @Email) show up there, so the docs always match the checks. A /// comment or @Describe('...') on a field becomes its description. See API docs with OpenAPI.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text: An MCP tool can use a DTO as its input. Extend McpDtoTool<T>, and handle gets the checked object, with the same rules as a controller. See Tools that take a DTO.

docs.title: Sharing with Flutter
docs.text: The generated DTO code is pure Dart, so a Flutter app can use the same DTO to check a form before it sends it. Put the DTO in a shared package and import dox_validation instead of dox_core. See Share code with Flutter.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A DTO is a normal Dart class. If you want to skip the checks in a test, for example to test a service, make one directly:

CreateUser input = const CreateUser(name: 'Ann', email: 'ann@dox.dev');

To test the checks, use safeValidateMap on the schema. It never throws:

ParseResult<CreateUser> result = await CreateUser.schema.safeValidateMap(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'A',
  'email': 'not-an-email',
});

expect(result.success, isFalse);
expect(result.errors['email'], 'The email is not a valid email');

validateMap does the same, but returns the object or throws. Pass source: Source.query to read the map like a query string, and params: {'id': '5'} to give path params. @Unique and @Exists need a test database.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• All @Dto(...) options are in Keys and DTO options.
  • The content type of the body decides how Dox reads it. See Body types.
  • The generator stops with a clear error for a field it can not use, like a field that is not final. See What the generator checks.
  • A trailing Dto in the make:dto name is removed: dox make:dto CreateUserDto gives the class CreateUser.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Every error that a route throws goes to one exception handler, which logs it and sends an answer to the client.

The handler has two methods:

  • report(error, stackTrace) logs the error.
  • render(error, req) decides what the client gets.

You do not need to set anything up. The default handler already gives good answers. You only write your own handler when you want to change them.

docs.title: The default answer
docs.text:
This is what the client gets with the default handler:

Error Status Body an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code {"code": "not_found", "message": "Not Found"} a ValidationException (bad input) 422 the field errors, like {"name": "The name is required"} a ValidationException on a request with a session that does not want JSON, like a form post 302 a redirect back. The errors and the old input are in the session. a URL with no route 404 {"code": "not_found", "message": "GET /x not found"} any other error 500 {"code": "server_error", "message": "Server Error"}

For a 500, the error text is sent only when APP_ENV is development or local. In production the client never sees it, because it can hold SQL, file paths or hosts.

See HTTP exceptions for the built-in exception classes.

docs.title: Which errors are logged
docs.text: report is called for every error, except an IHttpException with a 4xx code. A 4xx exception (like 404) is a normal answer, so it is not logged. A 5xx exception, like InternalErrorException, is logged. The default report prints the error and the stack with the logger.

docs.title: An HTML error page
docs.text:
By default an error is sent as JSON, so a browser that opens a bad URL sees JSON, not a page. In development or local, a 500 is plain text with the error text.

If you want browsers to get an HTML page, turn on htmlErrors:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  // ...
);

The page shows the status and its title, like 404 Not Found. It loads no files from outside. When APP_ENV is development or local, the page also shows the error text and the stack trace.

Only a request that does not want JSON gets the page. A JSON client, a validation error and an answer from your own render stay the same.

docs.title: Your own error page
docs.text:
To make your own page, set errorPage. It gets the status, the error, the stack trace and a debug flag. debug is true when APP_ENV is development or local. Escape every value you put in the page.

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  errorPage: (int status, Object error, StackTrace stack, bool debug) =>
      '<h1>Sorry, error $status</h1>',
  // ...
);

The default page is defaultErrorPage. You can call it from your own function, for example for the statuses you do not handle.

docs.title: Your own handler
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to send errors to an error tracker, or give your own exception a special answer. For this, extend ExceptionHandler and override one method or both:

lib/app/exception_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class PaymentRequiredException implements Exception {}

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    // send it to your error tracker
    print('ERROR $error\n$stackTrace');
  }

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    if (error is PaymentRequiredException) {
      return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Please pay'})
          .statusCode(402);
    }
    // everything else: the default answer
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}

Then set it in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);

docs.title: What render can return
docs.text:
render can return anything a controller can return: a DoxResponse, a map or a string. If you return the error itself, the client gets the default answer. This is what super.render does.

req is the raw HttpRequest. It is there even when the error came before Dox read the body. Use it to read headers, like req.headers.value('accept').

See Custom errors for a full example with your own exception classes.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• A request wants JSON (DoxRequest.expectsJson()) when it has an Accept header with json, a JSON body, or X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest. An Inertia request does not want JSON, so it gets the HTML page.
  • If render itself throws, Dox logs that error and sends the default answer. The client always gets a response.
  • Errors outside a request, like a future that nobody awaits or an error in the shutdown() of a provider, also go to report. The server keeps running.
  • The responseHandler of AppConfig still runs after render, so it sees error responses too. Use render to change errors, and responseHandler to change all responses.

docs.title: Inertia
docs.text:
Inertia lets you build a single page app with React, Vue or Svelte, and keep routes and controllers in Dox.

You do not write an API. A controller gives a page name and its props, and Inertia shows the page in the browser. The first visit gets a full HTML page. After that, links and forms get only JSON, and the page changes without a reload.

The dox_inertia package is the server side of Inertia. Use it with Vite and the Inertia 3 client for your front-end (@inertiajs/react, @inertiajs/vue3 or @inertiajs/svelte, version 3).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the package with the CLI:

dox add inertia

It does steps 1 to 3 of Set it up by hand: the root view, the config and the provider. Then do steps 4 to 6 (Vite, the built files and the middleware) yourself. The command prints a short list of them. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text:
If you do not use dox add, add the package yourself:

dart pub add dox_inertia

docs.title: 1. Root view
docs.text:
The root view is the HTML page of the first visit. Dox puts the script and style tags in place of @vite, and the page in place of @inertia. It is plain HTML, with no template engine. It can hold {{ key }} marks for values like the title. See Root view data.

resources/views/app.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My app</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: 2. Config
docs.text:
The config tells Dox where your Vite files are:

lib/config/inertia.dart
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  /// the Vite entry files
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],

  /// load the scripts from the Vite dev server. null in production.
  devServerUrl: 'http://localhost:5173',

  /// add the React Fast Refresh code in dev mode
  reactRefresh: true,
);
Option Default What it does rootView resources/views/app.html the HTML page of the first visit. One request can use another file with Inertia.setRootView entryPoints ['resources/js/app.js'] the Vite entry files publicPath public the folder of public files buildDirectory build the folder in publicPath where vite build writes its files devServerUrl null the url of the Vite dev server, see Vite reactRefresh false add the React Fast Refresh code in dev mode version hash of the manifest the asset version, see Asset version encryptHistory false encrypt the browser history of every page, see History encryption ssr null server side rendering, see SSR

Paths are from the project root, where the app runs.

docs.title: 3. Provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up Inertia in every isolate. Put it in lib/, so the generated container finds it:

lib/providers/inertia_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

import '../config/inertia.dart';

class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);
}

With no provider, Dox uses the defaults of InertiaConfig.

docs.title: 4. Vite
docs.text:
Set up Vite so it writes a manifest into public/build:

vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  plugins: [react()],
  // public/ holds the Dox public files. The build goes into public/build,
  // so do not let Vite copy public/ into the build.
  publicDir: false,
  // the built files are served from /build/
  base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/',
  server: { origin: 'http://localhost:5173' },
  build: {
    manifest: true,
    outDir: 'public/build',
    rollupOptions: { input: 'resources/js/app.jsx' },
  },
}))

Then start the Inertia app in your entry file:

resources/js/app.jsx
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
  },
})

docs.title: 5. Serve the built files
docs.text:
In production the browser loads /build/assets/.... Add a route for them, or let your proxy (nginx, Caddy) serve public/build:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.get('/build/{path*}', (String path) {
  if (path.contains('..')) throw NotFoundHttpException();
  // the file names have a hash, so the browser can keep them for a year
  return response(File('public/build/$path')).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
});

docs.title: 6. Middleware
docs.text:
Add three middleware to globalMiddleware, in this order:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
    HandleInertiaRequests(),
  ],
  // ...
);
  • SessionMiddleware gives each request a session. Inertia uses it for validation errors and flash data.
  • CsrfMiddleware stops cross site form posts. It sets the XSRF-TOKEN cookie. The Inertia client reads it and sends it back in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header. You do not write any code for this.
  • HandleInertiaRequests is your InertiaMiddleware, see Shared props. With no props to share, use const InertiaMiddleware().

If only some routes are Inertia pages, you can add them to a router instead, in the same order.

docs.title: Rendering pages
docs.text:
Call inertia with the request, the page name and the props. The page name is the file in resources/js/Pages, without the extension:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
    return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
      'title': 'Users',
      'users': () => User().query().all(),
    });
  }
}

A normal request gets the root view as HTML. An Inertia request (a link or a form) gets the page as JSON.

A prop can be a function, like users above. It runs only when the prop is sent, and it can give a Future. Props become JSON, so a model or any object with toJson() works. A DateTime becomes ISO text.

Inertia.render(req, 'Users/Index', {...}) does the same as inertia(...).

docs.title: Shared props
docs.text:
Some props are needed on every page, like the signed in user or the app name. Extend InertiaMiddleware and return them from share. Then add it to globalMiddleware (see Middleware):

lib/app/http/middleware/handle_inertia_requests.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

class HandleInertiaRequests extends InertiaMiddleware {
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> share(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'appName': 'My app',
      'auth': () => req.auth?.toJson(),
    };
  }
}

A page prop with the same name wins over a shared prop. share can be async. You can also share from any middleware or controller with Inertia.share(req, {...}).

docs.title: Global values
docs.text:
For a value that is the same for the whole app, use Inertia.shareGlobal(key, value). Call it once in the setup() of your InertiaProvider, so it runs in every isolate:

class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Inertia.shareGlobal('appName', 'Dox');
  }
}

A global value is kept for all users and all requests. So use it only for a constant, or a function that does not read a request. Data of one user, like the signed in user, must go in InertiaMiddleware.share.

docs.title: Partial reloads
docs.text:
Sometimes a page only needs new data for one prop. The client can ask for some props only, with router.reload({ only: ['users'] }). Dox then sends only those props, and function props that are not sent do not run.

These helpers change when a prop is sent.

docs.title: Optional props
docs.text:
Inertia.optional sends the prop only when a partial reload asks for it:

'stats': Inertia.optional(() => Stats.load()),

docs.title: Always props
docs.text:
Inertia.always sends the prop on every request, also on a partial reload that does not ask for it:

'notices': Inertia.always(notices),

docs.title: Deferred props
docs.text:
A slow prop can make the first visit slow. Inertia.defer leaves it out of the first visit, and the page loads it right after:

'comments': Inertia.defer(() => Comment().query().all()),

Deferred props of the same group load in one request. The default group is default:

'likes': Inertia.defer(() => Like().query().count(), group: 'side'),

docs.title: Merging props
docs.text:
For infinite scroll, the page should add the new items to the old ones, not replace them. Use Inertia.merge for this:

'posts': Inertia.merge(posts),

A deferred prop can merge too:

'feed': Inertia.defer(() => Post().query().all()).merge(),

This table shows when each prop is sent:

Helper First visit Partial reload plain value or function sent sent when asked Inertia.optional not sent sent when asked Inertia.always sent always sent Inertia.defer not sent, listed in deferredProps sent when asked Inertia.merge sent, listed in mergeProps sent when asked

docs.title: Forms and validation errors
docs.text:
A form post needs no extra code for errors. This is how it works:

  1. The page posts the form: router.post('/users', data) or useForm.
  2. The controller validates. The validation fails.
  3. Dox flashes the errors and the old input to the session, and redirects back.
  4. The page loads again. It gets the errors in the errors prop.
Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  await req.validateSchema(
    v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
      'name': v.string().min(2),
      'email': v.string().email(),
    }),
  );
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users');
}

The page reads the errors from the form:

const { data, setData, post, errors } = useForm({ name: '', email: '' })
// errors.email holds the message, or is undefined

Every page gets errors, also on a partial reload. It is {} when there are no errors. The old input is in req.session.old('email'). Password fields are not kept.

docs.title: Error bags
docs.text: If one page has two forms, the errors of one form should not show on the other. Pass errorBag in the post, like router.post(url, data, { errorBag: 'login' }) or form.post(url, { errorBag: 'login' }). Then the errors are under the bag name: errors.login.email.

docs.title: Redirects
docs.text:
After a form, redirect with redirect(url) or back(req) from Dox:

Future<DoxResponse> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users'); // 303 for an Inertia PUT
}

After PUT, PATCH or DELETE, the browser must follow the redirect with GET, not with the same method. So InertiaMiddleware turns a 302 into 303 for these requests. You do not need to do anything.

If a controller returns nothing to an Inertia request, InertiaMiddleware sends the browser back to the page it came from, like back(req).

docs.title: External redirects
docs.text:
To go to an outside site, or any page that is not an Inertia page, use Inertia.location. The client then loads the url with a full page load:

return Inertia.location(req, 'https://checkout.example.com/pay/1');

docs.title: Flash data
docs.text:
Flash data is a short message for the next page, like "User saved". Use Inertia.flash, and the next page gets it in page.flash, once:

Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... save the user
  Inertia.flash(req, 'message', 'User saved');
  return redirect('/users');
}

Read it on the page:

import { usePage } from '@inertiajs/react'

const { flash } = usePage()
// flash.message is 'User saved'

The client also fires a flash event, and calls the onFlash callback of the visit. Inertia.flash needs SessionMiddleware.

docs.title: Vite
docs.text:
In dev mode, @vite loads the entry files from the Vite dev server, so you get hot reload. In production, Dox reads public/build/.vite/manifest.json and gives the <link> and <script> tags of the built files.

Dox is in dev mode when devServerUrl is set, or when the file public/hot exists. So set devServerUrl from the env, and production does not use it:

lib/config/inertia.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  devServerUrl: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'development'
      ? 'http://localhost:5173'
      : null,
  reactRefresh: true,
);

docs.title: Asset version
docs.text:
When you deploy new JavaScript, a browser that is still open has the old files. The asset version fixes this. When the version changes, the next link click loads the whole page again, with the new files.

The default version is a hash of the Vite manifest. Dox reads it once per isolate, so restart the server after vite build (a deploy does this). To set your own, use version in the config, for example the git commit.

docs.title: Root view data
docs.text:
Page props go to the JavaScript page. Sometimes the root view itself needs a value, like the <title> or a CSRF meta tag. Use Inertia.withViewData for that.

Write {{ key }} in the root view:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrfToken }}">
    <title>{{ title }}</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>

Set the values in the controller:

Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.withViewData(req, <String, Object?>{'title': 'Users'});
  return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
