    'users': () => User().query().all(),
  });
}

The values are for the root view only. They are not page props, so an Inertia request (a link or a form) does not get them. You can call withViewData many times, also in a middleware, and the data is merged.

Each value is HTML escaped. Put a value in text or in a quoted attribute only. It is not safe inside a <script> block, an unquoted attribute or a link address.

{{ csrfToken }} is filled for you with the CSRF token of the session. It needs SessionMiddleware.

A {{ key }} that you did not set stays as it is, so set every key that the root view uses.

A title set this way is for the first page load only, because later visits do not load the root view again. There, the <Head> component of the Inertia client changes the title. So set the title in <Head> too.

docs.title: Another root view for some pages
docs.text:
Sometimes a part of the app needs another HTML page, like an admin area. Inertia.setRootView uses another file for one request:

Future<DoxResponse> dashboard(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.setRootView(req, 'resources/views/admin.html');
  return inertia(req, 'Admin/Dashboard');
}

RootViewMiddleware does the same for every page of a router:

class AdminRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const RootViewMiddleware('resources/views/admin.html'),
  ];

  // ...
}

The path is from the project root, like rootView in the config. Use a fixed path. Never pass a value from the request, because it could show any file of the server as the page.

docs.title: History encryption
docs.text:
The browser keeps the props of each page in its history, so the back button is fast. After a logout, the back button can still show a page with private data. History encryption stops this.

With it, the browser encrypts the page data before it goes into the history. When you clear the history, the old pages can not be read any more, and the back button asks the server for the page again. The browser can only encrypt on HTTPS, and on localhost.

Turn it on for all pages in the config:

lib/config/inertia.dart
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  encryptHistory: true,
);

Or for one page, in the controller. false turns it off for one page when the config turns it on:

Future<DoxResponse> show(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.encryptHistory(req);
  // Inertia.encryptHistory(req, false);
  return inertia(req, 'Account/Show', props);
}

Or for all pages of a router, with EncryptHistoryMiddleware:

class AccountRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[const EncryptHistoryMiddleware()];

  // ...
}

Call Inertia.clearHistory(req) to clear the history, for example on logout:

Future<DoxResponse> logout(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... sign the user out
  Inertia.clearHistory(req);
  return redirect('/login');
}

The next Inertia page tells the browser to clear its history, once. The mark is kept in the session, so it works with a redirect. It needs SessionMiddleware.

docs.title: Server side rendering (SSR)
docs.text:
By default, the first visit gets an empty page, and the browser renders it. With SSR, the first visit gets the full HTML of the page. Search engines can read it, and the visitor sees the page sooner.

The page is rendered by the Inertia SSR server. It is a Node process that you build with Vite and run next to your Dox app. On a first visit, Dox sends the page to it and puts the answer in the root view. Inertia requests (links and forms) never use it.

docs.title: 1. The SSR entry file
docs.text:
Write an entry file for the SSR server:

resources/js/ssr.jsx
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import createServer from '@inertiajs/react/server'
import ReactDOMServer from 'react-dom/server'

createServer(
  (page) =>
    createInertiaApp({
      page,
      render: ReactDOMServer.renderToString,
      resolve: (name) => {
        const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
        return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
      },
      setup: ({ App, props }) => <App {...props} />,
    }),
  { host: '127.0.0.1' },
)

Vue and Svelte have the same createServer, in @inertiajs/vue3/server and @inertiajs/svelte/server.

The SSR server listens on port 13714. Set host to 127.0.0.1, so only your own machine can reach it.

docs.title: 2. Hydrate in the browser
docs.text:
The browser must reuse the HTML from the server, and not render the page again. Change setup in your app file:

resources/js/app.jsx
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot, hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    if (el.hasAttribute('data-server-rendered')) {
      hydrateRoot(el, <App {...props} />)
    } else {
      createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
    }
  },
})

The else part is for a page that was sent without SSR.

docs.title: 3. Build and run
docs.text:
Build the browser files, then the SSR file. Then start the SSR server with Node:

vite build
vite build --ssr resources/js/ssr.jsx --outDir bootstrap/ssr
node bootstrap/ssr/ssr.js

The file is ssr.js when your package.json has "type": "module". Else it is ssr.mjs. The SSR file loads your packages from node_modules, so keep that folder on the server.

Keep the Node process running with your process manager, like the Dox app. Build and start it again on each deploy.

docs.title: 4. Turn it on
docs.text:
Set ssr in the config:

lib/config/inertia.dart
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  ssr: InertiaSsr(),
);

With no ssr, SSR is off. InertiaSsr has two options:

Option Default What it does url http://127.0.0.1:13714/render the render url of the SSR server timeout 2 seconds how long Dox waits for the answer. Then it stops the request.

The url must be a full http or https url. A wrong url gives an error when the app starts.

To use SSR only in production, set it from the env:

ssr: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'production' ? InertiaSsr() : null,

docs.title: The root view with SSR
docs.text:
The root view needs no change. The HTML from the SSR server goes in place of @inertia. The head tags of the page (from the <Head> component, like <title>) go right before </head>.

When your pages set a title with <Head>, remove the <title> from the root view, so the page does not have two.

docs.title: When the SSR server fails
docs.text: If the SSR server is down, is too slow, or gives a bad answer, the visitor gets the normal page and the browser renders it. No error is shown. Dox prints one warning for the first failure, and no more until the SSR server works again.

docs.title: Not included
docs.text:
• The Inertia 1 and 2 clients. They read the page from <div id="app" data-page="...">. Use the Inertia 3 client.
  • Once props, scroll props (infinite scroll), prependProps, deepMergeProps and matchPropsOn.
  • Partial reloads of nested props with dots, like only: ['auth.user']. Ask for the top level prop (auth).
  • Starting the SSR server from Dox. You run the Node process yourself.

Inertia needs sessions for the errors, flash data and redirects. The client sends the CSRF token by itself, see CSRF.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

  • @inertia becomes <script data-page="app" type="application/json">{"component":"Home",...}</script><div id="app"></div>. In the JSON, <, > and & are written as \u003c, \u003e and \u0026, so a prop can not end the script tag.
  • An Inertia request has X-Inertia: true. Its answer has X-Inertia: true and Vary: X-Inertia.
  • A Dart int above 2^53 in a prop loses precision, because JavaScript reads the page JSON. Send such a number as a string.
  • The page lists the names of the shared props in sharedProps. The client keeps them on an instant visit. A prop shared for the request wins over a global one.
  • Inertia.lazy is the same as Inertia.optional. A deferred prop with .merge() (or merge: true) is also listed in mergeProps when it is sent.
  • With an error bag, the client sends the X-Inertia-Error-Bag header. You do not need to pass errors yourself, but a page prop named errors still wins.
  • An empty 200 answer to an Inertia request goes back only to a Referer of the same site. Any other Referer goes to /. A request without X-Inertia gets the empty answer as it is.
  • Inertia.location gives an Inertia request 409 with X-Inertia-Location. Other requests get 302. An old asset version on an Inertia GET also gets 409 with X-Inertia-Location.
  • In dev mode, @vite loads @vite/client too. With reactRefresh: true it adds the React Fast Refresh code first. In production, @vite gives a <link> tag for the css of each entry and of the chunks it imports, and a <script type="module"> tag for each entry.
  • public/hot holds the dev server url. Some Vite plugins write it while vite runs. Dox ignores it only when APP_ENV is production (in any case), and prints a warning. Other values, like staging or an empty value, still use it.
  • Root view data: the escaped characters are &, <, >, " and '. A null value gives empty text. For the same key, the last call wins. A key has letters, digits and _, and the spaces are optional: {{title}} works too. With no session, {{ csrfToken }} stays as it is. Your own csrfToken value wins. Only {{ key }} in the root view file is replaced, not the same text in a prop or in the SSR HTML.
  • With SSR, the <Head> title is also added to the first page, so use only one of withViewData and <Head> for the title.
  • Another root view works like the default one, with @vite, @inertia and {{ key }}.
  • History encryption keeps its key in the browser, in session storage. With no session, clearHistory only works when the same request renders a page with inertia(...).
  • With SSR, head tags need a </head> tag (</HEAD> works too). A root view with no </head> gets no head tags. The SSR HTML holds the page data and the rendered <div id="app">.

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
Middleware is code that runs before the controller, and if you want, after it too.

Use it for checks like login, logging or rate limits, or to change the response. For example, an auth middleware checks the user. If the user is not logged in, it sends an error, and the controller never runs.

docs.title: Defining middleware
docs.text:
Make a middleware with the CLI:

dox make:middleware Logger

It writes lib/app/http/middleware/logger.middleware.dart. Write your code in handle:

lib/app/http/middleware/logger.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class LoggerMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) {
    print('${req.method} ${req.uri.path}');
    return req; // go on to the next middleware
  }
}

handle takes an IDoxRequest, not a DoxRequest. It can be async, and Dox waits for it. A middleware does one of these:

  • Return the request. Dox goes on to the next middleware, then to the controller.
  • Return something else (a String, a Map, a response(...)). Dox sends it as the response. The controller does not run.
  • Throw an exception, like NotFoundHttpException(). Dox sends the error response. See Response: errors.

Warning

Do not forget return req. A middleware that returns null ends the request with an empty 200, and the controller does not run. When APP_ENV is development or local, Dox prints a warning the first time a middleware does this.

docs.title: Function middleware
docs.text:
A function that takes a DoxRequest also works as middleware. This one checks an API key:

lib/app/http/middleware/api_key.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

dynamic apiKeyMiddleware(DoxRequest req) {
  String apiKey = Env.get<String>('API_KEY');
  String given = req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '';
  if (apiKey.isEmpty || !Hash.equals(given, apiKey)) {
    return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Unauthorized'}).statusCode(401);
  }
  return req;
}

The key comes from the API_KEY env variable, not from the code. Use Hash.equals and not == to compare secrets. It takes the same time for every wrong key, so the time does not tell an attacker how much of the key was right.

docs.title: On a route
docs.text:
Put the middleware in a list before the controller. They run from left to right, and you can mix class and function middleware:

Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[
  LoggerMiddleware(),
  apiKeyMiddleware,
  (WebController c) => c.pong, // the controller is always last
]);

docs.title: On a group of routes
docs.text:
Use Route.middleware to run a middleware for many routes:

Route.middleware(<dynamic>[LoggerMiddleware()], () {
  Route.get('/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
  Route.post('/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
});

docs.title: On a router
docs.text:
For all routes of one router, set its middleware list:

lib/routes/api.dart
class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[LoggerMiddleware()];

  @override
  void register() {
    // every route here runs LoggerMiddleware
  }
}

docs.title: Global middleware
docs.text:
For all routes, set globalMiddleware in the app config:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    LogMiddleware(enabled: env.appEnv != 'production'),
  ],
  // ...
);

A package can add global middleware from the setup() of its provider, with Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(...). It runs before the app's globalMiddleware:

class AuditProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(AuditMiddleware());
  }
}

docs.title: The order
docs.text:
Middleware runs in this order: package middleware from providers, then the app's global middleware, then router middleware, then group middleware, then route middleware. If one returns a value or throws, the rest do not run:

flowchart LR
    G["Global"] --> R["Router"] --> P["Group"] --> T["Route"] --> C["Controller"]

docs.title: Run code after the controller
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to change the response after the controller made it. For this, a middleware can get a next function. await next() runs the rest of the middleware and the controller, and gives you the response. Change it, then return it:

lib/app/http/middleware/see_other.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// a redirect after a form post becomes 303, so the browser does a GET
class SeeOtherMiddleware implements IDoxNextMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<DoxResponse> handle(DoxRequest req, Next next) async {
    // before the controller
    DoxResponse res = await next();
    // after the controller
    if (res.status == 302 && req.httpRequest.method != 'GET') {
      res.statusCode(303);
    }
    return res;
  }
}

The response from next() is always a DoxResponse, so you can use all its methods, like statusCode(...) and header(...). Read the status with res.status (null means 200) and the headers with res.headers.

If the controller throws an error, next() does not throw. It gives the error response from the ExceptionHandler, like a 404 or a 422. So the code after next() always runs. To stop early, return a response and do not call next().

A function works too. It takes the request and next:

Future<DoxResponse> timerMiddleware(DoxRequest req, Next next) async {
  Stopwatch watch = Stopwatch()..start();
  DoxResponse res = await next();
  return res.header('X-Time', '${watch.elapsedMilliseconds}ms');
}

docs.title: Run code after the answer is sent
docs.text:
Some work should not make the client wait, like logs, metrics or cleanup. A middleware can do it in a terminate method, which runs after the answer has gone to the client. Implement IDoxTerminableMiddleware:

lib/app/http/middleware/metrics.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class MetricsMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware, IDoxTerminableMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) => req; // before the controller

  @override
  void terminate(DoxRequest req, DoxResponse res) {
    // the answer is already sent
    print('${req.method} ${req.uri.path} ${res.status}');
  }
}

res.status is the status that was sent, also for an error answer. terminate can be async. An error in it goes to ExceptionHandler.report, and it never changes the answer.

docs.title: From any code, with AfterResponse
docs.text:
A middleware must be on the route. If you want to add work after the answer from any code (a controller, a service, a package), use AfterResponse. The code does not need the request.

It is off by default. Turn it on in the setup() of a provider. setup() runs in every isolate, so each isolate turns it on:

lib/providers/app_provider.dart
@override
void setup() {
  AfterResponse.enable();
}

Then add work anywhere in the request:

AfterResponse.run(() => mailer.sendWelcome(user));

The work runs after the answer is sent, one after the other. An error in it goes to ExceptionHandler.report, so it never reaches the client.

A request that adds no work costs almost nothing. The list of work is made on the first run.

The work is not saved anywhere. When the server stops, work that did not run yet is lost. So use a queue for work that must run. To run a queue job this way, see dispatchAfterResponse() in Queue.

docs.title: Request id
docs.text:
When you look for one request in your logs, an id helps. RequestId gives each request an id. It is sent back in the X-Request-Id header, and you can read it as req.requestId:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const RequestId(),
    LogMiddleware(enabled: true),
  ],
  // ...
);

Put RequestId before LogMiddleware, so each log line gets http.request_id. The default ExceptionHandler.report prints the id with the error. In your own report, read ExceptionHandler.requestId.

When the client (or a proxy) sends a safe X-Request-Id, Dox keeps it. Else it makes a new one. RequestId(trustClient: false) always makes a new one.

docs.title: ETag and 304 Not Modified
docs.text:
If a client asks for the same data again and nothing changed, you can save bandwidth. ETag adds an ETag header to GET and HEAD answers. When the client sends the same ETag back in If-None-Match, Dox answers 304 Not Modified with no body:

Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[const ETag(), (PostController c) => c.index]);

It works on 200 answers with a body in memory: a String, a Map, a List or a model. Files and streams are not touched. The controller still runs, so a 304 saves bandwidth, not server time.

docs.title: Request timeout
docs.text:
A slow route should not keep the client waiting forever. .timeout answers 503 Service Unavailable when the middleware after it and the controller take too long:

Route.get('/report', (ReportController c) => c.show)
    .timeout(Duration(seconds: 30));

This is the same as the RequestTimeout middleware. For every route, add RequestTimeout(...) to globalMiddleware:

Route.get('/report', <dynamic>[
  RequestTimeout(Duration(seconds: 30)),
  (ReportController c) => c.show,
]);

The answer is the normal error JSON:

{"code": "request_timeout", "message": "The request took too long"}

Dart can not stop a running Future, so the controller keeps running in the background. Its late result is dropped, so nothing is sent twice.

docs.title: Server timing
docs.text:
When a page is slow, you want to see where the time goes. ServerTiming adds a Server-Timing header, and the browser dev tools show it in the Network tab, under Timing:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'development') const ServerTiming(),
  ],
  // ...
);

Development or trusted clients only

The header tells every client how long your code takes. An attacker can use that, for example to guess if an email has an account. ServerTiming is off unless you add it. Turn it on in development, or only for clients you trust.

It always sends two times, in milliseconds. handler is the time in the controller. total is the time of the middleware after ServerTiming and the controller.

To add your own time to the current request, use add. You do not pass the request:

ServerTiming.add('db', Duration(milliseconds: 4));

measure runs a function and adds the time it took, also when it throws:

String html = await ServerTiming.measure('render', () => view.render());

The header looks like this:

Server-Timing: db;dur=4.10;desc="3 calls", handler;dur=12.34, total;dur=13.02

When you add the same name again, the times are added together, and the text shows the count, like "3 calls". Pass description: to set your own text.

docs.title: Timing database queries
docs.text:
To add the time of every database query, listen to the queries once, in setup() of a provider. The listener runs inside the request that made the query, so add finds that request:

lib/providers/query_timing_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart'; // SqlQueryBuilder and QueryEvent

void onQuery(QueryEvent event) {
  ServerTiming.add('db', event.time);
}

/// Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class QueryTimingProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    SqlQueryBuilder().listen(onQuery);
  }
}

The header then shows the total query time and the count, like db;dur=4.10;desc="3 calls". See Listen to queries.

Each listen call adds the listener again. If setup() runs a second time (for example in tests), each query is counted twice. Call SqlQueryBuilder().removeListener(onQuery) first, or when you are done.

docs.title: More middleware
docs.text:
Dox has more middleware on other pages:

  • LogMiddleware from dox_core logs one line per request. See Details for its options.
  • AuthMiddleware from dox_auth checks the JWT token. AuthMiddleware(optional: true) lets guests through too. GuestMiddleware lets only guests through, for login pages. See Authentication.
  • RateLimit answers 429 when a client sends too many requests. See Rate limiting.
  • SecurityHeaders adds safe headers like X-Frame-Options to every answer. See Security headers.
  • SessionMiddleware gives each request a session. See Session.
  • CsrfMiddleware stops cross site request forgery. See CSRF protection.
  • ValidateSignature checks signed urls. See Signed URLs.
  • MethodOverride lets HTML forms send PUT, PATCH and DELETE. See Routing.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: LogMiddleware
docs.text:
• It follows LoggerConfig: enabled, level and prettyPrint. If the logger is off, LogMiddleware(enabled: true) does not turn logs on. enabled: false turns only the request logs off. Leave it unset to follow the logger.
  • With prettyPrint it prints colored text that starts with [request], like [request] GET /users => {...}. Without it, it prints one JSON line with status, source (request), message, network.client.ip, http.method, http.url, http.request_id and payload.
  • The filter can change status, message and the other fields. It can not change timestamp or logger, because Logger sets them.
  • Headers are logged only with withHeader: true.
  • Body fields and headers whose name has a word like password, secret, token, authorization, cookie or api_key in it (upper or lower case) are logged as [REDACTED]. Change the list with redact:.
  • The new project turns it off when APP_ENV is production.

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• A route with no next or terminate middleware pays nothing extra for these features.
  • A class can implement only IDoxTerminableMiddleware, with no handle.
  • AfterResponse work runs in the order it was added. The next one starts only when the one before it ends, so work that never ends blocks the rest for that request. Outside a request, or when it is off, the work runs soon, after the current code.
  • Dox().addGlobalMiddleware skips a second add of the same middleware. The list is cleared at each start, before the providers run, so add it from setup(). Use a top-level function or a const instance. dox route:list does not run providers, so it does not show this middleware.
  • A safe X-Request-Id is 1 to 128 characters of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -. A new id is 32 hex characters.
  • ETag skips an answer that already has an ETag header or Cache-Control: no-store. The ETag is weak (W/"..."), made from a fast 64-bit hash of the body. It is not a secure hash.
  • RequestTimeout sends 503, not 504, because 504 Gateway Timeout is what a proxy sends. 503 says the app itself gave up.
  • ServerTiming names may only have letters, digits and !#$%&'*+-.^_`|~. Other characters become _, and an empty name is ignored. One answer keeps at most 32 names, plus handler and total.
  • A time you add named total or handler is sent as app_total or app_handler, so it does not change the built-in times.
  • If the answer already has a Server-Timing header, the times are added after it.
  • Without ServerTiming, or outside a request, add and measure do nothing. The cost is one small lookup.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
The request gives you the input, files, headers and cookies that the client sent.

There are two ways to read input. You can ask for a typed, checked object (a DTO). Or you can read the raw values from DoxRequest. Use a DTO when you can, because Dox checks the input for you.

docs.title: Typed input (recommended)
docs.text:
Ask for a DTO in your controller. Dox reads the body (or the query for GET, HEAD and DELETE), checks it, and gives you a typed object:

Route.put('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User?> update( // (1)!
    int id, // (2)!
    UpdateUser input, // (3)!
  ) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    user?.name = input.name;
    await user?.save();
    return user;
  }
}
  1. The return value is the response. Dox waits for a Future. A String is sent as text. A Map or a model is sent as JSON.
  2. A path param. It is {id} from the route. /users/abc answers 404, because abc is not an int.
  3. A DTO. Dox reads the body, checks it, and builds the object before this method runs.

Bad input gets 422 before your method runs. See DTOs and Validation.

docs.title: Raw input
docs.text: Sometimes you need a value that is not in a DTO. Add a DoxRequest parameter to read the raw values. These values are not checked.

docs.title: Retrieving an input value
docs.text:
The input method reads one value from the query string or the body. The body wins when both have the key:

@Inject()
class ApiController {
  String sayHello(DoxRequest req) {
    String? name = req.input('name');
    return 'Hello $name';
  }
}

The second argument is the default. You get it when the key is not there or is null:

String name = req.input('name', 'guest');

To read inside a map or a list, use a dot key:

req.input('user.name');
req.input('items.0.id'); // the id of the first item

docs.title: Retrieving all input
docs.text:
The all method returns all values from the query string and the body, as a Map:

Map<String, dynamic> data = req.all();

If you want only the body or only the query string, use body or query:

req.body;  // JSON or form data
req.query; // the query string

docs.title: Retrieving a part of the input
docs.text:
Use only to get some keys, or except to get all keys but some:

req.only(<String>['name', 'email']);

req.except(<String>['password']);

docs.title: Checking if a value exists
docs.text:
The filled method returns true when the key is there and not empty. A text of only spaces, an empty list and an empty map count as empty:

if (req.filled('name')) {
  // ...
}

The exists method returns true when the key is there, with any value (also '' or null). The missing method is the opposite:

req.exists('name');

req.missing('name');

There is also has. It returns true when the key is there as it is and not empty. It does not read dot keys, so req.has('user.name') is false for {"user": {"name": "Ann"}}. Use filled for that.

docs.title: Reading booleans and numbers
docs.text:
The boolean method returns true for true, 1, on and yes, and false for anything else. This is useful for checkboxes:

bool remember = req.boolean('remember');

The integer method gives the value as an int. The default is used when the key is not there or is not a number:

int page = req.integer('page', 1);

docs.title: Adding input
docs.text:
Sometimes a middleware needs to add values to the input. Use add for one value, or merge for a map:

req.add('key', value);

req.merge(<String, dynamic>{'key': value});

docs.title: Lists and maps in forms
docs.text:
Form and query keys with brackets give lists and maps:

Input req.input(...) gives tags[]=a&tags[]=b req.input('tags') is ['a', 'b'] address[city]=Yangon req.input('address') is {'city': 'Yangon'} items[0][name]=x req.input('items') is [{'name': 'x'}] name=a&name=b (no brackets) req.input('name') is 'b', the last value

docs.title: Route params
docs.text:
Ask for a path param as a typed parameter, like int id in the example above. See Controller: parameters.

The text values are also in req.param. They are URL-decoded, so /users/a%20b gives 'a b':

String? id = req.param['id'];

docs.title: Form data (File)
docs.text:
An uploaded file is a RequestFile. The request must be multipart/form-data.

Put the file in a DTO, so Dox checks its type and size:

lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}

Then store it in the controller:

lib/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart
@Inject()
class ApiController {
  Future<Map<String, String>> uploadImage(UploadImage input) async {
    String uploadedPath = await input.image.store('images');
    return <String, String>{'filename': uploadedPath};
  }
}

store() comes from the dox_storage package. Add it and import package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart.

Save the file before you return

A bigger upload is kept in a temp file, and the temp file is deleted when the response is sent. So call store, moveTo or stream before your controller returns.

docs.title: Files without a DTO
docs.text:
Without a DTO, req.file gives the RequestFile, or null when the field is not a file. These files are not checked:

RequestFile? image = req.file('image');

hasFile returns true when the field holds a file or a list of files. For a field with many files, use req.input('images'):

if (req.hasFile('image')) {
  // ...
}

docs.title: RequestFile
docs.text:
A RequestFile tells you about the file and lets you save it:

RequestFile file = req.input('video');

file.filename;        // name from the client
file.filetype;        // content type, like video/mp4
file.extension;       // mp4
file.length;          // size in bytes
await file.size;      // size in KB

To save the file, use store (needs dox_storage) or moveTo:

await file.store('videos');              // save to storage (needs dox_storage). returns the path
await file.moveTo('/data/videos/1.mp4'); // move it. returns the new File

To read the file, use stream to get it in chunks. bytes loads the whole file in memory, so avoid it for big files:

file.stream();        // read it in chunks
await file.bytes;     // the whole file in memory. avoid for big files

docs.title: Size limits
docs.text:
A body that is too big gets 413 Payload Too Large. You can change the limits in AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig(
  maxBodySize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,        // JSON and urlencoded, default 10 MB
  maxMultipartSize: 100 * 1024 * 1024,  // form-data uploads, default 100 MB
);

Set the same limit in your proxy, like client_max_body_size in nginx.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
The header method reads one header:

String? token = req.header('X-Token');

headers gives all of them. A repeated header is joined with ', ':

Map<String, dynamic> all = req.headers;

There are short methods for common headers:

req.userAgent();  // User-Agent header
req.host();       // Host header
req.origin();     // Origin header, or null
req.referer();    // Referer header, or null
req.locale;       // first language of Accept-Language, like 'th', or null
req.bearerToken(); // the token of 'Authorization: Bearer <token>', or null

To check the body type, use isJson or isFormData:

req.isJson();     // true for a JSON body
req.isFormData(); // true for multipart/form-data

docs.title: Path and URL
docs.text:
Use path and fullUrl to read the URL of the request:

req.path();                   // '/admin/users/5'
req.fullUrl();                // 'https://example.com/admin/users/5?tab=info'

To check where the request goes, use pathIs with a pattern, or routeIs with a route name. * matches any text:

req.pathIs('admin/*');        // true. `*` matches any text
req.routeIs('admin.users.*'); // true when the route name matches

routeIs is false for a route with no name. Give a route a name with .name('admin.users.show').

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
The cookie method reads a cookie. Dox encrypts cookies by default, so you get the decrypted value. For a cookie that is not encrypted, pass decrypt: false:

String? token = req.cookie('token');                 // decrypted value
String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);   // value as sent

See Response to set a cookie.

docs.title: Client IP and scheme
docs.text:
req.ip();       // client IP
req.scheme();   // http or https
req.isSecure(); // true for https

Behind a proxy, req.ip() shows the proxy, not the client. Set trustedProxies in AppConfig to fix it. See Deployment.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• A key that is in the input as it is wins over a dot key. So a body key 'a.b' is read before the b key inside a.
  • Dot keys also work in filled, exists, missing, boolean, integer, file and hasFile.
  • The flags onlyPresent and hasKeyOnly make only leave out missing keys and has only check the key. See Core flags.
  • An upload up to 1 MB stays in memory. A bigger one is written to a temp file while it arrives.
  • For the size limits, Dox checks Content-Length first. It also counts the bytes while it reads the body.
  • pathIs cleans the path like the router does. A / at the start or the end does not matter, and // counts as one /. So 'admin/*' and '/admin/*' are the same.

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
A controller returns a value, and Dox turns it into the response for the client.

Most of the time you just return a string, a map or a model. When you need to set the status, headers or cookies, use the response() helper.

docs.title: Return a value
docs.text:
Return the value from your controller. Dox sends a String as text, and a Map or a model as JSON:

// JSON
Map<String, String> hello(DoxRequest req) {
  return <String, String>{'message': 'hello world!'};
}

// a model
Future<Blog?> show(int id) async {
  return Blog().find(id);
}

This is what the client gets for each type:

You return The client gets a String the text a Map or a List JSON a model, a list of models, a serializer JSON (from toJson()) a DateTime the ISO 8601 text an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException() its status code and JSON: {"code": ..., "message": ...}, or a Map message as it is a File (from dart:io) the file, streamed a Stream<List<int>> the bytes, streamed StreamFile, DownloadableFile (also from Storage() of dox_storage) the file, streamed response(...) full control: status, headers, cookies

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
To answer with an error, throw or return an exception:

throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'Blog not found');

The client gets 404 with {"code":"not_found","message":"Blog not found"}. Each exception takes message:, errorCode: and code:. code in the JSON is the errorCode. A Map message is sent as it is.

Dox has these exceptions:

Exception Status BadRequestException() 400 NotFoundHttpException() 404 PayloadTooLargeException() 413 UnsupportedMediaTypeException() 415 TokenMismatchException() 419 ValidationException() 422 TooManyRequestsException() 429 InternalErrorException() 500

If you need another status, extend IHttpException:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ForbiddenException extends IHttpException {
  ForbiddenException({String message = 'Forbidden'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.forbidden;
    super.errorCode = 'forbidden';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

Any other error gets 500. It is also passed to the exception handler.

docs.title: Files and big responses
docs.text:
Return a File or a Stream<List<int>> to send a file. Dox sends it in chunks, so it does not load it all into memory:

import 'dart:io';

// a file from disk
Route.get('/video', (DoxRequest req) => File('storage/video.mp4'));

A File gets the right Content-Type, Content-Length and Accept-Ranges. It also answers Range requests with 206 Partial Content, so video players can seek and downloads can resume.

docs.title: Files from storage
docs.text:
If you use File Storage, return Storage().download() to make the browser save the file. It sends Content-Disposition:

import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

// a download from Storage
Future<DownloadableFile> download(DoxRequest req) async {
  // sends Content-Disposition, so the browser saves the file
  return Storage().download('report.pdf');
}

To show the file in the browser instead, return Storage().stream():

// a stream from Storage
Future<StreamFile> show(DoxRequest req) async {
  return Storage().stream('photo.jpg');
}

docs.title: The response() helper
docs.text:
Use response(content) when you need to set the status, headers or cookies. All methods return the response, so you can chain them:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

DoxResponse store(DoxRequest req) {
  return response(<String, String>{'status': 'created'})
      .statusCode(201)
      .header('X-Request-Id', 'abc')
      .contentType(ContentType.json);
}

docs.title: Setting the status
docs.text:
statusCode sets the status code. The default is 200:

response(data).statusCode(201);

docs.title: Setting headers
docs.text:
header sets one header. If a middleware already put the same header on the response, the old value stays and this one is added. Pass replace: true to replace it:

response(data).header('X-Key', 'value');

response(data).header('X-Key', 'value', replace: true);

withHeaders adds many headers. A key replaces the header with the same name, in any case. Other headers stay:

response(data).withHeaders(<String, String>{'X-One': '1', 'X-Two': '2'});

contentType sets Content-Type. ContentType is from dart:io:

response(html).contentType(ContentType.html);

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
cache sets Cache-Control. For example, Duration(minutes: 5) sends Cache-Control: max-age=300:

response(data).cache(Duration(minutes: 5));

docs.title: Changing the body
docs.text:
content changes the body, and stream sends a Stream<List<int>> as the body:

response('').content(value);

response('').stream(byteStream);

docs.title: Redirect
docs.text:
Use redirect to send the browser to another page. The status is 302, unless you pass another one:

// 302 to a path
return redirect('/login');

// another status
return redirect('/posts', status: 301);

back sends the browser back to the page the request came from (the Referer header). When there is no Referer, or it points to another host, it goes to /. This is useful after a form post:

return back(req);

See Session for flash messages and errors with a redirect.

docs.title: Cookie
docs.text:
To set a cookie, make a DoxCookie and add it with cookie:

DoxCookie cookie = DoxCookie('theme', 'dark');
return response('ok').cookie(cookie);

You can set the cookie options too:

DoxCookie token = DoxCookie(
  'token',
  'value',
  maxAge: Duration(days: 7), // sent as Max-Age in seconds. default 1 hour
  httpOnly: true, // default true: page scripts can not read it
  secure: true,   // default: Secure only when the request came over https
  path: '/',
  sameSite: SameSite.lax, // from dart:io. default: none sent
);
return response('ok').cookie(token);

To delete a cookie, pass setExpire: true:

return response('ok').cookie(DoxCookie('token', ''), setExpire: true);

Dox encrypts the cookie value with APP_KEY, and decrypts it when you read it. If the browser or another app must read the value, turn this off with DoxCookie(key, value, encrypt: false). Then read it with req.cookie(key, decrypt: false).

To read a cookie, see Request: cookies.

docs.title: Change every response
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to change every response in one place, for example to add a header. Set a responseHandler in AppConfig for this:

lib/app/http/handler.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    return res.header('X-Powered-By', 'Dox');
  }
}
lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  responseHandler: ResponseHandler(),
  // ...
);

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Some flags change this page: htmlStrings sends a string as text/html, replaceHeaders makes header() replace, and cookieDefaults sends Path=/ and SameSite=Lax when you set no path or sameSite. See Core flags.
  • Storage().stream() and Storage().download() on the local disk also stream the file.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
A route connects a URL and an HTTP method to the code that answers it.

Routing is the first step in the life of a request. When a request comes in, the router finds the route by its method, host and path, and calls its controller.

docs.title: Where routes live
docs.text:
Routes are in the lib/routes folder. Each file has one Router class. The prefix of the router is added in front of all its routes:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (DoxRequest req) => 'pong'); // GET /api/ping
  }
}

Dox finds every Router class by itself after dart run build_runner build. If you want to pick the order of routers, list them in routers: of AppConfig. See Dependency injection: routers and providers.

To see every route of your app, run dox route:list. It does not start the server. See dox route:list.

docs.title: Route methods
docs.text:
There is one method for each HTTP verb:

Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);
Route.post('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.store);
Route.put('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.update);
Route.patch('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.update);
Route.delete('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.destroy);

The leading / is optional, so 'ping' and '/ping' are the same route. A HEAD request runs the GET route of the same path, and the answer has no body.

docs.title: More than one method
docs.text:
Sometimes one handler should answer more than one method. Route.match adds it for a list of methods:

Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST'], '/contact', (ContactController c) => c.handle);

Route.any adds it for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE:

Route.any('/webhook', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);

HEAD comes with GET, so do not list it.

docs.title: The handler
docs.text:
The second argument is the code that answers the request. It can be a function:

Route.get('/ping', (DoxRequest req) => 'pong');

Or a controller method. The controller comes from the container. See Controller:

Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);

@Inject()
class WebController {
  String pong(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

Or a list. The last item is the controller, and the items before it are middleware:

Route.get('/ping', <dynamic>[
  LoggerMiddleware(),
  (WebController c) => c.pong,
]);

See Controller: parameters for the parameters a handler can ask for.

docs.title: Health check route
docs.text:
Route.health adds a route for your load balancer or uptime check. It answers 200 with {"status": "ok"}:

Route.health('/health');

docs.title: Redirect routes
docs.text:
If a page moved, Route.redirect sends the old path to the new URL. The status is 302 by default:

Route.redirect('/home', '/');
Route.redirect('/old-blog', '/blog', status: 301);

For a 301, you can also use permanentRedirect:

Route.permanentRedirect('/old-pricing', '/pricing'); // 301

The target is sent as it is. A param like {id} in the target is not filled in, and the query string is dropped. If you need these, use a normal route and return redirect(...) with the URL you build.

docs.title: Route params
docs.text:
Sometimes you need a part of the URL, like the id of a blog. Put the param in {}, and ask for it as a typed parameter in the controller:

Route.get('/blogs/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.show);

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  Future<Blog?> show(int id) async {
    return Blog().find(id);
  }
}

/blogs/abc answers 404, because abc is not an int. See Controller: parameters for all the rules.

docs.title: Optional param
docs.text:
A param with ? can be missing. Use a nullable type for it:

Route.get('/posts/{page?}', (int? page) {
  return 'page ${page ?? 1}'; // GET /posts and GET /posts/2 both match
});

docs.title: Catch-all param
docs.text:
A param with * matches the rest of the path, with slashes:

Route.get('/docs/{page*}', (String page) {
  return page; // GET /docs/a/b/c gives 'a/b/c'
});

docs.title: Param rules
docs.text:
If you want a route to match only some values, use .where(param, regex). When the param does not match, the router tries the next route. When no route matches, the client gets 404:

Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show).where('id', '[0-9]+');
Route.get('/users/{name}', (UserController c) => c.byName); // gets the rest

The regex must match the whole param text, so you do not need ^ or $. Use (?:...) for a group, not (...). Call .where more than once for more params.

docs.title: Prefix
docs.text:
If many routes start with the same path, put them in a group. The prefix goes in front of every path in the callback:

Route.group('/blogs', () {
  Route.get('/', (BlogController c) => c.index); // GET /blogs
  Route.get('/{id}', (BlogController c) => c.show); // GET /blogs/{id}
});

Groups can be nested. Route.group('blogs', ...) with Route.get('all', ...) makes /blogs/all.

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
Routes in a domain group match only when the Host header is that domain. Other hosts get 404:

Route.domain('dartondox.com', () {
  Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);
});

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
To run a middleware for many routes, use a middleware group. It runs after the global and router middleware:

Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
  Route.get('/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
  Route.post('/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
});

A group can also add a prefix to the route names inside it, with name:. To turn CORS on or off for some routes, see CORS.

docs.title: Resource routes
docs.text:
Most models need the same CRUD routes. Route.resource makes all of them in one line:

Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);

These are the routes it makes:

Method Path Controller method Route name GET /blogs index blogs.index GET /blogs/create create blogs.create POST /blogs store blogs.store GET /blogs/{id} show blogs.show GET /blogs/{id}/edit edit blogs.edit PUT, PATCH /blogs/{id} update blogs.update DELETE /blogs/{id} destroy blogs.destroy

If the controller does not have a method, no route is made for it. See Resource controllers to make one with the CLI.

The route names come from the path: / becomes ., and {params} are left out. So Route.resource('users/{user}/posts', ...) gives users.posts.index. Pass name: to pick another one: Route.resource('blogs', BlogController, name: 'posts').

docs.title: Naming the param
docs.text:
The param of one item is {id}. Pass parameter: to give it another name:

Route.resource('photos', PhotoController, parameter: 'photo');
// GET /photos/{photo}, PUT /photos/{photo}, ...

Then Route.bind('photo', ...) and model binding work on these routes.

docs.title: Forms with PUT, PATCH and DELETE
docs.text:
An HTML form can only send GET or POST. To reach a PUT, PATCH or DELETE route, add MethodOverride to the global middleware:

AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[const MethodOverride()],
);

Then send the form as POST with a _method field:

<form method="POST" action="/blogs/5">
  <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="DELETE">
</form>

CsrfMiddleware still checks the request, so send the _token field too. MethodOverride works only in globalMiddleware, not on a router or a route.

If a client can not send PUT, like an old proxy or JS client, it can send the X-HTTP-Method-Override header instead. Turn it on with header: true:

AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[const MethodOverride(header: true)],
);

docs.title: Named routes
docs.text:
You should give routes a name, so a path lives in one place. Then you build URLs from the name, and you can change the path later without breaking links:

Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show).name('users.show');

docs.title: Generating URLs
docs.text:
Use route() to build the path of a named route. Route.url() does the same:

route('users.show', params: <String, Object>{'id': 5});
// /users/5

To add a query string, pass query:. A param that is not in the path also goes to the query string:

route('users.show', params: <String, Object>{'id': 5}, query: <String, Object>{'tab': 'posts'});
// /users/5?tab=posts

Dox stops with a clear error when two routes have the same name, when route() gets a name that no route has, or when a {param} of the path has no value.

docs.title: Full URL
docs.text:
Pass absolute: true to get the full URL, with APP_URL in front:

route('users.show', params: <String, Object>{'id': 5}, absolute: true);
// https://example.com/users/5   (APP_URL=https://example.com)

To use another base, also pass baseUrl::

route('users.show', params: <String, Object>{'id': 5}, absolute: true, baseUrl: 'https://admin.example.com');
// https://admin.example.com/users/5

docs.title: Name prefix in a group
docs.text:
A group can put a prefix in front of the names inside it:

Route.group('admin', () {
  Route.get('users', (UserController c) => c.index).name('users'); // admin.users
}, name: 'admin.');

docs.title: Signed routes
docs.text:
Sometimes you send a link in an email, like "unsubscribe", and nobody should be able to change it. A signed URL has a signature in its query for this. Protect the route with ValidateSignature, and make the URL with Route.signedUrl:

Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');

Route.signedUrl('unsubscribe',
    params: <String, Object>{'user': 5}, expires: Duration(days: 7));
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?expires=...&signature=...

A changed or expired URL gets 403. See Signed URLs.

docs.title: Route model binding
docs.text:
Often a route param is the id of a model, and every controller loads the model first. A binder does this for you before the controller runs. Add it with Route.bind, before the routes that use it:

Route.bind<User>('user', (String id) => User().find(id));

Route.get('/users/{user}', (DoxRequest req, User user) {
  return user;
});

Every route with a {user} param now runs the binder first. The binder gets the raw text from the URL. If it returns null, the client gets 404.

Ask for a parameter of the bound type, like User user, at any place in the parameter list. You can also read it from the request with req.bound<User>('user'). Other path params still work next to it:

Route.get('/users/{user}/posts/{page}', (User user, int page) {
  return user.posts(page);
});

The binder runs after the middleware, so an auth middleware can stop the request before any database call.

A @DoxModel class does not need Route.bind, because Dox makes a binder for it. See Dependency injection: route model binding. Route.bind wins when both exist.

docs.title: Serve static files
docs.text:
Your app often has CSS, JavaScript and images. Route.staticFiles(prefix, folder) serves the files of a folder:

Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');

Build files with a hash in the name (like Vite's) never change, so give them a long maxAge. It sends Cache-Control: public, max-age=...:

Route.staticFiles('build', 'public/build', maxAge: Duration(days: 365));

Only GET and HEAD requests read files, and only when no route matches. .., dot files (like .env) and folders are never sent. No middleware runs for a file, but the global CORS config still applies.

Warning

Never save user uploads in this folder. An uploaded html or svg file would run its script on your site. Use dox_storage for uploads. It sends such files as downloads.

docs.title: Fallback route
docs.text:
Route.fallback answers a GET or HEAD request that matches no route and no static file. Use it for a custom 404 page, or to send index.html of a single page app:

lib/routes/web.dart
class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/', (WebController c) => c.home);

    Route.fallback((DoxRequest req) {
      return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Page not found'}).statusCode(404);
    });
  }
}

The handler decides the status. So return a 404 status for a "not found" page, or the client gets 200.

Add the fallback in a Router, so the global middleware (like security headers) runs for it. The built-in 404 and 405 answers do not run the global middleware.

docs.title: Serve storage files
docs.text:
Storage.route(path) from the dox_storage package serves the files of a storage disk at GET <path>/{key*}. By default only signed URLs work, and other requests get 403:

Storage.route('files');
Storage.route('public', disk: 'local', signed: false);

An html, svg, xml or javascript file is sent as a download, so a script in an uploaded file does not run on your site. For user uploads, download: true sends every file as a download, also images and PDFs:

Storage.route('uploads', download: true);

See File Storage.

docs.title: WebSocket routes
docs.text:
Route.websocket adds a raw WebSocket route:

Route.websocket('chat', handler, maxMessageSize: 64 * 1024);

By default any website can open it from a browser, with the cookies of the user. So you should check the Origin: pass allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example.com'], or set AppConfig(webSocketAllowedOrigins: [...]) for every WebSocket route. Then only pages of the same host and the listed sites can open it, and other origins get 403. [] means the same host only. When a WebSocket route has no check, Dox prints a warning at start.

A message over maxMessageSize bytes (default 16 MB) closes the socket with code 1009.

docs.title: Request body for the docs
docs.text:
post, put and patch take a body: schema, so the body shows in the OpenAPI docs. It does not check the request. To check input, use a DTO.

Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store, body: v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
  'title': v.string().min(3),
}));

docs.title: Mount a raw handler
docs.text:
Some packages need the raw request, before Dox reads it. Route.mount(prefix, handler) sends every request under a path prefix straight to a raw HttpRequest handler. The handler writes and closes the response itself. Socket.IO uses it for /socket.io/:

Route.mount('/socket.io/', io.handle);

The prefix matches whole path parts. So /admin matches /admin and /admin/users, but not /administrator. When two prefixes match, the longest one wins.

Warning

By default a mount skips all middleware, also the global middleware (security headers, CSRF, rate limit). Set middleware: true to run AppConfig.globalMiddleware before the handler. The global CORS config never applies to a mount. The handler must send its own CORS headers.

Route.mount('/admin', admin.handle, middleware: true);

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Route methods
docs.text:
• There are also Route.options, Route.copy, Route.view, Route.link, Route.unlink, Route.purge, Route.lock, Route.unlock and Route.propfind. Route.view is the WebDAV VIEW method. It does not render a template. To show a template, use a GET route with view() of dox_view: Route.get('welcome', (DoxRequest req) => view(req, 'welcome')).
  • (WebController c) => c.pong picks the method. Dox calls it once per isolate, at start.
  • An unknown method in Route.match throws an ArgumentError at start.
  • Route.any does not add OPTIONS, so Dox still answers the CORS preflight request for the path.
  • .where(...) and .timeout(...) after Route.match or Route.any work on every route it added. .name(...) names the last one.
  • Route.redirect works for the same methods as Route.any.
  • In a group, Dox puts one / between the parts. 'blogs' and '/blogs/' work the same.
  • Route.resource also takes a controller object: Route.resource('blogs', BlogController()). An error from the controller, other than a missing method, stops the app at start.

docs.title: Param rules
docs.text:
• A leading ^ and a trailing $ in a .where regex are dropped. A regex with a (...) group, or a param name that the path does not have, throws an ArgumentError at start.
  • .where('page', '.*') also matches slashes.
  • Routes without .where cost nothing extra.
  • The regex checks the param text two times: as it is in the URL, and again after % codes are decoded. Both checks must pass. A % code for a letter, a digit or -._~ is decoded before the router sees the path, so /users/%31 matches [0-9]+. So /files/x%2Fy does not match [^/]+, because %2F is /. In the second check, . also matches a new line (%0A), so .* still matches it.

docs.title: Forms and named routes
docs.text:
• MethodOverride changes only a POST request, and only to PUT, PATCH or DELETE. Other values are ignored. req.method gives the new method. When both the header and _method are there, the header wins.
  • In route(), param values are URL encoded. A missing {name?} param and a null value are left out. When params and query have the same key, query wins.
  • baseUrl: works only with absolute: true. With absolute: true and no APP_URL and no baseUrl:, route() throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Static files
docs.text:
• The one dot folder that is sent is .well-known at the top of the folder. It holds ACME (Let's Encrypt) challenges, security.txt and apple-app-site-association. Dot files inside it still get 404.
  • A file gets a weak ETag (from its size and change time) and Last-Modified, so the browser gets 304 when it already has the file. If-None-Match wins over If-Modified-Since. Range requests work. With If-Range, the Range is used only when it is the file's Last-Modified date.
  • The prefix follows Route.group, the router prefix and Route.domain.
  • The folder path is relative to the folder the app starts in. Symlinks are followed.
  • Behind a proxy, the proxy can serve the folder instead.
  • Storage routes send html, svg, xml and javascript files with Content-Security-Policy: sandbox. Every file response has X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

docs.title: Fallback route
docs.text:
• Other methods still get the normal 404 or 405. A GET to a path that only has a POST route gets the fallback, if one covers that path. If none does, the client gets 405.
  • Add the fallback before startServer(). A fallback added later only works in the isolate that added it.
  • It follows Route.group, the router prefix and Route.domain. In a group, it only answers paths under the group prefix. A prefix can have params, like {tenant}. When two fallbacks match, the one with the longest prefix wins.
  • The built-in 404 and 405 skip the global middleware because, for example, CsrfMiddleware would answer 419 to a POST to an unknown path, and SessionMiddleware would start a session for every bad link.

docs.title: Mounts
docs.text:
• A trailing / does not change the match, and the query string is not part of it. // counts as one /, so /admin//secure/x goes to a mount at /admin/secure.
  • The match uses the raw path. %2F stays encoded, so /admin/secure%2Fx goes to a mount at /admin. To protect a nested path, set middleware: true on the outer mount too.
  • With middleware: true, a middleware that gives a response (like 403) stops the request. The body is not read for the middleware, so a CSRF token must come in a header.
  • With middleware: true, the handler sends the answer itself. So the part of a middleware that runs after next cannot change it, and cookies it adds then (the session cookie, XSRF-TOKEN) are not sent. Get the CSRF token from a normal route. A terminate step still runs. RequestTimeout does not run for a mount.

docs.title: Serializer
docs.text:
A serializer sets the JSON shape of a response: which keys the client gets, their names and their values.

You often do not want to send a model as it is. Maybe the client needs other key names, a formatted date, or a field made from two columns. A serializer does this in one place. It works with any Dart type: a model, a plain class, or a map.

Tip

You do not always need a serializer. A controller can return a model, a Map or a List as it is. See Response. To only hide some model fields, use hidden.

docs.title: Create a serializer
docs.text:
Make a serializer with the CLI:

dox make:serializer Blog

This makes lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart. The file is for a model with the same name. Change the type to use it for something else.

docs.title: Writing a serializer
docs.text:
Extend Serializer<T> and write convert. convert gets one value of type T and gives back one JSON object:

lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

class BlogSerializer extends Serializer<Blog> {
  BlogSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Blog m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'uid': m.id,
      'title_en': m.title,
    };
  }
}

Return the serializer from a controller, and Dox sends its toJson(). You can give it one model or a list:

lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
class BlogController {
  Future<BlogSerializer> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    List<Blog> blogs = await Blog().all();
    return BlogSerializer(blogs); // a list
  }

  Future<BlogSerializer> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
    Blog? blog = await Blog().find(id);
    return BlogSerializer(blog); // one model
  }
}

The response of show:

{
  "uid": 1,
  "title_en": "This is title"
}

This is what the client gets for each input:

You give The client gets one value of type T one JSON object a List<T> a JSON list ([] when the list is empty) null (for example, find found nothing) null any other type null

The list type must be List<T>

A List<dynamic> is not a List<T>, so the response is null. This happens with a list from jsonDecode. Call .cast<T>() first. See JSON from another API.

docs.title: Change values
docs.text:
convert is plain Dart, so you can format dates, join fields and add new keys:

lib/app/serializers/user.serializer.dart
class UserSerializer extends Serializer<User> {
  UserSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(User m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'id': m.id,
      'name': '${m.firstName} ${m.lastName}',
      'is_active': m.status == 'active',
      'joined_at': m.createdAt?.toIso8601String(),
    };
  }
}

docs.title: A serializer inside a serializer
docs.text:
If a model has a relation, use its serializer inside the other one. Load the relation first, for example with preload:

lib/app/serializers/comment.serializer.dart
class CommentSerializer extends Serializer<Comment> {
  CommentSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Comment m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'id': m.id,
      'content': m.content,
      'user': UserSerializer(m.user).toJson(), // null when there is no user
    };
  }
}

Then preload the relation in the controller:

Future<CommentSerializer> index(DoxRequest req) async {
  List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
  return CommentSerializer(comments);
}

docs.title: With pagination
docs.text:
A paginated result has its own keys, like the page number. page.data is a List<User>, so put the serializer output in place of data:

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}

See Pagination for the full example.

docs.title: Examples without models
docs.text: T can be any type, so you do not need the ORM.

docs.title: A plain Dart class
docs.text:
A serializer for a plain class works the same way:

lib/app/serializers/weather.serializer.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class Weather {
  final String city;
  final double celsius;

  Weather(this.city, this.celsius);
}

class WeatherSerializer extends Serializer<Weather> {
  WeatherSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Weather m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'city': m.city,
      'celsius': m.celsius,
      'fahrenheit': m.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32,
    };
  }
}

WeatherSerializer today(DoxRequest req) {
  return WeatherSerializer(<Weather>[Weather('Yangon', 30)]);
}

docs.title: Rows from the query builder
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.table(...) gives rows as maps, not models. Use Serializer<Map<String, dynamic>> to pick and rename the keys:

lib/app/serializers/sales_report.serializer.dart
class SalesReportSerializer extends Serializer<Map<String, dynamic>> {
  SalesReportSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Map<String, dynamic> m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'product': m['name'],
      'sold': m['total'],
    };
  }
}

Future<SalesReportSerializer> report(DoxRequest req) async {
  List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('orders')
      .selectRaw('name, count(*) as total')
      .groupBy('name')
      .get();
  return SalesReportSerializer(rows);
}

docs.title: JSON from another API
docs.text:
jsonDecode gives a List<dynamic>, so cast it to the type of the serializer first:

Future<SalesReportSerializer> remote(DoxRequest req) async {
  String body = await fetchReport(); // your HTTP call
  List<dynamic> rows = jsonDecode(body);
  return SalesReportSerializer(rows.cast<Map<String, dynamic>>());
}

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • CLI: dox make:serializer

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
A session keeps data for one browser across many requests, so you can remember things like the logged in user or a shopping cart.

HTTP is stateless: each request knows nothing about the one before it. A session fixes this. Dox gives every browser a session cookie and keeps the data for that cookie between requests.

You need a session for web pages with forms and logins. An API that uses tokens does not need one.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add SessionMiddleware to globalMiddleware. Because session forms also need CSRF protection, add CsrfMiddleware right after it:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*']),
  ],
  // ...
);

Now every request has req.session. You can also add the middleware to only some routers or routes. If a route has no session middleware, using req.session there throws an error.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Set session in the app config. Every option has a default, so you only set the ones you want to change:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  session: const SessionConfig(
    driver: 'cache',
    store: 'redis',
    lifetime: Duration(hours: 2),
  ),
  // ...
);

The driver option decides where the session data is kept. Dox has two drivers:

  • cookie (the default): all data is in the session cookie, encrypted with your APP_KEY. There is nothing to store on the server.
  • cache: the cookie only holds a random session id. The data lives in a cache store, such as redis.

If you run more than one server, use the cache driver with a shared store like redis, so all of them see the same sessions. See Choosing a driver for more.

docs.title: Retrieving data
docs.text:
Use get to read a value. The second argument is the default, which you get when the key is not in the session:

String? name = req.session.get('name');

List<dynamic> cart = req.session.get('cart', <int>[]);

docs.title: Retrieving all data
docs.text:
The all method returns a copy of all session data:

Map<String, dynamic> data = req.session.all();

docs.title: Checking if a value exists
docs.text:
The has method returns true when the key is in the session and its value is not null:

if (req.session.has('cart')) {
  // ...
}

docs.title: Storing data
docs.text:
Use put to store a value:

req.session.put('cart', <int>[1, 2]);

Values must be JSON types: Map, List, String, num, bool or null. This is because the session is saved as JSON.

docs.title: Retrieving and deleting a value
docs.text:
The pull method reads a value and removes it in one step:

dynamic cart = req.session.pull('cart');

docs.title: Flash data
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to keep a value only for the next request. For example, after you save a form you redirect, and the next page shows "The post is saved". Use the flash method for this:

Route.post('/posts', (DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... save the post
  req.session.flash('message', 'The post is saved');
  return redirect('/posts');
});

Route.get('/posts', (DoxRequest req) {
  String? message = req.session.get('message'); // 'The post is saved'
  // ...
});

Flash data is there for the current request and the next one. Then Dox removes it.

If you need the flash data for one more request, use reflash. To keep only some keys, use keep:

req.session.reflash();

req.session.keep(<String>['message']);

docs.title: Deleting data
docs.text:
The forget method removes one value. The flush method removes all data:

req.session.forget('cart');

req.session.flush();

docs.title: Regenerating the session ID
docs.text:
You should give the user a new session id when they log in. This stops a session fixation attack, where someone makes a user log in with a session id the attacker already knows.

Use the regenerate method after login. It gives a new session id and a new CSRF token, and it keeps the data:

req.session.regenerate();

On logout, use invalidate. It removes all data and gives a new session id:

req.session.invalidate();

If you use session login from dox_auth, it does both for you.

docs.title: Validation errors and old input
docs.text:
When a form post fails validation on a route with a session, Dox redirects back to the form for you. It also flashes two things, so the form can show them:

  • the errors, like {'email': 'The email is not a valid email'}
  • the old input, so the user does not have to type it again (password fields and files are never kept)

Read them on the form page:

Route.get('/register', (DoxRequest req) {
  Map<String, dynamic> errors = req.session.errors; // empty when there are none
  String? email = req.session.old('email');
  // ...
});

You can also do this yourself. flashErrors flashes the errors and the input, and back redirects to the page the request came from:

req.session.flashErrors(<String, String>{'email': 'The email is taken'}, input: req.all());
return back(req);

docs.title: The cookie driver
docs.text:
The cookie driver is the default because it needs no server storage. The data is encrypted with AES-GCM and your APP_KEY, so the browser can not read or change it.

It has two limits:

  • A cookie can hold about 4 KB. If the session gets bigger, you get an error. So keep the data small: store an id, not a whole object.
  • An old copy of the cookie still works after logout, until the session lifetime ends. This is because the server keeps nothing it could delete.

If either limit is a problem, use the cache driver.

docs.title: The cache driver
docs.text:
The cache driver keeps the data in a cache store, and the cookie only holds an encrypted session id. On logout the data is deleted, so old cookies stop working.

Pick the store with the store option:

  • redis shares sessions between all isolates and servers. To set a command timeout or other Redis options, see Redis options.
  • database also shares sessions, if you have no Redis. See Database store.
  • memory keeps sessions in the main isolate of this server. The other isolates read and write them there, so all isolates of one server see the same sessions. They are lost when the server stops, and each server has its own. Expired sessions are removed by the memory store. Good for tests and a single server.
SessionConfig(driver: 'cache', store: 'redis')

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
client.withSession() gives a test client that keeps cookies like a browser. It also sends the CSRF token back, so CsrfMiddleware lets its posts in:

DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();
await browser.get('/cart/add?id=1');
(await browser.get('/cart')).expectJson(isNotEmpty);

See Testing: keep a session.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: All options
docs.text:
Option Default What it does driver cookie cookie or cache. store null The cache store for the cache driver, like redis, memory or file. null uses the default store of AppConfig.cache. cookie dox_session The name of the session cookie. lifetime 2 hours The session ends after this long with no use. The cookie driver keeps the save time inside the encrypted cookie, so a copied old cookie also stops working after this time. path / Path of the cookie. domain null Domain of the cookie. null means only the host that set it. httpOnly true Page scripts can not read the cookie. secure null null sets Secure when the request came over https. sameSite SameSite.lax SameSite of the cookie (from dart:io).

You can also give a config to one middleware: SessionMiddleware(SessionConfig(...)).

docs.title: Other cases
docs.text:
• regenerate(keepToken: true) keeps the CSRF token, so forms open in other tabs keep working. Do not use it at login.
  • A request that wants JSON gets a 422 JSON answer instead of a redirect when validation fails.
  • Code with no request, like a Socket.IO login, can load the session from the raw cookie value with await SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value). Changes to it are not saved.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
This page lists every annotation you can put on a @Dto field, with its error code and default message.

Use it to look up a rule. To learn how DTOs work, read Validation first.

How to read the tables:

  • Code is the error code. Use it in @Dto(messages: ...) and in a MessageResolver.
  • Message is the default English text. {field} is the last key of the path.
  • Every annotation also takes message:. It wins over every other message.
  • All limits include the limit itself, unless the table says "exclusive".
  • On a List<T> field, a value rule checks each item. Only the list rules check the list itself.

docs.title: Type errors
docs.text:
You get these errors when a value does not fit the field type. They have no annotation.

Code When Message required a required field is missing, null, or "" The {field} is required string not a string The {field} must be a string integer not a whole number The {field} must be an integer numeric not a number (double, num) The {field} must be a number boolean not a bool The {field} must be a boolean date not an ISO 8601 date The {field} must be a date in not a name of the enum The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values} array not a list The {field} must be an array object not an object (nested DTO, Map) The {field} must be an object file not a file The {field} must be a file unrecognized_keys unknown key, with @Dto(strict: true) The {field} field is not allowed

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
Use these rules on String fields (and List<String> items):

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @Length(min: 3, max: 50) length_between The {field} must be between {min} and {max} characters minLength, maxLength @Length(min: 6, max: 6) length The {field} must be exactly {length} characters minLength, maxLength @MinLength(3) min_length The {field} must be at least {min} characters minLength @MaxLength(50) max_length The {field} may not be greater than {max} characters maxLength @Email() email The {field} is not a valid email format: email @Url() url The {field} must be a url format: uri @Uuid() uuid The {field} is invalid uuid format: uuid @Ulid() ulid The {field} must be a valid ULID pattern @Ip() ip The {field} must be an ip address anyOf ipv4 / ipv6 @Regex(r'[a-z]+') regex The {field} format is invalid pattern @In(['a', 'b']) in The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values} enum @NotIn(['root']) not_in The {field} field cannot be {value} not: {enum} @StartsWith('dox') start_with The {field} must start with {prefix} pattern @EndsWith('.dev') end_with The {field} must end with {suffix} pattern @Alpha() alpha The {field} must be an alphabetic pattern @AlphaNumeric() alpha_numeric The {field} must be only alphabetic and number pattern @AlphaDash() alpha_dash The {field} must be only alphabetic, number, dash and underscore pattern
  • @Length has min: and max:. Both are optional, but you must give one. With only min: it acts like @MinLength, with only max: like @MaxLength.
  • Length counts characters (Unicode code points). é counts as 1.
  • @Url() needs http or https and a host.
  • @Uuid() takes any version. Upper or lower case.
  • @Ulid() takes 26 Crockford base32 characters, upper or lower case. The first one is 0 to 7.
  • @Regex(pattern, {message}) must match the whole value. You do not need ^ and $. The regex is checked when the generator runs. A bad regex stops the build.
  • @Alpha(), @AlphaNumeric() and @AlphaDash() use ASCII letters a-z, A-Z. @AlphaDash() also allows digits 0-9, - and _.
  • @In and @NotIn compare exactly (case matters).

docs.title: More text rules
docs.text:
These are also for String fields:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @Json() json The {field} is not a valid json contentMediaType: application/json @Digits(6) digits The {field} must be {digits} digits pattern @DigitsBetween(4, 6) digits_between The {field} must be between {min} and {max} digits pattern @DateFormatted('Y-m-d') date_format The {field} must match the format {format} @HexColor(), @HexColor(short: true) hex_color The {field} must be a hex color like #1a2b3c pattern @Password(min: 8, ...) password The {field} must have {rules} minLength
  • @HexColor() takes # and 6 hex digits, in any case. @HexColor(short: true) also takes 3 digits, like #abc.
  • @Digits and @DigitsBetween take only 0-9. No sign, no dot. Use a String field, so leading zeros stay.
