  • @DateFormatted uses these letters: day d, j, D (Mon), l (Monday), N, w, S (st), z; month m, n, M (Jan), F (January), t; year Y, y, L; time a, A, g, h, G, H, i, s, v, u; time zone e, T, P, p, O, Z, I; full U, c, r. Put \ before a letter to use it as text, like Y-m-d\TH:i. Any other letter stops the build (and throws an ArgumentError in v.string().dateFormat()). Other characters must be there as they are. j, n, g, G, z and U take no leading zero: j/n/Y rejects 01/02/2024. e and T take any name that looks like a time zone. They do not check that it is a real one. The date must exist: 2023-02-29 fails. Names need the case shown (Jan, not jan). A day name must fit the date. The field stays a String. Use a DateTime field for ISO 8601 dates.
  • @Password options: min (default 8), letters, mixedCase (one upper and one lower case letter), numbers, symbols. They are all off by default. Letters, numbers and symbols are Unicode, so é is a letter. {rules} lists the options you set, like at least 8 characters, one number, and one symbol, or at least 8 characters and one number. It does not check leaked passwords.

docs.title: Other fields
docs.text:
Sometimes a field depends on another field. For example, a password must match its confirmation, or a VAT number is required only for a company. These rules read another key of the same object.

The other key is the input key, like account_type, not the Dart name accountType. If you give the Dart name of a field with another key, the build stops.

Annotation Code Message @Confirmed() confirmed The {field} confirmation does not match @Same('email') same The {field} must match {other} @RequiredIf('type', 'company') required_if The {field} is required when {other} is {values} @RequiredWith(['phone']) required_with The {field} is required when {others} is present @RequiredUnless('type', 'guest') required_unless The {field} is required unless {other} is {values} @RequiredWithout(['email']) required_without The {field} is required when {others} is not present @RequiredWithoutAll(['email', 'phone']) required_without_all The {field} is required when none of {others} are present @Different('old_password') different The {field} and {other} must be different @ProhibitedIf('type', 'guest') prohibited_if The {field} is prohibited when {other} is {values} @GreaterThanField('min_price') greater_than The {field} must be greater than {min} @GreaterThanOrEqualField('min_price') min The {field} must be greater than or equal {min} @LessThanField('max_price') less_than The {field} must be less than {max} @LessThanOrEqualField('max_price') max The {field} must be less than or equal {max}
  • @Confirmed and @Same compare the raw input of both keys, so @Trim does not change the compare.
  • @Confirmed() on password needs the key password_confirmation with the same value. The error is on password. Use @Confirmed(other: 'password_again') for another key. The DTO does not need a field for the confirmation key.
  • Text and numbers match by text, both ways: 1234 matches "1234", and "1234" matches 1234.
  • @RequiredIf and @RequiredWith work on a nullable field, a Maybe field or a field with a default. On an always-required field the build stops.
  • @RequiredIf('type', ['company', 'shop']) takes a list: any of the values makes the field required. "true" matches true, "1" matches 1. An enum value matches its name: @RequiredIf('role', Role.admin) matches "admin".
  • @RequiredWith(['phone', 'email']): the field is required when any of the keys is there and not empty.
  • @RequiredUnless('type', 'guest') makes the field required unless type is guest. A missing type counts as null, so the field is required then. It takes a list of values like @RequiredIf.
  • @RequiredWithout(['email']): the field is required when any of the keys is missing or empty. @RequiredWithoutAll(['email', 'phone']): when all of them are missing or empty.
  • @RequiredUnless, @RequiredWithout and @RequiredWithoutAll follow the same rules as @RequiredIf: a nullable, Maybe or default field, and input keys.
  • @Different('old_password') needs a value that is not the same as the other key. It compares the raw input like @Same. A missing other key passes.
  • @ProhibitedIf('type', 'guest') means: when type is guest, the field must be missing or empty. Empty is null, blank text, an empty list or an empty map. 0 and false fail. This is not the same as @Prohibited(), which fails on null and []. It reads type and matches like @RequiredIf.
  • @GreaterThanField, @GreaterThanOrEqualField, @LessThanField and @LessThanOrEqualField compare a value with another field. They are for int, double and num fields. They read the raw input of the other key: a number, or number text from a form. A missing other key (or one that is not a number) fails. {min} and {max} in the message are the other key. They use the codes of @GreaterThan, @Min, @LessThan and @Max.
  • On a List<T> field, @Different checks the whole list, not each item. The field compare rules do not fit a list.
  • Missing means: not there, null, blank text, an empty list or an empty map.
  • They run in step 1, with the other "required" checks. @Confirmed and @Same run in step 2.

docs.title: Present or missing
docs.text:
Use these rules to check if a key is sent and has a value:

Annotation Code Message @Filled() filled The {field} must have a value @Present() present The {field} must be present @Prohibited() prohibited The {field} is prohibited @Accepted() accepted The {field} must be accepted @Declined() declined The {field} must be declined
  • @Filled(): a missing key passes. A key that is sent must have a value: not null, not blank text, not an empty list.
  • @Present(): the key must be sent. Its value may be null or empty.
  • @Filled() and @Present() are for a nullable, Maybe or default field, like @RequiredIf. They run in step 1.
  • @Prohibited(): the key must be missing, or blank text like "" or " ". Any other sent value fails, also null, [], {}, 0 and false. It reads the raw input, so it runs before the type check, in step 1. It is for a nullable, Maybe or default field.
  • @Accepted() takes true, 1, "1", "true", "yes" and "on". @Declined() takes false, 0, "0", "false", "no" and "off". The text is case sensitive. Use them on a bool field with no default. Then a missing value fails with required. In a form, yes and on turn into true first. In a JSON body a bool field takes only true and false, unless the DTO has @Dto(coerce: true).
@Accepted()
final bool terms;

@Present()
final String? note; // the key must be there, null is fine

docs.title: Skip a field
docs.text:
Sometimes a field only matters for some input. For example, a VAT number is only for a company. These rules skip the field for the other cases:

Annotation Does @ExcludeIf('type', 'person') when type is person, the field is skipped @ExcludeUnless('type', 'company') unless type is company, the field is skipped
  • A skipped field is not read and not checked. It gets its default, null or Maybe.missing(), as if it was not sent. The field is left out of the validated data.
  • They read the raw input of the other key, and match like @RequiredIf (also with a list of values).
  • @ExcludeIf: a missing other key does not skip. @ExcludeUnless: a missing other key counts as null, so the field is skipped.
  • They are for a nullable, Maybe or default field. On an always-required field the build stops.
  • The fluent schemas have .excludeIf() and .excludeUnless(). There the key is left out of the output. See Skip a field.
final String type;

@ExcludeIf('type', 'person')
@MinLength(5)
final String? vatNumber; // not checked for a person

docs.title: Change text
docs.text:
These change the value before the rules run. For example, @Trim removes the spaces a user typed by mistake.

They always run in this order, wherever you put them: @Trim, then @Lowercase or @Uppercase, then the "empty string is missing" check.

Annotation Does @Trim() removes spaces at the start and the end @Lowercase() makes the text lower case @Uppercase() makes the text upper case @AllowEmpty() keeps "" as a value. Without it, "" counts as missing.

They have no error and no JSON Schema output. @Lowercase() and @Uppercase() together stop the build.

docs.title: Bad value to default
docs.text:
Sometimes a bad value should just give the default, like page=abc in a list page:

Annotation Does @OrDefault() a bad value gives the default of the field (or null, or Maybe.missing()), not an error.
  • It drops type errors and the errors of the normal rules of the field.
  • Errors from async rules (@Unique, @Exists, your AsyncRule) and from validate() are not dropped. They still give 422.
  • The field needs a default, a nullable type or a Maybe type. Else the build stops.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
Use these rules on int, double and num fields (and list items):

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @Min(18) min The {field} must be greater than or equal {min} minimum @Max(100) max The {field} must be less than or equal {max} maximum @Range(1, 10) between The {field} must be between {min} and {max} minimum, maximum @Positive() greater_than The {field} must be greater than 0 exclusiveMinimum: 0 @GreaterThan(0.5) greater_than The {field} must be greater than {min} (exclusive) exclusiveMinimum @LessThan(100) less_than The {field} must be less than {max} (exclusive) exclusiveMaximum @In([1, 2, 3]) in The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values} enum @NotIn([0]) not_in The {field} field cannot be {value} not: {enum}

The values are num. @Min(1.5) on an int field stops the build. @Range checks that a number is between two values.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
Use these rules on List<T> fields. They check the list, not the items:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @MinItems(1) min_items The {field} must have at least {min} items minItems @MaxItems(5) max_items The {field} may not have more than {max} items maxItems @UniqueItems() unique_items The {field} must not have duplicate items uniqueItems: true

@UniqueItems() works for String, numbers, bool, enums and DateTime. On a list of DTOs it stops the build.

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
Use these rules on DateTime fields:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @After('2000-01-01') after The {field} must be a date after {date} format: date-time @Before('now') before The {field} must be a date before {date} format: date-time @AfterOrEqual('today') after_or_equal The {field} must be a date after or equal to {date} format: date-time @BeforeOrEqual('end_date') before_or_equal The {field} must be a date before or equal to {date} format: date-time
  • The value is one of:
    • an ISO 8601 date, like '2000-01-01',
    • a word: 'now' (the time of the request), 'today', 'tomorrow' or 'yesterday'. These are in UTC, and 'today' is the start of the day,
    • the input key of another DateTime field of the same DTO, like 'start_date'.
  • With another field, the check uses its converted value. When that field has no value, the check passes.
  • A text that is not a date, a word or a DateTime field stops the build.
  • @After and @Before are exclusive: @After('2000-01-01') does not accept 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z. @AfterOrEqual and @BeforeOrEqual accept the same time.
  • Words and other fields need one build_runner run.
final DateTime startDate;

@After('start_date')
@BeforeOrEqual('tomorrow')
final DateTime endDate;

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Use these rules on RequestFile and List<RequestFile> fields:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @MaxSize('2MB') max_size The {field} may not be larger than {max} maxLength (bytes) @Mimes(['pdf', 'png']) mimes The {field} must be a file of type: {types} contentMediaType @Image() image The {field} must be an image contentMediaType: image/* @MinSize('10KB') min_size The {field} must be at least {min} minLength (bytes) @MimeTypes(['image/png', 'image/*']) mime_types The {field} must be a file of type: {types} contentMediaType @Dimensions(minWidth: 100, ratio: 3 / 2) dimensions The {field} has invalid image dimensions contentMediaType: image/*
  • @MaxSize and @MinSize units: B, KB, MB, GB. 1KB = 1024 bytes. A bad size text stops the build.
  • @Mimes takes file extensions. Dox finds the real type from the first bytes of the file. The file name extension must not name another type, or a type a browser runs (like html or svg). So x.html with GIF bytes does not pass. An empty or unknown extension is fine. For zip based types (like docx or xlsx), the file name extension must match too. For types without a byte signature (like txt or csv), it uses the file name extension.
  • @Image() is @Mimes(['jpg', 'jpeg', 'png', 'gif', 'webp', 'bmp']). No svg.
  • @MimeTypes takes MIME types. Dox turns each one into file extensions, then checks the real bytes like @Mimes. It does not trust the content type the client sent. image/* means: jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp, bmp, tif, tiff, ico, heic, heif, avif and psd. No svg. This is wider than @Image(), and browsers can not show most of the extra types. For images that browsers can show, use @Image() or list the MIME types. Write image/jpeg, not image/jpg. image/jpg is not a real MIME type, so it never matches. An unknown MIME type never matches.
  • @Dimensions checks the width and height in pixels. Limits: width, height (exact), minWidth, maxWidth, minHeight, maxHeight and ratio (width / height, like 3 / 2). Give at least one limit, or the build stops. It reads only the image header of PNG, GIF, WebP and JPEG files, never the whole file. Any other file, or a broken or cut short header, fails. For a JPEG over 1 MB, Dox reads the first 128 KB. A JPEG with more photo metadata than that before its size fails. A ratio passes when it is off by less than one pixel.
  • The JSON Schema of a file is {"type": "string", "format": "binary"}, plus the keys above.

With fluent schemas, the same rules are on v.file(). Sizes there are in bytes, not text:

v.file()
    .maxSize(2 * 1024 * 1024) // 2 MB
    .mimeTypes(<String>['image/jpeg', 'image/png'])
    .dimensions(minWidth: 100, maxWidth: 2000);

The fluent methods are maxSize(bytes), minSize(bytes), mimes(types), mimeTypes(types), dimensions(...), image() and extensions(types).

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
These rules come from dox_orm. They read the database, so they run after all other checks passed:

Annotation Code Message @Unique(table, {column, ignoreParam, ignoreColumn, connection}) unique The {field} has already been taken @Exists(table, {column, connection}) exists The selected {field} is invalid
  • @Unique column default: the input key. @Exists column default: id.
  • They read the table, not the model. So soft-deleted rows count too.
  • ignoreParam: 'id' skips the row where ignoreColumn (default id) equals the path param {id}.
  • They add nothing to the JSON Schema.

See Database rules.

In a fluent schema, use v.string().unique('users', column: 'email') and v.int().exists('teams'). See Fluent schemas.

docs.title: Keys and DTO options
docs.text:
These options change how the whole DTO reads its input:

Annotation Does @Name('emailAddress') the input key for this field. Default: the field name in snake_case. @Dto() marks the class. @Dto(source: Source.query) where to read: Source.auto (default), Source.query, Source.body. @Dto(keyCase: KeyCase.field) keys: KeyCase.snake (default) or KeyCase.field (the Dart name as is). @Dto(strict: true) unknown keys are errors. Default false: they are dropped. @Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true) "" is read as null, not as missing. Default false. @Dto(trim: true) trims every String field and text item, like @Trim() on each. Default false. @Dto(coerce: true) a JSON body may send text for numbers and bools, like a form. Default false. @Dto(messages: {...}) messages by code or key.code. A dotted path like address.city.required or tags.*.required works too. A short rule name works too, like name.min. See Short rule names. @Dto(attributes: {...}) the names shown for {field}, by key, like {'first_name': 'first name'}. See Names for {field}. @Describe('...') on a field: a short text for the description of the field in the JSON Schema. It does not change the checks.

A /// doc comment on a field becomes its description in the JSON Schema. @Describe wins over the /// comment. Use it when the text is for API users and MCP clients, not for the code. The OpenAPI docs and MCP tools (McpDtoTool) show it.

@Describe('Category ID (see list_categories).') final int categoryId;

docs.title: Types in detail
docs.text:
This is how each field type reads input. The short table is in Types.

  • JSON is strict. In a JSON body, "18" is not an int. You get the error integer. With @Dto(coerce: true), JSON is read like form text for int, double, num and bool, and a bool also takes 1 and 0.
  • Query and form data are text. Dox turns the text into the field type first. If it can not, you get the type error.
  • int takes 18 or 18.0, never a fraction. "4.5" or 4.5 gives integer.
  • bool in text takes true, 1, yes, on and false, 0, no, off (any case).
  • DateTime takes 2024-01-31 or 2024-01-31T10:00:00Z. A value without a time zone is read as UTC. The result is always UTC (isUtc == true). A number (timestamp) is not allowed.
  • An enum matches the Dart name exactly. "Admin" does not match Role.admin. Custom wire values (like "ADMIN") are not supported.
  • Object? and dynamic take any value. They are not checked.
  • Map<String, dynamic> must be an object. Its values are not checked.
  • In query and form data, one value for a List<T> field gives a list with one item.
  • In bracket keys, list indexes are sorted and packed: items[3] alone gives a list with one item.
  • In query and form data, a list can have at most 1000 items, and keys can nest at most 10 levels. More gives 422 with the key _root.

docs.title: Body types
docs.text:
The content type of the body decides how Dox reads it:

Body Result application/json (or any +json type) read with strict JSON types application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data read as text, then converted any other content type 415 Unsupported Media Type JSON that is not valid 400 Bad Request JSON that is not an object (like [1, 2]) 422 with the key _root

docs.title: The order of checks
docs.text:
Dox checks the input in four steps:

  1. Read the input and convert types. Change text (@Trim, @Lowercase, @Uppercase). Find missing required fields.
  2. The field rules, top to bottom. The first rule that fails stops the other rules of that field. So there is no @Bail. A fluent schema runs all rules, unless you add .bail(). See Stop at the first error.
  3. The validate() method (nested DTOs first, then the parent).
  4. Async rules (@Unique, @Exists, your AsyncRule), one at a time, in field order.

Each step runs only when the step before it had no errors. So the database is never asked about input that is already wrong.

  • Steps 1 and 2 run per DTO. So one answer can have a type error in address and a rule error in items.1.
  • Inside one step, Dox collects the errors of all fields.
  • A default value is not checked by the field rules. Async rules check the final value.

docs.title: What the generator checks
docs.text:
The build stops with a clear error when:

  • a field is not final, or is not a parameter of the unnamed constructor,
  • a field type is not supported (see Types),
  • a rule does not fit the field type (like @Email() on an int),
  • a Maybe<T> field has no const Maybe.missing() default,
  • @RequiredIf, @RequiredWith, @RequiredUnless, @RequiredWithout, @RequiredWithoutAll, @Filled, @Present, @Prohibited, @ProhibitedIf, @ExcludeIf or @ExcludeUnless is on a field that is always required,
  • @OrDefault() is on a field that is always required (no default, not nullable and not a Maybe),
  • a rule that reads another key (like @RequiredIf, @Same, @Different, @ExcludeIf or @GreaterThanField) names a Dart field (like accountType) instead of its input key (account_type),
  • @After, @Before, @AfterOrEqual or @BeforeOrEqual has a text that is not a date, a word or another DateTime field,
  • @DateFormatted has a letter it does not know,
  • two @Dto classes in the app have the same name,
  • the class is generic, or extends another class (other than Object).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation checks the request input with a typed DTO class, so your controller only gets good data.

You write a class with @Dto() and put rules on its fields. Then you ask for it in your controller. Dox reads the request, checks it, and gives you a typed object. When the input is wrong, Dox answers 422 with the errors, and your controller does not run.

lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'create_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class CreateUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Email()
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  @Min(18)
  final int? age; // nullable, so optional

  const CreateUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
    this.age,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema = $CreateUserDto;
}
lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
class UserController {
  Future<User> store(CreateUser body) async {
    // body is already checked
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();
    return user;
  }
}

To create a DTO, register it with the app, and use it for the body, the query string or files, see DTOs. This page is about the rules and the error messages.

docs.title: Required and optional fields
docs.text:
The Dart type decides if a field is required, so you do not write required or nullable:

Field Key missing Value null final String name; error required error required final int? age; null null final Role role; with this.role = Role.user Role.user error required

Rules on an optional field run only when it has a value. A default value is used only when the key is missing, and the rules do not check it.

docs.title: Empty strings and spaces
docs.text:
An empty string counts as missing. So a required String rejects "". Add @AllowEmpty() to keep "".

Spaces are kept. So " " passes required, unless the field has @Trim(). To trim every text field of a DTO, use @Dto(trim: true). Then " " counts as missing.

If you want "" to be null instead, use @Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true).

docs.title: Using the default for bad values
docs.text:
Sometimes a bad value should not be an error. For example, page=abc in a list page should just give page 1. @OrDefault() turns a bad value into the default, with no error:

@OrDefault()
@NotIn(<int>[0])
final int page; // with this.page = 1, page=abc and page=0 give 1

The field needs a default, a nullable type or a Maybe type.

docs.title: Missing or null? (for PATCH)
docs.text:
In a PATCH request, a missing key means "do not change it", and null means "clear it". A T? field gives null for both. To know the difference, use Maybe<T>:

@Length(max: 500)
final Maybe<String?> bio; // default: const Maybe.missing()

// in the controller
if (body.bio.isPresent) {
  user.bio = body.bio.value; // can be null: the client cleared it
}

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Put rules on a field as annotations. They run from top to bottom, and the first rule that fails gives the error:

@Trim()
@Lowercase()
@Email()
@MaxLength(255)
final String email;

A rule on a list checks each item, like @Email() on a List<String>. Only the list rules check the list itself. For a few allowed values, use a Dart enum, or @In(<String>['draft', 'published']).

These are the rules. Every rule, with its error code and message, is in Validation rules:

Kind Annotations Text @Length, @MinLength, @MaxLength, @Email, @Url, @Uuid, @Ulid, @Ip, @Regex, @In, @NotIn, @StartsWith, @EndsWith, @Alpha, @AlphaNumeric, @AlphaDash Change text @Trim, @Lowercase, @Uppercase, @AllowEmpty Numbers @Min, @Max, @Range, @Positive, @GreaterThan, @LessThan, @In, @NotIn Lists @MinItems, @MaxItems, @UniqueItems Dates @After, @Before, @AfterOrEqual, @BeforeOrEqual Other fields @Same, @Confirmed, @Different, @GreaterThanField, @GreaterThanOrEqualField, @LessThanField, @LessThanOrEqualField, @ProhibitedIf Present or missing @RequiredIf, @RequiredUnless, @RequiredWith, @RequiredWithout, @RequiredWithoutAll, @Filled, @Present, @Prohibited, @Accepted, @Declined Skip a field @ExcludeIf, @ExcludeUnless Files @MaxSize, @MinSize, @Mimes, @MimeTypes, @Image, @Dimensions Database @Unique, @Exists

docs.title: Checks across fields: validate()
docs.text:
Some checks need more than one field. Add a validate(DtoErrors errors) method to the DTO. Dox calls it after all field rules passed:

void validate(DtoErrors errors) {
  if (password != passwordConfirmation) {
    errors.add('password_confirmation', 'The passwords do not match');
  }
}

The key is the input key (snake_case). Use _root for an error about the whole body. errors.has(key) tells you if a key already has an error.

The method can be async. Do not throw for bad input. Add an error.

docs.title: Database rules: @Unique and @Exists
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to check the database, for example that an email is not taken yet. @Unique and @Exists do this. They come from dox_orm, so add import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart'; to the DTO file:

@Unique('users', column: 'email')
final String email;

@Exists('teams') // column defaults to id
final int teamId;

For an update, skip the row you are updating with ignoreParam:

// PUT /users/{id}
@Unique('users', column: 'email', ignoreParam: 'id')
final String email;

These rules read the database, so they run last. All options are in Validation rules: database. The full order of checks is in The order of checks.

docs.title: The error response
docs.text:
When a check fails, Dox answers 422 with one message per field:

{
  "email": "The email is not a valid email",
  "tags.0": "The tags may not be greater than 20 characters",
  "items.1.quantity": "The quantity must be greater than 0"
}

The key is the path to the value, with the input keys. List items use the index.

On a form post with a session, Dox redirects back with the errors instead.

If you need another error shape, read error.issues of the ValidationException in your ExceptionHandler. Each issue has its dottedPath, its rule code (like min_length), its message and its params.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Sometimes you want your own error text. You can change a message in three places. The first one wins.

On the rule:

@Email(message: 'Please check your email')
final String email;

On the DTO, by code or by key.code. Use * for list items, like 'tags.*.required':

@Dto(messages: <String, String>{
  'email.required': 'We need your email',
  'integer': 'The {field} must be a number',
})

For the whole app, with a MessageResolver. Use it for other languages:

class AppMessages extends MessageResolver {
  static const Map<String, Map<String, String>> _texts = <String, Map<String, String>>{
    'th': <String, String>{'required': 'กรุณากรอก {field}'},
  };

  @override
  String resolve(MessageRequest request) {
    String? template = _texts[request.locale]?[request.code]; // locale from Accept-Language
    if (template == null) {
      return super.resolve(request);
    }
    return format(template, request.params);
  }
}

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  validationMessages: AppMessages(),
  // ...
);

A message can use placeholders: {field} (the last key), {value}, and rule values like {min} and {max}.

docs.title: Names for {field}
docs.text:
By default {field} is the key, like The first_name is required. To show a nicer name, give attribute names on the DTO:

@Dto(attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'})
class CreateUser { ... }
// The first name is required

Or for the whole app (and for fluent schemas), in the MessageResolver:

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  validationMessages: MessageResolver(
    attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'},
  ),
  // ...
);

A key with no name still shows the key. Only the text changes. The key in the error response stays the same.

docs.title: Short rule names in message keys
docs.text:
Some error codes are long, like min_length. With the opt-in flag laravelMessageKeys, a message key can also use a short name. So 'name.min' gives the message for the min_length error of name. Without the flag, only the full codes match. Set the flag in a provider's setup(), like the other flags:

Validator.flags = const ValidationFlags(laravelMessageKeys: true);

The error code in the response does not change: it is still min_length. These are the short names:

Dox code Short name min_length min max_length max length size length_between between start_with starts_with end_with ends_with alpha_numeric alpha_num greater_than gt less_than lt min_items min max_items max unique_items distinct min_size min max_size max mime_types mimetypes datetime date

docs.title: Custom rules
docs.text:
If no built-in rule fits, write your own. Extend Rule<T>. T is the field type (or the item type, for a list):

class Slug extends Rule<String> {
  const Slug({super.message});

  @override
  String get name {
    return 'slug'; // the error code
  }

  @override
  String get defaultMessage {
    return 'The {field} must be a slug';
  }

  @override
  bool check(String value, RuleContext context) {
    return _pattern.hasMatch(value);
  }

  static final RegExp _pattern = RegExp(r'^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$');
}

Then use it like any rule:

@Slug()
final String slug;
  • If the rule has values, add final fields and override params. They become placeholders.
  • context.lookup('other.key') reads another input value.
  • context.sibling('key') reads the raw input of a field next to this one, in the same object. For example, context.sibling('password_confirmation') in a rule on password. It gives undefined when the field is missing.
  • If the rule needs the database, extend AsyncRule<T> and write checkAsync.

docs.title: Dynamic input
docs.text:
Sometimes the shape of the input is known only at runtime, like form fields from the database. Use a fluent schema for this:

Map<String, dynamic> data = await req.validateSchema(v.object(fields));

See Fluent schemas. Use a DTO for everything else.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: To test the checks of a DTO, use safeValidateMap on its schema. See DTOs: testing.

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
• The flag laravelErrors sends {"message": "...", "errors": {"field": ["..."]}} as the error response. See Core flags.
  • Three opt-in flags change how DTOs are checked: get all errors at once, reject [] in a required list, and reject "" in a Maybe field.

docs.title: Empty values and defaults
docs.text:
• @Dto(trim: true) works like @Trim() on each String field and on the text items of its lists and maps. A nested DTO uses its own @Dto(trim:). The same is true for @Dto(coerce:).
  • With @Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true) and @Dto(trim: true), blank text like " " is null as well. Then {"bio": ""} clears a Maybe<String?> field. A required field still gets required. A field that is not nullable but has a default gets required too, because null is not a missing key.
  • @OrDefault() works on any field, in a body or a query. A Maybe field gets Maybe.missing(). Errors from async rules (@Unique, @Exists, your AsyncRule) and from validate() are not dropped. They run later, on the built object, and still give 422.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
• In @Dto(messages:), a full dotted path works too, like 'address.city.required'. It also reaches a nested DTO. A message in the nested DTO itself, like 'city.required', wins over it.
  • A name for {field} is looked up by the dotted path (address.city), then with * for list items (items.*.qty), then by the field name (city).
  • The names of the DTO win over the names of the MessageResolver. A nested DTO uses its own names first, then the names of the outer DTO.
  • MessageResolver.setAttributes(...) adds names to a resolver. A custom resolver can override attributeName(path).
  • {other} and {others} (the other keys of rules like @RequiredIf and @Same) show their names too.
  • @Dto(attributes:) needs one build_runner run.
  • With laravelMessageKeys, the full code is tried first at each step of the lookup, then the short name. So 'name.min_length' wins over 'name.min'. A key with a path still wins over a key with only a code: 'name.min' wins over 'min_length'.
  • Short names work in @Dto(messages:) and in a MessageResolver. A code that is already short (like email or required) needs nothing. With the flag on, a key min or max with no path fits text, list and file errors too, not only numbers.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
Views are HTML templates that Dox fills with your data and sends as the response.

Writing HTML in a controller gets messy fast. A view keeps the HTML in its own file, so the controller only gives the data. The dox_view package has the template engine. Templates are .dox.html files in resources/views.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the package with the CLI:

dox add view

It adds the package, the provider, the resources/views folder and a sample view. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text:
If you do not use dox add, add the package yourself:

dart pub add dox_view

Add the provider in lib/, so every isolate sets up the engine:

lib/providers/view_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart';

class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());
}

To make a view file, run dox make:view emails/welcome. It writes resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html. See dox make:view.

docs.title: Rendering views
docs.text:
view() renders a template and sends it as HTML. Leave out the .dox.html extension:

DoxResponse show(DoxRequest req) {
  return view(req, 'users/show', <String, dynamic>{
    'user': user,
    'posts': posts,
  });
}

This renders resources/views/users/show.dox.html:

<h1>{{ user.name }}</h1>

If you need the HTML as a string, for example for an email, use View.render():

String html = View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});

docs.title: Displaying data
docs.text:
{{ }} prints a value. It escapes HTML, so a user can not add a <script> tag to your page:

<p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>

{{{ }}} prints a value with no escape. Use it only for HTML you trust:

<article>{{{ post.html }}}</article>

null prints nothing, and a variable that does not exist prints nothing too. true prints true, false prints false, and 10.0 prints 10.0. The bladeOutput and strictVariables options change this. See Strict options.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
A comment is not in the output:

{{-- only you see this --}}

To print {{ or a tag as text, put @ before it: @{{ name }} prints {{ name }}, and @@if prints @if.

docs.title: Stay safe
docs.text:
{{ }} escapes HTML, but it does not make every place in a page safe. Follow these three rules:

  • Always quote attributes. Write href="{{ url }}", not href={{ url }}. Without quotes, a space in the value starts a new attribute, like onclick=....
  • Check URLs from users. href="{{ url }}" does not block a javascript: URL. A click on javascript:alert(1) runs the code. Allow only http:// and https:// URLs (or your own paths) before you print them.
  • <script> and <style> are not safe for {{ }}. Inside them, {{ }} only escapes HTML. It does not make a value safe for JavaScript or CSS. Do not print user data there with {{ }}. In a <script>, use @json. See JSON for JavaScript. Or put the value in a quoted data- attribute, and read it in your script.
<a href="{{ profile.website }}">Website</a>  {{-- only after you check it is http or https --}}

<div id="app" data-user-name="{{ user.name }}"></div>
<script>
  const name = document.getElementById('app').dataset.userName;
</script>

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Inside {{ }} and tags, you can use these expressions:

What Example Values 'text', "text", 42, 1.5, true, false, null Lists and maps [1, 2], { name: 'Ann', 'full name': 'Ann Lee' } Fields user.name, user?.name, items[0], map['key'] Math +, -, *, /, %, ~/ Compare ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= (=== and !== work too) Logic &&, \|\|, !, a ?? b, a ? b : c Functions route('users.show', { id: 5 }), name.toUpperCase()

+ joins text: {{ 'Hi ' + name }}. Fields work on maps, and on objects with a toJson() method, like Dox models.

Some methods work too:

  • Lists, maps and text have length, isEmpty and isNotEmpty.
  • Lists also have first, last, contains(), join() and indexOf().
  • Text has toUpperCase(), toLowerCase(), trim(), contains(), startsWith(), endsWith(), split(), replaceAll(), substring() and indexOf().
  • Numbers have toStringAsFixed(), round(), floor(), ceil() and abs().

In @if and ?:, these values are false: null, false, 0, '', an empty list and an empty map. With the stringZeroIsFalse option, the text '0' is false too. See Strict options.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
Use @if, @elseif and @else to show a part only in some cases. Close it with @end:

@if(user.isAdmin)
  <a href="/admin">Admin</a>
@elseif(user.isEditor)
  <a href="/posts">Posts</a>
@else
  <p>Welcome</p>
@end

@unless(x) is @if(!x). A tag alone on its line leaves no empty line in the output.

A tag can not come right after a letter or a digit, so me@mail.com stays text. Put a space before the tag, or use {{ on ? 'active' : '' }}.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
Use @each to print a list. The @else part shows when the list is empty:

<ul>
  @each(user in users)
    <li>{{ user.name }}</li>
  @else
    <li>No users yet</li>
  @end
</ul>

If you need the index too, or the key of a map, use two names:

@each((user, index) in users)
  {{ index + 1 }}. {{ user.name }}
@end

@each((value, key) in settings)
  {{ key }}: {{ value }}
@end

docs.title: The loop variable
docs.text:
$loop tells you where the loop is. For example, to put a comma after every item but the last:

@each(tag in tags)
  {{ tag }}{{ $loop.last ? '' : ', ' }}
@end
Field What it is $loop.index the round, from 0 $loop.iteration the round, from 1 $loop.first true in the first round $loop.last true in the last round $loop.count the number of items. $loop.length is the same. $loop.remaining the rounds left after this one $loop.even true when iteration is even: the 2nd, 4th, ... round $loop.odd true when iteration is odd: the 1st, 3rd, ... round $loop.depth 1 for a loop, 2 for a loop inside a loop $loop.parent the $loop of the loop around this one. null when there is none.

In a loop inside a loop, $loop.parent reads the outer loop:

@each(row in rows)
  @each(cell in row)
    <td class="{{ $loop.parent.odd ? 'light' : 'dark' }}">{{ cell }}</td>
  @end
@end

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
@let makes a variable, and @assign changes it:

@let(total = 0)
@each(item in cart)
  @assign(total = total + item.price)
@end
Total: {{ total }}

docs.title: Partials
docs.text:
Some parts are the same on many pages, like a nav bar. @include puts another template in this one, and it sees the same variables:

@include('partials/nav')

To give it more variables, pass a map as the second argument:

@include('partials/card', { title: 'Profile', user: post.author })

On the same name, the map wins. The map is only for this include, so the page does not see it after the include.

To include a template only when a condition is true, use @includeIf or @includeWhen. The two tags do the same. The condition is the first argument, the template name is the second, and the map is the third:

@includeIf(user, 'partials/account')
@includeWhen(user.isAdmin, 'partials/admin', { level: 2 })

docs.title: More tags
docs.text:
Dox has more tags for common cases. Close a block tag with @end. @else works in all of them, but not in @once and @verbatim.

Tag What it does @isset(user.phone) ... @end shows when the value is not null. A field of null is not an error here. @empty(items) ... @end shows when the value is false: null, false, 0, '', an empty list or map. With stringZeroIsFalse, '0' too. @auth ... @end shows when the user is logged in (req.auth) @guest ... @end shows when the user is not logged in @env('local') ... @end shows when APP_ENV is this value. A list works too: @env(['local', 'staging']). Case does not matter. @production ... @end shows when APP_ENV is production @once ... @end shows only the first time in one render, for example a <script> in a component @verbatim ... @end prints the text as it is: no {{ }} and no tags run inside it @extends('layouts/app') the layout of the page. See Layouts with sections. @section('name') ... @end fills a section. Short form: @section('title', 'Home'). @yield('name') prints a section. @yield('title', 'My app') has a default. @stack('scripts') prints every push of the stack. See Stacks. @push('scripts') ... @end adds to the end of a stack @prepend('scripts') ... @end adds to the start of a stack @csrf the hidden _token field. See Forms. @method('PUT') the hidden _method field @error('email') ... @end shows when the field has a validation error. See Forms. @json(value) the value as JSON. See JSON for JavaScript. @includeWhen(condition, 'name') includes a template when the condition is true. See Partials. @datetime(...) a tag of your app. See Your own tags.

Put @auth, @guest, @production, @once and @verbatim alone on their line. In the middle of text, like @once upon a time, they stay text.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
@auth shows its body when the user is logged in, and @guest when not:

@auth
  <a href="/logout">Log out</a>
@else
  <a href="/login">Log in</a>
@end

They use the req.auth that view() gets. In View.render there is no request, so @guest shows.

docs.title: Verbatim
docs.text:
Some JavaScript frameworks also use {{ }}. @verbatim prints its text as it is, so Dox does not run it. It ends at the first @end, so the text inside can not have @end:

@verbatim
  <div id="app">{{ message }}</div>
@end

docs.title: Attributes from conditions
docs.text:
These tags print an HTML attribute when a condition is true:

<a @class(['link', { active: isActive, muted: !isActive }])>Home</a>
<input type="checkbox" name="news" @checked(user.news)>
<option value="en" @selected(lang == 'en')>English</option>
<button @disabled(saving)>Save</button>

@class takes text, a map of class name to a condition, or a list of these. It prints class="..." with the names whose condition is true. @checked, @selected and @disabled print the attribute name when the value is true.

docs.title: Layouts and components
docs.text:
A component is a template with its own props and slots. You can use one for the page layout, so every page has the same head and header:

resources/views/layouts/main.dox.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>{{ title ?? 'My app' }}</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>{{ $slots.header }}</header>
    <main>{{ $slots.main }}</main>
  </body>
</html>

A page then puts its content in the component:

resources/views/home.dox.html
@component('layouts/main', { title: 'Home' })
  @slot('header')
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
  @end

  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
  • The second argument is the props. In the component they are variables (title), and also $props.title.
  • @slot('name') ... @end fills a named slot. Everything else goes into $slots.main. $slot is the same as $slots.main.
  • A slot is HTML, so {{ }} does not escape it again.
  • A component does not see the variables of the page. It only sees its props, $props, $slots, $slot, $attributes, the globals and the request helpers of view() (see Forms).

@!component(...) is a component with no body and no @end.

docs.title: Components as tags
docs.text:
A template in resources/views/components/ is also a tag with its name. A . in the tag is a folder:

resources/views/components/button.dox.html
<button class="btn btn-{{ type ?? 'primary' }}">{{ $slots.main }}</button>

Then use the tag:

@button({ type: 'danger' })
  Delete
@end

@!form.input({ name: 'email' })   {{-- components/form/input.dox.html --}}

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Often a component should pass its props on as HTML attributes, like id or type. $attributes has the props as HTML attributes, and {{ $attributes }} prints them, like id="save" title="Save". The values are escaped.

$attributes.merge({ ... }) adds default attributes. A prop wins over a default, but class is joined:

<button {{ $attributes.merge({ class: 'btn', type: 'button' }) }}>{{ $slot }}</button>

@button({ class: 'btn-big', type: 'submit' })
  Save
@end

This prints <button class="btn btn-big" type="submit">.

Only text, numbers and true are attributes. true prints the name alone, like hidden. null, false, lists, maps and objects are left out. You can still read any prop, like $attributes.type.

$attributes keeps any attribute name, like onclick. So do not pass a map from the user as the props of a component.

docs.title: Layouts with sections
docs.text:
A page can also name its layout with @extends. The page fills sections, and the layout prints them with @yield:

resources/views/layouts/app.dox.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>@yield('title', 'My app')</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <main>@yield('content')</main>
  </body>
</html>
resources/views/home.dox.html
@extends('layouts/app')

@section('title', 'Home')

@section('content')
  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
  • @extends must be the first thing in the template. A template can have only one.
  • @section('name') ... @end fills a section. The short form @section('title', 'Home') takes a value, which is escaped like {{ }}.
  • @yield('title', 'My app') prints the second value when the page has no such section.
  • Only the sections reach the layout. Text outside a section is not printed.
  • A section and the layout both see the variables of the page.
  • A layout can extend another layout. When a page and its layout fill the same section, the page wins.

Use @extends for the page layout. Use a component when you need props or more than one copy on a page.

docs.title: Stacks
docs.text:
Sometimes a page or a component needs its own script or style in the layout's <head>. A stack collects HTML from many templates and prints it in one place. The layout prints the stack with @stack:

<head>
  @stack('styles')
</head>
<body>
  @yield('content')
  @stack('scripts')
</body>

A page or a component adds to it with @push:

@push('scripts')
  <script src="/js/chart.js"></script>
@end

@push adds to the end of the stack, and @prepend adds to the start. A push works from the page, its layout, an @include and a component. @stack can come before the @push, and it still prints every push.

Put @once inside @push in a component, so the script is added one time only.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Forms need a CSRF token, the old input and the validation errors. With SessionMiddleware, view() adds these to every template:

Name What it is csrfField() the hidden _token field for CsrfMiddleware. @csrf prints the same. csrfToken() the CSRF token errors the flashed validation errors, like errors.email old('email') the input of the request before session('key') a value from the session 
<form method="POST" action="/register">
  {{ csrfField() }}
  <input name="email" value="{{ old('email') }}">
  @error('email')
    <p class="error">{{ message }}</p>
  @end
  <button>Register</button>
</form>

docs.title: Validation errors
docs.text:
@error('field') ... @end shows its body when errors has a message for the field. Inside the body, message is that message. With no error for the field, the @else part is printed instead, if there is one.

A name with dots, like @error('user.email'), works for nested fields. The name can also be a variable, like @error(name) in an input component.

docs.title: CSRF and method fields
docs.text:
@csrf prints the same hidden field as csrfField(). Put it alone on its line.

A browser form can only send GET and POST. For a PUT, PATCH or DELETE route, send a POST and add @method. It prints the hidden _method field that the MethodOverride middleware reads:

<form method="POST" action="/posts/{{ post.id }}">
  @csrf
  @method('PUT')
  <input name="title" value="{{ post.title }}">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>

This prints <input type="hidden" name="_token" value="..."> and <input type="hidden" name="_method" value="PUT">.

Every template from view() also has request.path, request.method and request.query. Components and layouts see all of these too, so a layout can use request.path and a form component can use csrfField().

docs.title: Globals
docs.text:
Some values are needed in every template, like the app name. Globals are variables and functions that every template can use. route() is there by default:

const ViewConfig(globals: <String, Object?>{'appName': 'My app'});

View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
View.global('money', (num cents) => (cents / 100).toStringAsFixed(2));

Then use them in any template:

<footer>{{ appName }} {{ year }}</footer>
<a href="{{ route('users.show', { id: user.id }) }}">Profile</a>
<p>{{ money(order.total) }}</p>

Each isolate has its own engine. So add globals in your provider, after super.setup(). Then every isolate gets them:

lib/providers/view_provider.dart
class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
  }
}

If a global holds HTML, make it a SafeString. It is printed with no escape:

View.global('logo', const SafeString('<img src="/logo.svg" alt="Logo">'));

docs.title: JSON for JavaScript
docs.text:
Sometimes your JavaScript needs data from the server. @json(value) prints a value as JSON:

<script>
  const user = @json(user);
</script>

<div data-tags='@json(tags)'></div>

Maps, lists, text, numbers, true, false and null work. An object with a toJson() method works too, like a Dox model.

The output is safe in two places: inside a <script> block, and inside an attribute in single quotes. Do not put it in an attribute in double quotes, because JSON has " in it, and that ends the attribute.

json(value) does the same as a function. Use it where you need an expression:

@!chart({ points: json(points) })

In Dart, SafeString.json(value) gives the same text.

docs.title: Your own tags
docs.text:
If you print the same thing in many places, like a date format, you can add your own tag. A directive is a tag that your app adds. Write a class with a render method. It gets the values between ( and ), and gives the text to print:

class DateTimeDirective implements ViewDirective {
  @override
  Object? render(List<Object?> args, Scope scope) {
    Object? value = args[0];
    DateTime time = value is DateTime ? value : DateTime.parse('$value');
    return '${time.day}/${time.month}/${time.year}';
  }
}

View.directive('datetime', DateTimeDirective());

Then use it in a template:

<time>@datetime(post.createdAt)</time>

The text is escaped, like {{ }}. Give a SafeString to print HTML as it is. scope.lookup('name') reads a variable of the template. A directive has no body and no @end.

Each isolate has its own engine. So add directives in your provider, after super.setup(), like globals. You can also give them in the config: ViewConfig(directives: <String, ViewDirective>{'datetime': DateTimeDirective()}).

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Set the options in ViewConfig:

Option Default What it does path resources/views the folder of the templates extension .dox.html the file extension cache on, but off when APP_ENV is development or local keep parsed templates in memory globals {} variables for every template directives {} your own tags, by name strictVariables false a variable that does not exist throws a ViewException. See Strict options. stringZeroIsFalse false the text '0' is false in a condition bladeOutput false print true as 1, false as nothing and 10.0 as 10 bladeWarnings true warn about tag names from other template engines that are not Dox tags. See Unknown tag warnings.

With the cache off, a changed template shows on the next request, with no restart.

docs.title: Strict options
docs.text:
These three options are off by default. Turn each one on in ViewConfig:

const ViewConfig(
  strictVariables: true,
  stringZeroIsFalse: true,
  bladeOutput: true,
);

strictVariables: a variable that does not exist throws a ViewException. The message has the name of the variable, the template and the line. So a typo like {{ titel }} shows as an error, not as an empty spot on the page. When it is off, a variable that does not exist prints nothing.

A variable that is there with the value null is fine. These ways to read a variable that may not exist never throw:

Code What it gives when user does not exist @isset(user) ... @end the body is not printed @empty(user) ... @end the body is printed {{ user ?? 'Guest' }} Guest {{ user?.name }} nothing

The rule covers the variable on the left of ?? and ?.. In {{ a ?? b ?? 'x' }}, both a and b can be missing. {{ user.name ?? 'Guest' }} still throws when user does not exist: write {{ user?.name ?? 'Guest' }}.

stringZeroIsFalse: the text '0' is false in @if, @unless, @empty, ?:, &&, ||, !, @class, @checked, @selected, @disabled, @includeIf and @includeWhen. Other text, like '0.0' or '00', is still true. When it is off, '0' is true, like any text that is not empty.

bladeOutput: {{ }} and {{{ }}} print true as 1, false as nothing, and a number with no fraction, like 10.0, as 10. The values of @yield, @section and @method, and the numbers in $attributes, are printed the same way. Joining text with + does not change: {{ 'a' + true }} is still atrue. When it is off, true prints true, false prints false, and 10.0 prints 10.0.

docs.title: Unknown tag warnings
docs.text:
Some tag names from other template engines, like @foreach, are not Dox tags. Dox prints them as plain text. To help you find them, Dox writes a warning to stderr when it reads a template that has one:

dox_view: warning: posts/index:12 "@foreach" is not a Dox tag. Use "@each(item in items) ... @end".
Other name Dox {!! html !!} {{{ html }}} @foreach, @forelse, @for @each(item in items) ... @else ... @end @endif, @endforeach, @endsection and the other @end... names, @stop @end @switch @if ... @elseif ... @else ... @end @php, @endphp @let(name = value) @show @end, then @yield('name') @parent not there. Use @stack and @push to add content.

The output of the template does not change. The warning is only a hint, and each one is written one time. ViewConfig(bladeWarnings: false) turns the warnings off.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A syntax error, or an error in an expression, throws a ViewException. The message has the template name and the line:

ViewException: expected ")" but found the end (in "users/show", line 12)

docs.title: Prettier
docs.text:
Prettier formats .html files, and it does not know the @ tags. Add this line to .prettierignore:

*.dox.html

docs.title: Details
docs.text: This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

docs.title: When a tag is text
docs.text:
• A tag can not come right after a letter or a digit. Write on @else off, not on@else off. L@yield('s') also stays text.
  • @extends, @section, @yield, @stack, @push, @prepend, @method, @error, @json, @includeWhen and your own directives need ( ). With no ( ), like @section in a sentence, they stay text.
  • With no space before the (, like @empty(items) or @json(user), a tag is always a tag.
  • With a space before the (, in the middle of a line, it is a tag only when its args are one valid expression (one or two for @section and @yield). So see @class (see docs) stays text.
  • With a space, alone on its line, it is a tag even when its args are not valid, unless a rule below says it stays text. Then the args give an error.
  • A tag with a body, like @isset, @empty, @env, @section and @push, also needs its own @end after it. The @end of a block around it does not count. So @empty (none) stays text, also alone on its line.
  • @extends, @section, @yield, @stack, @push, @prepend, @method and @error with a space also need text in quotes as the first argument. So git @push (force) stays text, but @yield ('title') is a tag. If such a tag stays text, its @end gives the error "@end has no matching tag before it".
  • @json and @includeWhen are never tags with a space. So the @json (format) stays text.
  • When resources/views/components/ has a template with the same name as a tag or a directive, like class.dox.html, the component wins.

docs.title: Partials, loops and components
docs.text:
• @include with a second argument that is not a map throws a ViewException.
  • A loop in an @include counts the loop around the @include as its parent. A loop in a component starts at depth 1.
  • $slot and $slots.main are always there. They are empty when the component has no body.
  • In $attributes, a number prints like {{ }}: 1.0 is title="1.0", or title="1" with bladeOutput.

docs.title: Sections and stacks
docs.text:
• In a page with @extends, @let and @push outside a section still work. The @yield default value is escaped too.
  • The names of sections and stacks must be plain text in quotes, like 'title'.
  • The first @section with a name wins. So a @section inside @each keeps only the first round.
  • A @yield('s') that comes before the @section('s') in the same file prints nothing.
  • An @include or a component with its own @extends prints its layout in place. It shares the section names with the page.
  • The pushes are printed in the order they run. A page with @extends runs before its layout.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
• If your app has a global named errors, the global shows when the request has no validation errors. When there are validation errors, they win over the global.
  • When the value in errors is a list, message is its first item.
  • With no session, and in View.render, there are no errors, so the @error body is not printed. It does not throw. With no session, @csrf throws a ViewException.
  • @error('user.email') reads the key 'user.email' of errors first. That is how the validator names a nested field. When there is no such key, it reads email inside user.
  • message is only there inside the @error body. After @end, a message variable of your page has its own value again.

docs.title: Globals, JSON and directives
docs.text:
• You can add globals before or after View.configure(). The engine keeps them. When a name is in both, the value in ViewConfig.globals wins.
  • @json writes <, >, &, ' and the line separators U+2028 and U+2029 as \uXXXX, so a value can not close the <script> block or the attribute. A value that can not be JSON, like a DateTime or an object with no toJson(), throws a ViewException. {{ json(value) }} does not escape the text again.
  • A directive that returns null prints nothing. Its name can have letters, digits and _. The name of a built-in tag, like if, section or json, throws a ViewException.

docs.title: Which names warn
docs.text:
• @end... names warn anywhere in a line. The other names warn only with the ( right after the name, like @foreach(...), or alone on their line. So a sentence like the @foreach loop does not warn.
  • Text in a {{-- --}} comment, in @verbatim, and a name with @@ before it, do not warn. A name in an HTML comment, like <!-- @endif -->, does warn.

docs.title: Build a blog API
docs.text:
This tutorial takes you from an empty folder to a small blog API that runs as one native binary.

Every step has the full code and a curl command, so you can check your work after each step.

The finished project is on GitHub: examples/blog-api. CI builds it and runs its tests on every push, so the code on these pages always works.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
You will build a JSON API for blog posts. Anyone can read posts, but only a logged in user can write them:

Method Path Who What it does GET /api/posts anyone list all posts GET /api/posts/{id} anyone one post, or 404 POST /api/posts logged in user make a post (201, or 422 on bad input) PUT /api/posts/{id} logged in user change a post POST /api/auth/register anyone make an account, get a token POST /api/auth/login anyone log in, get a token GET /api/auth/user logged in user the user of the token

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Dart 3.13 or newer. Check it with dart --version.
  • curl, to call the API.
  • About 15 minutes.

You do not need Docker or a database server, because the app uses SQLite. SQLite keeps the whole database in one file in your project.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Create the project
  2. Model and migration
  3. Routes and controller
  4. Validation
  5. Login with dox_auth
  6. Test
  7. Build and deploy

docs.title: The finished project
docs.text:
This is the project at the end. Files that you make or change are marked with *. The template has more files, like queue, scheduler and storage, but this tree only shows the ones you need here.

blog/
├── bin/
│   ├── migrate.dart              runs the dox migration:* commands
│   ├── server.dart               runs the migrations, starts the server
│   └── queue.dart, schedule.dart, seed.dart
├── db/migration/
│   ├── ..._create_posts_table.dart   *
│   ├── ..._create_users_table.dart
│   └── migrations.dart           the list of migrations (Dox writes it)
├── lib/
│   ├── app/http/controllers/
│   │   ├── auth.controller.dart  *
│   │   └── post.controller.dart  *
│   ├── app/dtos/
│   │   ├── login_user/login_user.dto.dart   *
│   │   ├── register_user/register_user.dto.dart *
│   │   └── save_post/save_post.dto.dart    *
│   ├── app/models/
│   │   ├── post/post.model.dart  *
│   │   └── user/user.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart              * adds the DTO list
│   │   ├── database.dart
│   │   └── env.dart              the .env keys, typed
│   ├── routes/api.dart           *
│   ├── providers/
│   │   ├── auth_provider.dart    *
│   │   └── orm_provider.dart
│   └── generated/
│       ├── container.g.dart      * generated
│       └── dtos.g.dart           * generated
├── test/http_test.dart           *
├── .env                          made by dox create
├── Dockerfile
└── pubspec.yaml                  * adds dox_auth

Start with step 1: create the project.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the project
docs.text: In this step you make a new Dox project, start the dev server and call the first route.

docs.title: 1. Make the project
docs.text:
First install the dox command line tool. Then use it to make a project named blog:

dart pub global activate dox
dox create blog
cd blog
dart pub get

dox create downloads the dox-sample template and names the package blog. So every import in this tutorial starts with package:blog/.

docs.title: 2. Look at the database settings
docs.text:
You do not need to change anything here. dox create made a .env file with a new random APP_KEY, and the template already uses SQLite:

.env
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<your new random key>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite

Dox makes the file db/dox.sqlite at the first start. SQLite does not use the other DB_* lines. The app reads these keys through the typed class in lib/config/env.dart. See Environment variables.

The folder must exist

Dox makes the database file when it is missing, but not its folder. If you set DB_NAME=storage/blog.sqlite, run mkdir storage first.

docs.title: 3. Start the server
docs.text:
Start the dev server:

dox s

dox s runs the code generator and the server. When you save a file in lib/app/, it hot reloads your code. When you change routes, config or other start-up code, it restarts the server.

The first start is slower, because it compiles the SQLite library. It also runs the migrations of the template. At the end you see this log line:

[server] Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

The number of isolates is the number of CPU cores on your machine.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Call the ping route from a second terminal:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping

You should see:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
...

pong

The route is in lib/routes/api.dart. The ApiRouter has the prefix api, so /ping is served at /api/ping.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 2: Model and migration

docs.title: Step 2: Model and migration
docs.text: In this step you make the posts table with a migration, and a Post model to read and write it.

docs.title: 1. Make the model and the migration
docs.text:
Stop dox s first with Ctrl+C. You need to do this because dox s restarts the server when a new file appears, and the server runs new migrations at start. So it would run the new migration before you add the columns.

Now make the model and its migration:

dox make:model Post -m

This makes two files and updates one:

File What it is lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart the model (new) db/migration/<date>_create_posts_table.dart the migration (new) db/migration/migrations.dart the list of all Dart migrations. Dox writes it. Do not edit it.

The dox migration:* commands run bin/migrate.dart, which the template already has.

docs.title: 2. Add the columns to the migration
docs.text:
A new migration has no columns yet. Open the new file in db/migration and add title and body:

db/migration/2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreatePostsTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('title');
      table.text('body');
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('posts');
  }
}
  • table.id() makes an auto increment primary key.
  • table.timestamps() makes created_at and updated_at. The model fills them for you.

docs.title: 3. Add the fields to the model
docs.text:
The model needs one field for each column you added:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'posts')
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>[];

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? body;
}

Every column field is nullable, because a new Post() has no values yet. You do not declare id, createdAt and updatedAt, because they come from PostGenerator.

docs.title: 4. See how migrations run
docs.text:
You do not need to change anything here. The template's bin/server.dart already runs the migrations before the server starts:

bin/server.dart
import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);

  await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
  ).migrate();

  await Dox().startServer();
}

This also works in the native binary of step 7.

docs.title: 5. Run the migration and the generator
docs.text:
Run the new migration now:

dox migration:run

Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table

The migration ran too early?

If dox s was still running, the posts table may already exist without title and body. Run dox migration:rollback, then dox migration:run again.

The model also needs its generated file post.model.g.dart. dox s makes it while it runs. If dox s is not running, run the generator once:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
See which migrations ran:

dox migration:status

You should see:

Migration                                 Batch  Status
2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table   1      Ran
2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables  1      Ran
2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table      2      Ran

The first two come with the template. The server ran them at the first start in step 1.

Now start the server again with dox s.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 3: Routes and controller

docs.title: Step 3: Routes and controller
docs.text: In this step you add a controller and the routes to list, create and show posts.

docs.title: 1. Make the controller
docs.text:
A controller holds the code that answers a request. Make one for posts:

dox make:controller Post -r

-r makes a resource controller with the seven CRUD methods. You only need three of them now, so replace the file with this:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = req.input('title')
      ..body = req.input('body');
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}

What the code does:

  • @Inject() puts the controller in the container, so Dox can make it for you. The code generator adds it to lib/generated/container.g.dart, and a new project already uses that file. So you change nothing else.
  • When a method returns a model or a list of models, Dox sends it as JSON.
  • response(post).statusCode(201) sets the status code.
  • show(int id) gets the {id} from the URL. /api/posts/abc answers 404, because abc is not an int.
  • req.input('title') reads the input without any check. You add checks in step 4.

docs.title: 2. Add the routes
docs.text:
Routes connect a URL to a controller method. Open lib/routes/api.dart and add Route.resource:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    Route.resource('posts', PostController);
  }
}

Route.resource makes one route for each method the controller has:

Method Path Controller method GET /api/posts index POST /api/posts store GET /api/posts/{id} show

The controller has no update or destroy yet, so those routes are not made. You do not need to register the router anywhere, because Dox finds every Router class by itself.

docs.title: 3. Start the server
docs.text:
If the server is not running, start it:

dox s

If it is already running, it restarts by itself when you save a file.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Make a post:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post."}'

You should get 201 and the new post:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}

List the posts:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts

[{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}]

Show one post:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}

Ask for a post that does not exist. You should get 404:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/posts/99

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
...

{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 4: Validation

docs.title: Step 4: Validation
docs.text: In this step you check the input of create and update with a @Dto class, so bad input gets a 422 answer and the controller does not run.

docs.title: 1. Make the DTO
docs.text:
A DTO is a class that describes the input you expect, with a rule on each field. Make one:

dox make:dto SavePost

Create and update need the same fields, so one class is enough for both. Replace the file with this:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'save_post.dto.g.dart';

/// Typed, checked input. Run `dox build_runner:build` after a change.
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}
  • A field that is not nullable and has no default is required.
  • The rules run from top to bottom. @Trim() removes spaces first, so an empty string then counts as missing.
  • See Validation for all rules.

docs.title: 2. Give the DTO list to the app
docs.text:
The code generator writes a list of all DTOs to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. Dox needs this list, because it does not use reflection. Add two lines to lib/config/app.dart:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// DTOs (generated list in lib/generated/dtos.g.dart)
  dtos: dtos,

  // ... the rest stays the same
);

docs.title: 3. Use the DTO in the controller
docs.text:
Now ask for SavePost as a parameter of the controller method. Dox checks the body and gives you a typed object. This version also adds update, so you can change a post:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    return _find(id);
  }

  /// PUT /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> update(int id, SavePost body) async {
    Post post = await _find(id);
    post
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return post;
  }

  Future<Post> _find(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}

You do not need to change the routes. Route.resource sees the new update method and adds PUT and PATCH /api/posts/{id}.

docs.text:
dox s runs the generator for you. If it is not running, run it once:

dart run build_runner build

It writes lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.g.dart and lib/generated/dtos.g.dart.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Send a title and a body that are too short:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hi","body":"Short"}'

You should get 422 with one message for each field:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"title":"The title must be between 3 and 100 characters","body":"The body must be at least 10 characters"}

Send an empty body:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'

{"title":"The title is required","body":"The body is required"}

Good input still gives 201:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Second post","body":"Validation works now."}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

Update the first post:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited."}'

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:59:13.539886Z"}
